🛡️ Kubernetes CKS — Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist

Complete Security Hardening Guide with anihpj Django Project (jobpost app)

From CKA-certified administrator to CKS-certified security specialist. Learn cluster hardening, system hardening, microservice vulnerability minimization, supply chain security, monitoring, logging, runtime security, and incident response — all through hands-on examples securing a real Django application.

🟢 CKA Prerequisite 🛡️ Kubernetes Security v1.31+ 🐍 Django / Python 📚 38 Chapters ⏱️ ~50 Hours 🎓 CKS Exam — 100% Coverage 📋 7 Appendices

🛡️ Your CKS Security Journey

🔐 Welcome! This guide takes you from CKA-certified administrator to CKS-certified Kubernetes security specialist. Every concept is explained with real examples securing the anihpj/jobpost Django project — you'll learn by hardening, not just reading. Covers all CKS exam domains: Cluster Setup (15%), Cluster Hardening (15%), System Hardening (10%), Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities (20%), Supply Chain Security (20%), and Monitoring, Logging & Runtime Security (20%).

🎯 The Six CKS Domains — At a Glance

🔧
Cluster Setup (15%)

CIS benchmarks, kube-bench, Network Policies, Ingress TLS, node metadata protection, platform binary verification. Ch 4-7

🔒
Cluster Hardening (15%)

RBAC, Service Accounts, API server access restriction, Node Restriction, version upgrades. Ch 8-12

🖥️
System Hardening (10%)

OS attack surface, AppArmor, Seccomp, ports/packages minimization, cloud IAM, AIDE file integrity. Ch 13-16

📦
Microservice Vulnerabilities (20%)

Pod Security Standards, SecurityContext, secrets encryption, Vault, sandboxed containers, multi-tenancy, mTLS. Ch 17-22

🔗
Supply Chain Security (20%)

Image scanning (Trivy), admission controllers, static analysis (kube-linter, kubesec), cosign signing, SBOM, SLSA. Ch 23-27

🔍
Runtime Security (20%)

Audit logging, Falco, incident response, immutable containers, behavioral analytics, compliance monitoring. Ch 28-32

📋 Implementation Strategy — How to Study with This Guide

1
Learn (Ch 1-12)

Foundation + Setup + Hardening. Read the theory, study diagrams, answer practice questions. ~18 hours.

2
Practice (Ch 13-32)

System hardening through runtime security. Hands-on labs with anihpj. Drill muscle memory commands. ~30 hours.

3
Master (Ch 33-38)

End-to-end hardening simulation. Mock exam scenarios. Last-mile review. Exam strategy. ~15 hours.

⚡ CKS Exam Day — Quick Reference

WhatDetails
Exam FormatPerformance-based, hands-on. Solve real tasks on a live Kubernetes cluster via command line.
Duration2 hours (120 minutes). 15-20 tasks. ~6-8 minutes per task average.
Passing Score67/100 points. Partial credit exists — always attempt every task.
Kubernetes Versionv1.34 (aligned with latest minor version within 4-8 weeks of release).
PrerequisitesValid CKA certification required. No exceptions.
Exam SimulatorTwo Killer.sh attempts included. 17 questions each. 36 hours of access per attempt.
Certification Validity2 years. One retake included. 12-month eligibility window.
Allowed ResourcesKubernetes official docs (kubernetes.io/docs). No other tabs, notes, or bookmarks.
Strategy3-pass: Pass 1 (30m) quick wins → Pass 2 (60m) medium tasks → Pass 3 (30m) hard tasks.

🧭 Which Path Should You Take?

🔍 Are you new to Kubernetes security?
✅ YES → Start at Part 1 (Ch 1-3). Build foundation. Then follow the guide linearly through Part 9.
❓ No — I have security experience. Continue.
🔍 Do you have your CKA certification?
✅ YES → You meet the prerequisite. Focus on Parts 2-6 (Ch 4-32) for exam domains.
❌ NO → CKA is required before CKS. Take CKA first, then return to this guide.
🔍 Is your exam scheduled within 2 weeks?
✅ YES → Skip to Ch 36-38 (Exam Strategy, Mock Scenarios, Last-Mile Review). Drill muscle memory.
✅ NO → Follow the 3-phase study plan above. ~60 hours total preparation.

🔴🟢 Before vs After — Hardening the anihpj Cluster

🔴 Before: Default K8s (No Hardening)
  • Pods run as root with full capabilities
  • No NetworkPolicies — flat network, all pods reachable
  • Secrets in plaintext base64 in etcd
  • Dashboard with cluster-admin exposed
  • Images from public Docker Hub, no scanning
  • No audit logging, no Falco, no runtime detection
  • kubesec score: 2/10
🟢 After: CKS-Hardened (This Guide)
  • Pods run as non-root (UID 10001), ALL caps dropped
  • Zero-trust NetworkPolicy — deny-all + specific allows
  • Secrets encrypted at rest + Vault integration
  • Dashboard: read-only SA, kubectl proxy only
  • Images from private registry, Trivy-scanned, cosign-signed
  • Full audit logging + Falco + behavioral analytics
  • kubesec score: 8/10

Chapter 1: Introduction to Kubernetes Security

Kubernetes is the most powerful container orchestration platform ever built — and with that power comes an enormous attack surface. A single misconfiguration can expose every workload in your cluster. This chapter lays the foundation: why K8s security is uniquely challenging, what the 4Cs security model means in practice, and how you'll apply five core security principles to protect anihpj/jobpost throughout this guide.

Understanding "Why" Is Critical on the CKS Exam

The CKS is a performance-based exam (2 hours, ~15-20 hands-on tasks in a live terminal). Unlike multiple-choice exams, every question requires you to configure security controls — not just identify them. Understanding why each control matters helps you reason through unfamiliar scenarios:

  • Defense in Depth — The CKS tests your ability to LAYER controls. If one fails, the next must hold. Always think: "What's my backup?"
  • Least Privilege — Every RBAC question tests whether you grant ONLY what's needed. Over-permission = lost points.
  • Assume Breach — The CKS assumes attackers are already trying. Your job is to detect and stop them before they reach data.
  • Verification — The exam GRADES on verification. After every configuration, run a check command to prove it works.

🗺️ What You'll Actually DO on the CKS Exam — Preview of Skills You'll Master

By the end of this guide, you will be able to perform ALL of these tasks from memory in under 2 hours:

🔐
Run kube-bench & Fix Findings

Scan a cluster against CIS benchmarks, identify FAIL/WARN results, and apply the exact fixes — editing API server manifests, kubelet configs, and etcd settings directly on the node.

🌐
Write NetworkPolicy from Scratch

Create default-deny and specific-allow policies. Test them with kubectl exec and ping. Know exactly which CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy and which don't.

👥
Create RBAC with Least Privilege

Define Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, and ClusterRoleBindings. Test with kubectl auth can-i --as=user. Never grant more than needed — the exam deducts points for over-permission.

🛡️
Apply AppArmor & Seccomp Profiles

Load AppArmor profiles on nodes, annotate pods to use them. Create custom Seccomp profiles that block specific syscalls. Verify the profiles are actually enforced at runtime.

🔍
Scan Images & Sign with cosign

Run Trivy to find CVEs, fix Dockerfiles to eliminate them. Generate cosign keypairs, sign images, and configure Kyverno to verify signatures before admitting pods.

🦅
Deploy Falco & Write Detection Rules

Install Falco, write custom rules that detect shell spawns, file access to /etc, and unexpected network connections. Trigger alerts and verify they fire correctly.

💡 Pro Tip: Every CKS exam task falls into one of these six categories. If you can do these from memory, you can pass the exam. This guide builds each skill systematically, chapter by chapter.

1.1 Why Kubernetes Security Is Different

Imagine your anihpj/jobpost Django application is running on Kubernetes. Employers post jobs, candidates browse listings, and user data flows through your cluster. Now imagine an attacker finds a way in. How many layers do they have to breach before they reach your database?

📖 Key Concept: The K8s Attack Surface

Attack surface is the sum of all points where an attacker can try to enter or extract data. Kubernetes has a uniquely large attack surface because it manages networking, storage, secrets, identities, and application lifecycle — all through a single API. As a CKS specialist, your job is to reduce, monitor, and defend every inch of that surface.

5 Inconvenient Truths About Default Kubernetes Security

Out of the box, a freshly installed Kubernetes cluster is insecure by default. Knowing these defaults is essential — because every CKS exam question is essentially asking you to fix one of them:

🔴
Truth 1: All Pods Can Talk to Each Other

No NetworkPolicy exists by default. Any pod in any namespace can reach any other pod on any port. This means a compromised jobpost container could directly connect to your PostgreSQL database — no firewall, no barrier, nothing. CKS Fix: Chapter 6 — Network Policies.

🔴
Truth 2: Containers Run as Root (UID 0)

Unless you explicitly set runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser, every container runs with full root privileges. If an attacker exploits a CVE in your app, they get root on the container — and potentially the node. CKS Fix: Chapter 18 — Security Contexts.

🔴
Truth 3: All 38+ Linux Capabilities Are Enabled

Default containers have SYS_ADMIN, NET_RAW, SYS_PTRACE, and dozens more. Each capability is a potential privilege escalation path. You must explicitly drop: [ALL] and add back only what's needed. CKS Fix: Chapter 18 — capabilities drop ALL.

🔴
Truth 4: Secrets Are Stored as Plain Base64 in etcd

kubectl create secret stores your database passwords, API keys, and TLS certificates as base64-encoded text — not encrypted. Anyone with etcd access can decode them. Encryption at rest must be explicitly configured. CKS Fix: Chapter 19 — EncryptionConfiguration.

🔴
Truth 5: No Audit Logging by Default

By default, Kubernetes records ZERO information about who did what. If an attacker deletes your production namespace at 3 AM, you'll have no record of who, how, or when. Audit logging must be explicitly enabled and configured. CKS Fix: Chapter 28 — Audit Logging.

🏙️ Think of Your K8s Cluster as a City — and Security as Infrastructure
  • 🏛️ Control Plane = City Hall — If someone breaks in, they control everything. Lock every door and window (API server hardening).
  • 🏘️ Worker Nodes = Residential blocks — Your apps live here. Each home needs its own lock (SecurityContext, seccomp).
  • 🌐 Network = Roads — By default, every building has a door to every other building. Install gates between districts (NetworkPolicy).
  • 📦 Containers = Delivery packages — Anyone can send one. Scan every package before accepting it (image scanning, admission control).
  • 🦅 Falco = CCTV cameras on every street — You'll know the moment something suspicious happens.
  • 📋 Audit Logs = Visitor registry — Every entry and exit is recorded forever.
⚠️ Real-World Kubernetes Security Breaches

These are not hypothetical. Major companies have suffered K8s security incidents:

  • Tesla (2018) — Crypto-mining malware deployed via an exposed Kubernetes dashboard with no authentication. Attackers used Tesla's cloud resources to mine cryptocurrency.
  • Capital One (2019) — A misconfigured WAF allowed an attacker to access AWS credentials from a K8s pod, leading to the exposure of 100+ million customer records.
  • Shopify (2020) — Rogue employees accessed customer data through overly permissive K8s RBAC roles that had not been properly scoped.

Common thread in ALL K8s breaches: Default configurations left unchanged, excessive permissions, and no runtime detection. Everything you will learn in this guide directly prevents these exact scenarios.

Time to Detect — The Most Brutal Statistic

🔴 Without CKS Controls — Average Time to DETECT a Breach 204 days
🔴 Without CKS Controls — Average Time to CONTAIN After Detection 73 days
🟡 With Basic Auditing — Detection Time ~7 days
🟢 With Falco + Audit Logs + AlertManager — Detection Time Minutes to hours

Why this gap exists: Without Falco (Ch 29) and audit logging (Ch 28), there is zero runtime visibility into your cluster. You find out about a breach when your cloud bill arrives, when customers complain, or when a security researcher emails you — not from your own monitoring. The 204-day average is not because breaches are hard to detect. It is because most organizations have no detection infrastructure at all. Every chapter in this guide closes a piece of that gap.

Traditional IT Security vs Kubernetes Security

Everything you know about traditional security still applies — but Kubernetes adds a new dimension of complexity:

Traditional IT SecurityKubernetes Security
One server = one firewall rule1000 pods = 1000 potential targets
Static IPs and hostnamesEphemeral pods, rotating IPs
Update OS once a monthImages rebuilt & deployed daily
Users log in via SSHPods authenticate with SA tokens
Audit logs in /var/log/auth.logAudit logs via K8s API policy
Firewall blocks at edgeNetworkPolicy inside the cluster
Manual security reviewsPolicy-as-code enforced at admission

Secret in /etc/app.conf🔴 Secret in etcd (unencrypted!)
Patch = update one binaryPatch = rebuild + redeploy image

How Attackers Actually Breach Kubernetes — The Attack Chain

Understanding how attackers operate is the first step to stopping them. Below is a realistic attack chain against an unsecured Kubernetes cluster running anihpj/jobpost, mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Each stage shows the attacker's action on the LEFT and the CKS control that stops it on the RIGHT.

The 7-Stage Kubernetes Attack Chain — Attack vs CKS Defense
🔓 STAGE 1: Initial Access

Attacker scans internet for open Kubernetes API servers (port 6443). Finds your cluster with --anonymous-auth=true (the DEFAULT!). Result: Full cluster access with NO credentials needed.

🛡️ CKS Defense

Anonymous auth disabled (Ch 8). TLS client certificates required. NetworkPolicy blocks external access to API server port.

🔍 STAGE 2: Discovery

Attacker runs kubectl get pods --all-namespaces → sees anihpj-prod, postgres, redis. Runs kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces → finds database-passwords, api-keys, tls-certs — all in plain base64!

🛡️ CKS Defense

RBAC with least privilege — attacker's stolen credential can only access specific namespace (Ch 9). Secrets encrypted at rest in etcd — even if accessed, unreadable (Ch 19).

🔑 STAGE 3: Credential Access

Attacker reads SA token from pod: cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. This token has cluster-admin permissions (the DEFAULT!). Attacker now has permanent API access.

🛡️ CKS Defense

ServiceAccount with automountServiceAccountToken: false, zero API permissions (Ch 10). Token projected with limited lifetime.

↔️ STAGE 4: Lateral Movement

From compromised anihpj pod, attacker connects to postgres:5432 (dumps entire database), redis:6379 (reads sessions), and probes every reachable pod. ALL connections succeed — NO NetworkPolicies exist!

🛡️ CKS Defense

Default-deny NetworkPolicy. anihpj pod can ONLY reach postgres:5432. Everything else is BLOCKED (Ch 6).

⬆️ STAGE 5: Privilege Escalation

anihpj container runs as ROOT (UID 0). All 38 Linux capabilities enabled. Attacker exploits CVE in Python Pillow → writes malicious binary to /usr/bin/ → sets SUID bit → persistent access. Even tries container escape via /proc/1/ns/.

🛡️ CKS Defense

runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000 (Ch 18). drop ALL capabilities — even if CVE exploited, can't write to /usr. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true — nothing modifiable (Ch 31). Seccomp blocks dangerous syscalls (Ch 15).

💾 STAGE 6: Persistence

Attacker creates a CronJob running every hour, downloading a reverse shell. Even if original pod is killed, CronJob recreates the backdoor. Also modifies Deployment to pull malicious image from docker.io/evil/reverse-shell.

🛡️ CKS Defense

OPA/Kyverno admission control blocks images not from approved registries (Ch 24). cosign signature verification rejects unsigned images (Ch 26). RBAC prevents creating CronJobs.

📤 STAGE 7: Exfiltration

Attacker slowly streams entire jobpost database (user emails, passwords, resumes) to external server. No egress controls = data flows freely. No monitoring = nobody notices for 204 days.

🛡️ CKS Defense

NetworkPolicy egress rules block all external connections. Audit logging records every API call (Ch 28). Falco detects anomalous network patterns and triggers alerts within seconds (Ch 29).

🔴 WITHOUT CKS

7/7 Stages Succeed

Complete data breach. Full cluster compromise. Zero detection.

🟢 WITH CKS

0/7 Stages Succeed

Attack fails at every layer. Defense-in-depth works.

The Shared Responsibility Model — Who Secures What?

Kubernetes security is a shared responsibility between the cloud provider, the cluster administrator (YOU), and the developers. Understanding where your responsibility begins and ends is critical for the CKS exam:

LayerCloud Provider (AWS/GCP/Azure)🔑 YOU — The CKS AdminDeveloper
Physical / Hardware ✅ Physical security, hardware — —
OS / Kernel ✅ Host OS patching (managed K8s) 🔑 Node OS hardening, kernel params, AppArmor, Seccomp profiles on nodes —
Kubernetes Control Plane ✅ API server HA (managed K8s) 🔑 API server hardening flags, audit policy, encryption config, RBAC, admission controllers —
Kubernetes Networking — 🔑 CNI plugin choice, NetworkPolicies, Ingress TLS, CoreDNS config —
Container Runtimes — 🔑 Runtime selection (runc vs gVisor), runtimeClass config —
Container Images — 🔑 Image scanning policy, registry allowlists, admission webhooks ✅ Write secure Dockerfiles, use minimal base images
Pod Security — 🔑 PSS enforcement labels on namespaces, PodSecurity admission config ✅ Write SecurityContext in pod specs, run as non-root
Application Code — — ✅ Secure coding, dependency scanning, secrets in env vars (from K8s Secrets)
Monitoring / Detection — 🔑 Falco deployment, audit log collection, SIEM integration, alert routing —
💡 CKS Exam Focus: The Middle Column Is Your Domain

Every CKS exam question falls into the "YOU — The CKS Admin" column. The exam does NOT test cloud provider configuration (that's cloud certs) and does NOT test application code (that's CKAD). Your job is everything in between: the cluster, the nodes, the networking, the policies, and the detection. If you're not sure whether to harden the OS or fix the app code, the answer is almost always: harden the OS.

😰 Scenario: anihpj/jobpost running on Kubernetes WITHOUT CKS hardening
  • 💸 Financial Impact: Average cloud data breach cost: $4.45M (IBM 2023 report). Crypto-mining on stolen compute drains resources immediately.
  • 🏢 Business Impact: jobpost user emails exposed → user trust destroyed. Company credentials leaked → all cloud resources at risk. Service taken offline → job seekers cannot access listings.
  • ⏱️ Time to Detect (without CKS): Average: 204 days to DETECT a breach. Average: 73 days to CONTAIN it. With Falco + Audit Logs: minutes to hours.

The Shared Kernel Architecture — Why K8s Security Is Fundamentally Harder

At the heart of Kubernetes security lies an uncomfortable truth: every container on a node shares the exact same Linux kernel. This is not a bug. It is the defining architectural property of containerization — and the reason container security is qualitatively different from VM security. Understanding this deepens every decision you make in the chapters ahead.

VM Isolation vs Container Isolation — The Kernel Is the Difference
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VIRTUAL MACHINE MODEL (e.g., VMware, KVM, EC2)                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐                      │
  │  │   VM 1      │  │   VM 2      │  │   VM 3      │                      │
  │  │  App A      │  │  App B      │  │  App C      │                      │
  │  │  Kernel A   │  │  Kernel B   │  │  Kernel C   │  ← SEPARATE kernels  │
  │  │  (Linux 5.10)│  │  (Linux 5.15)│  │  (Linux 6.1) │    per VM          │
  │  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘                      │
  │         │                │                │                              │
  │  ┌──────┴────────────────┴────────────────┴──────┐                      │
  │  │        HYPERVISOR (ESXi / KVM / Xen)          │  ← Hardware-enforced  │
  │  │        CPU ring -1 isolation                   │     boundary         │
  │  └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘                      │
  │                         │                                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐                      │
  │  │              PHYSICAL HARDWARE                 │                      │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SECURITY MODEL: Kernel exploit in VM1 affects ONLY VM1.                │
  │  The hypervisor enforces hardware-level isolation between VMs.          │
  │  Breaking out of VM1 requires BOTH a kernel exploit AND a hypervisor    │
  │  escape — two independent vulnerabilities.                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CONTAINER MODEL (Docker, containerd, CRI-O)                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐      │
  │  │  Pod A   │ │  Pod B   │ │  Pod C   │ │  Pod D   │ │  Pod E   │      │
  │  │  Django  │ │  Nginx   │ │  Redis   │ │  Postgres│ │  Attacker│      │
  │  │  UID 1000│ │  UID 101 │ │  UID 999 │ │  UID 70  │ │  UID 0   │      │
  │  └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘      │
  │       │            │            │            │            │              │
  │  ┌────┴────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴─────┐      │
  │  │               CONTAINER RUNTIME (containerd / runc)           │      │
  │  │               Namespace isolation (no hardware boundary)     │      │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘      │
  │                                 │                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┐      │
  │  │               SINGLE LINUX KERNEL (shared by ALL containers)  │      │
  │  │               Version 5.15.0-91-generic                       │      │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘      │
  │                                 │                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┐      │
  │  │                    PHYSICAL HARDWARE                          │      │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SECURITY MODEL: A SINGLE kernel exploit affects ALL containers.        │
  │  If Pod E exploits CVE-2022-0185 in the 5.15 kernel, the attacker       │
  │  escapes the namespace and gains access to Pods A, B, C, D — AND       │
  │  the host OS. Every container's security depends on the integrity       │
  │  of one shared kernel. There is no hypervisor to escape.                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The implication for CKS: Every security control you learn in this guide exists because the shared kernel model creates a single point of failure. NetworkPolicies (Ch6) prevent Pod E from even reaching Pods A-D. SecurityContext with non-root (Ch18) means Pod E's exploit needs TWO vulnerabilities (kernel + privilege escalation). Seccomp (Ch15) blocks the syscalls the kernel exploit needs. AppArmor (Ch14) blocks the files the exploit needs to read. Each control is a layer of defense against the inevitable truth that all containers on a node share one kernel, and kernels have bugs.

How Traditional Security Tools Fail in Kubernetes — And What Replaces Them

When organizations first adopt Kubernetes, they try to apply their existing security toolkit. This almost always fails — not because the tools are bad, but because they were built for a fundamentally different computing model. Here is what breaks and why:

Traditional ToolWhat It DidWhy It Fails in K8sCKS Replacement
Host-based Firewall (iptables on each server)Block ports per static IPPod IPs are ephemeral — change every restart. 1000 pods = 1000 changing firewall rules. Static rules become stale in minutes.NetworkPolicy (Ch6) — label-based, dynamic, auto-applied to new pods.
SSH-based Admin AccessSSH into each server as rootPods don't run SSH daemons. You can't SSH into a container (and shouldn't). Admin access must go through the K8s API.RBAC + kubectl exec (Ch9) — API-mediated access with audit trail.
Static Vulnerability Scanners (Nessus, Qualys)Scan server IPs for open ports and CVEsPods come and go in seconds. A scan that runs hourly misses 99% of pod lifecycles. Images change in CI/CD, not on servers.Trivy in CI/CD (Ch23) — scan images BEFORE they become pods. Admission control (Ch24) blocks vulnerable images at deploy time.
Filesystem Integrity Monitoring (AIDE, Tripwire)Alert when /etc/passwd or /bin/ changesContainers are immutable (or should be). Change detection on ephemeral filesystems generates noise. The real change happens in the image registry.Image signing (Ch26) + Immutable containers (Ch31) — verify the image hasn't changed before it runs. No filesystem changes allowed at runtime.
User Account Auditing (lastlog, wtmp)Track who logged in and whenK8s has ServiceAccounts, not Linux users. Pods authenticate with JWT tokens, not passwords. Linux audit trails don't capture K8s API activity.K8s Audit Logging (Ch28) — captures every API operation with user, timestamp, resource, and verb.
Antivirus (ClamAV, McAfee)Signature-based malware detection on filesContainers don't persist files. Malware in a container disappears on restart. The attack surface is the running process, not stored files.Falco (Ch29) — behavioral detection at the syscall level. Alerts on suspicious process behavior, not file signatures.

The mindset shift: Security in Kubernetes is not about protecting servers. It's about protecting a dynamic system where identities (ServiceAccounts), network endpoints (pods), and execution environments (containers) are constantly created and destroyed. The tools that work are the tools that understand this dynamism — which is why every tool in the CKS curriculum is Kubernetes-native or Linux-kernel-native, not server-native.

1.2 The 4Cs of Cloud Native Security (The Layered Model)

The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) defines a four-layer security model for cloud-native applications. Each layer builds on the security of the layer below it. If the Cloud layer is insecure, nothing above it matters. Every layer must be independently secured. This model — Cloud → Cluster → Container → Code — is the foundation of every CKS exam question.

📖 The 4Cs

Cloud → Cluster → Container → Code: Think of these as nested Russian dolls. The Cloud is the outermost doll (the infrastructure). The Cluster is inside (Kubernetes itself). The Container is inside the cluster (how your app runs). The Code is the innermost doll (your actual application). A breach at any outer layer compromises ALL inner layers.

The 4Cs — Nested Security Layers

Cloud (outermost) → Cluster → Container → Code (innermost)

Security Decision Flowchart — Which 4C Layer Does This Belong To?

Use this decision tree to map any security concern to the correct 4C layer
  You identify a security concern. Ask:

  Is it about cloud infra (VPC, IAM, firewall)?
    YES → ☁️  CLOUD layer → fix at cloud provider level
    NO  ↓

  Is it about K8s API, RBAC, nodes, networking, policies?
    YES → ☸️  CLUSTER layer → fix with RBAC, NetworkPolicy, etc.
    NO  ↓

  Is it about how a container runs (user, caps, filesystem)?
    YES → 📦 CONTAINER layer → fix SecurityContext, Seccomp, AppArmor
    NO  ↓

  Is it about the software, libraries, or secrets IN the image?
    YES → 💻 CODE layer → fix with scanning, signing, dep updates

What Happens When Each 4C Layer Fails — A Failure Walkthrough

Understanding what each layer protects against is one thing. Understanding what happens when a layer FAILS is what separates CKS-certified specialists from everyone else. Here's what actually happens at each failure point for anihpj:

☁️
When the CLOUD Layer Fails...

If your node's IAM role has AdministratorAccess and an attacker compromises that node, they can delete every S3 bucket, terminate every EC2 instance, and exfiltrate every RDS snapshot. The fix must happen at the cloud provider level — Kubernetes cannot protect you from overly permissive cloud IAM. This is why NodeRestriction exists: it limits what each kubelet can modify via the API server, creating a boundary between node compromise and cluster-wide disaster.

☸️
When the CLUSTER Layer Fails...

If anonymous auth is enabled (--anonymous-auth=true), anyone who can reach your API server on port 6443 has full cluster access — no credentials needed. They can kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces and extract every database password, API key, and TLS certificate stored in your cluster. This is the #1 most common K8s breach vector (see: Tesla 2018). The fix is simple but critical: --anonymous-auth=false and proper RBAC with least privilege.

📦
When the CONTAINER Layer Fails...

If your container runs as root (the default!) and a vulnerability exists in any library (e.g., CVE in Pillow, Requests, or even libc), an attacker who exploits that CVE immediately has root inside the container. From there, they can install backdoors, read /proc/1/environ for secrets, attempt container escape via nsenter, or write to any mounted hostPath volumes. This is why non-root + drop ALL + readOnlyRootFS is mandatory for every production pod.

💻
When the CODE Layer Fails...

If your CI/CD pipeline builds from python:3.11 (a 1GB+ image with compilers, curl, wget, and hundreds of unnecessary packages), every CVE in those packages becomes YOUR CVE. An attacker who exploits a curl vulnerability in your base image can make outbound connections to exfiltrate data — even if your APPLICATION code is perfectly secure. The fix: multi-stage builds, distroless images, and Trivy scanning at every CI/CD stage.

⚠️ The Most Dangerous Assumption in Kubernetes Security

Many administrators assume: "I deployed on a managed K8s service (EKS/GKE/AKS), so the cloud provider handles security." This is dangerously wrong. Managed K8s secures the CONTROL PLANE (API server, etcd, controller manager). It does NOT secure: your pod configurations, your NetworkPolicies, your RBAC rules, your container images, your node OS, your audit logging, or your runtime detection. Everything from the container level down is YOUR responsibility. The CKS exam tests exactly this boundary.

1.3 Security Principles You Will Apply Throughout This Guide

Every single CKS exam task — and every real-world security decision — flows from five core security principles. These are not just theory. They are the mindset you will apply to every kubectl command, every YAML file, and every security audit you perform on the anihpj/jobpost application.

The 5 Core Security Principles

🎯
Least Privilege

Grant ONLY what is needed. Nothing more, nothing less. Every RBAC role, every ServiceAccount, every IAM policy — start from zero and add only what's required.

🧅
Defense in Depth

Multiple layers of security; no single point of failure. If NetworkPolicy fails, SecurityContext still blocks. If Seccomp fails, Falco still alerts. Every layer is a backup.

🚫
Zero Trust

Trust no pod, user, or service by default. Every connection must be explicitly allowed. Default-deny is the starting position for every NetworkPolicy and every RBAC rule.

🧊
Immutability

Containers should not change once running. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Changes go through Git → CI/CD → image rebuild → new pod. Attackers cannot persist changes.

📋
Audit Everything

Log every API call, every access, and every anomaly. If you don't know it happened, you can't respond to it. Audit logs + Falco = complete visibility.

The anihpj Application Context for Security

Throughout this guide, every principle, tool, and technique is demonstrated using the anihpj/jobpost Django application. Here is what we need to protect:

  • jobpost app — serves public job listings; must not expose secrets or user data
  • Django admin interface — must be restricted by RBAC and NetworkPolicy
  • PostgreSQL database — must not be reachable from the internet
  • Media uploads — must be scanned for malware
  • API keys in settings.py — must be in Kubernetes Secrets, never in code

How Each Principle Applies to anihpj Daily

🎯
LEAST PRIVILEGE in Practice

anihpj pod's ServiceAccount → no API permissions (automount=false). CI/CD ServiceAccount → can only update Deployments, nothing else. Every identity in the cluster has the absolute minimum permissions required to function.

🧅
DEFENSE IN DEPTH in Practice

anihpj has: NetworkPolicy + PSS + SecurityContext + Falco + TLS. If NetworkPolicy fails → SecurityContext still prevents root exec. If image is vulnerable → Seccomp still blocks dangerous syscalls. Seven layers, no single point of failure.

🚫
ZERO TRUST in Practice

Default-deny NetworkPolicy in anihpj-prod: nothing in, nothing out. Each connection explicitly allowed: ingress→anihpj (port 8000), anihpj→postgres (port 5432), anihpj→DNS (port 53). Everything else is BLOCKED.

🧊
IMMUTABILITY in Practice

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true on all anihpj containers. Changes go through Git → CI/CD (scan + sign) → image rebuild → new pod. Attackers cannot persist changes inside a running container — any modification disappears on pod restart.

📋
AUDIT EVERYTHING in Practice

Audit policy logs: all secret reads, all pod exec, all deployments. Falco rule: alert on any shell in anihpj container. Trivy Operator: continuous CVE scan of running images. If anything happens in the cluster, you have a record of it.

Principle Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do (And What to Do Instead)

Understanding the principles is important. Avoiding the common anti-patterns is what saves you on exam day. Here are the five most dangerous security anti-patterns, with concrete code examples showing wrong vs right approaches:

❌ ANTI-PATTERN: Over-Permissive RBAC

kubectl create clusterrole anihpj-admin --verb=* --resource=*

Granting wildcard permissions defeats the purpose of RBAC entirely. A compromised pod with this role can delete every resource in every namespace.

✅ CORRECT: Least Privilege RBAC

kubectl create role anihpj-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods,deployments -n anihpj-prod

Grant ONLY the specific verbs and resources needed. Use namespaced Roles (not ClusterRoles) when possible. Always verify with kubectl auth can-i --as=sa.

❌ ANTI-PATTERN: Running as Root

containers:
- name: anihpj
image: anihpj:latest
(no securityContext — runs as root by default!)

✅ CORRECT: Non-Root with Drop ALL

securityContext:
runAsNonRoot: true
runAsUser: 1000
capabilities:
drop: [ALL]
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

❌ ANTI-PATTERN: Trusting Internal Traffic

No NetworkPolicy defined. All pods in all namespaces can reach anihpj on every port. PostgreSQL port 5432 is exposed to every container in the cluster.

✅ CORRECT: Zero-Trust NetworkPolicy

podSelector: app=anihpj
policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
ingress: [{from: [podSelector: app=ingress-nginx], ports: [8000]}]
egress: [{to: [podSelector: app=postgres], ports: [5432]}]
Everything else is implicitly denied.

💡 The CKS Exam Anti-Pattern Rule

On the CKS exam, if you find yourself typing * (wildcard) in an RBAC rule, you're probably losing points. If you leave runAsUser unspecified, you're losing points. If you don't verify after every configuration with a test command, you're losing points. The exam rewards precision, not speed.

🚫 Common Misconceptions About Kubernetes Security

Before you continue to Chapter 2, let's clear up the most common misconceptions that trip up CKS candidates:

  • ❌ "My cluster is behind a firewall, so it's secure."
    ✅ Firewalls protect north-south traffic (external ↔ cluster). They do NOTHING for east-west traffic (pod ↔ pod). A compromised pod can attack every other pod unless you have NetworkPolicies. Chapters 6, 20.
  • ❌ "I use RBAC, so my cluster is locked down."
    ✅ RBAC controls API access (who can run kubectl). It does NOT control what containers can do at runtime (run as root, access host filesystem, make syscalls). You need SecurityContext + Seccomp + AppArmor for that. Chapters 14-18.
  • ❌ "My images are scanned, so my supply chain is secure."
    ✅ Scanning finds KNOWN vulnerabilities. It does NOT prevent someone from pushing a malicious image to your registry. You need image signing (cosign) + admission control (OPA/Kyverno) to verify provenance. Chapters 23-26.
  • ❌ "Security is a one-time setup."
    ✅ New CVEs are discovered daily. New attack techniques emerge constantly. Security is continuous: scan continuously, monitor continuously, update continuously. Chapters 28-35.
  • ❌ "I'll just secure it before the exam."
    ✅ The CKS is a PERFORMANCE exam. You can't memorize your way through it. You need muscle memory: writing YAML from scratch, running kubectl commands blind, and troubleshooting broken clusters under time pressure. Practice, practice, practice.

📝 Chapter 1 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
You're auditing a Kubernetes cluster and discover that pods in the "default" namespace can communicate freely with pods in "kube-system". Which 4C layer does this vulnerability belong to, and which single Kubernetes resource would you apply to fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

Layer: Cluster layer. Fix: Apply a NetworkPolicy in the "default" namespace that restricts egress to kube-system. NetworkPolicy controls pod-to-pod communication at the cluster level.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-kube-system
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector: {}  # Only allow egress to pods in same namespace
Explanation

The 4Cs model (Cloud → Cluster → Container → Code) maps every security control to a layer. NetworkPolicy operates at the Cluster layer because it controls pod-to-pod communication enforced by the CNI plugin. Without a NetworkPolicy, Kubernetes allows all traffic between any pods in any namespace — this is the default "flat network" model. The CKS exam expects you to immediately identify which 4C layer a vulnerability falls into because it determines WHICH set of controls to apply. Pod-to-pod communication = Cluster layer = NetworkPolicy.

Q2
Explain the difference between Authentication (AuthN) and Authorization (AuthZ) in Kubernetes. If a user gets a 401 error vs a 403 error, which system rejected them and what should you check?
Show Answer
Answer

401 Unauthorized: Authentication failure — the API server doesn't recognize WHO you are. Check: is your certificate valid? Is your bearer token expired? Is your kubeconfig pointing to the right cluster? 403 Forbidden: Authorization failure — the API server knows who you are but you lack permission. Check: kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> -n <ns>. Review your Role/ClusterRole bindings.

Explanation

The API server processes every request through a chain: AuthN → AuthZ → Admission. AuthN answers "Who are you?" (certificates, tokens, OIDC). AuthZ answers "Can you do this?" (RBAC, Node, ABAC, Webhook). A 401 means your identity was rejected — check your kubeconfig credentials. A 403 means you're known but not allowed — use kubectl auth can-i to debug. On the CKS exam, when you get "forbidden" errors after applying RBAC, it's almost always because you forgot the namespace flag or used the wrong verb name.

Q3
A developer deploys a pod that runs as root (UID 0) with all Linux capabilities. Which 4C layer should catch this FIRST, and which Kubernetes mechanism would automatically reject this pod?
Show Answer
Answer

Layer: Container layer (caught at admission time by Cluster layer). Mechanism: Pod Security Admission (PSA) with the Restricted profile. If the namespace has pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted, the pod is REJECTED before creation because it violates: runAsNonRoot != true and capabilities.drop must include ALL.

kubectl label ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30
Explanation

Pod Security Admission (PSA) replaced PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) in Kubernetes 1.25. PSA defines three policy levels: privileged (unrestricted), baseline (minimally restrictive, prevents known privilege escalations), and restricted (heavily restricted, follows pod hardening best practices). The enforce label on a namespace REJECTS pods that violate the policy. This is a preventive control — the pod never gets created. The CKS exam tests PSA extensively because it's the native Kubernetes mechanism for container-level security.

Q4
What is the principle of "Least Privilege" in Kubernetes security? Give a concrete example using ServiceAccounts: what's the default behavior and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

Least Privilege means every entity (user, ServiceAccount, pod) should have ONLY the minimum permissions needed. Default problem: Every namespace has a "default" ServiceAccount that is automatically mounted to every pod unless explicitly overridden. This SA may have unintended RBAC permissions. Fix: Create a dedicated SA with no RBAC bindings, and set automountServiceAccountToken: false.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false  # No token = no API access
Explanation

In Kubernetes, every pod gets a ServiceAccount token mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token by default. If your pod is compromised, the attacker can use this token to make authenticated API calls — with whatever RBAC permissions the SA has. Two fixes: (1) set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the SA or pod spec to prevent the token mount entirely, and (2) never bind RBAC roles to the default SA. On the CKS exam, look for pods that mount tokens but don't need API access — that's a finding you must fix.

Q5
You are tasked with securing a new Kubernetes cluster from scratch. Draw or describe the 4Cs security model and for each layer, name ONE specific CKS control that applies. Which layer is entirely outside Kubernetes' control?
Show Answer
Answer
Layer Control K8s Managed?
Cloud IAM roles, VPC firewalls, KMS encryption keys, network ACLs ❌ No — cloud provider
Cluster RBAC, NetworkPolicy, Audit Logging, EncryptionConfiguration, Admission Controllers ✅ Yes
Container SecurityContext (non-root, readOnlyRootFS), Seccomp, AppArmor, PodSecurity, image scanning ✅ Yes
Code Static analysis (SAST), dependency scanning (SCA), SBOM generation, code signing ✅ Yes (CI/CD pipeline)
Explanation

The 4Cs model is the organizing framework for the entire CKS curriculum. The Cloud layer is critical because Kubernetes cannot fix cloud-level misconfigurations — an over-permissive AWS IAM role can expose etcd even if Kubernetes RBAC is perfect. The exam tests your ability to identify which layer a vulnerability belongs to so you know where to apply the fix. Remember: Cloud → security of the infrastructure, Cluster → security of Kubernetes itself, Container → security of what runs inside pods, Code → security of what you build.

Q6
You SSH onto a control plane node and run ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. You see four YAML files: kube-apiserver.yaml, etcd.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml. What type of pods are these, who manages them, and what happens if you edit kube-apiserver.yaml and save the file?
Show Answer
Answer

These are Static Pods. They are managed by the kubelet directly, NOT by the kube-apiserver or any controller. The kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and starts/stops pods based on the files there.

If you edit kube-apiserver.yaml and save: The kubelet detects the file change, terminates the current kube-apiserver container, and recreates it with the new configuration. Your kubectl connection WILL drop for 30-60 seconds while the new container starts. After the restart, the API server runs with the updated flags.

# Check which kubelet is watching
ps aux | grep kubelet | grep -- --pod-manifest-path
# Common path: --pod-manifest-path=/etc/kubernetes/manifests

# Restart a static pod by editing its manifest
vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add: --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# Save → kubelet auto-restarts kube-apiserver with audit logging enabled
Explanation

Static pods are the mechanism Kubernetes uses to bootstrap itself — the control plane components run as static pods so they don't depend on the API server being available (which would be a chicken-and-egg problem). The kubelet uses the CRI (Container Runtime Interface) to manage these pods directly. On the CKS exam, you'll frequently need to edit static pod manifests to add security flags (--audit-policy-file, --encryption-provider-config, --authorization-mode). Always be aware that editing the API server manifest causes a brief outage — this is expected and not an error.

Q7
Explain the Defense in Depth principle using a real CKS scenario. An anihpj pod is compromised. Describe at least FOUR different security layers that should limit the blast radius, and what specific CKS control each layer uses.
Show Answer
Answer
🧱 Layer 1: NetworkPolicy

Default-deny egress blocks the compromised pod from reaching other pods or the internet. The attacker can't exfiltrate data or pivot laterally.

👤 Layer 2: SecurityContext

runAsNonRoot: true + readOnlyRootFilesystem: true — even inside the container, the attacker can't install tools or modify system files.

🛡️ Layer 3: Seccomp/AppArmor

A restricted Seccomp profile blocks dangerous syscalls (nsenter, mount, ptrace). AppArmor denies access to /proc and /sys.

🔔 Layer 4: Runtime Detection

Falco detects the shell spawn inside the container and triggers an alert. Audit logs record every API call the compromised SA attempts.

Explanation

Defense in Depth means no single control is your only protection. If NetworkPolicy fails, SecurityContext still limits the attacker. If SecurityContext is bypassed via a kernel exploit, Seccomp still blocks the syscall. If all preventive controls fail, Falco still detects and alerts. This is the "Swiss cheese" model — each layer has holes, but the holes don't line up. The CKS exam tests your ability to stack controls rather than relying on any single mechanism. A common exam task: given a pod spec, add ALL applicable security controls, not just one.

Q8
A cluster has --anonymous-auth=true on the API server (the default). What can an unauthenticated attacker do, and which flag should you change to what value? What's the verification command?
Show Answer
Answer

With anonymous auth enabled, an attacker can reach any API endpoint that doesn't explicitly require authentication. Depending on RBAC, the system:anonymous user may have cluster-wide read access if someone mistakenly bound a ClusterRole to it.

Fix: Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml and change --anonymous-auth=true to --anonymous-auth=false.

# Verify anonymous access is blocked
kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: Error from server (Forbidden)

# Verify the flag is set
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep anonymous-auth
# Should show: --anonymous-auth=false

# Or check the manifest
grep anonymous-auth /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
Explanation

--anonymous-auth=true is the DEFAULT in Kubernetes. It creates a user called system:anonymous that represents all unauthenticated requests. If any ClusterRole/Role is bound to system:anonymous or to system:unauthenticated group, anonymous users gain those permissions. On the CKS exam, setting --anonymous-auth=false is a common task. After the change, the API server restart takes 30-60s — your kubectl connection will drop briefly. Also verify that --authorization-mode includes RBAC (it should: --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC).

Q9
What is the Immutability principle in Kubernetes security, and how does it apply to both container images AND running pods? Give specific CKS-relevant Kubernetes configurations that enforce immutability.
Show Answer
Answer

Immutability means that once deployed, nothing changes. Instead of patching a running container, you rebuild the image and redeploy. This eliminates configuration drift and makes it impossible for attackers to persist changes.

Pod-level immutability:

securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # Can't write to container filesystem
  runAsNonRoot: true               # Can't install packages
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # Can't gain more privileges than parent

Image-level immutability: Use digest-based image references instead of tags. Tags are mutable (an attacker can push a malicious anihpj:v2.1). Digests are immutable.

# BAD: Mutable tag
image: anihpj:v2.1

# GOOD: Immutable digest
image: anihpj@sha256:a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0
Explanation

Immutability is a cultural shift from traditional server management. In Kubernetes, you never SSH into a container to fix it — you fix the Dockerfile, rebuild, scan, sign, and redeploy. The CKS exam tests this via readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (pod spec) and image digest pinning (admission controllers like Kyverno can enforce digest-only images). Immutability also makes forensic analysis easier: if an attacker compromises a pod, you can kill it and replace it with a known-good image — the attacker can't survive a pod restart because they can't persist files.

Q10
You're performing a security audit and need to discover the complete attack surface of a live cluster. List the commands you would run and what each reveals. Include at least ONE command for each 4C layer.
Show Answer
Answer
Layer Command Reveals
Cloudkubectl get nodes -o wideNode IPs, OS, kernel version
Clusterkubectl api-resources --verbs=list -o wideEvery resource type, its API group, and available verbs
Clusterkubectl get pods,svc,secrets,cm -AAll workloads, exposed services, sensitive data
Clusterkubectl auth can-i --list -AYOUR current permissions (attacker's first command)
Containerkubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true)'All pods running as root
Containerkubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged == true)'All privileged pods
Codekubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].image'All running images (check for :latest tags, old versions)
Explanation

This audit approach is what you'd perform on the CKS exam when given a cluster and told to "find all security issues." The key insight: use kubectl's JSON output with jq to query across all namespaces at once. kubectl auth can-i --list is the attacker's first command after gaining access — it reveals exactly what damage they can do. Running pods as root is the #1 finding in real-world CKS audits. The exam rewards you for automation: write a one-liner that finds all issues rather than manually inspecting each pod.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. List ALL API resources (know your attack surface)
kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o wide

# 2. Check YOUR permissions (what can an attacker with your SA do?)
kubectl auth can-i --list -n default
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:anihpj-sa

# 3. Find all pods running as root (common exam task)
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true) | .metadata.name'

# 4. Quick cluster component check
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/  # Static pods: kube-apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager
kubectl get componentstatuses  # Deprecated but still in some clusters
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 1 Traps
  • Static pod ≠ regular pod: Editing /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml auto-restarts the API server. Your kubectl connection WILL drop for 30-60s. Don't panic — just wait and reconnect.
  • kubectl explain lies sometimes: kubectl explain pod.spec shows the API, not what your cluster version supports. Always check kubectl version --short first.
  • Namespaces aren't security boundaries: A pod in namespace-A can still talk to a pod in namespace-B unless NetworkPolicy blocks it. Namespaces are organizational, not isolation.

⚡ Ch 1 Visual Cheat Sheet — Cluster Architecture

🧠
API Server

Single entry point. All kubectl commands go through it. Stateless, horizontally scalable.

🗄️
etcd

Cluster brain. Stores all state. Only API server talks to it. Backup before any change.

📅
Scheduler

Decides which node runs each pod. Watches for unscheduled pods, scores nodes, binds.

🎮
Controller Manager

Runs control loops: node controller, replication controller, endpoints controller.

🤖
Kubelet

Node agent. Registers node, starts pods via CRI. Watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ for static pods.

🌐
kube-proxy

Network rules on every node. Implements Service abstraction via iptables/IPVS.

📦
Container Runtime

CRI-compliant: containerd, CRI-O. Pulls images, starts/stops containers.

🔌
CNI Plugin

Pod networking. Calico, Cilium, Flannel. Assigns IPs, routes traffic between pods across nodes.

📋 Exam Quick-Reference — Cluster Architecture
🎯 Exam Task Simulator — Verify Cluster Component Security
1SSH to control plane: ssh master-node
2Check static pod manifests: ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — verify kube-apiserver.yaml, etcd.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml exist.
3Verify API server flags: grep -E "authorization-mode|anonymous-auth|enable-admission-plugins" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
4Test connectivity: kubectl get nodes — if this works, API server is reachable. Then curl -k https://localhost:6443/healthz for health check.
5Verify: kubectl cluster-info and kubectl get componentstatuses (deprecated but shows scheduler/controller-manager status on older clusters).
⚠️ Top 2 Failure Modes
  • API server not responding after manifest edit: You edited kube-apiserver.yaml with wrong YAML indentation. The kubelet can't parse it → API server won't start. Fix: docker logs <api-server-container> or check /var/log/pods/kube-system_kube-apiserver-* for parse errors.
  • kubectl "connection refused": API server is restarting (30-60s after manifest edit). Wait and retry. If persistent: check kubelet is running with systemctl status kubelet.
⚡ CKS Speed Tips
  • kubectl api-resources --verbs=list -o wide — lists every resource type and which verbs you can use on them. Faster than searching docs.
  • kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive — complete pod spec reference without leaving the terminal.
  • Alias: alias k=kubectl saves ~2 seconds per command × 50 commands = 100 seconds saved on exam.

Chapter 2: The Threat Landscape — What Attackers Target

Before you can defend a Kubernetes cluster, you must understand how attackers think. This chapter maps the entire attack surface of a K8s cluster, walks through four real-world breaches that cost companies millions, introduces the STRIDE threat model, and shows you exactly how attackers would target your anihpj/jobpost application — and how CKS controls stop them at every stage.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Threat Analysis 🛡️ Attack Surface

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The 7 most common Kubernetes attack vectors and how each one works
  • ✅ Detailed walkthroughs of Tesla, Capital One, Shopify, and SolarWinds breaches
  • ✅ The STRIDE threat model applied to Kubernetes — with CKS-specific mitigations
  • ✅ MITRE ATT&CK framework mapped to K8s attack techniques and CKS defenses
  • ✅ The complete attacker kill chain — and exactly where CKS stops each stage
  • ✅ How the anihpj/jobpost Django application would be attacked without CKS hardening
🎓 CKS Relevance
Foundation ALL DOMAINS Cluster Setup 15% Monitoring 20%
Think Like an Attacker to Pass the CKS

The CKS exam doesn't ask you to "describe a threat." It asks you to configure a defense against a specific attack scenario. Understanding the attack is half the battle:

  • If the question mentions "pod-to-pod communication" → the attacker is doing lateral movement → NetworkPolicy is your answer.
  • If the question mentions "shell access" or "kubectl exec" → the attacker is executing commands → Falco rules + audit logging is your answer.
  • If the question mentions "secrets visible" or "database credentials" → the attacker found plaintext secrets → encryption at rest + Vault is your answer.
  • Every CKS task maps to a specific attack stage. Know the kill chain, and you'll know which tool to deploy.

2.1 How Kubernetes Gets Attacked — The Attack Surface

The Kubernetes attack surface is massive. Unlike a traditional server with one entry point (SSH), a K8s cluster has the API server, the kubelet on every node, the etcd database, the container runtime, the network overlay, and hundreds of pods — each a potential entry point. Here are the seven most common attack vectors, ranked by real-world frequency:

The 7 Most Common Kubernetes Attack Vectors

1️⃣
Exposed API Server (No Authentication)

The API server listens on port 6443. If --anonymous-auth=true (the default!), anyone who can reach that port has full cluster access. This is how Tesla was breached in 2018. Attackers scan the internet for open K8s API ports using Shodan and Masscan. Fix: Chapter 8.

2️⃣
Misconfigured RBAC — Over-Permission

Developers get cluster-admin "to make things easier." ServiceAccounts default to full namespace access. A single compromised credential gives attackers the keys to the kingdom. Fix: Chapter 9.

3️⃣
Vulnerable Container Images — Known CVEs

The average container image contains 100+ known vulnerabilities. If you deploy python:3.9 without scanning, you're shipping CVEs directly into production. Attackers exploit known CVEs in frameworks like Django, Flask, or even the base OS packages. Fix: Chapter 23.

4️⃣
Secrets in Plaintext — Environment Variables & Git

Database passwords in configmap.yaml. API keys in .env files committed to Git. ServiceAccount tokens mounted in every pod by default. A single kubectl describe pod or a Git history search reveals everything. Fix: Chapters 10, 19, 20.

5️⃣
Privilege Escalation — Root Containers

Containers run as root by default. If an attacker exploits any application vulnerability, they immediately have root inside the container. From there: container escape, node compromise, cluster takeover. Fix: Chapters 14, 15, 18.

6️⃣
Lateral Movement — Flat Network

No NetworkPolicies = every pod can reach every other pod on every port. One compromised pod gives attackers access to your database, your cache, your message queue, and every other service in the cluster. Fix: Chapter 6.

7️⃣
Supply Chain — Malicious Images

Pulling images from docker.io/random-user/app without verification. No image signing. No registry allowlist. Attackers publish typosquatted images with backdoors. Fix: Chapters 24, 26, 27.

Evolution of Kubernetes Attack Sophistication (2018–2025)

Kubernetes attacks have not stayed static. They have evolved through four distinct eras, each building on the lessons of the previous one. Understanding this progression is critical because every attack pattern from every era still works today on unhardened clusters. Attackers don't abandon old techniques — they layer new ones on top. A cluster that would have been breached in 2018 is still breachable today if you haven't applied the fixes.

The timeline below maps each era to a specific breach, the new attack surface that emerged, and the CKS domain that addresses it. Notice how the attacks grow more sophisticated — from simple port scanning to supply chain subversion to AI-assisted automation — yet the root cause remains the same: security features that are available but not enabled.

🚗
2018
Exposed Dashboards

Tesla breach. Attackers scanned for open dashboards and APIs. No auth = instant admin. Simple internet-wide scans.

❌ No auth defaults
☁️
2019
Cloud Metadata SSRF

Capital One breach. Attackers exploited pod→metadata API paths to steal IAM roles. Cloud + K8s attack surface emerged.

❌ Metadata exposed
🔗
2020
Supply Chain Compromise

SolarWinds. Attackers targeted build pipelines. Signed malware distributed as trusted updates to 18,000 organizations.

❌ Build trust broken
🧠
2022+
AI-Assisted Recon

Attackers use LLMs to analyze K8s configurations, generate exploits, and automate lateral movement. Defense must be automated too.

⚠️ Auto-defense needed

Era 1 (2018) — Exposed Dashboards: The simplest attack. Kubernetes Dashboard shipped with --enable-skip-login and cluster-admin privileges by default in many distributions. Attackers used Shodan (the "Google for internet-connected devices") to find port 6443 or 8001, and walked straight in. No exploit needed — just a browser. The Tesla breach proved that Fortune 500 companies were running clusters with zero authentication. CKS response: Chapters 5 (Dashboard auth), 8 (API server hardening), and 9 (RBAC) directly address this era.

Era 2 (2019) — Cloud Metadata SSRF: As organizations moved Kubernetes to the cloud, a new attack surface emerged: the cloud provider's metadata API at 169.254.169.254. Every pod on every EC2 node can reach this IP by default. If any pod has a Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability, the attacker can steal the IAM role credentials attached to the underlying node. This is not a Kubernetes vulnerability — it's an architectural blind spot where cloud and container meet. Capital One's $270 million breach was this exact pattern. CKS response: Chapters 13 (metadata concealment), 16 (IAM minimization), and 6 (NetworkPolicy egress) close this gap.

Era 3 (2020) — Supply Chain Compromise: Attackers realized they didn't need to breach running clusters — they could compromise the software before it ever reached the cluster. By infiltrating build pipelines (CI/CD systems, source repositories, base image registries), attackers injected malicious code that was then signed and distributed as trusted software. SolarWinds demonstrated that even digitally signed software from a reputable vendor could be trojanized if the build system itself was compromised. CKS response: Chapters 25 (static analysis), 26 (cosign/image signing with key management), and 27 (SBOM + SLSA provenance) create a verifiable chain of trust from source to runtime.

Era 4 (2022+) — AI-Assisted Attacks: The latest evolution. Attackers now use large language models to analyze Kubernetes manifests for misconfigurations, generate context-aware exploit code, and plan multi-stage lateral movement campaigns automatically. A single misconfigured RBAC rule that might have taken a human attacker weeks to find can now be identified by an LLM in seconds. The defense must now be equally automated: policy-as-code (OPA/Gatekeeper), automated vulnerability scanning (Trivy), and runtime anomaly detection (Falco) are no longer optional — they are baseline requirements. CKS response: Chapters 24 (admission control), 23 (image scanning), 29 (Falco), and 32 (continuous compliance) build the automated defense layer.

Attack Vector Likelihood × Impact — Risk Heat Map

Not all attack vectors are equally dangerous. The risk heat map below ranks each vector by exploitability — how easy it is for an attacker to succeed — expressed as a percentage. These percentages are drawn from real-world penetration testing data and incident response reports across thousands of Kubernetes clusters. Think of each bar as answering the question: "If I deploy anihpj with default K8s settings, what are the odds an attacker succeeds at this vector?"

The pattern is unmistakable: the highest-percentage vectors are the ones that require zero exploit development. Exposed API servers and root containers are not vulnerabilities — they are defaults. An attacker does not need to find a bug; they just need to find your cluster. The lower-percentage vectors (unsigned images, supply chain) require more sophistication, but their impact is potentially far greater because they can affect thousands of organizations simultaneously — as SolarWinds proved.

How to read this chart: A 95% bar means that in 95 out of 100 unhardened clusters, this attack vector would succeed. The color intensity (red for critical/high, orange for medium) corresponds to the combined risk score — likelihood multiplied by potential business impact. As you progress through this guide, every CKS chapter you complete will drive these percentages down toward zero. By the end, your anihpj cluster should have every bar below 20%.

🔴 Exposed API Server / Dashboard (Critical) 95% exploitable — internet-scanable
🔴 Root Containers — Privilege Escalation (Critical) 90% — default container config
🟡 Flat Network — Lateral Movement (High) 85% — no NetworkPolicy by default
🟡 Plaintext Secrets in etcd (High) 80% — etcd stores secrets unencrypted
🟡 Overly Broad RBAC (High) 75% — cluster-admin is common
🟠 Unscanned Images with CVEs (Medium) 65% — average image has 100+ CVEs
🟠 Unsigned Images / Supply Chain (Medium) 55% — most orgs don't sign images
