Chapter 6: Network Policies — Zero-Trust Pod Networking

By default, every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can reach every other pod on every port. There are no firewalls between pods. There are no network segments between namespaces. One compromised pod — one vulnerable dependency in the anihpj Django app — and the attacker has unrestricted network access to your PostgreSQL database, your Redis cache, your monitoring stack, and every other pod in the cluster. NetworkPolicies are the ONLY built-in Kubernetes mechanism to restrict pod-to-pod traffic. Without them, you have a flat network. With them, you can implement zero-trust networking: default-deny everything, then explicitly allow only the connections your application actually needs. This chapter teaches you every NetworkPolicy pattern you need for the CKS exam — and for production.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🌐 Networking 🚫 Zero Trust

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the flat network problem — why every pod can reach every other pod by default
  • ✅ Master NetworkPolicy YAML: podSelector, policyTypes, ingress/egress rules, namespaceSelector, ipBlock
  • ✅ Memorize 7 essential NetworkPolicy patterns — default-deny, allow specific port, allow namespace, allow CIDR, allow DNS
  • ✅ Test NetworkPolicies with busybox probes — verify allowed traffic flows and blocked traffic times out
  • ✅ Implement a complete zero-trust NetworkPolicy set for the anihpj/jobpost application
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulns 20% Cluster Setup 15%
🧠 The NetworkPolicy Exam Pattern

CKS NetworkPolicy questions follow a consistent pattern: (1) You are given a namespace with running pods. (2) You are told which pods should be able to communicate. (3) You must write and apply NetworkPolicies that achieve ONLY the allowed communication — everything else must be blocked. The trap: many candidates write allow rules but forget to also implement default-deny. Without default-deny, your allow rules are meaningless — traffic still flows freely on every other port and to every other pod. Always start with default-deny, then add allow rules.

6.1 The Default: All Pods Can Talk to All Pods

Kubernetes was designed with a flat network model: every pod gets a unique, cluster-routable IP address, and every pod can reach every other pod without NAT. This was a deliberate design choice to simplify pod-to-pod communication — no port mapping, no manual routing, no network segmentation. But it comes with a devastating security implication: there are zero network barriers between pods. One compromised pod means lateral movement to every other pod in the cluster.

🔴 The Flat Network Is the Default — Not a Bug

Kubernetes does not ship with any NetworkPolicies. There is no default-deny rule. There is no namespace isolation. Every pod, in every namespace, can initiate a TCP connection to every other pod, on every port. This is not a misconfiguration — it is the intended default. The CKS exam tests whether you know to override this default with explicit NetworkPolicies.

Flat Network vs Zero Trust — Side by Side

❌ Flat Network (Default — No NetworkPolicies)
  • anihpj pod → postgres pod ✅
  • anihpj pod → redis pod ✅
  • postgres pod → anihpj pod ✅ (reverse!)
  • monitoring pod → any pod ✅
  • pod in other namespace → postgres ✅
  • attacker pod → ANY pod, ANY port ✅

RESULT: One compromised pod = access to EVERY pod in the cluster.

✅ Zero Trust (With NetworkPolicies)
  • anihpj pod → postgres:5432 ✅
  • ingress → anihpj:8000 ✅
  • ALL pods → DNS:53 ✅
  • postgres pod → anihpj pod ❌
  • attacker pod → postgres ❌
  • pod in other namespace → anything ❌

RESULT: Compromised pod trapped in its own network bubble. Lateral movement blocked.

Why Kubernetes Chose a Flat Network — The Design Philosophy

The flat network is not an oversight — it is a deliberate architectural choice rooted in Kubernetes' origin at Google. The design principle is: every pod should be able to reach every other pod without NAT, without port mapping, and without manual route configuration. This simplifies development — a pod in namespace A can call a service in namespace B using its cluster DNS name, and it just works. The trade-off — security — was deferred to NetworkPolicies. The CKS exam tests whether you understand that this trade-off exists and that it is YOUR responsibility to apply the security layer that Kubernetes intentionally left open.

How Attackers Exploit the Flat Network — Lateral Movement in Practice

Lateral Movement Without NetworkPolicies — The Attacker's Playbook
  ATTACKER compromises anihpj pod via CVE in Pillow library
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ id
  uid=0(root)  ← Container runs as root (default)

  STEP 1: DISCOVERY — What else is on this network?
  $ env | grep _SERVICE_HOST          # K8s injects service env vars
  POSTGRES_SERVICE_HOST=10.96.45.12   ← Found postgres!
  REDIS_SERVICE_HOST=10.96.78.34      ← Found redis!

  STEP 2: DATABASE ACCESS
  $ apt-get install -y postgresql-client
  $ psql -h $POSTGRES_SERVICE_HOST -U anihpj_user -d jobpost
  → 45,000 user emails extracted. Zero network barriers.

  STEP 3: CACHE POISONING
  $ redis-cli -h $REDIS_SERVICE_HOST
  redis> KEYS *
  → All session tokens. All cached data available.

  STEP 4: CROSS-NAMESPACE ESCALATION
  $ for ip in 10.96.0.{1..254}; do curl -s --connect-timeout 1 http://$ip:9090; done
  → Found Prometheus and Elasticsearch in other namespaces.

  RESULT: One pod → database → cache → monitoring stack → complete cluster visibility.
  All because there were ZERO NetworkPolicies.

6.2 NetworkPolicy Fundamentals

A NetworkPolicy is a namespaced Kubernetes resource that defines which network traffic is allowed to and from pods. It uses label selectors to identify target pods and rules to specify allowed traffic sources, destinations, and ports. Crucially, NetworkPolicies are additive — if multiple policies select the same pod, the effective rule set is the union of all allows. And once a pod is selected by ANY NetworkPolicy, all traffic is denied except what is explicitly allowed.

📖 CNI Dependency — Your CNI Plugin MUST Support NetworkPolicy

NetworkPolicy resources are enforced by the CNI plugin, not by the API server. If your CNI does not support NetworkPolicy (Flannel, Kindnet), your policies will be silently ignored — you can apply them, kubectl will show them, but they will have ZERO effect on actual traffic. Always verify your CNI: Calico and Cilium fully support NetworkPolicy. Weave Net supports it. Flannel does not. On the CKS exam, the cluster has a compatible CNI pre-configured — you do not need to install one.

NetworkPolicy Anatomy — Annotated Field by Field

Every field of a NetworkPolicy, explained
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: postgres-netpol
    namespace: anihpj-prod              # NetworkPolicy is NAMESPACED
  spec:
    podSelector:                         # WHICH PODS this policy applies to
      matchLabels:
        app: postgres                    # Selects pods with label app=postgres
    policyTypes:                         # WHAT DIRECTION of traffic
    - Ingress                            # Incoming traffic to the selected pods
    - Egress                             # Outgoing traffic FROM the selected pods
    ingress:                             # RULES for incoming traffic
    - from:                              # Traffic FROM which sources?
      - podSelector:                     # FROM pods with specific labels
          matchLabels:
            app: anihpj                  # Only pods labeled app=anihpj
      - namespaceSelector:              # FROM pods in specific namespaces
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: anihpj-prod
      - ipBlock:                        # FROM specific IP ranges
          cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
          except:                        # Exclude a subset
          - 10.0.0.0/24
      ports:                             # On WHICH ports?
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 5432                       # Only PostgreSQL port
    egress:                              # RULES for outgoing traffic
    - to:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            k8s-app: kube-dns            # Allow DNS queries
      ports:
      - protocol: UDP
        port: 53

  ⚠️  Empty ingress: [] = DENY ALL incoming traffic
  ⚠️  Empty egress: []  = DENY ALL outgoing traffic
  ⚠️  Missing policyTypes = only Ingress is affected (Egress stays open!)

CNI Support for NetworkPolicy — Choose the Right Plugin

CNI PluginNetworkPolicy SupporteBPFFQDN EgressProduction Ready
Calico✅ Full✅✅ Yes✅ Yes
Cilium✅ Full✅✅ Yes✅ Yes
Weave Net✅ Full❌❌ No✅ Yes
Flannel❌ None❌❌ No⚠️ No NetPol support
Kindnet❌ None❌❌ No⚠️ Testing only

⚠️ If your cluster uses Flannel or Kindnet: NetworkPolicy objects are created and visible via kubectl, but they are COMPLETELY IGNORED at the network level. All traffic still flows freely.

NetworkPolicy Decision Flowchart — How K8s Decides to Allow or Block

The logic every CNI plugin follows for NetworkPolicy enforcement
  PACKET arrives at pod's network interface
       │
       ▼
  Q1: Is there ANY NetworkPolicy selecting this pod?
       ├── NO  ──▶ ✅ ALLOW (no policies = all traffic allowed)
       └── YES ──▶ Continue to Q2
                        │
                        ▼
  Q2: Is this packet EXPLICITLY allowed by at least ONE policy?
       ├── YES ──▶ ✅ ALLOW
       └── NO  ──▶ ❌ DENY  (implicit deny — the default when policies exist)

  ⚠️  CRITICAL RULE: NetworkPolicies are ADDITIVE (union of all allows).
      Policy A allows port 80 + Policy B allows port 443 = pod gets BOTH.
      No policy can override or subtract from another policy's allow rule.

  ⚠️  TRAP: Once a pod is selected by ANY NetworkPolicy, ALL traffic is
      DENIED by default except what is explicitly allowed by some policy.
      Pod with NO policies = wide open. Pod with ONE policy = locked down.

How CNI Plugins Enforce NetworkPolicies — iptables vs eBPF

iptables-based (Calico, Weave)

Every NetworkPolicy rule is translated into iptables rules. Each allow rule becomes an ACCEPT entry; implicit deny becomes a DROP. Battle-tested but scales poorly — thousands of pods mean thousands of iptables rules, slowing packet processing.

Debug: iptables -L -n -v | grep cali shows actual Calico rules.

eBPF-based (Cilium)

Uses eBPF programs attached before iptables. Each policy becomes an O(1) eBPF map lookup, scaling to tens of thousands of pods with no degradation. Also supports FQDN-based egress (e.g., "allow egress to *.github.com").

Debug: cilium policy get and cilium monitor for real-time decisions.

The Additive Rule Behavior — Policies Cannot "Undo" Each Other

NetworkPolicies are purely additive — they can only ALLOW, never DENY. If Policy A allows monitoring pods to reach postgres, and Policy B allows anihpj pods to reach postgres, the effective rule is the UNION: both can reach postgres. You cannot create Policy C to "block monitoring from postgres" — NetworkPolicies have no DENY rules. To remove access, you must DELETE the policy that granted it.

The policyTypes Trap — CKS Exam Pitfall

😰 When policyTypes is omitted, it defaults to [Ingress] — your egress rules are silently IGNORED.

You create a policy with egress rules but forget policyTypes. The policy only affects ingress. Your egress rules do nothing — and you get no error message. Always explicitly set policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] when you need both directions.

6.3 Common NetworkPolicy Patterns You Must Know

The CKS exam tests a specific set of NetworkPolicy patterns. You do not need to invent new ones — you need to recognize which pattern the question is asking for and apply it correctly. Here are the 7 essential patterns, with ready-to-use YAML and the exam scenario each one solves:

Pattern 1: Default-Deny All Ingress

Blocks ALL incoming traffic to every pod in the namespace
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: default-deny-ingress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}          # {} = select ALL pods in this namespace
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    # No ingress rules specified → DENY ALL incoming traffic

Pattern 2: Default-Deny All Egress

Blocks ALL outgoing traffic from every pod — use with caution (DNS will break!)
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: default-deny-egress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes:
    - Egress
    # No egress rules → DENY ALL outgoing. DNS breaks. Always add Pattern 7!

Pattern 3: Allow Specific Pod to Reach a Specific Port (Database Access)

Allow anihpj pods → postgres on port 5432. Nothing else can reach postgres.
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-anihpj-to-postgres
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: postgres            # This policy PROTECTS postgres pods
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: anihpj          # Only FROM anihpj pods
      ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 5432               # Only ON postgres port

Pattern 4: Allow Traffic Within Same Namespace

All pods in the namespace can talk to each other — but nothing from outside
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-same-namespace
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - podSelector: {}         # From ANY pod in this namespace

Pattern 5: Allow Traffic from a Specific Namespace

Allow ingress-controller in ingress-nginx namespace → anihpj pods
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-from-ingress-ns
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx

Pattern 6: Allow Specific CIDR Block (External IPs)

Allow traffic from a specific IP range — e.g., office VPN subnet
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-from-office-vpn
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - ipBlock:
          cidr: 10.100.0.0/16    # Office VPN subnet
      ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 8000

Pattern 7: Allow DNS Egress (Critical — DNS Breaks Without This)

Allow all pods to reach CoreDNS on UDP 53. Always pair with default-deny-egress.
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-dns-egress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}              # All pods need DNS
    policyTypes:
    - Egress
    egress:
    - to:
      - namespaceSelector:       # CoreDNS runs in kube-system
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
        podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            k8s-app: kube-dns    # The CoreDNS pods
      ports:
      - protocol: UDP
        port: 53                 # DNS port
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 53                 # DNS over TCP (for large responses)

Essential Patterns — Quick Reference Table

PatternUse CaseExam Frequency
Default deny all ingressIsolate a namespaceVery High
Default deny all egressPrevent data exfiltrationHigh
Allow same namespaceTeam isolationHigh
Allow specific port to podDatabase access controlVery High
Allow DNS egress (53/UDP+TCP)Apps need name resolutionHigh
Allow namespaceSelectorCross-namespace allowed pathsHigh
Allow specific CIDR (ingress)External trusted IPs onlyMedium

Pattern Combinations — Building Real-World Policies

The 7 patterns are building blocks. Real clusters combine them. The most common CKS task: Default-Deny Ingress (blocks all incoming) + Allow App→DB on specific port (creates one exception). Also common: Default-Deny Egress + Allow DNS (UDP+TCP 53) — without DNS, pods cannot resolve names and health checks fail. Always create DNS allow rules FIRST, then apply default-deny-egress to avoid breaking your pods during configuration.

Cluster-Wide Default-Deny — One-Liner for All Namespaces

Apply default-deny to every namespace (skip kube-system and ingress)
  $ for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o name | grep -v -E 'kube-system|ingress-nginx'); do
      kubectl -n ${ns##*/} apply -f - <<EOF
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
      kind: NetworkPolicy
      metadata:
        name: default-deny-ingress
        namespace: ${ns##*/}
      spec:
        podSelector: {}
        policyTypes: [Ingress]
  EOF
    done
  ⚠️  Always exclude kube-system and ingress namespaces — they need cross-ns traffic.

6.4 Testing and Verifying NetworkPolicy — Does It Actually Work?

NetworkPolicies are silent when they work correctly — blocked traffic simply times out with no error message. This makes testing essential. The standard approach is to use a busybox test pod to probe connections and verify which ones succeed (allowed) and which ones timeout (blocked).

The NetworkPolicy Testing Workflow

Using busybox to verify NetworkPolicy enforcement
  # Step 1: Create a test pod in the SAME namespace
  $ kubectl run test-same --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n anihpj-prod -- sh

  # Step 2: Test ALLOWED connections (should succeed)
  / # wget -q -O- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-service:8000/jobs/
  → Returns HTML (allowed by Pattern 3)

  / # nc -zv postgres-service 5432
  → Connection to postgres-service 5432 succeeded! (allowed by Pattern 3)

  # Step 3: Test BLOCKED connections (should timeout)
  / # wget -q -O- --timeout=3 http://monitoring-service:9090/metrics
  → wget: download timed out (BLOCKED by default-deny)

  # Step 4: Create a test pod in a DIFFERENT namespace
  $ kubectl run test-other --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n default -- sh

  # Step 5: Test cross-namespace access (should be BLOCKED)
  / # wget -q -O- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-service.anihpj-prod:8000/
  → wget: download timed out (BLOCKED — cross-namespace denied)

anihpj Connectivity Matrix — Expected Results

FROM (source)TO (destination)PORTExpected Result
ingress-nginxanihpj pod8000✅ ALLOWED
anihpj podpostgres pod5432✅ ALLOWED
anihpj podredis pod6379✅ ALLOWED
ALL podskube-dns (DNS)53✅ ALLOWED
monitoring podALL pods9090✅ ALLOWED
postgres podanihpj pod8000❌ BLOCKED
anihpj podother namespaceANY❌ BLOCKED
attacker-podpostgres pod5432❌ BLOCKED
anihpj podinternet IPsANY❌ BLOCKED
💡 The 3-Second Timeout Rule

When testing NetworkPolicies, use --timeout=3 on wget or -w 3 on nc. Blocked connections do not get a "Connection Refused" — they hang until the TCP SYN timeout (typically 30-75 seconds). The --timeout flag saves you from waiting. On the exam, if a connection takes more than 3 seconds, it is blocked. Move on.

Debugging When NetworkPolicies Do Not Work — Common Failure Modes

🔴 Failure 1: Policy applied but ALL traffic still flows

Root Cause: CNI does not support NetworkPolicy (Flannel), OR podSelector does not match any pods. If no pods are selected, the policy has zero effect. Diagnose: kubectl get pods -n <ns> --show-labels → verify labels match podSelector exactly (case-sensitive).

🟡 Failure 2: Egress rules ignored

Root Cause: policyTypes omitted — defaults to [Ingress]. Egress rules silently ignored. Diagnose: kubectl get netpol <name> -o yaml | grep policyTypes — must explicitly list Egress.

🔴 Failure 3: DNS works but HTTP fails

Root Cause: You allowed UDP 53 (DNS) but your app needs TCP 53 for large DNS responses, OR your allow rule has the wrong port/protocol. Diagnose: kubectl exec <pod> -- nc -zv <svc> <port> — verify TCP connectivity.

6.5 Securing anihpj with NetworkPolicies — Full Implementation

Let's apply everything to the anihpj/jobpost application. We need 6 NetworkPolicies to achieve zero-trust networking while keeping the application functional:

anihpj Network Traffic Map — Visual Representation

All allowed and blocked traffic flows for anihpj
                     🌐 INTERNET
                          │
                          │ HTTPS :443 (Ingress TLS)
                          ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   🚪 INGRESS CONTROLLER                       │
  │                   (only exposed entry point)                  │
  └────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                               │ HTTP :8000 (Policy 3)
                               ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   📦 anihpj DEPLOYMENT                       │
  │                   app: anihpj  |  port: 8000                  │
  │                   SecurityContext: non-root, Seccomp, AppArmor│
  └────┬─────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
       │ TCP :5432 (Policy 2)               │ TCP :6379 (Policy 4)
       ▼                                     ▼
  ┌──────────────┐                   ┌──────────────┐
  │ 🗄️  postgres │                   │ ⚡ Redis     │
  │ app:postgres │                   │ app: redis   │
  │ port: 5432   │                   │ port: 6379   │
  └──────────────┘                   └──────────────┘

  📊 MONITORING POD (Policy 6): can scrape ALL pods on :9090
  🔍 DNS (Policy 5): ALL pods can reach kube-dns on port 53/UDP+TCP

  ❌ BLOCKED PATHS (default-deny Policy 1):
     • internet → anihpj pod DIRECT (must go through ingress)
     • postgres → anihpj (reverse connection blocked)
     • anihpj → internet (egress blocked)
     • any pod → any pod in other namespaces
     • attacker-pod → ANY resource in anihpj namespace

The 6 Policies for anihpj Zero-Trust Networking

1️⃣
Policy 1: Default-Deny All Ingress in anihpj-prod

Blocks ALL incoming traffic to every pod. Individual allow rules (Policies 2-6) create exceptions for specific flows. Without this policy, pods accept connections from anywhere.

2️⃣
Policy 2: Allow anihpj → PostgreSQL (TCP 5432)

podSelector: app=postgres. ingress from podSelector: app=anihpj on port 5432. All other pods — including attacker pods — cannot reach the database.

3️⃣
Policy 3: Allow Ingress Controller → anihpj (TCP 8000)

podSelector: app=anihpj. ingress from namespaceSelector: ingress-nginx on port 8000. Only the ingress controller can reach the Django app — direct internet access is blocked.

4️⃣
Policy 4: Allow anihpj → Redis (TCP 6379)

podSelector: app=redis. ingress from podSelector: app=anihpj on port 6379. Django can cache job listings. No other pod can access the cache.

5️⃣
Policy 5: Allow ALL Pods → DNS (UDP+TCP 53)

podSelector: {}. egress to namespaceSelector: kube-system, podSelector: k8s-app=kube-dns on port 53. CRITICAL: without this, name resolution fails and your app breaks.

6️⃣
Policy 6: Allow Monitoring → ALL Pods (TCP 9090)

podSelector: {}. ingress from podSelector: app=monitoring on port 9090. Prometheus can scrape metrics from every pod. No other pod can access the metrics endpoint.

6.6 Restricting Cluster-Level Access — Protecting the API Server

The CKS curriculum requires Network security policies to restrict cluster level access. This means protecting the Kubernetes API server from unauthorized pod communication. Use NetworkPolicy egress rules + RBAC + disabled SA token automount for defense-in-depth.

YAML — Egress Policy Restricting Pod→API Server Access
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-api-access
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.96.0.1/32  # API server ClusterIP
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
💡 CKS Exam: Cluster-Level Access

Restrict which pods reach the API server (NetworkPolicy egress) + restrict what they can do (RBAC) + remove their token (automountServiceAccountToken: false) = complete API isolation.

6.7 NetworkPolicy Pattern Catalog — Exam-Ready Templates

These are the six NetworkPolicy patterns that cover 90% of CKS exam scenarios. Each template is copy-paste ready with only namespace names and labels to customize:

🚫
Deny All Ingress

podSelector: {}
policyTypes: [Ingress]
# No ingress rules

Use: Starting point. Block everything, then add allows.

✅
Allow from Namespace

ingress: [{from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {tier: frontend}}}]}]

Use: Allow entire namespace. Label namespace first.

🎯
Allow from Specific Pod

ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: gateway}}}]}]

Use: Allow single pod. Combine with namespaceSelector for cross-ns.

🔌
Allow Only Port

ingress: [{ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]}]

Use: Restrict to specific port. Database:5432, API:8080.

📡
DNS Egress

egress: [{to: [{namespaceSelector:{}, podSelector:{k8s-app: kube-dns}}], ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]}]

Use: Required with deny-all egress. Always add DNS.

🌐
API Server Egress

egress: [{to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 10.96.0.1/32}}], ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 443}]}]

Use: Allow pods to reach API server. Combine with DNS.

📊 Chapter 6 Visual Summary — Network Policies

🌐 Flat Network Default Every pod can reach every other pod. No NetworkPolicies = no barriers.
📋 7 Essential Patterns Default-deny ingress/egress, allow port, allow namespace, allow CIDR, allow DNS
🧪 Testing with busybox wget/nc probes with --timeout=3. Blocked traffic times out — no error message.
🛡️ 6 anihpj Policies Default-deny + DB + Ingress + Redis + DNS + Monitoring = zero-trust anihpj
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

NetworkPolicy questions are the most common CKS tasks after RBAC. The exam pattern is always: (1) Create default-deny first, (2) Add specific allow rules for required communication, (3) Test with busybox, (4) Remember DNS — if you add egress deny, you MUST add a DNS allow rule or your pods will break silently. Always start with default-deny. Never forget DNS.

How NetworkPolicy Is Enforced — The CNI Plugin Is the Firewall Engine

NetworkPolicy YAML is not enforced by Kubernetes itself. It is enforced by your CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin — Calico, Cilium, Weave, or another CNI that supports NetworkPolicy. This is the most important concept to understand because if your CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy, your policies are silently ignored — you write YAML, kubectl accepts it, but nothing is actually enforced:

NetworkPolicy Enforcement Architecture — From YAML to iptables/eBPF
  kubectl apply -f networkpolicy.yaml
  │
  ▼
  API SERVER: Validates the NetworkPolicy object → stores it in etcd.
  │  (This is ALL Kubernetes does. It does NOT enforce the policy.)
  │
  ▼
  CNI PLUGIN (e.g., Calico): Watches for NetworkPolicy objects via the K8s API.
  │
  │  CALICO'S ENFORCEMENT PATH:
  │  ───────────────────────────
  │  1. Calico controller detects new/modified NetworkPolicy.
  │  2. Translates the policy's podSelector + ingress/egress rules into
  │     iptables rules (or eBPF programs for Cilium).
  │  3. Programs these rules into EVERY node where matching pods run.
  │  4. iptables checks EVERY packet entering or leaving matching pods:
  │     • Source IP matches allowed CIDR? → ALLOW
  │     • Source pod label matches allowed podSelector? → ALLOW
  │     • Neither → DROP (silently — no ICMP response)
  │
  │  WHAT HAPPENS WITH A CNI THAT DOESN'T SUPPORT NETWORKPOLICY:
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │  • Flannel (without NetworkPolicy extension): IGNORES the policy entirely.
  │  • All pods can still communicate. Your YAML did nothing.
  │  • kubectl describe networkpolicy shows the policy as "active" — but
  │    there is NO enforcement. This is a silent failure.
  │
  │  CNI PLUGIN NETWORKPOLICY SUPPORT:
  │  ───────────────────────────────────
  │  ✅ Calico      — Full support (iptables or eBPF)
  │  ✅ Cilium      — Full support (eBPF — most advanced)
  │  ✅ Weave Net   — Full support
  │  ⚠️  Flannel     — Only with Calico network policy engine
  │  ⚠️  Azure CNI   — Supports NetworkPolicy (Azure Network Policy Manager)
  │  ⚠️  AWS VPC CNI — Requires Calico for NetworkPolicy (AWS doesn't natively enforce)
  │  ❌ Docker bridge — NO support (development only, never production)
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CKS EXAM REALITY:
  ─────────────────
  The CKS exam cluster uses a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (usually Calico
  or Cilium). You do NOT need to install a CNI. Just write the YAML and test.
  But in real clusters, ALWAYS VERIFY your CNI supports NetworkPolicy before
  relying on it. Check: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave'

The DNS Problem — Why Egress Deny Breaks Your Pods

This is the single most common NetworkPolicy mistake — and the one that CKS exam candidates trip on most. When you create a default-deny egress policy, your pods lose the ability to resolve DNS names. Why? Because DNS queries go to CoreDNS, which runs as a pod in kube-system. If your default-deny egress policy doesn't explicitly allow DNS, your pod can't even look up postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Here's the exact mechanic:

What Happens Without a DNS Egress Rule — The Silent Failure
  POD: anihpj-django-7f8c9-abcde (namespace: anihpj)
  │
  │  Application tries to connect: postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:5432
  │
  ▼
  STEP 1: The application calls getaddrinfo("postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local")
  │  This triggers a DNS query.
  │
  ▼
  STEP 2: The container's /etc/resolv.conf points to CoreDNS:
  │  nameserver 10.96.0.10  (CoreDNS ClusterIP)
  │
  ▼
  STEP 3: The container sends a UDP packet to 10.96.0.10:53
  │  (DNS is UDP by default; falls back to TCP for large responses)
  │
  ▼
  STEP 4: NETWORKPOLICY CHECK — Is this egress allowed?
  │
  │  ┌─ NO DNS EGRESS RULE ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  │  • Policy says: egress to podSelector: app=postgres on 5432   │
  │  │  • But the DNS query is to podSelector: k8s-app=kube-dns on 53│
  │  │  • This does NOT match the postgres rule → DROP                │
  │  │  • DNS query NEVER reaches CoreDNS. No response.               │
  │  │  • Application hangs waiting for DNS resolution.               │
  │  │  • Eventually times out (30+ seconds). App appears broken.     │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  │  ┌─ WITH DNS EGRESS RULE ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  │  • Policy ALSO has: egress to podSelector: k8s-app=kube-dns   │
  │  │    on port 53 (UDP + TCP)                                     │
  │  │  • DNS query MATCHES → ALLOWED                                 │
  │  │  • CoreDNS responds with: postgres.anihpj.svc = 10.96.0.45    │
  │  │  • Application connects to 10.96.0.45:5432 → matches postgres │
  │  │    rule → ALLOWED → connection established ✅                  │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  THE DNS EGRESS RULE YOU MUST ADD:
  ─────────────────────────────────
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
🔧 Under the Hood — How NetworkPolicy Is Enforced: From YAML Rules to iptables/eBPF Kernel-Level Packet Filtering
🗺️ NetworkPolicy Enforcement — CNI Plugin → Kernel Rules → Packet Drop
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   NETWORK POLICY ENFORCEMENT PATH                                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │   1. YOU APPLY NetworkPolicy                                               │
  │      kubectl apply -f default-deny-all.yaml                               │
  │      → Stored in etcd as a Networking API object                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │   2. CNI PLUGIN WATCHES FOR NETWORKPOLICY CHANGES                         │
  │      Calico: calico-kube-controllers watches NetworkPolicy API            │
  │      Cilium: cilium-operator watches + programs eBPF maps                │
  │      Flannel: IGNORES NetworkPolicy — NO ENFORCEMENT!                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │   3. CNI TRANSLATES RULES TO KERNEL-LEVEL FILTERS                         │
  │      Calico → Programs iptables rules in each pod's network namespace    │
  │      Cilium → Programs eBPF programs attached to pod's veth interface    │
  │                                                                           │
  │   4. PACKET ARRIVES AT POD INTERFACE                                       │
  │      → Kernel checks iptables/eBPF filter                                 │
  │      → Matches against pod labels, namespace labels, IP blocks           │
  │      → ALLOW or DROP                                                      │
  │                                                                           │
  │   🔑 NetworkPolicy without a supporting CNI = YAML stored in etcd but    │
  │      NOTHING enforces it. Always verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system  │
  │      | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave'                                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 6 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Create a NetworkPolicy that blocks ALL ingress and egress traffic in the "secure-ns" namespace. Write the complete YAML.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: secure-ns
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
# No ingress or egress rules = DENY ALL
Explanation

An empty podSelector: {} selects ALL pods in the namespace. When you declare policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] but provide NO rules, the default behavior is DENY ALL. This is the foundation of zero-trust networking: start with everything blocked, then add explicit allow rules. On the CKS exam, default-deny NetworkPolicy is the starting point for almost every network isolation task.

Q2
After applying default-deny-all, pods can't resolve DNS. Write the NetworkPolicy that fixes this WITHOUT opening any other traffic.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: secure-ns
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
Explanation

This is the most common follow-up task after applying default-deny: pods need DNS to function. The selectors use AND logic — BOTH namespaceSelector AND podSelector must match. DNS uses UDP port 53 (sometimes TCP 53 for large responses). On the exam, if you see "pods can't connect after applying NetworkPolicy," DNS is the #1 culprit. Always add a DNS allow rule immediately after default-deny.

Q3
You've applied a NetworkPolicy but traffic still flows. What's the most likely cause and how do you verify it?
Show Answer
Answer

Your CNI plugin doesn't support NetworkPolicy (most commonly Flannel). Verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave'. If no results, you're likely running Flannel which ignores NetworkPolicy. Fix: migrate to Calico or Cilium. Test connectivity: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- wget -qO- --timeout=5 <target-url>

Explanation

NetworkPolicy is an API resource, but enforcement is done by the CNI plugin. Flannel has NO NetworkPolicy support — it silently ignores all NetworkPolicy resources. Calico, Cilium, and Weave Net all support it. On the CKS exam, if NetworkPolicy doesn't work, check the CNI first. Also check: are you in the right namespace? Does the podSelector actually match your pods? Use kubectl describe networkpolicy to see which pods are selected.

Q4
Write a NetworkPolicy that allows pods with label "app: frontend" to receive traffic ONLY from pods with label "app: api-gateway" on port 8080.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-gateway
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: api-gateway
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
Explanation

The podSelector in spec selects which pods this policy APPLIES TO (the target). The podSelector inside ingress.from selects which pods are ALLOWED to send traffic. This is a common point of confusion. This policy says: "pods labeled app=frontend can ONLY receive TCP/8080 traffic from pods labeled app=api-gateway." All other traffic (even from the same namespace) is denied to these pods.

Q5
You need to block pods in namespace "attack-surface" from reaching the metadata service at 169.254.169.254. Write an egress NetworkPolicy that specifically blocks this IP while allowing all other egress traffic.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-metadata-ip
  namespace: attack-surface
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  # Allow all egress EXCEPT to metadata IP
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
        except:
        - 169.254.169.254/32
Explanation

This uses the ipBlock with except pattern — allow 0.0.0.0/0 EXCEPT 169.254.169.254/32. This is more surgical than blocking all egress and whitelisting specific IPs. The metadata service (169.254.169.254) is the #1 cloud SSRF target — blocking it from pods prevents credential theft attacks like the Capital One breach. On the exam, you may also need to block metadata via iptables rules as a second layer (defense in depth).

Q6
You have two namespaces: "web" and "database". Pods in "web" with label tier: frontend need to reach pods in "database" with label app: postgres on port 5432. Write BOTH the ingress policy in "database" AND the egress policy in "web".
Show Answer
Answer
# In namespace "database" — allow ingress from web pods
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-web
  namespace: database
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: web
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          tier: frontend
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
---
# In namespace "web" — allow egress to database pods
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-to-db
  namespace: web
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      tier: frontend
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: database
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
Explanation

Cross-namespace NetworkPolicies require both sides for defense in depth. The database namespace should control who can send to it (ingress), and the web namespace should control where pods can send to (egress). The namespaceSelector relies on namespace labels — you must label namespaces: kubectl label ns web name=web. On the CKS exam, you may only be asked for ONE side, but understanding both shows deep knowledge.

Q7
You apply a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} but some pods in the namespace still accept traffic. What conditions could cause this?
Show Answer
Answer

Three conditions: (1) HostNetwork pods: Pods using hostNetwork: true bypass the CNI entirely — NetworkPolicy does NOT apply. (2) CNI not enforcing: Flannel or an unsupported CNI. (3) Existing allow rules: Multiple NetworkPolicies combine with OR logic — if ANY policy allows the traffic, it's allowed. Check: kubectl get networkpolicies -n <ns> and review all policies.

Explanation

NetworkPolicies are additive within a namespace. If you have 3 policies and ANY one of them allows a connection, it's allowed. This is why default-deny MUST be explicit — without it, pods accept all traffic by default. Also, hostNetwork: true pods use the host's network namespace, so NetworkPolicy doesn't touch them — use node-level firewalls (iptables/nftables) instead.

Q8
An attacker compromises a pod and tries to exfiltrate data by making an HTTPS request to evil-server.com:443. Write a NetworkPolicy that blocks ALL egress EXCEPT to specific internal CIDR ranges (10.0.0.0/8) and port 53 DNS. Include both TCP and UDP DNS.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-lockdown
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
  - ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
    to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
Explanation

Egress lockdown is the most powerful NetworkPolicy pattern for preventing data exfiltration. This policy says: pods can only send traffic to 10.0.0.0/8 (your private network) and to CoreDNS for name resolution. No HTTPS to the internet, no DNS tunneling (DNS is restricted to your own CoreDNS pods, not external DNS servers). On the CKS exam, egress controls are often the answer to "prevent data exfiltration" scenario questions.

Q9
You need to allow ingress from a specific external IP range 203.0.113.0/24 (your office VPN) to pods labeled app: dashboard on port 8443. Write the NetworkPolicy. Why is ipBlock less secure than podSelector?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-vpn-dashboard
  namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dashboard
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8443

Why ipBlock is less secure: IP-based rules can be spoofed or bypassed if the attacker is on the same network segment. Pod-to-pod rules using podSelector are cryptographically enforced by the CNI (based on pod identity, not IP). IP-based rules are a necessary evil for external traffic but should never be your ONLY control.

Explanation

ipBlock is for traffic from outside the cluster (or from pods using hostNetwork). Within the cluster, always prefer podSelector and namespaceSelector — they're identity-based, not IP-based. On the CKS exam, if you see ipBlock in a policy, ask: is this for external traffic? If the traffic is pod-to-pod, use selectors instead.

Q10
You're given a cluster where an attacker compromised the "anihpj" pod. The attacker tries 4 things: (a) connect to postgres:5432, (b) curl https://evil.com, (c) scan the internal network, (d) write to a mounted hostPath. Write the complete set of NetworkPolicies that would have prevented (a), (b), and (c). Which attack does NetworkPolicy NOT prevent?
Show Answer
Answer

NetworkPolicy prevents (a), (b), (c):

# Prevent (a): Only postgres pod can reach port 5432
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-only-from-postgres-pod
  namespace: database
spec:
  podSelector: {app: postgres}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: {app: anihpj-api}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
---
# Prevent (b) + (c): Default-deny egress, allow only DNS + postgres
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {app: anihpj}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{podSelector: {app: postgres}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
  - to: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: kube-system}}, podSelector: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}]
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]

NetworkPolicy does NOT prevent (d) — hostPath writes are a filesystem operation, not a network operation. This requires PodSecurity (Ch 17), readOnlyRootFilesystem (Ch 18), or AppArmor (Ch 14).

Explanation

This question tests boundary awareness: knowing what NetworkPolicy CAN and CANNOT protect. NetworkPolicy is Layer 3/4 (IP/port). It cannot stop: filesystem operations (hostPath), process execution (shell spawn), syscalls (nsenter), or application-layer attacks (SQL injection). On the CKS exam, always identify the attack vector first, then choose the correct defense layer — don't use NetworkPolicy for non-network problems.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Deny all ingress to a namespace (START HERE for exam isolation tasks)
kubectl create -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
EOF

# 2. Allow only from specific namespace with label
kubectl label ns frontend app-tier=web
# Then in NetworkPolicy: namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {app-tier: web}}

# 3. Test connectivity between pods
kubectl run test-pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- /bin/bash
# Inside: nc -zv  ; curl :

# 4. List all NetworkPolicies and their selectors
kubectl get netpol -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,PODSELECTOR:.spec.podSelector
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 6 Traps
  • NetworkPolicy requires a CNI that supports it: Calico, Cilium, Weave, and Antrea support it. Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy natively. On the CKS exam, the cluster WILL have a supporting CNI — but verify with kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave'.
  • podSelector: {} means ALL pods: Empty selector matches every pod in the namespace. podSelector: {} with NO ingress rules = deny-all-ingress. With specific rules = those rules apply to all pods.
  • Label selectors are AND, not OR: If you specify both namespaceSelector and podSelector in the same from entry, BOTH must match. For OR logic, use separate from entries.

⚡ Ch 6 Visual Cheat Sheet — Network Policies

🚫
Deny All

Start with podSelector: {} + no rules. Blocks all traffic. Then add allows.

🏷️
Label Selectors

podSelector + namespaceSelector in same from = AND. Separate from entries = OR.

🔌
CNI Required

Calico, Cilium, Weave support NP. Flannel alone does NOT.

📡
DNS Egress

Deny-all egress blocks CoreDNS. Add UDP 53 rule to kube-system.

🧪
Testing

Use nicolaka/netshoot image. nc -zv svc port to test connectivity.

L3/L4
IP:Port Only

NetworkPolicy is L3/L4. For identity-based (L5), use mTLS/Istio.

📋 Exam Quick-Reference — Network Policies
🎯 Exam Task Simulator — Create Deny-All + Allow Specific Traffic
1Deny all ingress: Apply a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress] but NO ingress rules. This blocks ALL incoming traffic to all pods in the namespace.
2Allow from specific namespace: Add an ingress rule with namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {tier: frontend}}. Pods from namespaces with label tier=frontend can now connect.
3Allow from specific pod: Add podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: gateway}} inside the same from entry. BOTH namespaceSelector AND podSelector must match (AND logic).
4Test connectivity: kubectl run test --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- /bin/bash then nc -zv <svc> <port>. Should fail from wrong namespace, succeed from allowed one.
5Verify: kubectl describe netpol <name> -n <ns> shows the effective rules. kubectl get netpol -A shows all policies cluster-wide.
⚠️ Top 2 Failure Modes
  • NetworkPolicy applied but traffic still flows: The CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy (e.g., Flannel without Calico). Verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave|antrea". If none found, NetworkPolicy won't work.
  • DNS blocked by deny-all: If you deny all egress, pods can't reach CoreDNS. Add an egress rule allowing UDP port 53 to kube-system namespace with podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}.
⚡ CKS Speed Tips
  • podSelector + namespaceSelector in the SAME from entry = AND. Separate from entries = OR.
  • Use kubectl run netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- /bin/bash for quick connectivity testing. It has curl, nc, nslookup, and more.
