Ch 5: Dashboard Security — Dashboard SA uses RBAC → Ch 10: Service Accounts — The subject RBAC binds to → Ch 19: Secrets — RBAC controls who reads Secrets → Ch 28: Audit Logging — Every RBAC decision is logged.

📋 Exam Quick-Reference — RBAC for Security
🎯 Exam Task Simulator — Grant Least-Privilege Access
1Identify needed access: Read pods in ns X? Create deployments? Be specific.
2Create Role: kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n prod. For cluster-wide: use ClusterRole.
3Bind: kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=prod:sa -n prod.
4Test ALLOWED: kubectl auth can-i get pods -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:sa — must return "yes".
5Test DENIED: kubectl auth can-i create pods -n prod --as=<sa> — MUST return "no".
⚠️ Top 2 Failure Modes
  • Role created without -n: Creates in default namespace, not the intended one. Always specify -n.
  • ClusterRoleBinding gives GLOBAL access: Use RoleBinding for namespace-scoped permissions.
⚡ CKS Speed Tips
  • kubectl auth can-i --list -n <ns> --as=<subject> — shows ALL permissions at once.
  • Verbs: lowercase (get, list, create, delete, update, patch, watch). Resources: lowercase plural (pods, secrets).

⚡ Ch 9 Visual Cheat Sheet — RBAC

📋
Role (Namespaced)

Grants permissions within ONE namespace. kubectl create role ... -n <ns>

🌐
ClusterRole

Grants cluster-wide permissions. Nodes, PVs, namespaces. No -n flag.

🔗
Binding

RoleBinding (namespaced). ClusterRoleBinding (global). Links role to user/SA/group.

🚫
Deny by Default

No explicit deny rules. If no Role grants it, it's denied. Least privilege only.

Chapter 10: Service Accounts — Securing Pod Identity

Every pod in Kubernetes has an identity — a ServiceAccount. By default, every pod gets the default ServiceAccount in its namespace, and that ServiceAccount's JWT token is automatically mounted into the pod at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. Any process inside the pod can read this token and use it to authenticate to the Kubernetes API. If the ServiceAccount has RBAC permissions — even accidentally — every pod using it inherits those permissions. If the token is stolen (via a compromised container, a leaked log, or a misconfigured volume), the attacker has a permanent, non-expiring credential. This chapter teaches you to control pod identity: disable token auto-mounting for pods that do not need API access, create dedicated ServiceAccounts with minimal RBAC, and use bound tokens that automatically expire — eliminating the risk of stolen credentials granting persistent access.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🤖 ServiceAccounts 🔑 Pod Identity

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand how every pod authenticates to the API server using a mounted ServiceAccount token
  • ✅ Recognize the dangers of the default ServiceAccount — one shared identity for all pods
  • ✅ Create dedicated ServiceAccounts with minimal RBAC for each workload
  • ✅ Disable automountServiceAccountToken for pods that never need API access
  • ✅ Use bound (projected) tokens that auto-expire — eliminating permanent credential theft
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15% Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%
🧠 The ServiceAccount Exam Pattern

CKS ServiceAccount tasks follow a consistent pattern: (1) Identify which pods need API access and which do not, (2) For pods that do NOT need API access, set automountServiceAccountToken: false, (3) For pods that DO need API access, create a dedicated ServiceAccount with minimal RBAC, (4) Verify the pod can (or cannot) access the API. The exam always tests both cases: pods that should have access AND pods that should not.

10.1 How Pods Authenticate to the API Server

Every pod, when it starts, has a specific set of files mounted into it by the kubelet. These files are the pod's identity documents — and any process inside the container can read them:

What the kubelet mounts into every pod — the identity files
  $ kubectl exec anihpj-pod -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
  ca.crt       ← Cluster CA certificate (to verify the API server's TLS cert)
  namespace    ← The pod's namespace (plain text: "anihpj-prod")
  token        ← THE JWT TOKEN — this IS the pod's identity

  $ kubectl exec anihpj-pod -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJrdWJlcm5ldGVzL3NlcnZpY2VhY2NvdW50Iiwia3ViZXJu
  ZXRlcy5pby9zZXJ2aWNlYWNjb3VudC9uYW1lc3BhY2UiOiJhbmlocGotcHJvZCIsImt1YmVybmV0ZXMuaW8vc2Vy
  dmljZWFjY291bnQvc2VydmljZS1hY2NvdW50Lm5hbWUiOiJkZWZhdWx0Iiwic3ViIjoic3lzdGVtOnNlcnZpY2Vh
  Y2NvdW50OmFuaWhwai1wcm9kOmRlZmF1bHQifQ...

  # Decode the JWT payload (middle section between the dots):
  $ echo "eyJpc3Mi..." | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d | python -m json.tool
  {
    "iss": "kubernetes/serviceaccount",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace": "anihpj-prod",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/secret.name": "default-token-xxxxx",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/service-account.name": "default",
    "sub": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default"
  }
  → This pod identifies as: system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default

How the Pod Uses Its Token — The Full Flow

From pod to API — authentication, authorization, response
  1. Pod starts → kubelet creates the token volume mount
     Mount path: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
     Files: token (JWT), ca.crt (CA cert), namespace

  2. App inside pod reads the token file
     $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

  3. App calls the K8s API with the token as a Bearer header
     $ curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/pods \
         --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt \
         -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/.../token)"

  4. API server receives the request:
     a. Validates the JWT signature (signed by the SA token controller)
     b. Extracts: username = system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default
     c. Looks up RBAC: does this SA have "list pods" in anihpj-prod?
     d. If RBAC allows → returns pod list. If not → 403 Forbidden.

  IF automountServiceAccountToken: false:
     Step 1 never happens → /var/run/secrets/ is EMPTY
     → Pod CANNOT call the K8s API at all ✅

How the ServiceAccount Token Controller Works — Behind the Scenes

Three Kubernetes components collaborate to make ServiceAccount tokens work. Understanding this chain helps you diagnose token issues and understand why bound tokens are fundamentally more secure:

The ServiceAccount Token Pipeline — 3 Components
  1. SERVICEACCOUNT CONTROLLER (kube-controller-manager)
     ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Watches: ServiceAccount creations
     Action: Creates a Secret (type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token)
             containing a signed JWT for the SA.
     ⚠️  This is LEGACY behavior — for STATIC tokens only.
         Bound tokens are NOT created by this controller.

  2. TOKEN CONTROLLER (kube-controller-manager)
     ─────────────────────────────────────────────
     Watches: ServiceAccount deletions
     Action: Deletes all Secrets associated with a deleted SA.
     Also: Signs the JWT using the cluster's ServiceAccount private key
           (--service-account-private-key-file on kube-controller-manager).

  3. KUBELET (on every node)
     ────────────────────────
     Action: Mounts the token into every pod's filesystem.
     For STATIC tokens: reads the Secret, writes the token file.
     For BOUND tokens: calls the TokenRequest API to get a fresh,
     time-limited token on every pod start AND on rotation.

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Bound tokens NEVER touch a Secret. The kubelet
     calls the TokenRequest API directly, gets a JWT with an expiry,
     and writes it to a tmpfs volume. No Secret. No persistence.
     When the token expires, the kubelet gets a new one automatically.

The TokenRequest API — How Bound Tokens Are Created

The TokenRequest API is the modern replacement for static ServiceAccount tokens. Instead of creating a permanent Secret, you request a temporary token with a specific audience and duration. This API is what the kubelet uses internally for projected tokens — and you can use it directly to generate short-lived tokens for CI/CD pipelines or debugging:

Using the TokenRequest API — Generate a Short-Lived Token
  # Create a 1-hour token for the anihpj-sa ServiceAccount
  $ kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n anihpj-prod --duration=1h
  eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6Ii...truncated...

  # Use it directly with curl
  $ TOKEN=$(kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n anihpj-prod --duration=1h)
  $ curl -k https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/pods \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
  → Returns pods if SA has RBAC, 403 if not.

  # This token expires in 1 hour. No Secret exists. Nothing to clean up.
  # This is the recommended way to generate tokens for CI/CD, not static Secrets.

  ⚠️  kubectl create token requires K8s 1.24+. For older versions,
      use kubectl create token -- requested via the raw API.

10.2 The Dangers of the Default Service Account

Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount — created automatically by the namespace controller. Unless a pod explicitly specifies serviceAccountName, it uses this default SA. The danger: every pod in the namespace shares the same identity. If you grant any RBAC permissions to the default SA, every pod inherits them. If one pod is compromised and its token is stolen, the attacker can impersonate every other pod in that namespace.

❌ Default ServiceAccount — Shared Identity
  • All pods → "default" SA
  • Grant permissions to default → ALL pods get permissions
  • One compromised pod = all pods' identity stolen
  • Token never expires (old-style static token)
  • Default SA appears in every namespace

Compromised anihpj pod → can read Secrets as default SA → can access API across namespace.

✅ Dedicated ServiceAccounts — Isolated Identity
  • anihpj pod → anihpj-sa
  • postgres pod → postgres-sa
  • Each SA → minimal, specific RBAC permissions
  • Tokens can be time-limited (projected tokens)
  • Automount disabled for pods that don't need API

Compromised anihpj pod → can only do what anihpj-sa allows → nothing else.

🔴 The Default SA Is Shared — Never Give It Permissions

The default ServiceAccount should have zero RBAC permissions in every namespace. If you need a pod to access the API, create a dedicated ServiceAccount for that specific workload and grant permissions only to that SA. Never create a RoleBinding that references the default SA. If you see system:serviceaccount:<ns>:default in any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding, that is a security finding that must be remediated immediately.

Auditing Default ServiceAccount Permissions — Find the Gaps

Use these commands to audit every namespace for default SA permissions. Any non-empty result is a security finding:

One-Liner: Find All Permissions Granted to Default ServiceAccounts
  # Find every RoleBinding that references a default SA
  $ kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o json | jq -r \
      '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | select(.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .name=="default")) |
       "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name) → default SA"'

  # Sample output (each line is a FINDING):
  # anihpj-prod/anihpj-admin-binding → default SA 🔴
  # kube-public/default-view → default SA 🟡 (intentional for kube-public)

  # Check what the default SA can actually do in a namespace
  $ kubectl auth can-i --list \
      --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default -n anihpj-prod
  → Must return NO permissions. If any appear, investigate immediately.

  # Find namespaces where the default SA has ANY RBAC binding
  $ for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o name | cut -d/ -f2); do
      count=$(kubectl get rolebindings -n $ns -o json | jq \
        '[.items[]? | select(.subjects[]? | select(.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .name=="default"))] | length')
      if [ "$count" -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "🔴 $ns: default SA has $count RoleBinding(s)"
      fi
    done

Attack Scenario: What Happens When a ServiceAccount Token Is Stolen

Understanding the risk requires seeing the attack. Here is exactly what happens when an attacker compromises an anihpj pod and extracts its ServiceAccount token — and how the outcome differs dramatically depending on whether the SA has permissions and whether the token is static or bound:

Scenario A: Pod with DEFAULT SA + Accidental RBAC Permissions
  ATTACKER compromises anihpj pod via CVE → gains shell as root
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ whoami
  root     ← Container runs as root

  $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6Ii...   ← THE POD'S IDENTITY

  $ curl -s https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/secrets \
      --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/.../token)"
  {
    "items": [
      {"metadata":{"name":"anihpj-db-credentials"}},
      {"metadata":{"name":"anihpj-tls"}},
      {"metadata":{"name":"aws-s3-backup-key"}}
    ]
  }
  → Attacker can LIST all Secrets in the namespace!
    Because someone granted "get secrets" to the default SA.

  $ curl .../secrets/anihpj-db-credentials ...
  → Returns DATABASE_URL with username and password.
  → Attacker now has production database credentials.

  IMPACT: Full database access. All user data. All job listings.
  CAUSE: Default SA + accidentally granted Secret read permission.
Scenario B: Pod with DEDICATED SA + Zero Permissions
  ATTACKER compromises anihpj pod via CVE → gains shell as root
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ whoami
  root

  $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  → FILE NOT FOUND (automountServiceAccountToken: false)

  $ ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
  → DIRECTORY EMPTY

  $ curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/secrets
  → curl: (77) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate
  → Cannot even verify the API server's TLS cert (no ca.crt mounted)

  IMPACT: Zero. No token. No API access. No lateral movement via K8s API.
  CAUSE: automountServiceAccountToken: false + dedicated SA with no RBAC.
  Attacker must find another path — and NetworkPolicies (Ch 6) block that too.

ServiceAccount Lifecycle — From Creation to Token Rotation

📝
Create SA kubectl create
serviceaccount
→
🔑
Token Gen kubelet calls
TokenRequest API

📦

to tmpfs volume

🔑 With automountServiceAccountToken: false, the flow stops at Step 1 — no token is ever generated.

10.3 Bound Service Account Tokens (Projected Tokens)

Legacy ServiceAccount tokens (the kind stored as Kubernetes Secrets) are non-expiring, non-revocable, and valid for any API server audience. If an attacker steals one — from a compromised container, a leaked log file, or a misconfigured volume — they have permanent API access. Bound tokens (also called projected tokens) solve this: they are time-limited, audience-scoped, and automatically rotated by the kubelet. No Secret is created. No permanent credential exists.

Old vs New ServiceAccount Tokens

FeatureOld (Static) TokenNew (Bound) Token
Stored asKubernetes Secret (auto-created per SA)Projected volume (tmpfs, never on disk)
ExpiryNever expires 🔴1 hour (default), configurable ✅
AudienceAny K8s API server 🔴Specific audience (e.g., "vault") ✅
RotationManual only 🔴Automatic (kubelet rotates before expiry) ✅
RevocableOnly by deleting the Secret 🔴Expires automatically ✅
If stolenPermanent access 🔴Access expires within 1 hour ✅
Available sinceKubernetes 1.0Kubernetes 1.21+ (enabled by default in 1.24+)

Configuring a Bound Token — Pod Spec

Pod YAML with a projected ServiceAccount token (1-hour expiry)
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-secure
  spec:
    serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa         # Dedicated SA, not default
    automountServiceAccountToken: false    # Disable the default token mount
    containers:
    - name: anihpj
      image: anihpj:v2
      volumeMounts:
      - name: token
        mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens # Custom path, not the default
        readOnly: true
    volumes:
    - name: token
      projected:
        sources:
        - serviceAccountToken:
            path: token                    # The token file name
            expirationSeconds: 3600        # 1 hour expiry ← KEY FIELD
            audience: api                  # Audience claim in the JWT
  # ⚠️  The old default mount at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/
  #     is EMPTY because automountServiceAccountToken: false.
  #     Only THIS projected token exists, and it expires in 1 hour.

What Happens When a Bound Token Expires Mid-Request

A common concern with bound tokens: "What if my pod is in the middle of a long-running operation and the token expires?" The answer depends on your Kubernetes version and configuration. In K8s 1.22+, the kubelet automatically rotates the token BEFORE it expires — typically at 80% of its lifetime. The new token is written to the same file atomically, and any process that re-reads the file gets the new token. For HTTP clients that reuse connections (keep-alive), the existing connection continues to work — token validation only happens at connection establishment. For new connections, the pod reads the updated token file and presents the fresh token. Best practice: set expirationSeconds to at least 3600 (1 hour) to give the kubelet time to rotate. Avoid very short expirations (less than 600 seconds) unless your application explicitly handles token refresh.

Disabling Legacy Tokens Cluster-Wide

Even after you configure bound tokens for your pods, the old static token Secrets may still exist — and they never expire. The CKS exam may ask you to ensure that legacy tokens are not in use. The API server flag --service-account-extend-token-expiration=false (K8s 1.24+) prevents the legacy token controller from creating auto-mounted Secrets for new ServiceAccounts. Combined with --service-account-issuer and --service-account-signing-key-file (which configure the bound token issuer), you can ensure that all new tokens are bound tokens — no static Secrets created, no permanent credentials lingering in your cluster.

10.4 Securing anihpj Service Accounts

Let's apply everything to the anihpj application. We have four workloads, each with different API access needs:

anihpj ServiceAccounts — Each with least privilege
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # SA 1: anihpj-sa — Web application (NO API access)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # No API access needed
  # The Django app serves HTTP — it never calls the K8s API.
  # Even if Django is compromised, there is no token to steal.

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # SA 2: postgres-sa — Database (NO API access)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: postgres-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # No API access needed

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # SA 3: anihpj-operator-sa — Needs to read ConfigMaps
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-operator-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  ---
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Role
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-operator-role
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]      # Only ConfigMaps, only read
  ---
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: RoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-operator-binding
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: anihpj-operator-sa
  roleRef:
    kind: Role
    name: anihpj-operator-role
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # SA 4: ci-deployer-sa — Updates Deployments
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: ci-deployer-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  ---
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Role
  metadata:
    name: ci-deployer-role
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "update", "patch"]
  ---
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: RoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: ci-deployer-binding
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: ci-deployer-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  roleRef:
    kind: Role
    name: ci-deployer-role
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

Verifying anihpj ServiceAccounts — What Each Can Do

ServiceAccountAPI Access?PermissionsToken Auto-Mount?
anihpj-sa❌ NoNonefalse ✅
postgres-sa❌ NoNonefalse ✅
anihpj-operator-sa✅ Yesget/list/watch ConfigMaps in anihpj-prod onlytrue (needed)
ci-deployer-sa✅ Yesget/list/update/patch Deployments in anihpj-prod onlytrue (needed)

Decision Tree: Does My Pod Need API Access?

Walk through this decision tree for every pod in your cluster. The most common CKS mistake is either disabling the token on a pod that needs it (breaking functionality) or leaving the token mounted on a pod that does not need it (leaving a credential exposed):

🔍 Does this pod call the Kubernetes API? (kubectl, client-go, any /api/ endpoint?)
❌ NO → automountServiceAccountToken: false. Create a dedicated SA with zero RBAC. The anihpj web app does NOT call the K8s API — it serves HTTP.
✅ YES → Continue. The pod needs a token.
📋 Does it need read-only access (get/list/watch) to specific resources?
✅ YES → Create dedicated SA + Role with only get/list/watch on only the needed resources. Example: anihpj-operator-sa → ConfigMaps only.
❌ NO → Continue.
✏️ Does it need to modify resources (create/update/delete)?
✅ YES → Create dedicated SA + Role with only the needed verbs on only the needed resources. Example: ci-deployer-sa → update deployments only. Use bound tokens with 1-hour expiry.
🎉 Your pod needs API access but NOT to modify resources. Verify with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>. Every verb listed beyond get/list/watch is a finding.

ServiceAccount Security Maturity Model

Where is your cluster on the ServiceAccount security maturity curve? Each stage eliminates a class of attack:

🔴
Stage 0
Default Everywhere

All pods use the default SA. Token auto-mounted in every pod. Static tokens never expire.

❌ Extremely vulnerable
🟠
Stage 1
Dedicated SAs

Each workload has its own SA. Default SA has zero RBAC. But tokens are still static and auto-mounted everywhere.

⚠️ Still using static tokens
🟡
Stage 2
Auto-Mount Disabled

automountServiceAccountToken: false on all pods that do not need API access. Token only present where needed.

⚠️ Static tokens still expire never
🟢
Stage 3
Bound Tokens

All tokens are projected, time-limited, audience-scoped. Auto-rotated. No static Secrets. CKS target state.

✅ CKS Hardened

📊 Chapter 10 Visual Summary

🔑 Pod Identity Every pod has a ServiceAccount. Token mounted at /var/run/secrets/ — any process can read it.
🚫 Default SA Danger One shared identity for all pods. Never grant permissions to the default SA.
⏰ Bound Tokens Time-limited (1hr), audience-scoped, auto-rotated. No permanent credentials.
✅ Least Privilege SAs 4 dedicated SAs for anihpj — two with zero API access, two with minimal RBAC.
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Every CKS ServiceAccount task has two parts: (1) disable the token for pods that do not need it (automountServiceAccountToken: false), and (2) create a dedicated SA with minimal RBAC for pods that do. Always verify BOTH: kubectl exec <pod> -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ — if the directory is empty, the token is disabled. If it contains a token, verify the SA has only the expected permissions with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>.

JWT Token Lifecycle — How ServiceAccount Tokens Work at the Kernel Level

A ServiceAccount token is a JSON Web Token (JWT) — a signed, base64-encoded JSON document that proves the pod's identity. Understanding the token lifecycle explains why long-lived, non-expiring tokens are so dangerous and why bound tokens are the fix:

ServiceAccount JWT Token — Creation, Mounting, and Validation
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LEGACY TOKEN (pre-1.22, still default in many clusters)                  │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  • Created: Automatically when the SA is created.                         │
  │  • Stored: As a Secret (type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token).       │
  │  • Expiry: NEVER. The token is valid forever.                             │
  │  • Revocation: ONLY by deleting the Secret. Changing RBAC does NOT       │
  │    invalidate an existing token — it already passed auth.                 │
  │  • Mounted: Token is mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/          │
  │    serviceaccount/token via a projected volume.                           │
  │  ⚡ DANGER: If this token is stolen (log file, compromised pod, leaked   │
  │    ConfigMap), the attacker has PERMANENT API access as that SA.          │
  │    The only fix is to delete the Secret (revoking the token) AND           │
  │    change the RBAC bindings (in case the attacker already used the token  │
  │    to create backdoor credentials).                                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BOUND TOKEN (TokenRequest API, 1.22+) — CKS exam standard               │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────                       │
  │  • Created: On-demand when the pod is created, via the TokenRequest API. │
  │  • Stored: NOT stored in etcd. Generated on-the-fly and mounted.         │
  │  • Expiry: Configurable — typically 1 hour, renewable.                    │
  │  • Bound to: The specific POD that requested it. Cannot be used by any   │
  │    other pod, even if the token string is copied.                         │
  │  • Revocation: Automatic on expiry. No cleanup needed.                    │
  │  • Mounted: Same path, but kubelet rotates the token BEFORE expiry.      │
  │  ⚡ ADVANTAGE: A stolen token is useless after 1 hour. A token stolen     │
  │    from Pod A cannot be used by Pod B (pod-bound).                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  TOKEN PROJECTION MECHANICS (how the token file stays fresh):
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • kubelet mounts a PROJECTED VOLUME at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/
    serviceaccount/.
  • The projected volume contains a symlink: token → ..data/token
  • ..data/token is a NEW file each time kubelet rotates the token.
  • The symlink updates ATOMICALLY (rename()) — the pod always reads
    the current token without needing to restart.
  • Token rotation happens at 80% of the token's TTL (e.g., at 48 min
    for a 60-min token).

Default vs Dedicated ServiceAccount — Security Comparison

Why You Should NEVER Grant Permissions to the Default ServiceAccount
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  ❌ DEFAULT SERVICEACCOUNT   │   │  ✅ DEDICATED SERVICEACCOUNT │
  │                              │   │                              │
  │  All pods → "default" SA    │   │  anihpj pod → anihpj-sa     │
  │  Grant permissions to default│   │  postgres pod → postgres-sa │
  │  → ALL pods get permissions  │   │  Each SA → minimal permissions│
  │                              │   │                              │
  │  Compromised pod:            │   │  Compromised anihpj pod:     │
  │  → can access API as default │   │  → can only do what         │
  │  → may reach secrets across  │   │    anihpj-sa is allowed     │
  │    the namespace             │   │  → nothing else              │
  │                              │   │                              │
  │  🔴 If default SA has        │   │  🟢 anihpj-sa has NO        │
  │     cluster-admin binding:   │   │     permissions at all.     │
  │     EVERY pod = cluster-admin│   │     Postgres-sa also none.  │
  │     → CATASTROPHIC breach   │   │     Least privilege.        │
  └──────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────────┘

Service Account Token Flow — How a Pod Uses Its Identity

Pod → Token → API Server → RBAC Check — The Complete Flow
  1. Pod starts → kubelet creates projected volume
     Mount path: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
     Files: token (JWT), ca.crt (cluster CA), namespace

  2. App inside pod reads the token file
     $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
     → eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

  3. App calls K8s API with Authorization: Bearer <token>
     $ curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/pods \
       -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/.../token)"

  4. API server validates token → extracts SA identity → RBAC check → respond

  IF automountServiceAccountToken: false:
     Step 1 never happens → /var/run/secrets/ is EMPTY
     → Pod cannot call K8s API at all ✅

  🔑 THE CKS EXAM PATTERN: Tasks often ask you to create a pod that CANNOT
     access the API. The answer is always: ServiceAccount with
     automountServiceAccountToken: false.
🔧 Under the Hood — ServiceAccount Token Lifecycle: Token Creation → Projected Volume Mount → JWT Validation → Token Expiry
🗺️ SA Token Flow — From Secret to API Call
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   SERVICE ACCOUNT TOKEN LIFECYCLE                                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  1. TOKEN CREATION (by TokenController)                                   │
  │     • When a SA is created, TokenController generates a JWT               │
  │     • Claims: sub, iss, aud, exp, iat, kubernetes.io/namespace, sa/name  │
  │     • Signed with: --service-account-key-file (API server flag)           │
  │                                                                           │
  │  2. TOKEN MOUNTED (by kubelet, unless automount=false)                    │
  │     • Path: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/                │
  │     • Files: token (JWT), ca.crt (cluster CA), namespace (text)          │
  │     • Volume type: projected ServiceAccountTokenVolume                     │
  │     • Token is auto-rotated by kubelet when >80% of TTL elapsed          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  3. POD USES TOKEN (curl / python requests)                               │
  │     curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods \  │
  │       -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/.../token)"       │
  │       --cacert /var/run/secrets/.../ca.crt                                │
  │                                                                           │
  │  4. API SERVER VALIDATES TOKEN                                             │
  │     • Checks JWT signature against --service-account-key-file             │
  │     • Checks token hasn't expired (exp claim)                              │
  │     • Extracts username: system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>                 │
  │     • Proceeds to RBAC authorization                                       │
  │                                                                           │
  │  5. TOKEN EXPIRY                                                            │
  │     • Default TTL: 1 hour (configurable via --service-account-token-ttl)  │
  │     • kubelet auto-refreshes before expiry                                 │
  │     • Pod sees the new token automatically (projected volume)             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 10 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Create a ServiceAccount that has NO Kubernetes API access. Write the SA and the pod spec referencing it.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: isolated-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pod
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: isolated-sa
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
# Verify: kubectl exec test-pod -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/
# Should return: No such file or directory
Q2
What's inside a mounted ServiceAccount token? Decode it and explain each claim.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl exec pod -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d | jq .
# {
#   "aud": ["https://kubernetes.default.svc"],  # Who this token is for
#   "exp": 1753600000,                            # Expiration (Unix timestamp)
#   "iat": 1753596400,                            # Issued at
#   "iss": "https://kubernetes.default.svc",      # Issuer (API server)
#   "kubernetes.io": {
#     "namespace": "anihpj-prod",                  # Pod's namespace
#     "serviceaccount": {"name": "sa-name", ...}  # Which SA
#   },
#   "sub": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:sa-name"
# }
Q3
What happens if a pod's SA token expires while the pod is running? Does the pod lose API access?
Show Answer
Answer

No — the kubelet automatically rotates the token BEFORE it expires (when >80% of TTL has elapsed). The new token is written to the same projected volume path, and applications reading the file see the updated token. This is transparent to the application. The default TTL is 1 hour, and rotation happens around the 48-minute mark.

Q4
How do you verify that a specific ServiceAccount can (or cannot) perform an action? Write the exact command.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj-prod --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa
# Returns: yes or no

kubectl auth can-i --list -n anihpj-prod --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa
# Lists ALL permissions for that SA
Q5
What's the difference between a ServiceAccount token (JWT) and a client certificate for authentication? Which is preferred for pods and why?
Show Answer
Answer

SA Token (JWT): A signed JSON Web Token auto-mounted into pods. Contains claims (namespace, SA name, expiry). Automatically rotated by kubelet. Bound to a specific pod via projected tokens (K8s 1.21+). Client Certificate: An X.509 certificate used by kubectl and control plane components. Longer-lived, no automatic rotation. Pods use SA tokens because: (1) automatic provisioning — no manual cert generation, (2) automatic rotation — kubelet handles expiry, (3) pod-bound tokens prevent token reuse if the pod is deleted.

Explanation

Kubernetes 1.21+ introduced bound tokens: each token is tied to a specific pod UID. If the pod is deleted, the token becomes invalid even if not yet expired. This is a critical security improvement over legacy tokens that were valid until expiry regardless of pod state. The CKS exam tests knowledge of token types and when to use each.

Q6
You have 50 pods in a namespace. Only 5 of them need API access. What's the most efficient way to disable token mounting for the other 45 pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the ServiceAccount itself. Every pod using that SA inherits the setting. For the 5 pods that need API access, create a separate SA with automountServiceAccountToken: true (the default). This is more efficient than setting it on each of the 45 individual pod specs and ensures new pods automatically get the secure default.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-api-sa
  namespace: prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false  # All pods using this SA get no token
Explanation

The CKS exam rewards efficiency. Setting automountServiceAccountToken: false at the SA level is a single change that affects all pods using that SA. Setting it on each pod spec is error-prone — one forgotten pod is a security gap. Always think at the SA level for token mounting decisions.

Q7
What is a projected ServiceAccount token and how does it differ from the legacy token mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/? Write a pod spec using projected tokens.
Show Answer
Answer

Legacy token: Mounted as a Secret, valid until the Secret is deleted, NOT pod-bound. Projected token: Created via TokenRequest API, bound to a specific pod UID, has configurable TTL, auto-rotated by kubelet.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-pod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - name: token
      mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: token
    projected:
      sources:
      - serviceAccountToken:
          path: token
          expirationSeconds: 3600     # 1-hour TTL
          audience: api               # Bound to this audience
Explanation

Projected tokens (K8s 1.21+, GA in 1.24) are the modern standard. Key advantages: (1) pod-bound — token dies with the pod, (2) configurable TTL — set short lifetimes for sensitive pods, (3) audience-bound — token only works for specified audiences. On the CKS exam, use projected tokens with short expiration for pods that need temporary API access.

Q8
You discover that pods in namespace "legacy" are using ServiceAccounts that have automountServiceAccountToken: true but none of them need API access. Write the single command to find all such pods, and the fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Find pods with mounted tokens in namespace "legacy"
kubectl get pods -n legacy -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.automountServiceAccountToken != false) | {name: .metadata.name, sa: .spec.serviceAccountName, automount: .spec.automountServiceAccountToken}'

# Fix: Patch the default ServiceAccount in that namespace
kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n legacy -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}'

# Or create a dedicated SA for the namespace
kubectl create sa no-api -n legacy
kubectl patch sa no-api -n legacy -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}'
# Then update deployments to use this SA
Explanation

This is a common CKS audit task. The jq query filters for pods that haven't explicitly disabled automount. The default SA in every namespace has automount enabled by default. Patching the default SA is the fastest fix but may break legitimate API access. A safer approach: create a dedicated no-api SA and gradually migrate pods to it.

Q9
An attacker steals a pod's SA token file from /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token and exfiltrates it. They use it from an external server to query the Kubernetes API. What two Kubernetes features prevent this attack?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Pod-bound tokens (projected tokens): The token is bound to the pod's UID. When the API server receives a request with this token, it verifies the pod still exists. If the original pod was deleted (even if you created a new one with the same name), the token is rejected. 2. Token audience validation: The token's aud claim must match the API server's expected audience. An attacker can't reuse a token meant for the API server against a different service. 3. Short TTL: Projected tokens can have expiration as low as 600 seconds — the stolen token expires quickly.

Explanation

Legacy SA tokens (pre-1.21) had no pod binding — they were valid until the Secret was deleted, regardless of pod state. This was a significant security weakness. The CKS exam tests knowledge of projected tokens and their security properties. For production clusters, always use projected tokens with the shortest acceptable TTL.

Q10
You need to create a ServiceAccount for a monitoring agent that: can read pod metrics from the metrics API, cannot read Secrets, cannot create/modify anything, and has its token auto-rotated. Write the SA, ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, and the pod spec with projected token.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: monitoring-agent
  namespace: monitoring
automountServiceAccountToken: false  # We use projected tokens instead
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: pod-metrics-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: ["metrics.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: monitoring-metrics
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: monitoring-agent
  namespace: monitoring
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: pod-metrics-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: monitoring-agent
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  serviceAccountName: monitoring-agent
  containers:
  - name: agent
    image: monitoring-agent:v1
    volumeMounts:
    - name: sa-token
      mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: sa-token
    projected:
      sources:
      - serviceAccountToken:
          path: token
          expirationSeconds: 7200
          audience: https://kubernetes.default.svc
Explanation

This is the complete "least privilege monitoring agent" pattern tested on CKS. Key decisions: (1) SA has automount disabled because we use projected tokens. (2) ClusterRole is scoped to ONLY pods and metrics — no secrets, no configmaps, no write verbs. (3) ClusterRoleBinding is cluster-wide because the agent needs to see pods in all namespaces. (4) Projected token has 2-hour TTL — long enough for monitoring but short enough to limit stolen token risk.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Create SA with no API access (EXAM PATTERN)
kubectl create sa isolated-sa -n prod
kubectl patch sa isolated-sa -n prod -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}'
# Verify: kubectl get sa isolated-sa -n prod -o yaml | grep automount

# 2. Create a token for an SA
kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n prod --duration=24h

# 3. Check which SA a pod is using
kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'
kubectl get pod anihpj-api -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.automountServiceAccountToken}'

# 4. Verify SA has NO permissions (security check)
kubectl auth can-i --list -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:isolated-sa
# Should show: Resources: [], NonResourceURLs: []
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 10 Traps
  • Default SA in every namespace: Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount that is automatically mounted unless you set automountServiceAccountToken: false. Forgetting this means every pod gets API access by default.
  • SA token is a Secret: When you create an SA, K8s auto-creates a Secret containing the token. This Secret has RBAC protections just like any other Secret. If an attacker can read Secrets in the namespace, they can steal the SA token and impersonate the SA.
  • disableServiceLinks is not security: enableServiceLinks: false only prevents environment variable injection of service IPs — it does NOT prevent the SA token from being mounted. For no API access, use automountServiceAccountToken: false.

1Create the SA: kubectl create sa isolated-sa -n prod
2Disable auto-mount: kubectl patch sa isolated-sa -n prod -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}'. This prevents the token from being mounted by default.
3Reference in pod: spec.serviceAccountName: isolated-sa. If automount is false on the SA, no token is mounted even without pod-level override.
4Verify no API access: kubectl exec isolated-pod -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token — should fail (no file). Or check: kubectl exec isolated-pod -- curl -k https://kubernetes.default.svc — should fail with no token.
5Verify RBAC: kubectl auth can-i --list -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:isolated-sa — should show no permissions.
⚠️ Top 2 Failure Modes
  • Default SA still mounted: If you don't set serviceAccountName, pods use the default SA which HAS a token. Always explicitly set serviceAccountName.
  • automount false on SA but pod overrides: Pod can override SA-level automount with automountServiceAccountToken: true. Pod-level setting wins.
⚡ CKS Speed Tips
  • kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns> --duration=1h — generate a temporary token for testing without creating a long-lived Secret.
  • SA token location in pod: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. Check with: kubectl exec pod -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/.

Chapter 11: Node Restriction & Hardening Authorization

Every Kubernetes node runs a kubelet — the agent that starts pods, reports node status, and manages container lifecycles. The kubelet communicates with the API server to register its node and update pod statuses. If a kubelet is compromised — through a container escape, a node-level exploit, or stolen credentials — it can wreak havoc: modify other nodes' labels, evict pods from healthy nodes, or impersonate other kubelets to redirect traffic. NodeRestriction is the admission plugin that limits each kubelet to only its own node and its own pods. Combined with the Node authorization mode, which restricts what kubelets can even request, these controls form a critical defense layer that the CKS exam tests heavily.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ⚙️ Kubelet 🔐 Authorization

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Enable and verify the NodeRestriction admission plugin — limit kubelets to their own node
  • ✅ Understand the Node authorization mode and why it must be paired with RBAC
  • ✅ Compare all authorization modes and know which ones to NEVER use in production
  • ✅ Harden SSH access to nodes — disable root login, enforce key-only authentication
  • ✅ Protect the kubelet API (port 10250) from unauthorized access
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15% System Hardening 10%

11.1 The NodeRestriction Admission Plugin

NodeRestriction is an admission plugin — it intercepts API requests from kubelets and validates that each kubelet is only modifying resources it owns. Without NodeRestriction, a compromised kubelet on node-worker-2 can modify labels on node-worker-1 (impersonating another node), evict pods from node-worker-3, or modify pod labels to bypass scheduling constraints. With NodeRestriction, each kubelet is strictly limited to its own node object and the pods scheduled on it.

🔴 Without NodeRestriction — One Compromised Kubelet = Cluster-Wide Chaos

A compromised kubelet can: modify ANY node's labels (redirecting workloads), evict pods from ANY node (causing denial of service), modify pod labels to bypass affinity rules, and update node statuses to disrupt scheduling. NodeRestriction prevents ALL of this by enforcing: "kubelet on node-X can only modify node-X and pods on node-X."

NodeRestriction — What Each Kubelet Can and Cannot Touch

❌ WITHOUT NodeRestriction

Scenario: kubelet on node-worker-2 is compromised.

  • 🔴 Modify labels on node-worker-1 (impersonate other nodes)
  • 🔴 Evict pods from node-worker-3 (disrupt other nodes)
  • 🔴 Modify pod labels it doesn't run (bypass scheduling)
  • 🔴 Update any node's status to NotReady
  • 🔴 This enables privilege escalation across the entire cluster
✅ WITH NodeRestriction

Scenario: kubelet on node-worker-2 is compromised.

  • ✅ Can read its own node object (node-worker-2) — only
  • ✅ Can modify its own node status and labels — only
  • ✅ Can read/write pods scheduled ON node-worker-2 — only
  • ✅ Cannot touch node-worker-1 or node-worker-3 at all
  • ✅ Blast radius contained to ONE node

Enabling NodeRestriction — API Server Configuration

Add NodeRestriction to the admission plugin list and verify
  # Step 1: Edit the API server manifest
  $ vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

  # Find --enable-admission-plugins and add NodeRestriction:
  - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,AlwaysPullImages,...

  # Step 2: Save → kubelet restarts API server (10-30 seconds)

  # Step 3: Verify NodeRestriction is active
  $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* -o yaml | grep NodeRestriction
  → --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...  ✅

  # Step 4: Test — a kubelet CANNOT modify another node's labels
  $ kubectl label node node-worker-1 test=value
  → (From the compromised kubelet on node-worker-2)
  → Error: node "node-worker-1" cannot be modified (NodeRestriction)

How NodeRestriction Actually Works — The Internal Mechanism

NodeRestriction is not magic — it is a specific set of validation rules hardcoded into the API server's admission chain. Understanding exactly what it checks helps you diagnose when it blocks legitimate kubelet operations (rare, but possible during cluster upgrades or node replacements):

NodeRestriction Validation Rules — What Gets Checked
  RULE 1: kubelet identity is derived from the username "system:node:<nodeName>"
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  If a request comes from user "system:node:worker-2", NodeRestriction
  enforces that the kubelet can ONLY modify:
  • Node object: "worker-2" (its OWN node — not worker-1, not worker-3)
  • Pod objects: only pods where spec.nodeName == "worker-2"
  • Any attempt to modify worker-1 → REJECTED with "node 'worker-1' is not
    managed by node 'worker-2'"

  RULE 2: kubelet cannot modify taints on its own node with
          NoSchedule or NoExecute effects
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A compromised kubelet CANNOT taint its own node to attract or repel
  specific workloads. Only the API server (via scheduler) or cluster-admin
  can modify taints. This prevents a compromised kubelet from making its
  node a "preferred" target for sensitive pods.

  RULE 3: kubelet cannot set labels prefixed with
          "node-restriction.kubernetes.io/" on its own node
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  This label prefix is RESERVED. Only the NodeRestriction admission
  plugin itself can set these labels. Kubelets cannot modify them.

  RULE 4: kubelet can only update its own node's status sub-resources
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Node status updates (Ready, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure) are
  restricted to the kubelet's own node. A kubelet on worker-2 cannot
  mark worker-3 as NotReady.

What Happens When You Try to Bypass NodeRestriction

The CKS exam may present a scenario where NodeRestriction is disabled and ask you to enable it — or present a scenario where it IS enabled and ask you to diagnose why a kubelet operation is failing. Here is exactly what the API server returns when NodeRestriction blocks a request:

NodeRestriction Blocks — Error Messages and What They Mean
  ATTEMPT 1: Kubelet on worker-2 tries to label worker-1
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl --as=system:node:worker-2 label node worker-1 test=value
  Error: nodes "worker-1" is forbidden: node "worker-2" is not allowed
  to modify node "worker-1"
  → FIX: Legitimate. The kubelet should NOT touch other nodes.

  ATTEMPT 2: Kubelet on worker-2 tries to evict a pod on worker-3
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl --as=system:node:worker-2 delete pod anihpj-pod --grace-period=0
  Error: pods "anihpj-pod" is forbidden: node "worker-2" is not allowed
  to modify pods not assigned to it
  → FIX: The pod is on worker-3, not worker-2. This is NodeRestriction working correctly.

  ATTEMPT 3: Kubelet tries to set taint with NoSchedule
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl --as=system:node:worker-2 taint node worker-2 dedicated=user:NoSchedule
  Error: node "worker-2" is forbidden: node "worker-2" is not allowed to
  modify taint "dedicated"
  → FIX: Only cluster-admin can modify taints. The kubelet cannot.
