Chapter 14: AppArmor — Application-Level Sandboxing

Imagine a security guard who stands outside every door in a building and checks your badge before letting you through. That's AppArmor — a Linux Security Module (LSM) that sits between every process and the operating system, checking every file access, every network connection, every capability request against a profile that says exactly what that process is allowed to do. Without AppArmor, a compromised container process can read /etc/shadow, write to /proc, open raw network sockets, and access /dev devices. With AppArmor, even a fully compromised Django process in the anihpj container can only read its own application code, write to its media directory, and connect to the PostgreSQL and Redis ports — everything else is blocked at the kernel level before the process ever touches it. This chapter teaches you to write, test, and apply AppArmor profiles — the application-level sandbox that the CKS exam tests alongside Seccomp.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🛡️ Sandboxing 🐧 Linux Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What AppArmor is at the kernel level — how it differs from Seccomp, SELinux, and RBAC
  • ✅ The three AppArmor modes — disabled, complain (audit), and enforce (block) — and when to use each
  • ✅ How to generate AppArmor profiles automatically with aa-genprof and refine them manually
  • ✅ How to write production AppArmor profiles for the anihpj Django and PostgreSQL containers
  • ✅ How to apply AppArmor profiles in Kubernetes — both the annotation method (pre-1.30) and the native securityContext method (1.30+)
  • ✅ How to verify AppArmor is active and blocking violations in running pods
🎓 CKS Relevance
System Hardening 15% Minimize Vulnerabilities 20% Runtime Security 20%
🧠 AppArmor in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test

The CKS exam tests AppArmor in a very specific way. You will NOT be asked to write a complex profile from scratch. You WILL be asked to:

  • Load a profile onto a node: SSH to the node, copy the profile file to /etc/apparmor.d/, run apparmor_parser -a <profile>.
  • Apply a profile to a pod: Add either the annotation (container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<name>: localhost/<profile>) or the securityContext field.
  • Switch a profile between modes: aa-complain for testing, aa-enforce for production. Know the difference cold.
  • Verify the profile is active: aa-status | grep <profile> on the node, or check pod annotations with kubectl describe pod.
  • CRITICAL EXAM FACT: The profile MUST be loaded on EVERY node where the pod CAN run. If you load it on node-01 but the pod schedules on node-02, the pod will fail to start. The exam WILL test this.

14.1 What Is AppArmor and Why Does It Matter for Containers?

AppArmor (Application Armor) is a Linux Security Module (LSM) — a kernel-level framework that enforces mandatory access control (MAC) on processes. Unlike discretionary access control (DAC), where the file owner sets permissions (chmod, chown), MAC is enforced by the kernel and cannot be overridden by the process owner. Even root cannot bypass an AppArmor profile in enforce mode. This makes AppArmor fundamentally different from and complementary to traditional Unix permissions.

The Linux Security Module Landscape — Where AppArmor Fits

Security SystemWhat It ControlsLevelDefault OnProfile LocationCKS Chapter
DAC (Unix Permissions)File ownership and mode bits (rwx)User-spaceAlwaysFile inode metadataCh 13
AppArmorFile paths, network, capabilities, mounts, signalsKernel LSMUbuntu/Debian/etc/apparmor.d/Ch 14 (here)
SELinuxFile labels, process contexts, type enforcementKernel LSMRHEL/CentOSKernel policy storeMentioned here
SeccompSystem calls (syscalls)KernelDocker defaultJSON in pod spec or nodeCh 15
Kubernetes RBACAPI server operations (get, create, delete pods, etc.)K8s APIConfigured per clusterClusterRole/RoleBinding YAMLCh 9

AppArmor vs SELinux — The Two Linux MAC Systems

AppArmor and SELinux are the two major Mandatory Access Control systems in Linux. You need to understand both for the CKS exam because different cloud providers and distributions use different defaults:

🛡️ AppArmor
  • Default on: Ubuntu, Debian, OpenSUSE
  • Model: Path-based — profiles reference filesystem paths (/app/**, /etc/shadow)
  • Profiles: Simple text files in /etc/apparmor.d/
  • Learning curve: Low — paths are intuitive, auto-generation with aa-genprof
  • Granularity: Per-application profiles attached to executables
  • CKS exam: Uses AppArmor on Ubuntu nodes. You WILL encounter it.
🔒 SELinux
  • Default on: RHEL, CentOS, Fedora, Amazon Linux
  • Model: Label-based — every file, process, port, and socket gets a security context label
  • Policies: Complex compiled policy modules — much harder to write manually
  • Learning curve: High — labels are abstract, policy language is verbose
  • Granularity: System-wide policy with type enforcement across all objects
  • CKS exam: SELinux concepts may appear, but hands-on tasks use AppArmor on Ubuntu

The CKS exam uses Ubuntu nodes with AppArmor. If you see SELinux concepts in a question, the same principles apply — it's just a different syntax. Focus on AppArmor for the hands-on tasks.

AppArmor Concept — Before and After (The Security Badge Analogy)

Think of AppArmor like a security clearance badge. Without a badge, you can try to enter any room in the building. With a badge, the guard (the kernel) checks your badge against the room's access list before letting you through. Even if you're the CEO (root), if your badge doesn't list the nuclear reactor room, you don't get in.

AppArmor — The Security Badge System at Kernel Level
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  📦 Container WITHOUT AppArmor (Unconfined)                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Django process (anihpj) can access:                                     │
  │  ❌ /etc/shadow        → Read password hashes (credential theft)         │
  │  ❌ /proc/sysrq-trigger→ Trigger kernel emergency reboots                │
  │  ❌ /dev/sda           → Raw disk access (bypass all filesystem perms)   │
  │  ❌ /proc/1/ns/*       → Access init process namespaces (escape vector)  │
  │  ❌ Raw socket(AF_PACKET)→ Craft malicious network packets               │
  │  ❌ CAP_SYS_ADMIN      → Mount filesystems, load kernel modules          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ANY exploit in Django/Python/postgres → attacker has FULL system access │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                    LOAD APPARMOR PROFILE: aa-enforce anihpj-django
                                   │
                                   ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  📦 Container WITH AppArmor (Enforce) — Only what the badge allows       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Django process (anihpj) can ONLY:                                       │
  │  ✅ /app/** r          → Read its own application code (read-only!)      │
  │  ✅ /app/media/** rw   → Write uploaded files and generated static assets│
  │  ✅ /tmp/** rw         → Write temporary files (session data, uploads)   │
  │  ✅ network tcp        → Make TCP connections (postgres:5432, redis:6379)│
  │  ✅ /usr/bin/python3.* mr → Execute Python interpreter (mapped-read)     │
  │  🚫 EVERYTHING ELSE → DENIED + LOGGED by kernel BEFORE syscall completes │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Even a fully compromised Django process is TRAPPED in this sandbox.     │
  │  It cannot read /etc/shadow. It cannot touch /proc. It cannot escape.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How AppArmor Works at the Kernel Level — The Technical Flow

When a process inside a container tries to perform an operation — say, opening /etc/shadow for reading — the following chain of events occurs at kernel level. Understanding this flow is critical because it shows you exactly WHERE AppArmor blocks attacks and WHY it cannot be bypassed by the process:

Kernel Access Check — What Happens When a Process Tries to Open a File
  PROCESS: open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY)
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. SYSCALL ENTRY — Process calls open() → triggers sys_open()   │
  │     in the Linux kernel. The CPU switches from user mode to      │
  │     kernel mode (ring 0).                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  2. DAC CHECK (Discretionary Access Control) — FIRST             │
  │     • Kernel checks the file's UID/GID against the process's     │
  │       effective UID/GID.                                         │
  │     • Checks the file's mode bits (rwx) for owner/group/other.   │
  │     • If the file is mode 000 and the process is not owner →     │
  │       EACCES (Permission denied) returned immediately.           │
  │     • /etc/shadow is mode 000, owned by root:shadow.             │
  │     • If the process is root (UID 0), DAC PASSES — root can      │
  │       read any file under DAC. ⚡ THIS IS WHY APPARMOR EXISTS.   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼  (DAC passed — process is root)
  │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  3. LSM HOOK — The kernel calls the Linux Security Module hook   │
  │     • The kernel invokes security_file_open() — an LSM hook.     │
  │     • Every registered LSM gets a chance to veto the operation.  │
  │     • AppArmor checks: "Is this process confined by a profile?"  │
  │     • YES → AppArmor checks: "Does the profile allow reading     │
  │              /etc/shadow?"                                       │
  │     • The anihpj-django profile has:                             │
  │       deny /etc/shadow r,     ← ⬅⬅⬅ THIS LINE BLOCKS IT         │
  │     • Result: EACCES (Permission denied)                         │
  │     • Kernel returns -EACCES to the process. The open() syscall  │
  │       fails. The file is never touched. The process gets a       │
  │       "Permission denied" error.                                 │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ⚡ KEY INSIGHT: AppArmor blocks at the LSM hook — AFTER DAC     │
  │     but BEFORE the file is actually opened. Root cannot bypass   │
  │     this because the LSM hook runs in kernel space (ring 0),     │
  │     and the process cannot disable or modify the profile from    │
  │     inside its own confinement.                                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  4. AUDIT LOG — The denied access is logged                      │
  │     • kernel: audit: type=1400 audit(…): apparmor="DENIED"      │
  │       operation="open" profile="anihpj-django"                   │
  │       name="/etc/shadow" pid=12345 comm="python"                 │
  │       requested_mask="r" denied_mask="r"                         │
  │     • This log entry appears in:                                 │
  │       - /var/log/syslog (Ubuntu)                                 │
  │       - /var/log/audit/audit.log (if auditd is running)          │
  │       - journalctl -k | grep apparmor                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  RESULT: The attacker's process gets "Permission denied."
          The kernel logged the attempt.
          The file was never read.
          The attack failed at step 3 of 4.

What AppArmor CAN and CANNOT Protect Against

🟢
What AppArmor CAN Protect
  • ✅ Unauthorized file reads (secrets, configs, /etc/shadow)
  • ✅ Unauthorized file writes (backdoors, malware drops)
  • ✅ Execution of unauthorized binaries (downloaded exploits)
  • ✅ Network connections to unauthorized ports/hosts
  • ✅ Linux capability abuse (CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW)
  • ✅ Mount operations (preventing container escape via mount)
  • ✅ Signal sending (preventing process killing sprees)
  • ✅ Ptrace attach (preventing memory scraping of other processes)
🔴
What AppArmor CANNOT Protect
  • ❌ Kernel exploits that bypass LSMs (rare, high-severity CVEs)
  • ❌ CPU/memory exhaustion (resource DoS — use cgroups instead)
  • ❌ Network bandwidth abuse (use NetworkPolicy or CNI policy)
  • ❌ Application logic flaws (SQL injection, XSS — AppArmor doesn't parse SQL)
  • ❌ Data exfiltration via allowed channels (if the app can connect to postgres, it can exfiltrate data THROUGH postgres)
  • ❌ Side-channel attacks (Spectre, Meltdown — these are hardware bugs)

The takeaway: AppArmor is a filesystem, capability, and network access control system. It is NOT a behavior analysis system. It won't detect that your Django app is suddenly SELECTing all rows from the users table and sending them to an unknown IP — if that IP is reachable via an allowed network rule. That detection is the job of runtime security tools like Falco (Chapter 29). AppArmor + Falco together provide defense-in-depth: AppArmor restricts what the process CAN do; Falco alerts on what it IS doing.

How AppArmor Confinement Survives Container Boundaries

One of the most powerful properties of AppArmor is that its profiles are namespace-agnostic. When a process is confined by an AppArmor profile, that confinement follows the process across namespace boundaries. This means that even if a process inside a container calls unshare() to create new namespaces, setns() to join existing ones, or clone() with the CLONE_NEWNS flag — the AppArmor profile remains attached. The kernel checks the profile at every LSM hook point regardless of which namespaces the process is in.

AppArmor Profile Persistence Across Namespace Transitions
  PROCESS: anihpj-django (PID 12345) confined by "anihpj-django (enforce)"
  │
  ├─ In the container's MOUNT namespace: profile applies to /proc, /sys, /dev
  │  (these are the container's own mounts, not the host's)
  │
  ├─ Process calls unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) → creates a NEW mount namespace
  │  │  The process is NOW in a different mount namespace
  │  │  BUT: the AppArmor profile is still attached to PID 12345
  │  │  The kernel checks: "What profile confines PID 12345?"
  │  │  Answer: anihpj-django (enforce) — SAME profile, SAME rules
  │  │
  │  └─ KEY INSIGHT: AppArmor is attached to the TASK STRUCT (kernel's
  │     representation of the process), not to any namespace. Namespaces
  │     can change, but the task struct's security context stays the same
  │     unless explicitly changed by a privileged operation.
  │
  ├─ Process calls setns() to join a different container's network namespace
  │  │  The process now sees different network interfaces
  │  │  BUT: profile still says "network tcp" only — can't create raw sockets
  │  │  even in the new namespace. Profile rules are namespace-transparent.
  │
  └─ ⚡ CONTRAST WITH SELINUX: SELinux labels are namespace-aware. A process
     in container A has a different SELinux context than container B. AppArmor
     is simpler: the profile is the profile, regardless of context.

AppArmor vs SELinux — The Technical Architecture Difference That Matters

Many engineers treat AppArmor and SELinux as "the same thing, different distro." They are not. The fundamental architectural difference — path-based vs label-based — has profound implications for how you write, debug, and maintain security policies in production:

Architectural AspectAppArmor (Path-Based)SELinux (Label-Based)Why It Matters for K8s
Identity Model"What executable are you?" Profiles match by filesystem path of the binary."What context label do you carry?" Every process, file, port has a type label.In K8s containers, the executable path is known (/usr/bin/python). SELinux labels require RBAC integration — more complex.
File Access Model"What path are you accessing?" Rules use filesystem paths."What label does the target have?" Rules match source type → target type.AppArmor rule /app/** r, is immediately understandable. SELinux allow httpd_t user_home_t:file read; requires label knowledge.
Policy Developmentaa-genprof auto-generates from observed behavior. Edit text file, reload.audit2allow converts denial logs into policy. Compile into module, load into kernel.AppArmor: edit file → reload. SELinux: audit → convert → compile → semodule -i. AppArmor is faster for iteration.
Default PostureAllow what's listed, deny everything else (if in enforce mode). Unprofiled = unconfined.Deny everything by default. Every interaction must be explicitly allowed.SELinux is theoretically more secure (deny-by-default), but AppArmor's simplicity makes it more likely to be used correctly in practice.
K8s StateUbuntu default. CKS exam focus. Annotation + securityContext.RHEL default. Container-selinux policy. seLinuxOptions in securityContext.CKS exam tests AppArmor hands-on. SELinux appears as theory or comparison. Know both, practice AppArmor.

The path-based limitation you must understand: AppArmor identifies files by path. If an attacker creates a hard link from /app/harmless.txt to /etc/shadow, AppArmor evaluates the access against /app/harmless.txt — the path being opened — NOT /etc/shadow — the actual inode. However, the hard link can only be created if the profile allows writing to /app/ AND the filesystem is on the same partition, AND the attacker has permissions. This is why the profile has /app/** r, (read-only) — preventing writes that could be used to create such links. This is also why the explicit deny /etc/shadow r, rule exists: even if an attacker somehow opens /etc/shadow through an alias path, the explicit deny catches it.

14.2 AppArmor Modes — Disabled, Complain, Enforce

AppArmor profiles can operate in three distinct modes, and choosing the wrong mode in the wrong context is the difference between "my application mysteriously broke" and "my application is secure." The CKS exam expects you to know exactly what each mode does, when to use it, and — most critically — how to switch between modes without disrupting running workloads.

The Three Modes — Visual Comparison

ModeProfile Loaded?Violations Blocked?Violations Logged?Use CaseCommand
Disabled / Unconfined❌ No profile❌ Nothing blocked❌ Nothing loggedProcesses without a profile. The default for most containers.aa-disable <profile>
Complain (Learning)✅ Profile loaded❌ NOT blocked✅ Everything loggedProfile development — let the app run normally, collect ALL access patterns, then refine the profile.aa-complain <profile>
Enforce (Blocking)✅ Profile loaded✅ ALL violations blocked✅ Denials loggedProduction — the profile blocks everything not explicitly allowed. This is the goal state.aa-enforce <profile>

The AppArmor Profile Lifecycle — From Zero to Production

Creating an AppArmor profile is not a one-step process. It's a five-stage lifecycle that starts with automatic generation and ends with a production-hardened, enforce-mode profile applied to every pod. The CKS exam tests your understanding of this lifecycle — especially the transition from complain to enforce.

The Complete AppArmor Profile Lifecycle — Zero to Production in 5 Stages
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 1: GENERATE (auto-profile in complain mode)                      │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────                     │
  │  $ aa-genprof /usr/bin/python3                                          │
  │  → Starts profiling mode: launches the app, monitors ALL file,          │
  │    network, capability, and signal accesses the app makes.              │
  │  → As the app runs, aa-genprof records every access pattern.            │
  │  → When done (Ctrl+C or exit app), writes a draft profile to            │
  │    /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.python3 (auto-generated name).              │
  │  → The draft profile is LOADED in COMPLAIN mode automatically.          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 2: TEST in COMPLAIN mode (log violations, don't block)           │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────              │
  │  $ aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django                            │
  │  → Run the application through its NORMAL workflow: handle HTTP         │
  │    requests, connect to database, read/write files, serve static assets │
  │  → Meanwhile, monitor the logs for AppArmor events:                    │
  │    $ journalctl -k | grep apparmor | grep ALLOWED                       │
  │    (In complain mode, violations are tagged "ALLOWED" — meaning AppArmor│
  │     saw the access, would have blocked it in enforce mode, but let it   │
  │     through because we're in complain.)                                  │
  │  → These ALLOWED events are your TODO list: add them to the profile.    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 3: REFINE (iterate on the profile based on logs)                 │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────                     │
  │  Edit /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django and add:                            │
  │    • Paths that the app legitimately needs to access                    │
  │    • Network rules for database, cache, and API connections             │
  │    • Capabilities the app requires (rare — most apps need none)         │
  │  $ apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django  # Reload profile  │
  │  → Repeat STAGE 2-3 until no new ALLOWED events appear in logs.        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 4: ENFORCE (block violations — production mode)                  │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────                │
  │  $ aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django                             │
  │  → Profile now blocks everything not explicitly allowed.                │
  │  → Monitor logs for DENIED events (these are actual blocks):           │
  │    $ journalctl -k | grep apparmor | grep DENIED                        │
  │  → If the app breaks, check DENIED events → the app needed something   │
  │    you didn't add to the profile. Go back to STAGE 2, add it.          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 5: DEPLOY to Kubernetes (load on ALL nodes, apply to pods)      │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────       │
  │  • Copy profile to EVERY node: scp anihpj-django node-0X:/etc/apparmor.d/│
  │  • Load on EVERY node: ssh node-0X apparmor_parser -a anihpj-django     │
  │  • Apply to pod via annotation or securityContext (see 14.4)            │
  │  • Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/self/attr/current          │
  │    → Should show: anihpj-django (enforce)                               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Checking AppArmor Status — Essential Commands

Bash — AppArmor status, profile management, and log inspection 
# ── CHECK APPARMOR STATUS ──
aa-status
# Output shows:
#   apparmor module is loaded.
#   23 profiles are loaded.
#   18 profiles are in enforce mode.
#   5 profiles are in complain mode.
#   3 processes have profiles defined.

# ── LIST ALL LOADED PROFILES ──
aa-status | grep -E '^\s+\S+'
# Shows each profile name and its mode:
#   /usr/sbin/sshd (enforce)
#   anihpj-django (complain)

# ── CHECK A SPECIFIC PROFILE ──
aa-status | grep anihpj-django
# Output: anihpj-django (enforce)

# ── LOAD A NEW PROFILE ──
apparmor_parser -a /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
# -a = add/load the profile into the kernel

# ── RELOAD A MODIFIED PROFILE ──
apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
# -r = replace the currently-loaded profile with the updated file

# ── UNLOAD A PROFILE ──
apparmor_parser -R /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
# -R = remove the profile from kernel memory

# ── SWITCH A PROFILE TO COMPLAIN MODE ──
aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django

# ── SWITCH A PROFILE TO ENFORCE MODE ──
aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django

# ── DISABLE A PROFILE (unconfine the process) ──
aa-disable /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django

# ── VIEW APPARMOR LOGS (violations) ──
journalctl -k | grep apparmor
# Look for:
#   apparmor="ALLOWED" → complain mode, would be blocked in enforce
#   apparmor="DENIED"  → enforce mode, actually blocked

# ── CHECK IF APPARMOR IS ENABLED IN THE KERNEL ──
cat /sys/module/apparmor/parameters/enabled
# Y = enabled, N = disabled

# ── CHECK A RUNNING PROCESS'S APPARMOR PROFILE ──
cat /proc/$(pgrep -f gunicorn)/attr/current
# Output: anihpj-django (enforce)
# OR: unconfined (no profile)

The Complain-to-Enforce Transition — A Real-World Scenario

🟡 SCENARIO: Deploying an AppArmor Profile for anihpj Django

You've generated a profile with aa-genprof. It's currently in complain mode. The Django app is running fine. The logs show 47 ALLOWED events over the past hour — all legitimate file accesses that Django, Gunicorn, or Python libraries need. You've added them all to the profile. Now it's time to switch to enforce mode.

What you do:

  1. aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django — switch to blocking mode on one node first
  2. Run kubectl rollout restart deployment/anihpj-django — restart the pods on this node
  3. Watch the logs: journalctl -k -f | grep apparmor
  4. If you see DENIED events → the app needed something you missed. Your options:
    • If it's a legitimate access: Add the path/capability to the profile, reload with apparmor_parser -r, switch back to enforce
    • If it's NOT legitimate: The profile is working! The app should handle the Permission Denied error gracefully.
  5. If NO denied events after 30 minutes of normal traffic → profile is ready for production. Deploy to all nodes.

Common mistake: Switching to enforce mode on ALL nodes at once. If you missed a required access, ALL pods break simultaneously. Always test on ONE node first.

What Actually Happens in the Kernel — Complain Mode vs Enforce Mode

The difference between complain and enforce is not just "log vs block." There is a specific kernel code path that diverges based on the profile mode. Understanding this divergence explains why complain mode is safe for testing and why enforce mode cannot be bypassed:

Kernel Code Path — The Exact Difference Between Complain and Enforce
  PROCESS: open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY)
  │
  ▼
  DAC CHECK → passed (process is root)
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LSM HOOK: security_file_open() — AppArmor's apparmor_file_open() runs  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Step A: Look up the task's current profile from the task_struct        │
  │          → Found: "anihpj-django" (profile pointer in kernel memory)    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Step B: Walk the profile's file rules DFA (Deterministic Finite        │
  │          Automaton). AppArmor compiles path rules into a DFA at load     │
  │          time for O(1) path matching.                                    │
  │          → Match: "/etc/shadow" matches rule "deny /etc/shadow r,"      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Step C: Check the PROFILE MODE (this is where it diverges):            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─ IF MODE == COMPLAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  • Profile says "deny /etc/shadow r," but mode is COMPLAIN.       │  │
  │  │  • AppArmor does NOT return -EACCES to the kernel.                │  │
  │  │  • Instead, it generates an audit message with "apparmor=ALLOWED" │  │
  │  │    (meaning: "I would have blocked this if I were in enforce").   │  │
  │  │  • Returns 0 (success) to the LSM hook.                           │  │
  │  │  • The kernel proceeds to actually open the file.                 │  │
  │  │  • RESULT: File opened SUCCESSFULLY. Log entry created.           │  │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─ IF MODE == ENFORCE ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  • Profile says "deny /etc/shadow r," and mode is ENFORCE.        │  │
  │  │  • AppArmor generates an audit message with "apparmor=DENIED"     │  │
  │  │    (meaning: "I blocked this access").                            │  │
  │  │  • Returns -EACCES (Permission denied) to the LSM hook.           │  │
  │  │  • The kernel sees the non-zero return and ABORTS the open().     │  │
  │  │  • The syscall returns -1 with errno = EACCES to the process.     │  │
  │  │  • RESULT: File NOT opened. Process gets "Permission denied."     │  │
  │  │  • The inode is NEVER touched. The file is NEVER read.            │  │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CRITICAL INSIGHT FOR CKS:
  ─────────────────────────
  When you run aa-genprof or aa-complain, the profile is LOADED into the
  kernel with MODE=COMPLAIN. The DFA is built. The rule engine is active.
  But the return value from the LSM hook is always 0 (allow).

  When you run aa-enforce, the profile mode is TOGGLED to ENFORCE. The
  SAME DFA is used. The SAME rules are checked. The ONLY difference is
  that the return value is now -EACCES for denied operations.

  This is why the transition from complain to enforce is SAFE: the rules
  don't change. Only the enforcement behavior changes.

Profile Inheritance — How Child Processes Get Their Profiles

When a process with an AppArmor profile spawns a child process (via fork() + exec()), what profile does the child get? This is controlled by execute permissions in the parent's profile — specifically the difference between ix, Px, Cx, and Ux:

Execute PermissionChild Process ProfileWhen to UseRisk Level
/usr/bin/python ix,Inherit — child gets the SAME profile as parentGunicorn spawning worker processes — all workers share the Django sandbox🟢 Safe — same confinement
/usr/bin/postgres Px,Profile transition — child switches to its OWN profile (must exist)Running a different application with different security needs🟢 Safe — if profile exists
/usr/bin/helper Cx,Child profile — child gets a SUB-profile of the parent (parent//child naming)Fine-grained sub-confinement for specific child processes🟢 Safe — explicit sub-profile
/bin/bash Ux,Unconfined — child runs with NO profile at all⚠️ Almost never appropriate for K8s containers🔴 DANGEROUS — breaks containment

For Kubernetes containers, the most common scenario is ix (inherit). Your Django container runs Gunicorn as PID 1. Gunicorn forks worker processes to handle HTTP requests. All workers inherit the same AppArmor profile — they're all confined identically. You don't need separate profiles for each Gunicorn worker. The flags=(attach_disconnected) setting in the profile header ensures that even if a process detaches from its parent (becomes a daemon), the AppArmor profile remains attached.

AppArmor Profile Workflow — From Zero to Enforce

Complete AppArmor Profile Lifecycle — Generate → Test → Enforce → Verify
  STEP 1: GENERATE (auto-profile in complain mode)
  $ aa-genprof /usr/bin/python3
  → Runs app, records all file/network/cap accesses
  → Writes draft profile to /etc/apparmor.d/

  STEP 2: TEST in COMPLAIN mode (log violations, don't block)
  $ aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
  → Run anihpj normally, check syslog for denied events
  $ journalctl -k | grep apparmor | grep ALLOWED
  → Add needed paths/permissions to the profile

  STEP 3: ENFORCE (block violations)
  $ aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
  → Profile now active: violations → blocked + logged

  STEP 4: VERIFY profile loaded on all K8s nodes
  $ ssh node01 aa-status | grep anihpj-django
  → Should show: anihpj-django (enforce)

  STEP 5: APPLY to Kubernetes pod spec
  securityContext:
    appArmorProfile:
      type: Localhost
      localhostProfile: anihpj-django

  🔑 CKS EXAM PATTERN: The exam tests whether you know the profile
     MUST exist on the node BEFORE the pod is created. If you create
     the pod first, it will be stuck in ContainerCreating because the
     container runtime cannot find the profile. Always: node first,
     then pod.

AppArmor Modes Compared — When to Use Each

ModeBehaviourUse CaseCKS Notes
disabledNo AppArmor for this process. No restrictions whatsoever.None — never use in production.Some distributions ship with AppArmor disabled by default. Always check: aa-status
complainLogs violations to syslog/journalctl. Does NOT block them.Profile development: learn what your app actually accesses without breaking it.Use aa-genprof to auto-generate, then test in complain mode for 24-48 hours.
enforceBlocks ALL actions not explicitly allowed by the profile.Production. Every pod should have an enforcing profile.Once a profile passes complain testing, switch to enforce. Monitor for new denials after app updates.

14.3 Writing AppArmor Profiles for anihpj

An AppArmor profile is a plain text file that declares what a specific application is allowed to do. The syntax is straightforward — you specify file paths with permissions, network rules for protocols, and capability rules for Linux capabilities. Let's build profiles for the two critical containers in the anihpj stack: the Django/Gunicorn application and the PostgreSQL database.

Profile Anatomy — Understanding Every Directive

DirectiveSyntaxWhat It DoesExample
#include#include <file>Imports shared rules from another file (abstractions)#include <abstractions/base>
File permission/path/** rwklmGrants access to files matching the path glob/app/** r, (read-only for all files under /app)
Deny ruledeny /path/** rwExplicitly denies access — overrides broader allow rulesdeny /etc/shadow r,
Network rulenetwork <family> <type>Allows specific network protocol familiesnetwork tcp, network udp,
Capabilitycapability <name>,Grants a specific Linux capabilitycapability net_bind_service,
Mount rulemount, or deny mount,Allows or denies filesystem mount operationsdeny mount,
Signal rulesignal <set> <sig>,Controls which signals a process can sendsignal (receive) peer=unconfined,
Ptrace ruleptrace,Allows or denies process tracing (debugging)deny ptrace,
File Permission Flags Explained
r
Read

Allow reading file contents. Required for loading code, config files, libraries.

w
Write

Allow writing/modifying files. Only grant to directories that actually need writes (media/, tmp/, logs/).

m
Memory-Map

Allow mmap() with PROT_EXEC. Required for loading shared libraries (.so files). Use mr for library dirs.

k
Lock

Allow file locking (flock). Rarely needed for web apps. Usually safe to omit.

l
Link

Allow creating hard links. Needed by package managers (pip, npm). Not needed at runtime.

ix
Inherit-Execute

Execute the binary but keep the current profile. Use for child processes that should share the sandbox.

Px
Profile-Execute

Execute the binary with its OWN profile. Use for child processes that need a different sandbox.

Ux
Unconfined-Execute

Execute the binary with NO profile. ⚠️ Dangerous — avoid if possible.

AppArmor Profile for anihpj Django/Gunicorn

AppArmor Profile — /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# APPARMOR PROFILE: anihpj-django
# Purpose: Sandbox the Django/Gunicorn application process
# Applies to: anihpj Django container running Gunicorn
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

#include 

profile anihpj-django flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  # ── INCLUDE SHARED ABSTRACTIONS ──
  #include 
  #include 
  #include 
  #include      # DNS resolution

  # ── APPLICATION CODE (READ ONLY) ──
  /app/**                        r,      # Django source code, templates, static files
  /usr/lib/python3*/**           mr,     # Python standard library (need mmap for .so)
  /usr/local/lib/python3*/**     mr,     # pip-installed packages (Django, Gunicorn, etc.)

  # ── WRITABLE DIRECTORIES (only where app legitimately writes) ──
  /app/media/**                  rw,     # User-uploaded files (profile pics, documents)
  /app/staticfiles/**            rw,     # Collected static files (Django collectstatic)
  /tmp/**                        rw,     # Temporary files (session data, upload staging)

  # ── NETWORK (only the ports anihpj actually uses) ──
  network tcp,                           # TCP for PostgreSQL, Redis, HTTP responses
  # Do NOT grant network udp unless the app uses UDP (Django doesn't)

  # ── EXPLICIT DENIALS (belt-and-suspenders) ──
  deny /etc/shadow               r,      # Password hashes — NEVER accessible
  deny /etc/kubernetes/**        r,      # K8s configs, kubeconfig, certs
  deny /proc/**                  rw,     # Kernel interfaces — escape vector
  deny /sys/**                   rw,     # Kernel sysfs — escape vector
  deny /dev/**                   rw,     # Devices — escape vector
  deny /root/**                  rw,     # Root home directory
  deny /var/log/**               w,      # Write to system logs (use stdout/stderr)
  deny mount,                            # Cannot mount filesystems (escape vector)
  deny ptrace,                           # Cannot attach debugger to other processes
  deny capability sys_admin,              # Cannot mount, swapon, etc.
  deny capability sys_ptrace,            # Cannot use ptrace at all
  deny capability net_raw,               # Cannot create raw sockets
  deny capability sys_module,            # Cannot load kernel modules
}

AppArmor Profile for PostgreSQL (anihpj Database)

AppArmor Profile — /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-postgres 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# APPARMOR PROFILE: anihpj-postgres
# Purpose: Sandbox the PostgreSQL database process
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

#include 

profile anihpj-postgres flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include 
  #include 

  # ── POSTGRESQL BINARIES (execute only — read mapped) ──
  /usr/lib/postgresql/**/bin/postgres    mr,
  /usr/lib/postgresql/**/bin/*            mr,
  /usr/lib/postgresql/**/lib/**           mr,

  # ── DATA DIRECTORY (the only place postgres writes) ──
  /var/lib/postgresql/data/**            rw,
  /var/lib/postgresql/data/pg_wal/**     rw,
  /var/lib/postgresql/data/pg_log/**     rw,

  # ── TEMP AND CONFIG (minimal writes) ──
  /tmp/**                                 rw,
  /etc/postgresql/**                      r,
  /run/postgresql/**                      rw,

  # ── NETWORK (only PostgreSQL port) ──
  network tcp,                            # Listen on 5432, connect to replicas

  # ── REQUIRED CAPABILITIES ──
  capability ipc_lock,                    # Shared memory for connections
  capability sys_nice,                    # CPU priority adjustment

  # ── EXPLICIT DENIALS ──
  deny /etc/shadow               r,
  deny /etc/kubernetes/**        r,
  deny /proc/**                  rw,
  deny /sys/**                   rw,
  deny mount,
  deny ptrace,
  deny capability sys_admin,
  deny capability net_raw,
}

Loading Profiles to Nodes and Applying to Pods

Bash — Deploying AppArmor profiles to all nodes in the cluster 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DEPLOY APPARMOR PROFILES to ALL K8s NODES
# Profiles MUST be on every node before pods can use them
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PROFILES=("anihpj-django" "anihpj-postgres")
NODES=($(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}'))

for NODE in "${NODES[@]}"; do
    echo "=== Deploying profiles to node: $NODE ==="

    # STEP 1: Copy profile files to the node
    for PROFILE in "${PROFILES[@]}"; do
        scp /path/to/profiles/${PROFILE} root@${NODE}:/etc/apparmor.d/${PROFILE}
    done

    # STEP 2: Load each profile into the kernel
    for PROFILE in "${PROFILES[@]}"; do
        ssh root@${NODE} "apparmor_parser -a /etc/apparmor.d/${PROFILE}"
    done

    # STEP 3: Set all profiles to enforce mode
    for PROFILE in "${PROFILES[@]}"; do
        ssh root@${NODE} "aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/${PROFILE}"
    done

    # STEP 4: Verify profiles are loaded and in enforce mode
    ssh root@${NODE} "aa-status | grep -E '${PROFILES[0]}|${PROFILES[1]}'"
done

echo "✅ All profiles deployed to all nodes"

Profile Abstractions — The Shared Building Blocks That Save You Hours

AppArmor abstractions are reusable, pre-written rule sets that you include in your profiles. Instead of writing 50 lines of rules to allow basic C library operations, DNS resolution, or SSL certificate access, you include one line like #include <abstractions/base>. The CKS exam expects you to know which abstractions exist and when to use them — you don't need to memorize their contents, but you should know what each one covers:

📚
abstractions/base

The foundation. Allows reading /etc/ld.so.cache, /proc/filesystems, /proc/meminfo, basic device access to /dev/null, /dev/zero, /dev/random, /dev/urandom, and terminal I/O. Every profile should include this. Without it, your app can't even read shared library caches.

🐍
abstractions/python

Allows Python to function: read /usr/lib/python3*/** with mr (mapped-read), execute /usr/bin/python3*, access Python bytecode cache directories, and use Python's ctypes FFI library. Always include for Django/Gunicorn/Flask containers.

🔒
abstractions/ssl_certs

Allows reading TLS/SSL certificates from system trust stores: /etc/ssl/certs/, /usr/share/ca-certificates/, /etc/ca-certificates.conf. Include for any container that makes HTTPS connections (database TLS, external APIs, OAuth).

🌐
abstractions/nameservice

Enables DNS resolution: read /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/hosts, connect to systemd-resolved or nscd sockets. Without this, your app cannot resolve DNS names. Pods that need to reach services by name MUST have this.

💾
abstractions/postgresql

PostgreSQL-specific: access to data directory paths, shared memory, lock files. Use for PostgreSQL containers instead of writing all those rules manually.

🔧
Custom Abstractions

You can create your own abstractions in /etc/apparmor.d/abstractions/. Useful for organization-wide shared rules: "all our Django apps need these 10 paths" → one abstraction, included everywhere.

To see what an abstraction actually contains: cat /etc/apparmor.d/abstractions/base. Each abstraction is just a text file with AppArmor rules — no magic. If an abstraction grants too much access for your security requirements, don't include it; write your own more restrictive rules instead.

Multi-Process Applications — How Gunicorn Workers, Celery Tasks, and Cron Jobs Stay Confined

Modern web applications are not single-process. Django under Gunicorn spawns multiple worker processes. Celery spawns task workers. Cron jobs spawn short-lived processes. Each of these must remain confined by the AppArmor profile. Here's how the mechanics work for each case:

Process Tree Confinement — Every Child Stays in the Sandbox
  PID 1: gunicorn (confined: anihpj-django enforce)
  │
  ├─ PID 12: gunicorn worker (confined: anihpj-django enforce) ── ix
  │    │  Gunicorn master forks workers with execve("/usr/bin/python", ...)
  │    │  Profile rule: /usr/bin/python3.* ix,  ← inherit profile
  │    │  Worker gets the SAME profile. Same restrictions apply.
  │    │
  │    ├─ HTTP request → opens /app/media/upload.jpg → ALLOWED (rule: /app/media/** rw)
  │    └─ HTTP request → opens /etc/shadow → DENIED (rule: deny /etc/shadow r)
  │
  ├─ PID 13: gunicorn worker (confined: anihpj-django enforce) ── ix
  │
  ├─ PID 14: celery worker (confined: anihpj-django enforce) ── ix
  │    │  Celery also runs under Python. Same binary, same path.
  │    │  Profile rule: /usr/bin/python3.* ix,  ← inherit profile
  │    │  KEY: If Celery needs to write to /var/run/celery/, that path MUST
  │    │  be in the profile or the worker will crash on startup.
  │
  └─ PID 15: cron (confined: anihpj-django enforce) ── ix
       │  Cron runs manage.py commands. Same Python binary.
       │  BUT: cron jobs often need different permissions than web workers.
       │  Example: a cleanup cron job needs to delete old files from /app/media/
       │  If the profile only allows 'r' on /app/media/, the delete will fail.
       │
       │  SOLUTION: Use Cx (child profile) for processes that need different perms:
       │  /usr/bin/python3.* Cx -> anihpj-django//cron
       │  profile anihpj-django//cron { ... }  ← separate sub-profile for cron

  ⚡ THE attach_disconnected FLAG — CRITICAL FOR CONTAINERS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  In containers, PID 1 (the entrypoint) is the profile attachment point.
  When PID 1 forks a child that calls setsid() (becomes a session leader,
  common for daemonized processes), the child disconnects from the parent's
  process group. Without `flags=(attach_disconnected)`, AppArmor loses track
  of the child and it becomes UNCONFINED.

  With `flags=(attach_disconnected)`:
  • AppArmor follows the process through setsid() and daemon() calls
  • The kernel maintains the profile reference even after the process
    detaches from its parent's session
  • Every descendant of the original confined process stays confined

  This flag is ESSENTIAL for containers running Gunicorn (which daemonizes
  workers), Celery (which daemonizes task processors), or any multi-process
  Python application.

AppArmor Troubleshooting — When Your Profile Breaks the App

SymptomLikely CauseDiagnosis Command
Pod stuck in ContainerCreatingAppArmor profile does not exist on the node the pod was scheduled to.kubectl describe pod <name> → look for "cannot load profile" in Events. SSH to that node: ls /etc/apparmor.d/ — is the profile file there?
App crashes with "Permission denied"Profile is in enforce mode and blocking a legitimate operation. The app needs more paths/permissions.Switch to complain mode temporarily: aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/profile-name. Check syslog: journalctl -k | grep apparmor | grep DENIED. Add the denied path to the profile.
AppArmor not applied to podAnnotation typo or securityContext misconfiguration. The container runtime silently ignores unknown profiles.Check pod annotations: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'. For securityContext: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext}'.
Profile works on node A but not node BProfile was only loaded on one node. AppArmor profiles must be present on EVERY node where the pod could run.SSH to each worker: aa-status | grep profile-name. Use a DaemonSet to distribute profiles, or include them in your node provisioning (Terraform, Ansible).

14.4 Applying AppArmor in Kubernetes

Once your AppArmor profile is loaded on every node, you need to tell Kubernetes to attach that profile to your pod's containers. There are two ways to do this — the old annotation method (pre-1.30, still widely used and almost certainly on the CKS exam) and the new native securityContext method (1.30+). You must know BOTH.

Method Comparison — Annotation vs securityContext

FeatureAnnotation Method (pre-1.30)securityContext Method (1.30+)
Where definedmetadata.annotations in pod specspec.containers[].securityContext
GranularityPer containerPer container
Annotation keycontainer.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container-name>N/A — native field
Value formatlocalhost/<profile-name> or runtime/default or unconfinedNested object: type: Localhost, localhostProfile: <name>
StatusBeta (but stable in practice — on exam)GA in 1.30
CKS Exam✅ DEFINITELY tested — most clusters are pre-1.30⚠️ May appear — know the syntax

Method 1: Annotation-Based (Pre-1.30) — CKS Exam Primary

YAML — anihpj Django deployment with AppArmor via annotation 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-django
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-django
      annotations:
        # ⬅⬅⬅ APPARMOR VIA ANNOTATION (pre-1.30 method)
        # Format: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/: 
        #  can be:
        #   localhost/  → use a custom profile loaded on the node
        #   runtime/default      → use the container runtime's default AppArmor profile
        #   unconfined           → no AppArmor profile (INSECURE — avoid)
        container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj: localhost/anihpj-django
    spec:
      # ⚠️ IMPORTANT: The node must have the profile loaded at /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
      # BEFORE this pod is scheduled. If the profile doesn't exist, the pod fails to start.
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

Method 2: Native securityContext (1.30+) — Future-Proof

YAML — anihpj Django deployment with AppArmor via securityContext (1.30+) 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-django
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-django
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          # ⬅⬅⬅ APPARMOR VIA securityContext (1.30+ native field)
          appArmorProfile:
            type: Localhost                # Localhost | RuntimeDefault | Unconfined
            localhostProfile: anihpj-django # Profile name (must be loaded on node)

Verifying AppArmor Is Active in Running Pods

Bash — Multiple methods to verify AppArmor profile is applied and working 
# ── METHOD 1: Check pod annotation (for annotation-based profiles) ──
kubectl get pod -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-django \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.annotations}' | jq .
# Look for: "container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj"
# Value should be: "localhost/anihpj-django"

# ── METHOD 2: Check process's current AppArmor context INSIDE the container ──
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-django -- cat /proc/self/attr/current
# Output: anihpj-django (enforce)
# OR: unconfined (NO PROFILE — investigate immediately!)
# OR: anihpj-django (complain) (profile loaded but NOT blocking)

# ── METHOD 3: Check from the NODE (more reliable) ──
NODE=$(kubectl get pod -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-django -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.nodeName}')
ssh $NODE "aa-status | grep anihpj-django"
# Output: anihpj-django (enforce)

# ── METHOD 4: Check ALL pods' AppArmor status cluster-wide ──
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] |
  select(.metadata.annotations."container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/" != null) |
  "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name): \(.metadata.annotations)"'

# ── METHOD 5: Verify AppArmor is actually BLOCKING violations ──
# On a node running the pod:
journalctl -k --since "5 minutes ago" | grep apparmor | grep DENIED
# If you see DENIED entries for anihpj-django → profile is actively blocking
# If you see ALLOWED entries for anihpj-django → profile is in COMPLAIN mode
# (violations logged but NOT blocked — switch to enforce!)

Common AppArmor Mistakes on the CKS Exam — And How to Avoid Them

⚠️
Profile Not on All Nodes

You loaded the profile on node-01, but the pod scheduled on node-02. Result: pod stays in ContainerCreating forever. Fix: Copy profile to ALL nodes before deploying the pod. Use a DaemonSet or node bootstrap script to ensure profiles are present on every node.

⚠️
Wrong Annotation Name

You wrote container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj-django but the container is named anihpj. Result: AppArmor profile silently not applied. The container runs unconfined. Fix: The container name in the annotation must match spec.containers[].name exactly.

⚠️
Forgot to Switch to Enforce

Profile loaded with apparmor_parser -a, but never ran aa-enforce. Result: Profile defaults to complain mode. Violations are logged but NOT blocked. You think you're protected, but you're not. Fix: Always check with aa-status — it shows the mode next to each profile name.

Troubleshooting AppArmor Denials — A Systematic Debugging Workflow

When you apply an AppArmor profile and your application breaks, don't panic. AppArmor denials are deterministic — the profile says exactly what's allowed, and the kernel enforces exactly that. There is no "sometimes it works." If an operation is denied, the profile doesn't allow it. The debugging workflow is systematic:

1
CHECK THE MODE — Is the profile in enforce?

aa-status | grep anihpj-django
If it says (complain), that's why denials aren't being logged as DENIED — switch to enforce. If it says (enforce), continue to step 2.

2
FIND THE DENIAL — What exactly was blocked?

journalctl -k --since "5 min ago" | grep apparmor | grep DENIED
Each line shows: the profile name, the operation (open, mkdir, connect), the target path/port, and the PID. This is your exact TODO list.

3
CLASSIFY THE DENIAL — Legitimate or malicious?

Is the blocked path part of normal application behavior (e.g., Python reading a .pyc file) or is it suspicious (e.g., reading /etc/shadow)? Legitimate = add to profile. Suspicious = the profile is working — investigate the application.

4
ADD THE RULE — Grant the needed access

Edit /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django, add the path/permission, reload: apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django. The reload is atomic — existing processes keep their current profile until their next exec(). Restart the pod to pick up the new profile.

5
REPRODUCE AND VERIFY — The denial should disappear

Trigger the same operation. Check journalctl -k again — the previously denied operation should now succeed silently (no audit entry = allowed). If it's still denied, check your path syntax — glob patterns can be tricky.

Common auditing gotcha: Not all AppArmor events go to journalctl -k. If auditd is installed and running, denials may go to /var/log/audit/audit.log instead. Check both. On systems without auditd, AppArmor uses the kernel's standard audit subsystem which routes through journald. The CKS exam environment typically uses journald — no auditd installed — so journalctl -k is your primary debugging tool.

What Happens When AppArmor Blocks Pod Startup — The ContainerCreating Nightmare

This is the most painful AppArmor failure mode — and the one the CKS exam loves to test. When you reference an AppArmor profile that doesn't exist on the node, or when the profile blocks the container's entrypoint from even starting, the pod gets stuck in ContainerCreating state. There is no obvious error message on kubectl describe pod. Here's exactly what happens and how to diagnose it:

AppArmor Pod Startup Failure — The Complete Failure Chain
  kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml
  │
  ▼
  API SERVER: Pod created → assigned to node-02 → spec sent to kubelet
  │
  ▼
  KUBELET on node-02 receives the pod spec:
  │
  ├─ Reads annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj:
  │  localhost/anihpj-django
  │
  ├─ CHECKS: Does /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django exist on this node?
  │  │
  │  ├─ YES → Proceed to create container. Apply profile via runc/containerd.
  │  │
  │  └─ NO → ⚡ pod.status.phase = Pending
  │           pod.status.conditions[].reason = "AppArmorProfileNotFound"
  │           Event: "Warning  Failed  Cannot enforce AppArmor: profile
  │                   "anihpj-django" is not loaded on the node"
  │           The kubelet RETRIES every few seconds. The pod stays in
  │           ContainerCreating FOREVER until you fix it.
  │
  ├─ ALTERNATIVE: Profile EXISTS on node and IS loaded, but entrypoint
  │  is BLOCKED by the profile.
  │  │
  │  └─ Container runtime (containerd/runc) calls execve() on entrypoint.
  │     AppArmor checks: is this execution allowed?
  │     If NOT allowed (missing Px/ix rule for the binary):
  │     → Container starts, entrypoint gets EACCES
  │     → Entrypoint crashes immediately (exit code 126 or 1)
  │     → Container enters CrashLoopBackOff
  │     → kubectl describe pod shows: "Error: container create failed:
  │       cannot enforce AppArmor profile"
  │     → kubectl logs shows: "Permission denied" on the entrypoint binary
  │
  └─ DIAGNOSIS CHECKLIST:
     1. kubectl describe pod → look for events mentioning "AppArmor"
     2. kubectl get events -n anihpj --field-selector involvedObject.name=
     3. ssh to the node: aa-status | grep anihpj-django  (profile loaded?)
     4. ssh to the node: cat /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django  (profile exists?)
     5. If profile loaded but pod failing: check the entrypoint binary path
        against the profile's execution rules.

The exam trap: You'll be asked to apply an AppArmor profile to a pod. You create the pod, and it stays in ContainerCreating. You check everything — the YAML is correct, the annotation is correct. But you forgot to copy the profile to all nodes. The pod scheduled on node-03, and you only loaded the profile on node-01. The fix: copy the profile to ALL nodes, or use nodeSelector to pin the pod to the node that has the profile. For the exam, copying to all nodes is the expected answer.

📊 Chapter 14 Visual Summary — AppArmor at a Glance

🔍
AppArmor Basics (14.1)

What: Linux Security Module (LSM) for per-process file/network/capability control
Where: Kernel-level — cannot be bypassed by root
Default: Ubuntu/Debian
Exam: Profile paths, permissions (r/w/m/k/l), abstractions

🔄
Three Modes (14.2)

Disabled: No profile — insecure
Complain: Logs violations, doesn't block — for profile development
Enforce: Blocks ALL violations — production mode
Key command: aa-enforce <profile>

✍️
Writing Profiles (14.3)

Tool: aa-genprof for auto-generation
Refine: Check logs, add paths, reload, repeat
Key files: /etc/apparmor.d/
anihpj profiles: Django + PostgreSQL with deny rules

🚀
Kubernetes (14.4)

Method 1: Annotation (pre-1.30, exam primary)
Method 2: securityContext (1.30+)
Critical: Profile MUST be on EVERY node
Verify: cat /proc/self/attr/current in container

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

AppArmor tasks on the CKS exam follow a five-step workflow: (1) SSH to the node, copy the profile to /etc/apparmor.d/, (2) load it with apparmor_parser -a, (3) set to enforce mode with aa-enforce, (4) apply to the pod via annotation or securityContext, (5) verify with kubectl exec -- cat /proc/self/attr/current. Never skip step 1: if the profile isn't on the node BEFORE the pod is created, the pod will fail. Also: the annotation method uses the container name, not the pod name. If your container is named anihpj but your annotation says anihpj-django, AppArmor will silently not apply — and the container will run unconfined without any warning.

🔧 Under the Hood — AppArmor Profile Syntax Deep Dive: File Rules, Capability Rules, Network Rules — Complete Annotated Reference 
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   APPARMOR PROFILE ANATOMY — Every Rule Type Explained                     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  profile anihpj-apparmor flags=(attach_disconnected,mediate_deleted) {   │
  │    #include <abstractions/base>    ← Basic filesystem + network access   │
  │                                                                           │
  │    # FILE RULES: r=read, w=write, m=memory-map, x=execute, ix=inherit    │
  │    /app/**              r,        ← Read all app files (recursive)        │
  │    /tmp/**              rw,       ← Read+Write temp files                 │
  │    /usr/bin/python3     rix,      ← Execute Python (inherit profile)      │
  │    deny /etc/shadow     r,        ← EXPLICITLY DENY reading shadow file   │
  │                                                                           │
  │    # CAPABILITY RULES: grant specific Linux capabilities                  │
  │    capability setuid,              ← Allow setuid syscall                 │
  │    capability dac_override,        ← Allow overriding file permissions    │
  │    # All OTHER capabilities are IMPLICITLY DENIED                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │    # NETWORK RULES: control protocol access                               │
  │    network inet tcp,               ← Allow TCP (HTTP, DB connections)     │
  │    network inet udp,               ← Allow UDP (DNS)                      │
  │    # All OTHER protocols are IMPLICITLY DENIED                             │
  │  }                                                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 14 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Write an AppArmor profile that allows a container to read /app/**, write to /tmp/**, and use TCP networking. Deny everything else.
Show Answer
Answer
#include <tunables/global>
profile anihpj flags=(attach_disconnected,mediate_deleted) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  /app/** r,
  /tmp/** rw,
  network inet tcp,
  /usr/bin/python3 rix,
  /opt/venv/bin/** rix,
  /** r,
}
Q2
How do you apply an AppArmor profile to a running container? What's the difference between the annotation method and the securityContext method?
Show Answer
Answer

Annotation (older, deprecated in v1.30+): container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>: localhost/<profile>. securityContext (newer, preferred): securityContext.appArmorProfile.type: Localhost, localhostProfile: <name>. The securityContext method is type-safe and validated by the API server — use this on the CKS exam if the cluster version supports it.

Q3
After loading an AppArmor profile, how do you verify it's actually enforced on a running pod?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/self/attr/current
# Should output: anihpj-apparmor (enforce)

ssh node01 aa-status | grep anihpj
# Shows: anihpj-apparmor (enforce) — with process count
Q4
What's the difference between AppArmor complain mode and enforce mode? When would you use complain mode?
Show Answer
Answer

Enforce: Violations are BLOCKED and logged. Complain: Violations are only LOGGED (not blocked). Use complain mode when testing a new profile to see what would be blocked without actually breaking the application. Check logs: dmesg | grep apparmor or aa-logprof. Switch: aa-complain <profile> → aa-enforce <profile>.

Q5
Write an AppArmor profile that denies a container access to /etc/kubernetes/, /proc/sysrq-trigger, and /sys/kernel/. Why are these paths dangerous?
Show Answer
Answer
profile k8s-hardened flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  deny /etc/kubernetes/** rwxlkm,
  deny /proc/sysrq-trigger rw,
  deny /sys/kernel/** rw,
  /app/** r,
  /tmp/** rw,
}

Danger: /etc/kubernetes/ contains PKI certs and kubeconfig — reading these enables API server impersonation. /proc/sysrq-trigger allows emergency reboot/shutdown commands. /sys/kernel/ exposes kernel parameters that can disable security features.

Explanation

AppArmor denies take priority over allows. These deny rules form a safety net: even if the container somehow gains root and hostPath access to /etc/kubernetes/, AppArmor blocks the read. This is defense in depth — AppArmor is the last gate before the kernel.

Q6
A pod with an AppArmor profile in enforce mode is crashing. Logs show no AppArmor denials. What debugging steps do you take?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Switch the profile to complain mode: aa-complain <profile>. (2) Recreate the pod and let it run. (3) Check AppArmor logs: dmesg | grep -i apparmor | grep -i audit. (4) Use aa-logprof to analyze logs and suggest profile additions. (5) If the pod still crashes with no AppArmor denials, the issue is NOT AppArmor — check pod events: kubectl describe pod, check if the profile is loaded: aa-status | grep <profile>, verify the annotation is correct.

Explanation

Complain mode is the AppArmor debugging tool. It logs all would-be denials without blocking them, letting you see the complete picture of what the container needs. aa-logprof is interactive and will suggest new rules. Always test profiles in complain mode before enforcing them.

Q7
AppArmor vs SELinux — what's the practical difference for CKS? Which one runs on the exam, and how do you check which MAC system is active?
Show Answer
Answer

AppArmor: Path-based MAC. Profiles are simple text files referencing file paths. Default on Ubuntu/Debian. The CKS exam uses Ubuntu nodes → AppArmor is the tested MAC system. SELinux: Label-based MAC. Every file and process has a label. Default on RHEL/CentOS. More complex but more granular than AppArmor.

Check active MAC: aa-status (AppArmor) or getenforce (SELinux). If aa-status returns "apparmor module is loaded" → AppArmor. If getenforce returns "Enforcing" → SELinux.

Explanation

The CKS exam explicitly tests AppArmor, not SELinux, because the exam environment uses Ubuntu. Know how to: (1) write and load AppArmor profiles, (2) apply them to pods via annotation or securityContext, (3) debug with complain mode and aa-logprof. If you encounter a RHEL-based question, it will specify SELinux explicitly.

Q8
How do you make AppArmor profiles survive a node reboot? Where are profiles stored, and what command ensures they persist?
Show Answer
Answer

AppArmor profiles are stored in /etc/apparmor.d/. They are automatically loaded at boot by the apparmor systemd service which reads all profiles from this directory. No additional persistence configuration is needed — simply place your profile file in /etc/apparmor.d/ (e.g., /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj) and it will be loaded on next boot.

# To load immediately without rebooting:
apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj
# Verify persistence:
aa-status | grep k8s-anihpj  # Shows loaded profiles
# After reboot, check again — profile should still be loaded
Explanation

On the CKS exam, you may need to create a profile and ensure it survives a reboot. The key: profiles in /etc/apparmor.d/ are auto-loaded. If you create a profile elsewhere and load it with apparmor_parser, it won't survive reboot unless you copy it to /etc/apparmor.d/. Always place production profiles in the standard directory.

Q9
Write the pod securityContext (not annotation) that applies an AppArmor profile named "anihpj-restricted" to container "app". What Kubernetes version is required?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secured-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: anihpj-restricted

Requires Kubernetes 1.30+ (GA in 1.30). Before 1.30, use the annotation method. The securityContext approach is preferred because: (1) it's validated by the API server, (2) it's part of the PodSecurity standards, (3) it's visible in kubectl describe pod.

Explanation

The securityContext field for AppArmor graduated to GA in Kubernetes 1.30. On the CKS exam, if the cluster is 1.30+, use this method. For older clusters, use the annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/app: localhost/anihpj-restricted. The exam may test both methods depending on the cluster version provided.

Q10
An attacker compromises a container and runs cat /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt via a hostPath mount. AppArmor is in complain mode. What do you see in the logs, and why is complain mode NOT sufficient for production?
Show Answer
Answer

In complain mode, the access SUCCEEDS but is logged. You'd see in dmesg:

audit: type=1400 apparmor="ALLOWED" operation="open" profile="k8s-anihpj" 
name="/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt" pid=12345 comm="cat" 
requested_mask="r" denied_mask="r"

Why complain mode is insufficient: The attacker successfully reads the CA certificate. They can now use it to forge client certificates or validate stolen etcd certs. Complain mode LOGS attacks but doesn't STOP them. Production MUST use enforce mode. Complain mode is for development and testing ONLY.

Explanation

This scenario illustrates the critical difference between detection and prevention. Complain mode is detection-only — useful for building profiles but useless for stopping attacks. The CKS exam expects you to: (1) use complain mode to develop and test profiles, (2) switch to enforce mode BEFORE considering a node production-ready. Never leave production profiles in complain mode.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Load an AppArmor profile (EXAM PATTERN)
apparmor_parser -q /etc/apparmor.d/custom-profile  # Load profile
aa-status | grep custom-profile  # Verify loaded and mode (enforce/complain)

# 2. Apply AppArmor to a pod
# Annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>: localhost/<profile>
kubectl run test --image=nginx --annotations="container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx: localhost/custom-profile"

# 3. Test AppArmor by triggering a violation
dmesg | grep -i apparmor  # Shows DENIED messages
cat /var/log/syslog | grep apparmor  # Alternative log source

# 4. Switch profile mode without unloading
aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/custom-profile  # Switch to complain (log-only)
aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/custom-profile   # Switch to enforce (block)
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 14 Traps
  • Profile file must be loadable: AppArmor annotations reference profiles by name, but the profile must first be loaded into the kernel with apparmor_parser. If the profile isn't loaded, the pod fails to start with a "cannot enforce AppArmor" error.
  • Path-based MAC means paths matter: AppArmor profiles specify file paths. If your container has a different filesystem layout than expected (e.g., the binary is at /usr/local/bin/app instead of /usr/bin/app), the profile won't match. Test in complain mode first.
  • Not all nodes have AppArmor: AppArmor is default on Ubuntu/Debian. RHEL/CentOS use SELinux instead. On the CKS exam, nodes run Ubuntu — so AppArmor works. If the pod is scheduled to a node without AppArmor, it fails.
