16.3 Limiting Kernel Modules — Blacklisting Dangerous Ones

Kernel modules are pieces of code that can be loaded into the running kernel to extend its functionality — filesystem drivers, hardware drivers, network protocol handlers. Every loaded module increases the kernel's attack surface. The CIS Benchmark mandates blacklisting specific modules that have no legitimate use on a Kubernetes node:

CIS-Mandated Kernel Module Blacklisting

Bash — /etc/modprobe.d/cis-blacklist.conf — CIS-required module blocks 
#!/bin/bash
# Create the CIS blacklist configuration
cat > /etc/modprobe.d/cis-blacklist.conf << 'EOF'
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CIS KUBERNETES BENCHMARK — Mandated Kernel Module Blacklist
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# ── UNNECESSARY FILESYSTEM DRIVERS ──
install cramfs /bin/true       # Compressed ROM filesystem (embedded devices only)
install freevxfs /bin/true      # Veritas filesystem (legacy Unix)
install jffs2 /bin/true         # Journaling Flash filesystem (embedded devices)
install hfs /bin/true           # Apple HFS (Mac OS Classic — never on servers)
install hfsplus /bin/true       # Apple HFS+ (Mac OS Extended — never on servers)
install squashfs /bin/true      # SquashFS (compressed read-only — rare on servers)
install udf /bin/true           # Universal Disk Format (optical media — never on servers)

# ── DANGEROUS HARDWARE DRIVERS ──
install usb-storage /bin/true   # USB mass storage — physical attack vector
install firewire-core /bin/true # FireWire — DMA attack vector (direct memory access)

# ── DANGEROUS NETWORK PROTOCOLS ──
install dccp /bin/true          # Datagram Congestion Control Protocol
install sctp /bin/true          # Stream Control Transmission Protocol
install rds /bin/true           # Reliable Datagram Sockets
install tipc /bin/true          # Transparent Inter-Process Communication
EOF

# Verify the configuration
echo "=== Checking blacklisted modules ==="
for mod in cramfs freevxfs jffs2 hfs hfsplus squashfs udf usb-storage; do
    if lsmod | grep -q "^$mod "; then
        echo "⚠️  WARNING: $mod is currently loaded. Reboot to fully disable."
    else
        echo "✅ $mod is not loaded"
    fi
done

# Verify blacklist is preventing module load
echo ""
echo "=== Testing module load prevention ==="
modprobe --dry-run cramfs 2>&1
# Should show: modprobe: ERROR: could not insert 'cramfs': Operation not permitted

16.4 Cloud IAM for Kubernetes Nodes

In cloud environments, Kubernetes nodes run on cloud VMs that have their own identity — an AWS IAM role, a GCP Service Account, or an Azure Managed Identity. These cloud credentials are accessible to every pod running on that node via the instance metadata service (169.254.169.254). If the node's IAM role has excessive permissions, a compromised pod can steal those permissions and pivot to your entire cloud infrastructure. This was exactly how the Capital One breach worked.

Cloud IAM Least-Privilege — What Each Node REALLY Needs

AWS IAM Policy — Minimal permissions for an EKS worker node
  {
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
      {
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Action": [
          "ec2:DescribeInstances",
          "ec2:DescribeNetworkInterfaces",
          "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups",
          "ec2:DescribeSubnets",
          "ec2:DescribeVolumes"
        ],
        "Resource": "*"
      },
      {
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Action": [
          "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",
          "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability",
          "ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer",
          "ecr:BatchGetImage"
        ],
        "Resource": "*"
      }
    ]
  }
  ❌ NEVER INCLUDE: s3:*, iam:*, sts:AssumeRole (allows full cloud pivot)
  ✅ THIS IS SUFFICIENT: Describe EC2 (for pod networking) + pull ECR images

IMDSv2 — Protecting the Node's Cloud Credentials from Pods

The Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at 169.254.169.254 exposes the node's IAM credentials to every process on the node — including every pod. IMDSv2 adds a required session token, preventing simple curl from retrieving credentials. Combined with hop limit = 1, it prevents containers from accessing the metadata service at all:

Bash — Configure IMDSv2 on AWS (required for production EKS nodes)
# Enable IMDSv2 only (disable insecure IMDSv1)
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options \
  --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0 \
  --http-tokens required \
  --http-put-response-hop-limit 1

# Verify: from inside any pod, this should FAIL
kubectl run test-imds --rm -it --image=amazonlinux -- \
  curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
# Expected: 401 Unauthorized (IMDSv1 disabled, token required)

# With hop limit = 1, even IMDSv2 requests from pods fail
# (pod → host network namespace = 2 hops)

  ⚡ THE METADATA SERVICE ATTACK (how Capital One was breached):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. Attacker exploits an SSRF vulnerability in a web app running on an EKS pod.
  2. The app makes a request to: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
  3. AWS metadata service returns temporary IAM credentials for the node's role.
  4. If the node's IAM role has s3:ListBuckets + s3:GetObject → attacker can
     enumerate and download EVERY S3 bucket in the account.
  5. Capital One: The node's IAM role had excessive S3 permissions. 100+ million
     customer records were exfiltrated through the metadata service.

  DEFENSE: Use IAM roles for ServiceAccounts (IRSA) in EKS, Workload Identity
  in GKE, or Pod Identity in AKS to give individual pods their own limited
  IAM credentials — instead of all pods inheriting the node's role.

16.5 etcd Security — Restricting Who Can Read the Cluster Brain

etcd is the most sensitive component in your Kubernetes cluster. It stores every Secret, every ConfigMap, every pod spec, every RBAC rule — the entire state of your cluster. If an attacker reads etcd, they have everything. If they write to etcd, they own the cluster. etcd security is not optional — it is existential.

etcd Raft Consensus — Security Implications of the Protocol

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm to maintain consistency across multiple nodes. A write is committed only when a majority (quorum) of nodes acknowledge it. This has direct security implications that most K8s administrators never think about:

Raft Consensus Security — Why etcd Cluster Size Matters for Breach Scenarios
  etcd CLUSTER: 3 nodes (typical HA setup)
  ──────────────────────────────────────
  Quorum = floor(N/2) + 1 = floor(3/2) + 1 = 2 nodes

  SCENARIO A: Attacker compromises 1 etcd node
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Attacker can READ all data on the compromised node (full cluster state).
  • Attacker CANNOT modify data: writes to the compromised node will be
    rejected by the other 2 nodes (the compromised node can't form quorum alone).
  • RESULT: Data is READ but not CORRUPTED. Cluster continues operating normally.

  SCENARIO B: Attacker compromises 2 etcd nodes (quorum)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Attacker controls QUORUM. They can:
    → Delete any key (including Secrets, pod specs, RBAC rules)
    → Modify any key (redirect traffic, change pod specs, escalate RBAC)
    → Add a new node to the cluster (persistence via new etcd member)
  • RESULT: Full cluster compromise. Attacker OWNS the cluster state.

  ⚡ SECURITY IMPLICATION:
  ───────────────────────
  • 3-node etcd cluster: tolerates 1 node failure/compromise.
  • 5-node etcd cluster: tolerates 2 node failures/compromises (quorum=3).
  • Why 5 nodes is more secure: An attacker must compromise 3 nodes to control
    etcd, not just 2. But 5 nodes adds more operational complexity.
  • ALWAYS use an ODD number of etcd nodes (3, 5, 7) to avoid split-brain.

  DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH FOR etcd:
  ──────────────────────────
  • Restrict port 2379 to API server IPs ONLY (firewall).
  • Use TLS with mutual authentication for ALL etcd communication.
  • Do NOT co-locate etcd with user workloads (dedicated control plane nodes).
  • Encrypt Secrets at rest so even a compromised etcd directory reveals nothing.
  • Monitor etcd logs for unauthorized access attempts.
  • Take regular etcd snapshots for disaster recovery.

etcd Hardening Checklist — Five Critical Controls

🔒
1. TLS Everywhere — Client and Peer Communication

etcd must use TLS for ALL communication — both client (API server → etcd) and peer (etcd → etcd). The API server manifest must include: --etcd-certfile, --etcd-keyfile, --etcd-cafile. The etcd manifest must include: --cert-file, --key-file, --peer-cert-file, --peer-key-file, --trusted-ca-file. Without TLS, etcd traffic is plaintext — any network sniffing reveals every Secret in the cluster.

🔥
2. Firewall — Only the API Server Talks to etcd

Port 2379 (etcd client) must be firewalled to allow ONLY the API server's IP address. No other component — not kubelet, not scheduler, not any pod — should be able to reach etcd. Use iptables: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 2379 -s <API_SERVER_IP> -j ACCEPT followed by iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 2379 -j DROP.

📁
3. Data Directory Permissions — 700, Owned by etcd User

chmod 700 /var/lib/etcd && chown etcd:etcd /var/lib/etcd. Only the etcd process user should be able to read the data directory. The directory contains the entire cluster state in plaintext on disk — unless encryption at rest is configured (Chapter 19).

🔐
4. Peer Authentication — Mutual TLS Between etcd Members

etcd peers (when running in a multi-node cluster) must mutually authenticate using TLS certificates. The --peer-client-cert-auth=true flag ensures that only nodes with valid etcd peer certificates can join the cluster. This prevents an attacker from adding a rogue etcd node to steal data.

🔑
5. Encryption at Rest — Secrets Must Be Unreadable on Disk

By default, Secrets stored in etcd are base64-encoded — NOT encrypted. Anyone with disk access can decode them. EncryptionConfiguration (Chapter 19) encrypts Secrets before they are written to etcd, so even a compromised etcd data directory reveals nothing.

16.6 Linux Kernel Hardening Parameters (sysctl)

The Linux kernel exposes hundreds of tunable parameters via sysctl. Many of these have direct security implications — they control IP forwarding, ICMP redirects, source routing, SYN flood protection, and address space layout randomization (ASLR). The CIS Benchmark specifies required values for production Kubernetes nodes:

CIS-Required Kernel Hardening via sysctl

Bash — /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-cis.conf — CIS kernel hardening 
#!/bin/bash
cat > /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-cis.conf << 'EOF'
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CIS KUBERNETES BENCHMARK — Kernel Hardening Parameters
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# ── NETWORK HARDENING ──

# IP forwarding (REQUIRED for pod networking — DO NOT disable on K8s nodes)
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1

# Disable ICMP redirects (prevent MITM redirect attacks)
# An attacker can send ICMP redirects to change routing tables
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0

# Disable source packet routing (prevent IP spoofing)
# Attackers use source routing to bypass firewall rules
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0

# Disable sending ICMP redirects (this node is not a router)
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects = 0

# Enable TCP SYN cookie protection (DDoS SYN flood mitigation)
# When SYN queue is full, use SYN cookies instead of dropping connections
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1

# Enable reverse path filtering (prevent IP spoofing from pods)
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

# ── MEMORY / ASLR HARDENING ──

# Maximum ASLR entropy (randomize memory addresses for all processes)
# 0 = no ASLR, 1 = partial, 2 = full (including heap and stack)
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2

# ── KERNEL POINTER / KEXEC RESTRICTIONS ──

# Restrict kernel pointer access in /proc (prevent info leaks)
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2

# Disable kexec (prevent replacing running kernel)
kernel.kexec_load_disabled = 1

# ── PROCESS / CORE DUMP RESTRICTIONS ──

# Restrict ptrace to direct child processes only
kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1

# Set core dump pattern (prevent core dumps from leaking memory contents)
kernel.core_pattern = |/bin/false
EOF

# Apply all sysctl changes
sysctl --system

# Verify key parameters
echo "=== Verifying CIS sysctl parameters ==="
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space
sysctl kernel.kptr_restrict
sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope

What each parameter actually does: accept_redirects=0 prevents an attacker on the same network from sending fake ICMP redirect messages that reroute your node's traffic through the attacker's machine. tcp_syncookies=1 defends against SYN flood DDoS by using cryptographic cookies instead of allocating connection state for half-open connections. randomize_va_space=2 randomizes the memory addresses of the stack, heap, and shared libraries — making it exponentially harder for attackers to exploit buffer overflow vulnerabilities because they cannot predict where their shellcode will land in memory.

How ASLR and kptr_restrict Stop Real Exploits — A Technical Deep Dive

Two of the most important sysctl parameters — kernel.randomize_va_space and kernel.kptr_restrict — work together to defeat memory corruption exploits. Understanding exactly HOW they work helps you appreciate why setting them correctly is non-negotiable:

ASLR + kptr_restrict — How They Defeat Exploits Together
  WITHOUT ASLR (randomize_va_space = 0):
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Process memory layout is PREDICTABLE (same addresses every run):
  ┌─────────────────┐ 0x7fffffffffff
  │  Stack          │ ← ALWAYS at 0x7ffffffde000
  │  (function      │    Attacker knows exactly where their shellcode
  │   return addrs) │    will land. They craft the exploit to jump here.
  ├─────────────────┤ 0x7ffff7e00000
  │  Shared Libs    │ ← ALWAYS at 0x7ffff7a00000
  │  (libc.so, etc) │    Attacker knows libc's address and can call
  │                 │    system("/bin/sh") by jumping to its known offset.
  ├─────────────────┤ 0x555555554000
  │  Heap           │ ← ALWAYS at 0x555555758000
  │  (malloc data)  │    Attacker can spray heap with shellcode at known addr.
  ├─────────────────┤ 0x400000
  │  Code (.text)   │ ← ALWAYS at 0x400000
  └─────────────────┘

  EXPLOIT DEVELOPMENT: Attacker writes: jump_to(0x7ffffffde000 + offset)
  one time. Exploit works on EVERY run, EVERY machine with same kernel.

  WITH ASLR (randomize_va_space = 2):
  ─────────────────────────────────────
  Process memory layout is RANDOMIZED (different on every execution):
  ┌─────────────────┐ varying address
  │  Stack          │ ← Randomized: could be anywhere in a ~32TB range
  │                 │    (x86-64 has 48-bit virtual address space)
  ├─────────────────┤ varying address
  │  Shared Libs    │ ← Randomized: different offset per process
  ├─────────────────┤ varying address
  │  Heap           │ ← Randomized: brk() starts at random address
  ├─────────────────┤ varying address
  │  Code (.text)   │ ← Position-Independent Executable (PIE): randomized
  └─────────────────┘

  EXPLOIT DEVELOPMENT: Attacker needs an INFORMATION LEAK to discover
  where anything is in memory. This is where kptr_restrict comes in:

  WITH kptr_restrict = 0:
  ────────────────────────
  cat /proc/kallsyms shows ALL kernel symbol addresses:
  ffffffff81000000 T _text
  ffffffff81234567 T sys_execve
  ffffffff81800000 D init_task
  → Attacker now knows kernel addresses. Can craft kernel exploits.

  WITH kptr_restrict = 2:
  ────────────────────────
  cat /proc/kallsyms shows: 0000000000000000 T _text
                             0000000000000000 T sys_execve
  → All addresses hidden. Attacker has no kernel address information.
  → Must find ANOTHER information leak — much harder.

  COMBINED DEFENSE:
  ─────────────────
  ASLR randomizes USER-SPACE addresses (stack, heap, libs, code).
  kptr_restrict hides KERNEL-SPACE addresses (syscall table, kernel functions).
  Both needed: user exploits need ASLR bypass. Kernel exploits need kptr leak.
  Without both defenses, exploits become dramatically easier to write.

16.7 Verify Platform Binaries & Least-Privilege Cloud IAM

The official CKS curriculum requires you to verify platform binaries before deploying and use least-privilege identity and access management. These two competencies work together: verified binaries ensure trusted components, least-privilege IAM ensures minimal cloud permissions.

Verifying Platform Binaries

Bash — Verify Kubernetes Binaries
# Verify K8s package integrity (Debian/Ubuntu)
dpkg -V kubelet kubeadm kubectl
# No output = all files match package manifest (CLEAN)
# ??5?????? /usr/bin/kubelet = md5 mismatch (TAMPERED)

# AIDE file integrity check
aide --check
# Compares monitored files against baseline. Reports added/removed/changed.

# Verify binary checksum against official release
curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt | xargs -I{} sh -c 'curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/{}/bin/linux/amd64/kubelet.sha256'
sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet  # Compare with official checksum

Least-Privilege Cloud IAM Patterns

⚠️ CKS Exam: Cloud IAM

The exam tests cloud IAM minimization. Know: (1) AWS IRSA — pod gets its own IAM role via SA annotation, not the node's role. (2) GCP Workload Identity — maps K8s SA to GCP SA. (3) The Capital One breach happened because the NODE's IAM role had broad S3 access — every pod could exfiltrate data via the metadata service. Fix: per-pod IAM roles + IMDSv2 with hop limit 1.

ptrace: Restricted to children

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Node minimization on the CKS exam is about systematic auditing and removal. The exam workstation gives you SSH access to nodes. Use it to: (1) audit running services with systemctl list-units --type=service, (2) audit open ports with ss -tlnp, (3) audit installed packages with dpkg -l, (4) audit kernel modules with lsmod, (5) apply hardening via the commands in this chapter. Always verify after every change. And remember: AIDE is explicitly on the CKS curriculum — install it, initialize the database, and run a check. The exam may ask you to verify that specific system files have not been modified.

🔧 Under the Hood — Kernel Module Security: How Unnecessary Modules Create Attack Surface and How to Block Them 
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   KERNEL MODULE HARDENING — Attack Vectors and Defenses                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │   ATTACK: CVE-2022-0185 (filesystem context overflow)                     │
  │   • Affected: Linux kernel 5.1-rc1+ filesystem context functionality      │
  │   • Exploited via: unshare(CLONE_NEWNS|CLONE_NEWUSER) + mount()          │
  │   • Impact: Container breakout to root on host                             │
  │                                                                           │
  │   DEFENSE 1: Block unnecessary kernel modules                             │
  │   ────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │   lsmod | grep -v "kernel|module"  # List loaded modules                  │
  │   modprobe -r <module>             # Remove unused modules                │
  │   echo "blacklist <module>" >> /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist.conf           │
  │                                                                           │
  │   DEFENSE 2: Restrict kernel module loading                               │
  │   ────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │   echo 1 > /proc/sys/kernel/modules_disabled  # Block ALL future loads   │
  │   # ⚠️ Only do this after ensuring all needed modules are loaded          │
  │                                                                           │
  │   DEFENSE 3: Seccomp blocks create_module syscalls                        │
  │   RuntimeDefault already blocks: create_module, init_module,              │
  │   delete_module, finit_module                                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 16 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
How do you list all loaded kernel modules and identify which ones are unnecessary for a Kubernetes node?
Show Answer
Answer

lsmod lists all loaded modules. Essential modules: overlay, br_netfilter, iptable_nat, ip_vs (if using IPVS mode). Unnecessary: bluetooth, btusb, snd_* (audio), joydev (joystick), uvcvideo (webcam), nouveau/radeon (GPU — unless doing GPU workloads). Remove: modprobe -r <module>. Blacklist: echo "blacklist <module>" >> /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist.conf.

Q2
What's the risk of leaving unnecessary kernel modules loaded? Give a real CVE example.
Show Answer
Answer

Every loaded kernel module adds to the attack surface. CVE-2022-0185 exploited the filesystem context functionality in the kernel — a feature most containers don't need but was available because the module was loaded. CVE-2016-0728 exploited the keyring facility. Both were exploitable from inside containers. Removing unused modules eliminates these attack paths entirely.

Q3
How do you permanently disable kernel module loading on a production node, and what's the risk?
Show Answer
Answer

echo 1 > /proc/sys/kernel/modules_disabled blocks ALL future module loading AND unloading. This is irreversible without a reboot. Risk: if a security update requires a new kernel module, you'll need to reboot the node. Only set this after verifying all required modules are loaded and tested. For production, set via sysctl: kernel.modules_disabled=1 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-security.conf.

Q4
AIDE reports that /usr/bin/kubelet has been modified. What does this mean and what should you do?
Show Answer
Answer

AIDE detects file integrity violations. A modified kubelet binary means either: (a) a legitimate upgrade (verify with package manager: dpkg -V kubelet), or (b) an attacker replaced the binary with a backdoored version. If not a known upgrade: IMMEDIATELY cordon and drain the node, isolate it from the network, capture forensic evidence, and rebuild from a known-good image. This is a potential node compromise.

Q5
What Kubernetes-specific ports MUST be open on a worker node? List them with their default port numbers and which component uses each.
Show Answer
Answer
PortComponentPurpose
10250kubeletAPI server → kubelet (logs, exec, metrics)
10255kubelet (read-only)Should be DISABLED (readOnlyPort: 0)
30000-32767kube-proxyNodePort services
8472CNI (Flannel)VXLAN overlay (varies by CNI)
22SSHAdministrative access
Explanation

Worker nodes need minimal open ports. Everything else should be firewalled. The kubelet read-only port (10255) exposes pod info without authentication — it must be disabled. NodePort range (30000-32767) is needed only if you use NodePort services. On the CKS exam, run ss -tlnp and verify only these ports are listening.

Q6
How do you verify the integrity of installed Kubernetes packages? Write the exact command and explain what output indicates tampering.
Show Answer
Answer
# Debian/Ubuntu
 dpkg -V kubelet kubeadm kubectl
# Output: nothing = all good. If files are modified:
# ??5?????? c /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf  (config file changed — expected)
# ??5??????   /usr/bin/kubelet           (BINARY changed — INVESTIGATE!)
# RHEL/CentOS
rpm -V kubelet kubeadm kubectl
# Key: S=size, M=mode, 5=MD5, D=device, L=symlink, U=user, G=group, T=mtime

Missing output = all files pass verification. Any output for binaries (/usr/bin/*) is suspicious. Config files (/etc/*) changing is expected after edits.

Explanation

Package integrity verification is complementary to AIDE. dpkg -V checks files against the package manager's database (which should be trusted). AIDE checks against its own baseline (which could be compromised if the baseline was created after tampering). Use BOTH — package verification for known-good comparison, AIDE for ongoing monitoring.

Q7
A node has a GPU (NVIDIA) requiring a kernel module. How do you balance the need for the GPU module with the principle of minimizing kernel modules?
Show Answer
Answer

Keep the NVIDIA module but blacklist ALL other unnecessary modules. Create a whitelist approach: (1) Identify required modules: lsmod | grep nvidia. (2) Blacklist everything else: create /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-all.conf with all non-essential modules. (3) Set kernel.modules_disabled=1 AFTER loading NVIDIA (can't be undone without reboot, but prevents future module injection). (4) Document the exception with business justification for auditors.

Explanation

Security is about risk management, not absolute rules. GPU workloads need kernel modules — that's a legitimate business requirement. The principle is: load ONLY what's required, blacklist everything else, and lock down future changes. On the CKS exam, don't blindly blacklist everything — read the scenario. If a pod needs GPU access, blacklisting NVIDIA breaks the workload and you fail the task.

Q8
How do you set up a cron job to run AIDE daily and email results? Write the crontab entry and explain the AIDE flags.
Show Answer
Answer
# Crontab entry (runs at 3 AM daily)
0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check | mail -s "AIDE Report $(hostname) $(date +\%Y-\%m-\%d)" security@anihpj.com
# Flags:
# --check: Compare current filesystem against database
# --update: Update database after legitimate changes
# --init: Initialize new database
# --compare: Compare two databases
# After legitimate changes (upgrades), update:
aide --update && cp /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz
Explanation

Automated AIDE checks are a CIS benchmark recommendation. The daily cron job provides continuous file integrity monitoring. After any legitimate system change (package upgrade, config edit), run aide --update to update the baseline — otherwise tomorrow's check will report false positives. On the CKS exam, know when to use --check (audit) vs --update (after changes).

Q9
A node's cloud IAM role has s3:* and ec2:* permissions. What's the security risk for Kubernetes workloads, and how do you mitigate it without changing the node role?
Show Answer
Answer

Risk: Any pod on this node can reach the cloud metadata service (169.254.169.254) and obtain these IAM credentials. A compromised pod can delete S3 buckets, terminate EC2 instances, or exfiltrate data.

Mitigation without changing node role: (1) Block metadata service from pods: iptables rule to DROP 169.254.169.254, or NetworkPolicy egress block. (2) Use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — pods use their own IAM roles, not the node's. (3) Set automountServiceAccountToken: false — pods can't authenticate to cloud APIs without explicit credentials. (4) AppArmor profile denying network access to 169.254.169.254.

Explanation

This is the Capital One breach scenario. The cloud metadata service is the #1 cloud security risk for Kubernetes. Even if the node role is over-privileged, you can prevent pods from accessing it. On the CKS exam: (1) always block 169.254.169.254 from pods, (2) use IRSA for pod-level IAM, (3) never rely on node-level IAM for pod permissions.

Q10
After hardening a node by removing packages, blacklisting modules, and applying sysctl settings, how do you comprehensively verify the node is production-ready? List your verification checklist.
Show Answer
Answer
1
Service verification

systemctl status kubelet containerd — both must be active/running. kubectl get node <name> — must show Ready.

2
Port audit

ss -tlnp — only kubelet (10250), SSH (22), and containerd should listen.

3
Module audit

lsmod | grep -v -E "overlay|br_netfilter|iptable|ip_vs|nf_|xt_" — verify no unnecessary modules.

4
AIDE baseline

aide --init && cp /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz — establish clean baseline.

5
Scheduling test

kubectl run test --image=nginx -n default; kubectl get pod test -o wide — must be Running on the hardened node.

6
kube-bench re-run

kube-bench run --targets node — all CIS checks for nodes should PASS.

Explanation

This verification checklist is exactly what the CKS exam expects after a hardening task. Don't just make changes — VERIFY them. The most common exam failure: hardening a node but breaking kubelet → node goes NotReady → no points awarded even if the hardening was correct. Always verify the node is still Ready and can schedule pods.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Check open ports on the node (EXAM PATTERN)
ss -tulnp | grep -E "LISTEN|ESTABLISHED"  # All listening + established connections
netstat -tulpn | grep LISTEN  # Alternative if ss not available

# 2. AIDE file integrity check (EXAM PATTERN)
aide --init  # Initialize database (first run)
aide --check  # Compare current files against database
aide --update  # Update database after legitimate changes

# 3. Verify package integrity
dpkg -V kubelet kubeadm kubectl  # Verify all K8s package files (Debian/Ubuntu)
rpm -V kubelet kubeadm kubectl  # Same for RHEL/CentOS

# 4. Check IAM roles (cloud provider specific)
# AWS: aws iam get-instance-profile --instance-profile-name <name>
# GCP: gcloud compute instances describe <instance> --format='json(serviceAccounts)'
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 16 Traps
  • AIDE --init must run BEFORE --check: Running aide --check without first running aide --init produces meaningless results (no baseline to compare against). The exam will likely have AIDE already initialized — verify with ls /var/lib/aide/aide.db.
  • Port 10250 is kubelet (keep open): Kubelet API serves on 10250. Don't block this port — it's required for kubectl exec, kubectl logs, and metrics. Do block ports 10255 (read-only, deprecated) and ports used by removed services.
  • NodePort 30000-32767 are open by default: Even if you block these with iptables, Kubernetes can still allocate them. The correct fix is a NetworkPolicy, not a node firewall rule.

Chapter 17: Pod Security Standards — Admission-Level Enforcement

Before Pod Security Standards (PSS), Kubernetes used PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) — a complex, confusing, and ultimately deprecated mechanism for controlling pod security. PSS, introduced in Kubernetes 1.22 and stable in 1.25, replaces PSP with a simple, namespace-scoped, label-based system with three predefined security levels: Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted. PSS is enforced at admission time — when a pod is created, the API server checks whether the pod spec violates the namespace's PSS level. If it does, the pod is rejected BEFORE it ever reaches a node. This chapter teaches you to apply the right PSS level to every namespace in your anihpj cluster — ensuring that every pod in production runs with Restricted-level security, while system namespaces (kube-system) maintain the flexibility they need.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 📋 Admission Control 🛡️ Pod Hardening

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What PSS is and how it replaced PodSecurityPolicy — the three security levels
  • ✅ What each PSS level allows and blocks — Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted compared
  • ✅ How to apply PSS to namespaces via labels — enforce, audit, and warn modes
  • ✅ The decision flowchart for choosing the right PSS level for any namespace
  • ✅ How to configure PSS Restricted for anihpj-prod and verify compliance
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% System Hardening 15%
🧠 PSS in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test

The CKS exam tests PSS in a practical, namespace-level way:

  • Apply PSS labels to a namespace: Add pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted label. The exam expects you to know the exact label keys.
  • Fix a non-compliant pod: The exam may give you a pod that violates Baseline or Restricted. You must identify which fields are violating and fix them (add runAsNonRoot, drop capabilities, etc.).
  • Understand the label format: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL> where MODE = enforce | audit | warn and LEVEL = privileged | baseline | restricted.
  • CRITICAL EXAM FACT: PSS labels go on the NAMESPACE, not the pod. The pod spec itself doesn't declare a PSS level — the namespace decides.

17.1 What Are Pod Security Standards (PSS)?

Pod Security Standards define three security levels that restrict what pods can do. These levels are cumulative — Baseline includes everything in Privileged plus restrictions, and Restricted includes everything in Baseline plus more. Importantly, PSS is enforced by a built-in admission controller (PodSecurity), not by an external webhook. This means it works out of the box on any Kubernetes cluster 1.23+ without installing anything extra.

The Three PSS Levels — What Each Allows and Blocks

PSS Security Levels — From Most Permissive to Most Restrictive
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  🔴 PRIVILEGED — No Restrictions (least secure)                          │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  • Allows everything: hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, privileged mode     │
  │  • Allows all Linux capabilities, including dangerous ones               │
  │  • Allows running as root (UID 0)                                        │
  │  • Allows hostPath volumes, /proc mount, /dev access                     │
  │  • Allows custom AppArmor/SELinux/seccomp profiles (or none)             │
  │  ⚡ USE CASE: kube-system pods (CNI, CSI drivers, node exporters)        │
  │  ⚡ NEVER USE: For user-facing workloads like anihpj                     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  🟡 BASELINE — Prevents Known Privilege Escalations (medium)             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────                   │
  │  • DISABLES: hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC (prevents container escape)   │
  │  • DISABLES: privileged containers                                       │
  │  • DISABLES: hostPath volumes (prevents host filesystem access)          │
  │  • DISABLES: CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW, and other dangerous caps        │
  │  • ALLOWS: running as any user (root or non-root)                        │
  │  • ALLOWS: most Linux capabilities                                       │
  │  ⚡ USE CASE: Dev/staging namespaces, workloads being migrated to        │
  │     Restricted that still need flexibility                               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  🟢 RESTRICTED — Maximum Security (strongly recommended for production)   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────    │
  │  • ALL Baseline restrictions, PLUS:                                       │
  │  • REQUIRES: runAsNonRoot: true                                           │
  │  • REQUIRES: seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (or Localhost)               │
  │  • REQUIRES: capabilities: drop: [ALL]                                    │
  │  • RESTRICTS: volume types to ConfigMap, Secret, EmptyDir, PVC, and      │
  │    projected volumes only (no hostPath, no flexVolume, no CSI ephemeral) │
  │  • RESTRICTS: /proc mount type to default only                            │
  │  • REQUIRES: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (unless exception)              │
  │  ⚡ USE CASE: anihpj-prod, any production namespace                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

PSS vs PSP — Why the Switch Matters

FeaturePodSecurityPolicy (PSP - Deprecated)Pod Security Standards (PSS - Current)
Status❌ Removed in K8s 1.25✅ GA since 1.25
Where appliedCluster-wide (RBAC-based)Namespace-level (label-based)
ConfigurationComplex YAML with 30+ fieldsThree predefined levels (Privileged/Baseline/Restricted)
GranularityPer-user/per-ServiceAccountPer-namespace
Built-inRequired enabling admission pluginBuilt-in PodSecurity admission controller
ExtensibilityCould create custom policiesFixed predefined levels (use OPA/Kyverno for custom)
CKS ExamMay appear as theory question✅ Hands-on — apply labels, fix violations

Side-by-Side — What Each Level Enforces on a Typical Pod Spec

Pod Spec FieldPrivilegedBaselineRestricted
hostNetwork✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
hostPID / hostIPC✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
privileged: true✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
hostPath volumes✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
runAsNonRootNot requiredNot required✅ REQUIRED
seccompProfileNot requiredNot required✅ REQUIRED (RuntimeDefault)
capabilities.dropNot required⚠️ Drops dangerous caps✅ REQUIRED (drop ALL)
readOnlyRootFilesystemNot requiredNot required✅ REQUIRED
Volume types allowedAll types⚠️ Most (no hostPath)⚠️ Limited (no hostPath, flexVol, CSI ephemeral)

How the PodSecurity Admission Controller Works Internally

When a pod is created, the PodSecurity admission controller runs as part of the API server's admission chain. It checks the pod spec against the namespace's PSS labels and returns ALLOW or DENY. Understanding this internal logic helps you troubleshoot when pods are unexpectedly rejected or when violations aren't caught:

PodSecurity Admission Controller — Internal Validation Logic
  kubectl apply -f pod.yaml (namespace: anihpj-prod)
  │
  ▼
  API SERVER receives the CREATE Pod request
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: LOOK UP NAMESPACE LABELS                                        │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────                                        │
  │  The PodSecurity controller reads the namespace object for "anihpj-prod":│
  │  labels:                                                                  │
  │    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted                         │
  │    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.29                      │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 2: DETERMINE THE APPLICABLE POLICY                                  │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  enforce=restricted → The controller loads the "restricted" policy        │
  │  definition for version v1.29 from its built-in policy library.           │
  │  The policy is a set of CHECKS, not a single rule. Each check validates   │
  │  one aspect of the pod spec.                                              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 3: RUN EACH CHECK AGAINST THE POD SPEC                              │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                             │
  │  The controller iterates through ~15 checks for the Restricted level:     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 1: runAsNonRoot                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │
  │  Reads: pod.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot                             │
  │  AND: container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot (for EACH container)         │
  │  Rule: At least one must be explicitly set to true.                        │
  │  If BOTH are unset → FAIL: "runAsNonRoot != true"                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 2: seccompProfile                                                  │
  │  ────────────────────────                                                  │
  │  Reads: pod.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type                      │
  │  AND: container.securityContext.seccompProfile.type                       │
  │  Rule: type must be "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost".                      │
  │  If type is "Unconfined" or unset → FAIL                                 │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 3: capabilities                                                    │
  │  ──────────────────────                                                    │
  │  Reads: container.securityContext.capabilities.drop                       │
  │  Rule: drop must include ALL.                                              │
  │  If drop is missing or doesn't include ALL → FAIL                        │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 4: allowPrivilegeEscalation                                        │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────                                        │
  │  Reads: container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation                │
  │  Rule: must be explicitly set to false.                                    │
  │  If unset or true → FAIL                                                  │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 5-15: readOnlyRootFilesystem, volume types, /proc mount type,     │
  │  hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, privileged, hostPath volumes,             │
  │  AppArmor profile, SELinux type, sysctls, procMount...                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 4: AGGREGATE RESULTS                                                │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                                │
  │  ALL checks must pass → request is ALLOWED.                               │
  │  ANY check fails → ALL failures are aggregated into a single error        │
  │  message (so you see ALL violations at once, not one at a time).          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 5: RETURN DECISION                                                  │
  │  ────────────────────────                                                  │
  │  enforce mode: DENY → returns 403 Forbidden with violation details.       │
  │  audit mode: ALLOW → logs violation to audit log.                         │
  │  warn mode: ALLOW → returns warning to kubectl user.                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

17.2 Applying PSS to Namespaces

PSS is applied by adding labels to the Namespace object. Each label controls a specific enforcement mode for a specific security level. The label format is: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL>. You can apply multiple modes simultaneously — for example, enforce at Baseline but warn at Restricted to prepare for a future upgrade.

The Three Enforcement Modes

🚫
enforce

Violations are REJECTED. The pod is not created. The API server returns a 403 Forbidden error with details about which fields violated the policy. This is the mode you use in production.

📝
audit

Violations are LOGGED to the audit log but the pod is ALLOWED. Use this to discover which pods would fail a stricter level without breaking anything. This is how you prepare to upgrade from Baseline to Restricted.

⚠️
warn

Violations trigger a WARNING to the user who created the pod (visible in kubectl output), but the pod is ALLOWED. Use this to educate developers without blocking their work.

Namespace Label Examples — All Modes, All Levels

Bash — Applying PSS labels to namespaces 
# ── PRODUCTION: Enforce Restricted (maximum security) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── STAGING: Enforce Baseline, Warn on Restricted ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── DEV: Audit Restricted (log violations, don't block) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── KUBE-SYSTEM: Privileged (system pods need host access) ──
kubectl label namespace kube-system \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── VERIFY labels are applied ──
kubectl get namespace anihpj-prod --show-labels
# Look for: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

# ── REMOVE PSS labels (revert to no enforcement) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce- \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn- \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-

Testing PSS — What Happens When a Pod Violates Restricted

Bash — Test that PSS Restricted blocks a non-compliant pod 
# Create a namespace with Restricted enforcement
kubectl create namespace pss-test
kubectl label namespace pss-test pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

# Try to create a pod that runs as root (violates Restricted)
kubectl apply -n pss-test -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-root
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest
    # ❌ MISSING: runAsNonRoot: true (required by Restricted)
    # ❌ MISSING: seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (required by Restricted)
    # ❌ MISSING: capabilities: drop: [ALL] (required by Restricted)
EOF

# OUTPUT: Error from server (Forbidden): pods "test-root" is forbidden:
# violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.29": unrestricted capabilities
# (container "nginx" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]),
# runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "nginx" must set
# securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container
# "nginx" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault"
# or "Localhost")

# ✅ FIX the pod and try again
kubectl apply -n pss-test -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-fixed
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      capabilities:
        drop: [ALL]
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
EOF
# Pod created successfully ✅

The Admission Plugin Chain — Where PSS Fits in the Request Pipeline

PSS is just one admission plugin among many. When a pod creation request reaches the API server, it passes through a CHAIN of admission plugins, each with a specific responsibility. Understanding the order helps you troubleshoot: if a pod is rejected, was it PSS? NodeRestriction? An OPA webhook? Here's the exact chain:

Pod Creation Admission Chain — Every Plugin in Order
  CREATE POD REQUEST ENTERS ADMISSION CHAIN
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MUTATING PHASE (plugins can MODIFY the pod spec)                        │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  1. NamespaceLifecycle — Ensures namespace exists, is not terminating.   │
  │  2. MutatingAdmissionWebhook — External webhooks (Istio sidecar inject,  │
  │     Kyverno mutate rules). Can ADD containers, volumes, labels.          │
  │  3. PodSecurity (MUTATING) — Adds default seccompProfile if unset,       │
  │     adds default runAsNonRoot based on namespace policy (if configured). │
  │  ... (other mutating plugins)                                             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VALIDATING PHASE (plugins can ACCEPT or REJECT, but NOT modify)         │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                │
  │  4. PodSecurity (VALIDATING) ← ⬅⬅⬅ PSS CHECKS RUN HERE                   │
  │     Checks the (possibly mutated) pod spec against namespace PSS labels. │
  │     If enforce=restricted → REJECTS violations.                           │
  │  5. NodeRestriction — Ensures kubelets only modify their own pods/nodes. │
  │  6. ValidatingAdmissionWebhook — External webhooks (OPA, Kyverno verify).│
  │  7. ResourceQuota — Ensures namespace resource limits not exceeded.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚡ KEY INSIGHT: PSS runs AFTER mutating webhooks. This means:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • If Istio injects a sidecar, PSS validates the sidecar too.
  • If Kyverno adds a default seccompProfile, PSS sees the default.
  • BUT: If the original pod spec violates Restricted and a mutating webhook
    is supposed to fix it, PSS might reject the pod BEFORE the webhook runs
    (because PSS runs in BOTH mutating and validating phases).
  • The mutating PSS plugin runs FIRST in the mutating phase and can add
    defaults, then the validating PSS plugin runs later to check compliance.

17.3 PSS for the anihpj Namespace

Now let's apply PSS to the anihpj namespaces. The production namespace gets Restricted — every pod must run as non-root, with no capabilities, with RuntimeDefault Seccomp. The dev namespace gets Baseline (enforced) with Restricted warnings — developers can work freely but see warnings when their pods would fail production.

PSS Level Decision Flowchart — Which Level for Which Namespace?

🔍 Does this namespace contain workloads that NEED host-level access? (CNI plugins, CSI drivers, node exporters, monitoring daemons)
✅ YES → Use PRIVILEGED. But restrict with NetworkPolicy (Ch6) and RBAC (Ch9) to limit who can deploy to this namespace. Example: kube-system.
❓ No — the pods are user workloads. Continue.
🔍 Can ALL containers in this namespace run as non-root? (Dockerfiles have USER 1000 or equivalent)
❌ NO — some containers still need root → Use BASELINE (enforce). Add warn=restricted to nudge toward fixing. Example: anihpj-dev.
✅ YES — all containers are non-root ready. Continue.
🔍 Can ALL containers run with read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, and RuntimeDefault Seccomp?
❌ NO → Use BASELINE (enforce) + audit=restricted. Review the audit logs to identify what needs fixing.
🎉 YES → Use RESTRICTED! This is the maximum security level. All new pods will be validated against it. Example: anihpj-prod.

Complete PSS Configuration for anihpj Namespaces

Bash — Configure PSS for all anihpj namespaces 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# PSS CONFIGURATION FOR ANIHPJ CLUSTER
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# ── PRODUCTION: RESTRICTED (maximum security) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29 \
  --overwrite

# ── STAGING: RESTRICTED (same as prod — test what you deploy) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29 \
  --overwrite

# ── DEV: BASELINE enforce + RESTRICTED warn (flexibility + education) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29 \
  --overwrite

echo "✅ PSS configured for all anihpj namespaces"
echo ""
echo "Verification:"
kubectl get namespace anihpj-prod --show-labels | grep pod-security
kubectl get namespace anihpj-staging --show-labels | grep pod-security
kubectl get namespace anihpj-dev --show-labels | grep pod-security

Compliant anihpj Pod Spec for Restricted Level

YAML — anihpj Django deployment compliant with PSS Restricted 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj-prod  # ← This namespace has enforce=restricted
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-django
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-django
    spec:
      # ── PSS RESTRICTED COMPLIANCE ──
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true           # ✅ Required by Restricted
        runAsUser: 1000               # ✅ Specific non-root UID
        runAsGroup: 1000              # ✅ Specific non-root GID
        fsGroup: 1000                 # ✅ Filesystem group
        seccompProfile:               # ✅ Required by Restricted
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # ✅ Required by Restricted
          capabilities:
            drop: [ALL]                    # ✅ Required by Restricted
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # ✅ Required by Restricted
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp            # Writable emptyDir for temp files
        - name: media
          mountPath: /app/media      # Writable PVC for uploads
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}                 # ✅ Allowed volume type
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim:       # ✅ Allowed volume type
          claimName: anihpj-media

Migrating from Baseline to Restricted — A Real-World Scenario

Most organizations start with Baseline and gradually migrate to Restricted. This is not a one-day task — it requires updating Dockerfiles, fixing application code, and testing. Here's the systematic migration playbook:

🟡 SCENARIO: Migrating anihpj Namespaces from Baseline to Restricted

Current state: anihpj-prod has enforce=baseline. Pods run as root (UID 0) because the Dockerfile doesn't specify a USER. Seccomp is not configured. Capabilities are not dropped.

Goal: enforce=restricted without breaking production.

Migration playbook — 4 phases over 2 sprints:

  1. PHASE 1: DISCOVERY (Sprint 1, Week 1)
    • Add audit=restricted and warn=restricted labels to anihpj-prod (keep enforce=baseline).
    • For 1 week, collect audit logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* | grep "would violate PodSecurity"
    • Identify ALL pods that would violate Restricted. Document which fields need fixing for each.
  2. PHASE 2: FIX (Sprint 1, Week 2)
    • For each non-compliant pod, fix the root cause:
      • Dockerfile: Add USER 1000 at the end
      • Deployment YAML: Add runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, capabilities: drop: [ALL]
      • Identify writable paths: Add emptyDir or PVC volumes for /tmp, /var/log, etc.
    • Deploy fixes to staging (anihpj-staging) first. Verify pods start successfully with enforce=restricted.
  3. PHASE 3: ENFORCE (Sprint 2)
    • Change anihpj-prod label: enforce=restricted
    • Roll out fixed deployments one at a time (canary deployment).
    • Monitor: any pod that still violates Restricted will fail to create. Roll back and fix.
  4. PHASE 4: LOCK (Ongoing)
    • Add OPA/Kyverno policy (Ch24) to verify Dockerfiles have USER directives in CI/CD.
    • Add CI/CD check: every Deployment YAML must pass kubectl apply --dry-run=server against a Restricted namespace.
    • Goal: Prevent non-compliant pods from ever reaching the API server.

Common migration pitfalls:

  • Forgotten writable directories: App writes to /var/log/app.log but rootfs is read-only → crash. Fix: mount emptyDir at /var/log.
  • Port binding below 1024: App binds to port 80 as non-root → EACCES. Fix: use port 8000 or add NET_BIND_SERVICE capability (but then you lose Restricted).
  • Third-party images: The postgres:15 image runs as root by default. Fix: use postgres:15-alpine which runs as postgres user, or set securityContext explicitly.

📊 Chapter 17 Visual Summary — Pod Security Standards at a Glance

🔴
Privileged

Use for: kube-system pods (CNI, CSI)
Blocks: Nothing
Allows: Everything including host access
Risk: Highest — full node access

🟡
Baseline

Use for: Dev/staging namespaces
Blocks: hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged, hostPath
Allows: Root containers, most capabilities
Risk: Medium — known exploits blocked

🟢
Restricted

Use for: Production (anihpj-prod)
Blocks: Root, all capabilities, writable rootfs
Requires: non-root, Seccomp, drop ALL
Risk: Lowest — maximum pod hardening

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

PSS tasks on the CKS exam follow a three-step workflow: (1) Label the namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<level>, (2) Identify which fields in a given pod spec violate the level, (3) Fix the pod spec by adding the required fields (runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile, drop ALL, readOnlyRootFilesystem). Remember: the labels go on the NAMESPACE, not the pod. The pod spec must comply with the namespace's level. And the enforce-version label is important — it determines which version of the PSS policy definitions are used. Without it, the API server uses the latest built-in version, which may have slightly different rules.

PSS Selection Flowchart — Which Level Should You Choose?

Decision Tree: Privileged → Baseline → Restricted
  START: I need to secure my namespace
         │
         ▼
  Q1: Does this workload NEED host-level access?
      (hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, privileged?)
  YES → Use PRIVILEGED (but ask: is there another way?)
  NO  ↓
  Q2: Can the workload run as a non-root user?
      (Does the Dockerfile have USER 1000?)
  NO  → Use BASELINE (allows root, blocks known exploits)
  YES ↓
  Q3: Can the container run with read-only root filesystem?
      (Writable dirs handled via emptyDir / PVC mounts?)
  NO  → Use BASELINE (allows writable root fs)
  YES ↓
  Q4: Can you drop ALL Linux capabilities?
      (Does the app need NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN, etc.?)
  NO  → Use BASELINE + specific capabilities allowed
  YES ↓
  🎉  Use RESTRICTED — Maximum security for this workload!

  RECOMMENDED FOR ANIHPJ:
  ─────────────────────
  anihpj-prod → RESTRICTED (public job listings)
  anihpj-dev  → BASELINE (developer flexibility)
  kube-system → PRIVILEGED (CNI plugins NEED host access)
      → But: apply NetworkPolicy to restrict who reaches them

PSS Three Levels — Side-by-Side Visual Comparison

  ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐
  │  🔴 PRIVILEGED       │ │  🟡 BASELINE         │ │  🟢 RESTRICTED    │
  │  (Most permissive)   │ │  (Moderate security) │ │  (Maximum security)│
  ├─────────────────────┤ ├─────────────────────┤ ├───────────────────┤
  │                     │ │                     │ │                    │
  │  ✅ Allowed:        │ │  ❌ Blocked:        │ │  ❌ Blocked:       │

  🔒 ENFORCEMENT MODES (can combine all three):
  enforce = block the pod (hard stop)  │  audit = log violation only
  warn = show warning in API response  │  (use audit+warn first!)

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   PSS ENFORCEMENT — Label → Admission → Accept/Reject                      │
  │                                                                           │
  │   Namespace: anihpj-prod                                                  │
  │   labels:                                                                  │
  │     pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted                         │
  │                                                                           │

  │   → PodSecurity admission plugin checks namespace labels                 │
  │   → Evaluates pod against Restricted profile:                             │
  │     ✓ runAsNonRoot=true?  ✓ seccomp=RuntimeDefault?                      │

  │     ✓ no hostPath/hostNetwork/hostPID? ✓ allowPrivEscalation=false?     │

  │   • runAsNonRoot: true                                                    │
  │   • seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault or Localhost                       │
  │   • capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]                                            │
  │   • No privileged containers                                              │
  │   • No hostPath volumes                                                   │
  │   • No hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC                                       │
  │   • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false                                        │

📝 Chapter 17 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What single kubectl command enforces PSS Restricted on namespace "prod-ns"? Write the exact command.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl label ns prod-ns pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label ns prod-ns pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30
Q2
Name three pod spec fields that will cause a pod to be rejected by PSS Restricted.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Missing runAsNonRoot: true — pod could run as root, (2) hostPID: true or hostNetwork: true — breaks pod isolation, (3) privileged: true — grants all capabilities + device access, (4) capabilities.add (any) — Restricted requires drop ALL, (5) hostPath volumes — direct node filesystem access.

Q3
You're migrating from PSS Baseline to Restricted. What's the safest rollout strategy?
Show Answer
Answer

Phase 1: Add audit=restricted label — violations logged but pods still deploy. Phase 2: Add warn=restricted — developers see warnings. Phase 3: After all violating pods are fixed, add enforce=restricted. Never jump straight to enforce — existing non-compliant pods will be blocked from restarting.

Q4
What's the difference between PSS Baseline and PSS Restricted? Give 2 examples of pods that would pass Baseline but fail Restricted.
Show Answer
Answer

Baseline prevents KNOWN privilege escalations (privileged containers, hostPath, hostNetwork). Restricted adds STRONGER pod hardening (requires non-root, requires Seccomp, drops ALL capabilities). Pods that pass Baseline but fail Restricted: (1) A pod running as root with RuntimeDefault Seccomp — Baseline allows root, Restricted doesn't. (2) A pod without capabilities.drop=ALL — Baseline doesn't require capability dropping, Restricted does.

Q5
Write the PSS labels that audit, warn, AND enforce the Baseline standard on the "anihpj-prod" namespace. What's the purpose of all three?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30

Purpose: enforce (blocks), audit (logs to audit log), warn (shows kubectl warning). All three together provide defense in depth: even if enforce is accidentally removed, audit and warn still provide visibility.

Explanation

The three-label pattern is the CKS best practice. enforce provides the actual security. audit creates an audit trail for compliance. warn provides immediate feedback to developers. On the exam, always apply all three — it shows you understand defense in depth for policy enforcement.

Q6
A namespace has enforce=restricted. A pod with runAsNonRoot: false is submitted. What happens? What about a pod with runAsNonRoot: true but no seccompProfile?
Show Answer
Answer

runAsNonRoot: false → REJECTED. The pod is blocked at admission time with: violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.30": "runAsNonRoot != true".

runAsNonRoot: true, no seccompProfile → REJECTED. Restricted requires either seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault or seccompProfile.type: Localhost. If neither is specified, the pod is rejected with: violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.30": "seccompProfile". The API server does NOT auto-apply RuntimeDefault — it must be explicit in the pod spec.

Explanation

This is a common CKS exam trap. Restricted does not auto-apply defaults — it requires EXPLICIT security configurations. If you omit seccompProfile, the pod is rejected even if you intended RuntimeDefault. Always explicitly set seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault alongside runAsNonRoot: true when targeting Restricted namespaces.

Q7
What is the difference between PSS (Pod Security Standards) and PSA (Pod Security Admission)? Which is the policy definition and which is the enforcement mechanism?
Show Answer
Answer

PSS (Pod Security Standards): The POLICY DEFINITIONS — Privileged, Baseline, Restricted. These are documents that define what's allowed at each level. PSA (Pod Security Admission): The ENFORCEMENT MECHANISM — a built-in admission controller that enforces PSS. PSA reads the namespace labels and rejects pods that violate the specified standard. Think of it as: PSS = the law, PSA = the police.

Explanation

This distinction is tested on CKS. You can't "install PSS" — you enable PSA (the admission controller) and then apply PSS labels to namespaces. The admission controller PodSecurity must be in --enable-admission-plugins. If PSA isn't enabled, the PSS labels on namespaces have zero effect.

Q8
A namespace has enforce=restricted. A DaemonSet for node monitoring needs hostNetwork: true to collect node metrics. How do you handle this without removing Restricted from the namespace?
Show Answer
Answer

Option 1: Place the DaemonSet in a separate namespace (e.g., node-monitoring) with enforce=privileged but strong RBAC and NetworkPolicy. Option 2: Use pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged on the monitoring namespace but add compensating controls: AppArmor profile, custom Seccomp, readOnlyRootFilesystem. Option 3: Use a mutating admission webhook (Kyverno) to exempt specific pods from PSA enforcement. The key: you CANNOT make exceptions within a Restricted namespace — PSS is all-or-nothing per namespace.

Explanation

PSS is intentionally rigid — no exceptions within a namespace. This forces proper namespace segmentation. Privileged workloads go in privileged namespaces with compensating controls. On the CKS exam, the answer to "how to allow this privileged pod in a Restricted namespace" is always: "create a separate namespace with appropriate controls."

Q9
Write the pod securityContext that satisfies ALL Restricted requirements. Include runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile, capabilities, and readOnlyRootFilesystem.
Show Answer
Answer
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 3000
  fsGroup: 2000
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
containers:
- name: app
  image: nginx
  securityContext:
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    capabilities:
      drop:
      - ALL
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
Explanation

This is the golden pod securityContext for CKS. Every field serves a purpose: runAsNonRoot prevents root, seccompProfile restricts syscalls, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false prevents setuid binaries, capabilities.drop: [ALL] strips all Linux capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem prevents writing to the container image. Memorize this block — it's used in multiple CKS tasks.

Q10
You notice that after applying enforce=baseline to the "default" namespace, existing pods still run but new pods that violate Baseline are rejected. Why are existing pods not affected?
Show Answer
Answer

PSA only evaluates pods at creation time (CREATE and UPDATE operations). Existing pods were created before the label was applied and are grandfathered in. They continue to run even if they violate the policy. PSA does NOT enforce against already-running pods. This is why gradual rollout (audit → warn → enforce) is critical — you need time to fix existing pods before enforcement blocks their restarts.

Explanation

This is the most important operational detail about PSA. On the CKS exam: (1) applying enforce=restricted does NOT kill running pods, (2) but if those pods restart (node failure, rolling update, eviction), they will be BLOCKED from restarting, (3) always fix existing pods BEFORE applying enforce. Use kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o json | jq '.items[] | select(...violates...)' to identify pods that need fixing.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Apply PSS Restricted to a namespace (EXAM PATTERN)
kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted
kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

# 2. Check PSS violations in a namespace
kubectl get events -n prod --field-selector reason=FailedCreate | grep -i "pod-security"
kubectl describe ns prod | grep pod-security  # Show current PSS labels

# 3. Test if a pod would be rejected
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml --dry-run=server -n prod  # PSS runs BEFORE creation
# If rejected: "pods 'name' is forbidden: violates PodSecurity 'restricted:latest'"

# 4. Check current PSS admission controller
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep PodSecurity
# Should see: --enable-admission-plugins=...,PodSecurity,...
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 17 Traps
  • Restricted ≠ Baseline: Restricted adds non-root requirement, enforces seccomp RuntimeDefault, and requires capabilities.drop=ALL. Most existing deployments that pass Baseline will FAIL Restricted — you MUST update pod specs before applying Restricted.
  • PSS labels are per-namespace, not per-pod: You can't apply PSS to a single pod. It applies to ALL pods in the namespace. If you need per-pod granularity, use a ValidatingWebhook (OPA/Kyverno) instead of PSS.
  • warn/audit don't block: enforce blocks, warn shows a warning in kubectl output, audit logs to audit log. Always start with warn+audit, verify no violations, THEN enforce.
