Chapter 20: External Secret Management — Vault and Cloud KMS

Kubernetes Secrets (Chapter 19) solve the encryption-at-rest problem. But they don't solve several critical enterprise requirements: automatic rotation (changing database passwords every 30 days), dynamic secrets (one-time-use credentials that expire after use), audit logging (who accessed which secret and when), and centralized management (one place to manage secrets for Kubernetes, VMs, and serverless). This is where external secret management systems — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault — come in. This chapter teaches you how to integrate Vault with Kubernetes, use the External Secrets Operator (ESO) to sync external secrets into K8s Secrets, and implement a complete secret management strategy for the anihpj application.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🏦 Vault 🔐 Secret Management

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why Kubernetes Secrets alone are not enough for enterprise requirements
  • ✅ How HashiCorp Vault solves secret rotation, dynamic secrets, and audit logging
  • ✅ How the External Secrets Operator (ESO) syncs secrets from cloud providers into K8s
  • ✅ How to implement Vault for anihpj — Kubernetes auth, policies, and sidecar injection
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% Supply Chain Security 20%

20.1 Why Kubernetes Secrets Alone Are Not Enough for Enterprise

Chapter 19 solved the problem of encrypting Secrets in etcd. But encryption at rest is just one piece of the puzzle. Here are the gaps that Kubernetes Secrets alone cannot fill:

K8s Secrets vs External Secret Managers

RequirementKubernetes SecretsHashiCorp VaultAWS Secrets Manager
Encryption at rest✅ With EncryptionConfiguration (Ch19)✅ Always encrypted✅ Always encrypted
Automatic rotation❌ Manual only✅ Automatic with database plugins✅ Built-in rotation schedules
Dynamic secrets❌ Static only✅ Creates per-pod, auto-expiring creds❌ Static only
Access audit❌ Only via K8s audit logs (complex)✅ Built-in audit device✅ CloudTrail integration
Centralized mgmt❌ Per-cluster✅ One Vault for all clusters✅ Regional service
Multi-cloud❌ K8s only✅ K8s + VMs + serverless⚠️ AWS only

20.2 HashiCorp Vault — Enterprise-Grade Secret Management

Vault is the gold standard for secret management. It stores, leases, and rotates secrets; generates dynamic database credentials on demand; and provides a complete audit trail. For Kubernetes, Vault integrates via the Kubernetes auth method — pods authenticate to Vault using their ServiceAccount JWT tokens, and Vault verifies the token with the Kubernetes API before granting access:

Vault Kubernetes Auth Flow — Pod → ServiceAccount → Vault → Dynamic Secret
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VAULT + KUBERNETES INTEGRATION FLOW                                    │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 1: POD AUTHENTICATES TO VAULT                                     │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                                   │
  │  anihpj pod has a ServiceAccount token mounted at:                      │
  │  /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token                    │
  │                                                                         │
  │  Vault Agent (sidecar or init container) reads this token and sends it  │
  │  to Vault: POST /v1/auth/kubernetes/login                               │
  │  {                                                                       │
  │    "role": "anihpj-django",                                              │
  │    "jwt": ""                                         │
  │  }                                                                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 2: VAULT VERIFIES THE TOKEN                                       │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────                                      │
  │  Vault calls the Kubernetes TokenReview API:                             │
  │  POST https://kube-apiserver:6443/apis/authentication.k8s.io/v1/tokenreviews│
  │                                                                         │
  │  K8s API verifies: ✅ Token is valid, signed by the cluster's CA        │
  │                    ✅ Token belongs to SA "anihpj-sa" in ns "anihpj-prod"│
  │                                                                         │
  │  Vault checks its role binding: "anihpj-django" role allows SA          │
  │  "anihpj-sa" in namespace "anihpj-prod" → ✅ MATCH                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 3: VAULT RETURNS A VAULT TOKEN + SECRETS                          │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────                             │
  │  Vault issues a short-lived Vault token (TTL: 1 hour) and returns       │
  │  the secrets the anihpj-django role is allowed to read:                 │
  │  {                                                                       │
  │    "data": {                                                             │
  │      "database-password": "xyz-dynamic-cred-2026",                       │
  │      "django-secret-key": "50-char-random-string",                       │
  │      "redis-password": "redis-secret-xyz"                                │
  │    },                                                                    │
  │    "lease_duration": 3600,                                               │
  │    "renewable": true                                                     │
  │  }                                                                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 4: VAULT AGENT WRITES SECRETS TO POD FILESYSTEM                    │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  Vault Agent sidecar writes secrets to a shared volume:                 │
  │  /vault/secrets/database-password → "xyz-dynamic-cred-2026"             │
  │  /vault/secrets/django-secret-key → "50-char-random-string"              │
  │                                                                         │
  │  The anihpj app reads these files at startup (or watches for changes).  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Dynamic Database Secrets — How Vault Generates Per-Pod Credentials

One of Vault's most powerful features is dynamic secrets for databases. Instead of storing a static database password that every pod shares (and that never changes), Vault generates a unique username and password for each pod that automatically expires after a configurable TTL. When the pod terminates (or the lease expires), Vault revokes the credential on the database. This means a compromised database password is worthless after the TTL — and each pod has a unique credential, so you can trace database activity to a specific pod:

Vault Dynamic Database Secrets — Per-Pod, Auto-Expiring Credentials
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VAULT DYNAMIC DATABASE SECRET FLOW                                     │
  │                                                                         │
  │  SETUP (one-time):                                                      │
  │  ─────────────────                                                      │
  │  Vault admin configures the PostgreSQL database plugin:                 │
  │  vault write database/config/anihpj-postgres \                          │
  │    plugin_name=postgresql-database-plugin \                              │
  │    allowed_roles="anihpj-readonly" \                                      │
  │    connection_url="postgresql://{{username}}:{{password}}@postgres:5432/anihpj"│
  │    username="vault-admin" \                                               │
  │    password="vault-admin-password"                                        │
  │                                                                         │
  │  Vault creates a role that defines the SQL to create credentials:        │
  │  vault write database/roles/anihpj-readonly \                            │
  │    db_name=anihpj-postgres \                                              │
  │    creation_statements="CREATE USER \"{{name}}\" WITH PASSWORD '{{password}}'│
  │                         VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}'; \                    │
  │                         GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public     │
  │                         TO \"{{name}}\";" \                                  │
  │    default_ttl="1h" \                                                     │
  │    max_ttl="24h"                                                          │
  │                                                                         │
  │  RUNTIME (every pod startup):                                           │
  │  ────────────────────────────                                             │
  │  1. anihpj pod starts → Vault Agent requests database credentials:       │
  │     vault read database/creds/anihpj-readonly                            │
  │                                                                         │
  │  2. Vault connects to PostgreSQL AS vault-admin.                        │
  │  3. Vault executes the creation_statements SQL:                          │
  │     CREATE USER "v-anihpj-abc123" WITH PASSWORD 'xyz-dynamic'            │
  │     VALID UNTIL '2026-06-14 15:00:00';                                    │
  │     GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO "v-anihpj-abc123";    │
  │                                                                         │
  │  4. Vault returns the credentials to the pod:                            │
  │     username: v-anihpj-abc123                                            │
  │     password: xyz-dynamic                                                │
  │     lease_id: database/creds/anihpj-readonly/abc123                      │
  │     lease_duration: 1h                                                   │
  │                                                                         │
  │  5. Pod uses these credentials to connect to PostgreSQL.                │
  │                                                                         │
  │  AFTER 1 HOUR (TTL expiry):                                             │
  │  ────────────────────────────                                             │
  │  • Vault automatically connects to PostgreSQL and runs:                  │
  │    DROP USER "v-anihpj-abc123"                                            │
  │  • The credential is REVOKED on the database.                            │
  │  • The pod needs to request NEW credentials (or its lease was renewed). │
  │                                                                         │
  │  ⚡ SECURITY BENEFITS:                                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │
  │  • Stolen password → valid for MAX 1 hour (then auto-revoked)           │
  │  • Each pod has UNIQUE credentials → trace DB activity per pod          │
  │  • No static password in Secrets, ConfigMaps, or env vars               │
  │  • PostgreSQL never knows a long-lived password exists                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

20.3 External Secrets Operator (ESO)

The External Secrets Operator (ESO) takes a different approach from Vault Agent. Instead of injecting secrets directly into pods, ESO syncs secrets from external providers into Kubernetes Secrets. Your pods continue to use native K8s Secrets (envFrom, volume mounts) — they don't know the secrets came from AWS/GCP/Vault. This gives you external management with zero application changes:

YAML — ExternalSecret resource for anihpj using AWS Secrets Manager 
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-creds
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h              # Sync every hour
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager      # Which backend to pull from
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: db-creds                 # K8s Secret to create/update
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
  - secretKey: DATABASE_URL        # Key in the K8s Secret
    remoteRef:
      key: anihpj/prod/database    # Key in AWS Secrets Manager
      property: url

ESO vs Vault Agent — Which Architecture to Choose

Both ESO and Vault Agent solve the external-secrets problem, but with fundamentally different architectures. The choice depends on whether you want zero application changes (ESO) or maximum security with dynamic secrets (Vault Agent):

🔄 ESO (External Secrets Operator)
  • How: Syncs external secrets → K8s Secrets
  • App changes: ZERO (uses native K8s Secret API)
  • Refresh: Polling (1h interval typical)
  • Dynamic secrets: Not supported
  • Best for: AWS/GCP shops, lift-and-shift migrations
🏦 Vault Agent Sidecar
  • How: Injects secrets directly into pod filesystem
  • App changes: Read from /vault/secrets/ instead of env vars
  • Refresh: Continuous (renews lease before expiry)
  • Dynamic secrets: ✅ Fully supported
  • Best for: Zero-trust, dynamic DB creds, multi-cloud

Dynamic Secrets — The Killer Feature of Vault

Static secrets (like the ones in Kubernetes Secrets) are a "steal once, use forever" problem. Dynamic secrets are generated on-demand per request, automatically expire, and are unique to each consumer. Here's how Vault dynamic database credentials work for anihpj:

Dynamic Database Credentials — Generated per Pod, Auto-Expiring
  1. anihpj pod starts → Vault Agent sidecar reads SA token
  2. Sidecar authenticates to Vault: POST /v1/auth/kubernetes/login
     → Vault verifies token with K8s API → returns Vault token
  3. Sidecar requests database credentials:
     GET /v1/database/creds/anihpj-readonly
     → Vault creates TEMPORARY postgres user with limited permissions
     → Returns: username (v-token-anihpj-abc123), password (random),
        lease_duration: 1h, lease_id: database/creds/anihpj-readonly/xyz
  4. Sidecar writes credentials to pod filesystem:
     /vault/secrets/db-username, /vault/secrets/db-password
  5. Django reads these files → connects to postgres
  6. After 1 hour: credentials EXPIRE → Vault automatically revokes
     the temporary postgres user → App must request new credentials

  🔑 KEY ADVANTAGES:
  • Stolen credentials are useless after 1 hour
  • Each pod gets UNIQUE credentials (blast radius isolation)
  • Postgres audit log shows WHICH pod accessed data (per-credential)
  • No manual rotation — Vault handles everything
  • If pod is compromised: credentials expire in <1 hour automatically

20.4 Implementing Vault for anihpj

Here is the complete Vault configuration for the anihpj Django application. The Vault policy grants access to the secrets the Django app needs, the Kubernetes auth role binds the anihpj ServiceAccount to that policy, and the Vault Agent sidecar injects secrets into the pod:

HCL — Vault policy for anihpj Django application 
# Vault policy: anihpj-django-policy
path "secret/data/anihpj-prod/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
path "database/creds/anihpj-readonly" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
# Configure Kubernetes auth in Vault
vault auth enable kubernetes

vault write auth/kubernetes/config \
    token_reviewer_jwt="$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" \
    kubernetes_host="https://kube-apiserver:6443" \
    kubernetes_ca_cert="@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt"

# Bind the anihpj ServiceAccount to the policy
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/anihpj-django \
    bound_service_account_names=anihpj-sa \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj-prod \
    policies=anihpj-django-policy \
    ttl=1h

K8s Secrets Gaps (20.1)

No rotation, no dynamic secrets, no audit. External managers fill these enterprise gaps.

K8s auth → ServiceAccount JWT → Vault token → dynamic secrets → pod filesystem.

🔄

Syncs AWS/GCP/Vault → K8s Secrets. Zero app changes.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam may ask about external secret management concepts — know the difference between Vault Agent sidecar injection (direct to pod) and ESO (sync to K8s Secret). Understand the Vault Kubernetes auth flow: pod presents SA JWT → Vault calls TokenReview API → Vault verifies identity → Vault issues token + secrets. The exam focuses on CONCEPTUAL understanding of these integrations, not deep Vault configuration.

🔧 Under the Hood — Vault Kubernetes Auth Flow: Pod SA JWT → TokenReview → Vault Token → Secret Injection — Complete Sequence 
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   VAULT KUBERNETES AUTHENTICATION FLOW                                     │
  │                                                                           │
  │   1. POD STARTS — SA token automatically mounted (if not disabled)       │
  │      /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token                  │
  │                                                                           │
  │   2. VAULT AGENT (sidecar or init container) reads SA token              │
  │      → Sends token to Vault: POST /v1/auth/kubernetes/login              │
  │      → Body: { jwt: "<sa-token>", role: "anihpj" }                      │
  │                                                                           │
  │   3. VAULT CALLS KUBERNETES TokenReview API                               │
  │      → Validates the SA token is genuine (signed by API server)          │
  │      → Returns: { namespace, serviceAccountName, podName, uid }          │
  │                                                                           │
  │   4. VAULT VERIFIES THE SA MATCHES THE BOUND ROLE                         │
  │      → Checks: SA namespace + name match bound_service_account_*         │
  │      → Checks: SA is in the allowed namespaces                           │
  │      → If match → Issues Vault token with attached policies              │
  │                                                                           │
  │   5. VAULT AGENT USES TOKEN TO READ SECRETS                               │
  │      → GET /v1/secret/data/anihpj/prod                                    │
  │      → Vault evaluates policy: "anihpj-policy" allows read               │
  │      → Returns: { django-secret-key, db-password, redis-password }       │
  │                                                                           │
  │   6. SECRETS INJECTED INTO POD                                            │
  │      → Sidecar: writes to shared volume (/vault/secrets/)                │
  │      → CSI driver: mounts as tmpfs volume                                │
  │      → App reads secrets from file, NOT from env vars or K8s Secrets     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 20 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What's the key difference between storing secrets in Kubernetes Secrets vs HashiCorp Vault?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes Secrets: stored in etcd (encrypted at rest if configured), accessed via API server, no automatic rotation, no audit per-secret access. Vault: stored externally (never in etcd), injected at runtime via sidecar/CSI, supports dynamic secrets + automatic rotation, full audit trail per secret access, fine-grained access policies per secret path.

Q2
How does a Kubernetes pod authenticate to HashiCorp Vault? What credential does it use?
Show Answer
Answer

The pod uses its mounted ServiceAccount JWT token. The Vault agent sends this token to Vault's Kubernetes auth endpoint. Vault calls the Kubernetes TokenReview API to validate the token and extract the SA's identity (namespace, name, UID). Vault then checks if this SA matches a configured Vault role and issues a Vault token with the role's policies.

Q3
What is the External Secrets Operator (ESO) and how does it differ from Vault Agent Sidecar?
Show Answer
Answer

ESO: Syncs secrets from external providers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) into Kubernetes Secrets. The secret STILL ends up in etcd (but can be encrypted at rest). Apps read from K8s Secrets as usual. Vault Agent Sidecar: Injects secrets directly into the pod's filesystem as a shared volume. Secrets NEVER touch etcd. The app reads from a file, not a K8s Secret. ESO is simpler to adopt (no app changes), Vault Agent is more secure (secrets bypass etcd entirely).

Q4
What Vault command stores a secret and what command reads it back? Write both.
Show Answer
Answer
vault kv put secret/anihpj/prod django-secret-key="value" db-password="pass"
vault kv get secret/anihpj/prod
vault kv get -field=django-secret-key secret/anihpj/prod  # Get single field
Q5
How does Vault's dynamic secret engine for databases work? What security advantage does it provide over static secrets?
Show Answer
Answer

Vault connects to the database as a privileged user and creates a temporary, per-request database credential. Each pod gets a UNIQUE username/password that: (1) is valid for a short TTL (e.g., 1 hour), (2) is automatically revoked when the TTL expires, (3) has scoped permissions (e.g., read-only on specific tables). Advantage over static secrets: even if an attacker steals the credential, it expires quickly and can only access what's explicitly granted. No long-lived shared database password exists anywhere.

Explanation

Dynamic secrets are Vault's killer feature for CKS. Instead of storing a shared PostgreSQL password that never changes, each pod instance gets its own temporary credential. On the exam, if asked about "credential rotation" or "preventing lateral movement after credential theft," dynamic secrets are the answer.

Q6
Compare Vault Agent Sidecar Injector vs Vault CSI Provider. Which one requires application changes, and which is transparent to the app?
Show Answer
Answer

Vault Agent Sidecar: Injects a Vault agent container alongside your app. Secrets are written to a shared memory volume (/vault/secrets/). The app reads secrets from FILES. Requires some app awareness (knowing the file path). Vault CSI Provider: Uses the Kubernetes CSI (Container Storage Interface) to mount secrets as a volume. Secrets appear as files in the pod but NO sidecar container is needed. Completely transparent to the app. CSI is the newer, preferred approach on CKS because it's simpler and uses fewer resources.

Explanation

Both methods keep secrets out of etcd. The difference is implementation: Sidecar = extra container + shared volume, CSI = kernel-level volume mount. On the CKS exam, CSI Provider is the modern recommended approach. But you should know both exist — older clusters may use the sidecar method.

Q7
Write the Vault policy that allows an anihpj pod to read ONLY its own database password at secret/anihpj/prod and nothing else.
Show Answer
Answer
path "secret/data/anihpj/prod" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
# Deny everything else
path "*" {
  capabilities = ["deny"]
}

Bind this policy to a Vault role that maps to the anihpj-sa ServiceAccount in the prod namespace. The pod can only read secret/anihpj/prod — it cannot read secret/other-app/prod or write any secret.

Explanation

Vault policies follow the least privilege principle — exactly like Kubernetes RBAC. Each application should have its own Vault policy scoped to its own secret paths. On the CKS exam, you may need to write a Vault policy or explain how Vault RBAC maps to Kubernetes RBAC. The key concept: Vault policies are path-based (file-system-like), not resource-based (like K8s RBAC).

Q8
What is Vault's Kubernetes auth method, and what Kubernetes API does Vault call to validate a pod's identity?
Show Answer
Answer

Vault calls TokenReview API (POST /apis/authentication.k8s.io/v1/tokenreviews) to validate the pod's ServiceAccount JWT. The flow: (1) Pod sends its SA JWT to Vault. (2) Vault forwards the JWT to the Kubernetes API server's TokenReview endpoint. (3) API server validates the JWT signature and returns the SA identity (namespace, name, UID, groups). (4) Vault maps this identity to a Vault role. (5) Vault issues a Vault token scoped to that role's policies.

Explanation

This is Kubernetes-native authentication for external systems. Vault trusts the API server's token validation. The pod never needs a separate Vault credential — its Kubernetes identity IS its Vault identity. On the CKS exam, understand that Vault's Kubernetes auth method eliminates the need for static Vault tokens in pods.

Q9
An External Secrets Operator SecretStore fails to connect to AWS Secrets Manager with "AccessDenied." Where do you check the IAM permissions: on the node role, the pod's IRSA role, or the ESO controller's SA?
Show Answer
Answer

Check the ESO controller's ServiceAccount IRSA role (or the SecretStore's referenced credentials). ESO uses its own identity to fetch secrets from external providers. It does NOT use the node's IAM role or the application pod's SA. The flow: ESO controller → authenticates to AWS using its SA's IRSA → fetches secret from Secrets Manager → creates Kubernetes Secret → application pod reads the K8s Secret (no direct AWS access needed by the app pod).

Explanation

This is a common ESO debugging question. The SecretStore configuration determines which credentials ESO uses. In AWS, this is typically IRSA mapped to the ESO ServiceAccount. On the CKS exam: (1) ESO controller SA needs IAM permissions to read secrets, (2) application pods do NOT need IAM permissions, (3) node role is irrelevant for ESO.

Q10
You need to migrate 50 Kubernetes Secrets from plaintext etcd storage to Vault with zero application downtime. Describe the migration strategy using External Secrets Operator.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. Set up Vault + ESO: Deploy ESO, create SecretStore pointing to Vault.
  2. Import secrets to Vault: Export each K8s Secret → import to Vault: kubectl get secret <name> -o jsonpath='{.data}' | while read k v; do vault kv put secret/app/$k $(echo $v | base64 -d); done.
  3. Create ExternalSecrets: For each secret, create an ExternalSecret resource that maps Vault paths to K8s Secret keys. ESO syncs the secrets.
  4. Update Deployments: Change secretKeyRef references to point to the ESO-managed Secret names (same names, just now ESO-managed).
  5. Verify: Deploy to staging first. Confirm pods start and function. Rolling update to production.
  6. Cleanup: After verification, delete the original manually-created Secrets (ESO now owns them).
Explanation

This is a real CKS scenario: migrating from native K8s Secrets to an external provider. The key design decision: ESO creates K8s Secrets that look identical to manually-created ones — same names, same keys. Applications don't need to change how they consume secrets (secretKeyRef still works). The only difference is the Secret is now synced from Vault instead of manually created.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Store and retrieve a secret in Vault
vault kv put secret/anihpj/prod db-password=SuperSecret123 api-key=sk-abc123
vault kv get secret/anihpj/prod

# 2. Read a secret into a Kubernetes Secret using CLI
vault kv get -field=db-password secret/anihpj/prod | kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-file=password=/dev/stdin -n prod

# 3. Check External Secrets Operator status
kubectl get externalsecrets -A  # Shows all synced secrets
kubectl get secretstore -A       # Shows connected Vault/AWS/GCP backends

# 4. Verify Vault authentication (Kubernetes auth method)
vault write auth/kubernetes/login role=anihpj-role jwt=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 20 Traps
  • Vault token expiry: Vault tokens have a TTL. If the External Secrets Operator's Vault token expires, it stops syncing secrets — and existing Kubernetes Secrets remain with stale values. Always configure token renewal or use the Kubernetes auth method (which auto-renews).
  • Secrets are still in etcd: External Secrets Operator creates regular Kubernetes Secret objects — which are stored in etcd. The external backend (Vault/AWS/GCP) is the SOURCE OF TRUTH, but the Secret data still exists in etcd. Use encryption at rest (Ch 19) for defense-in-depth.

Chapter 21: Container Runtime Sandboxing — gVisor and Kata Containers

Every container on a Kubernetes node shares the same Linux kernel. This is the defining architectural property of containerization — and its greatest security weakness. A single kernel exploit (like CVE-2022-0185) in one container gives the attacker access to every other container AND the host. Seccomp (Ch15) and AppArmor (Ch14) reduce the attack surface by blocking syscalls and file access — but they cannot protect against a zero-day kernel vulnerability that bypasses those filters. Sandboxed runtimes — gVisor and Kata Containers — solve this by adding an additional isolation layer between the container and the host kernel. gVisor intercepts syscalls in userspace with a written-from-scratch kernel simulator (Sentry). Kata Containers runs each container in its own lightweight virtual machine with a dedicated kernel. This chapter teaches you how both work, how to select them via RuntimeClass, and when to use each for the anihpj application.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1 hour 📦 Sandboxing 🛡️ Runtime Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why the shared kernel model is the fundamental container security weakness
  • ✅ How gVisor (Sentry) intercepts syscalls in userspace — and what it blocks
  • ✅ How Kata Containers provides hardware-level isolation with lightweight VMs
  • ✅ How to use RuntimeClass to assign different runtimes to different pods
  • ✅ When to use sandboxed runtimes — the decision flowchart for anihpj
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% System Hardening 15%

21.1 The Container Isolation Problem

Standard containers (runc) use Linux namespaces and cgroups for isolation — software constructs in the shared kernel. There is no hardware boundary. When a process in one container exploits a kernel vulnerability, it breaks through the namespace boundaries and gains access to the shared kernel — and from there, to every process, file, and network socket on the node. Sandboxed runtimes add a barrier that even a kernel exploit cannot cross — either by intercepting syscalls before they reach the kernel (gVisor) or by giving each container its own kernel in a VM (Kata).

Three Levels of Container Isolation

How gVisor Sentry Actually Works — The Syscall Interception Mechanism

gVisor's Sentry is not a full kernel — it's a user-space application written in Go that implements the Linux syscall interface. When a containerized application makes a syscall (e.g., open("/etc/shadow")), the normal path would be: CPU switches to kernel mode → kernel executes sys_open() → returns result. With gVisor, this path is intercepted at the platform layer before it ever reaches the host kernel:

gVisor Architecture — How Syscalls Get from App to Host Kernel (Safely)
  APPLICATION: open("/app/config.py", O_RDONLY)
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SENTRY (User-Space Kernel) — Runs in the sandbox pod's process          │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────                       │
  │  1. App makes syscall → CPU switches to kernel mode → but gVisor uses    │
  │     ptrace/seccomp to INTERCEPT the syscall BEFORE the host kernel       │
  │     processes it.                                                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  2. Sentry receives the syscall: open("/app/config.py", O_RDONLY)        │
  │                                                                           │
  │  3. Sentry has its OWN VFS (Virtual File System):                         │
  │     • Maintains a file descriptor table for the sandboxed process         │
  │     • Checks permissions against its OWN rules (not the host's)           │
  │     • If the file should be accessible → forwards to Gofer                │
  │     • If the file is NOT allowed → returns EACCES (never touches host)   │
  │                                                                           │
  │  4. Sentry translates the request into a 9P protocol message and sends   │
  │     it to the Gofer process (runs in a SEPARATE process, outside Sentry): │
  │     "Gofer: open /app/config.py, read 4096 bytes"                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  5. Gofer makes the ACTUAL host syscall: open("/app/config.py") →         │
  │     Linux kernel processes it → returns file descriptor → Gofer reads    │
  │     4096 bytes → sends data back to Sentry via 9P → Sentry returns       │
  │     data to the application.                                               │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ⚡ WHY THIS IS SECURE:                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                     │
  │  • The application NEVER makes syscalls directly to the host kernel.     │
  │  • Sentry validates every syscall against its own rules BEFORE           │
  │    forwarding to Gofer.                                                    │
  │  • Gofer only performs a LIMITED set of host operations (file I/O,       │
  │    socket creation). No mounts, no ptrace, no module loading.            │
  │  • Sentry implements the syscall in USER SPACE — a memory bug in Sentry │
  │    corrupts Sentry's memory, NOT the host kernel.                         │
  │  • Kernel exploit in the application → the exploit runs inside Sentry,   │
  │    which is a user-space process. To reach the host kernel, the attacker │
  │    would need to exploit Sentry AND THEN exploit the host kernel —       │
  │    two completely independent vulnerabilities.                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

21.2 RuntimeClass — Selecting the Runtime in Kubernetes

Kubernetes uses RuntimeClass to let you specify which container runtime to use for each pod. You can run trusted pods with runc (fast, low overhead) and untrusted pods with gVisor or Kata (secure, isolated) — all in the same cluster:

YAML — RuntimeClass + Pod using gVisor 
# ── RuntimeClass resource ──
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc              # The CRI handler name for gVisor

# ── Pod using gVisor RuntimeClass ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: untrusted-workload
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor   # ← Uses gVisor instead of default runc
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: untrusted-code-executor:v1

How RuntimeClass Maps to CRI Handlers in containerd

The handler field in RuntimeClass is not a magic string — it maps directly to a CRI handler registered in the container runtime's configuration. containerd uses a runtime configuration file that maps handler names to actual binary paths:

TOML — containerd config.toml registering gVisor and Kata handlers 
# /etc/containerd/config.toml
version = 2

[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"

[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runsc]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runsc.v1"

[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.kata]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.kata.v2"
  privileged_without_host_devices = true

# HOW THIS CONNECTS:
# RuntimeClass handler: "runsc" → containerd looks up [runtimes.runsc]
# → executes /usr/bin/runsc (gVisor) to create the container
# RuntimeClass handler: "kata" → containerd looks up [runtimes.kata]
# → executes /usr/bin/kata-runtime (Kata) to create the container

Sandbox Performance Tradeoffs — When the Slowdown Is Worth It

Workload Typerunc (Default)gVisorKata ContainersRecommendation
Web API (Django)100% baseline~85% perf (syscall overhead)~75% perf (VM overhead)runc for anihpj (trusted code, needs speed)
Database (Postgres)100% baseline~70% perf (many syscalls)~65% perfrunc (performance-critical)
User upload handler100% baseline~85% perf~75% perfgVisor (untrusted user input!)
CI/CD build jobs100% baseline~80% perf~70% perfKata (hardware isolation for untrusted builds)
Third-party microservice100% baseline~85% perf~75% perfKata or gVisor (untrusted vendor code)

Attack Scenario — What gVisor Prevents That runc Allows

ATTACK SCENARIO CVE-2022-0185 — Linux Kernel Heap Overflow (CVSS 8.4)
1
Attacker crafts malicious filesystem command

Using the unshare syscall with CLONE_NEWNS|CLONE_NEWUSER flags, the attacker triggers a heap buffer overflow in the Linux kernel's legacy_parse_param function. This CVE affected ALL Linux kernels 5.1+ through early 2022.

2
With runc: ATTACK SUCCEEDS

runc containers share the host kernel. The attacker's exploit corrupts kernel memory → gains root privileges → escapes the container entirely. Full node compromise. Seccomp does NOT block unshare in RuntimeDefault!

🛡️
With gVisor: ATTACK FAILS

gVisor containers run on a USERSPACE kernel (Sentry). The attacker's exploit runs against Sentry, NOT the host Linux kernel. Sentry is written in Go (memory-safe language) — no heap overflow possible. Even if the attack "succeeds," the attacker only compromises Sentry, not the host. gVisor then applies a SECOND seccomp filter between Sentry and the host kernel for defense-in-depth.

21.3 When to Use Sandboxed Runtimes

Not every pod needs gVisor or Kata. The decision is a tradeoff between security and performance:

🔍 Is this pod running code from untrusted users? (User-uploaded code, third-party containers)
✅ YES → Use gVisor or Kata. Example: anihpj media processing container.
❓ No — trusted internal code. Continue.
🔍 Is this a multi-tenant cluster with different customers sharing nodes?
✅ YES → Use Kata Containers for hardware-level tenant isolation.
❓ No — single tenant. Continue.
🔍 Is this a system workload (CNI, CSI, monitoring) needing full kernel access?
✅ YES → Use runc (default). These pods need full syscall access.
✅ Standard business workload (anihpj Django) → runc + Seccomp + AppArmor is sufficient.

21.4 Multi-Tenancy Isolation Patterns

The official CKS curriculum explicitly calls out multi-tenancy as a key isolation technique. Multi-tenancy means multiple teams, customers, or business units sharing the same Kubernetes cluster — each needing strong isolation guarantees that prevent one tenant from accessing another tenant's data, pods, or resources.

Multi-Tenancy Isolation Levels — From Soft to Hard

LevelIsolation TypeWhat It SeparatesBypass RiskCKS Tool
1. NamespaceLogical (Soft)RBAC, ResourceQuota, NetworkPolicy per namespaceHigh — namespace is NOT a security boundaryCh 9, Ch 6
2. NetworkNetwork (Medium)NetworkPolicy, CiliumNetworkPolicy, Istio mTLSMedium — misconfigured NP allows lateralCh 6, Ch 22
3. Pod SecurityPod-Level (Medium)PSS Restricted, securityContext, Seccomp, AppArmorMedium — container escape may bypassCh 17, Ch 14, Ch 15
4. Runtime SandboxKernel (Hard)gVisor user-space kernel per sandboxLow — gVisor has its own syscall layerCh 21.1
5. Hardware VMHardware (Hardest)Kata Containers — dedicated lightweight VM per podVery Low — hardware-enforced isolationCh 21.2
6. Cluster-LevelPhysical (Maximum)Separate clusters per tenant with federationNone — no shared kernel or networkCluster API, vcluster

Multi-Tenancy Decision Framework

Which Isolation Level for Your Tenant?
  Q1: Do tenants share the same trust boundary?
      YES (same org) → Namespace + Network isolation (Level 1-2)
      NO (different customers) → Sandbox or Hardware VM (Level 4-5)

  Q2: Does any tenant run user-uploaded code?
      YES → Hardware VM isolation (Level 5-6)
      NO → Sandbox or Pod Security (Level 3-4)

  Q3: Is regulatory compliance required (PCI, HIPAA, SOC2)?
      YES → Hardware VM or separate cluster (Level 5-6)
      NO → Network + Pod Security sufficient (Level 2-3)
💡 CKS Exam: Multi-Tenancy

The exam may ask you to configure isolation for a specific tenant scenario. Key pattern: "Tenant A must not access Tenant B's pods" → NetworkPolicy with namespaceSelector. "Tenant A runs untrusted code" → gVisor RuntimeClass. "Tenant A needs PCI compliance" → Kata Containers or separate cluster.

The CKS exam tests RuntimeClass as a concept. You need to know: (1) RuntimeClass selects the container runtime per pod via spec.runtimeClassName, (2) Different pods can use different runtimes in the same cluster, (3) The architectural differences between runc, gVisor, and Kata — the exam may test this as a scenario-based question. The exam is unlikely to ask you to install gVisor or Kata — focus on the conceptual understanding and RuntimeClass YAML.

🔧 Under the Hood — Sandboxed Runtimes: runc vs gVisor vs Kata — System Call Interception Models Compared 
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   CONTAINER RUNTIME COMPARISON                                              │
  │                                                                           │
  │   runc (DEFAULT):                                                          │
  │   Application → Linux Kernel (shared) → Hardware                          │
  │   Isolation: Namespaces + Cgroups + Seccomp                               │
  │   Syscalls: ~300 direct to host kernel                                    │
  │   Risk: Kernel CVEs = container breakout                                   │
  │                                                                           │
  │   gVisor (USERSPACE KERNEL):                                               │
  │   Application → Sentry (user-space kernel) → Limited syscalls → Host     │
  │   Isolation: Application NEVER talks to host kernel directly              │
  │   Syscalls: ~200 implemented in userspace (not all)                       │
  │   Risk: gVisor CVEs (much smaller attack surface)                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │   Kata Containers (LIGHTWEIGHT VM):                                        │
  │   Application → Guest Kernel (dedicated) → KVM hypervisor → Host          │
  │   Isolation: Hardware virtualization — each pod gets its OWN kernel       │
  │   Syscalls: All — but to a DEDICATED guest kernel                         │
  │   Risk: VM escape (extremely rare)                                         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 21 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Create a RuntimeClass that uses gVisor and apply it to a pod. Write both YAML resources.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sandboxed-pod

    image: nginx
Q2
What's the key architectural difference between gVisor and Kata Containers?
Show Answer
Answer

gVisor implements a user-space kernel (Sentry) that intercepts syscalls and handles them in userspace — the application NEVER makes direct syscalls to the host kernel. Kata Containers runs each pod in a dedicated lightweight VM with its OWN Linux kernel — syscalls go to the guest kernel, not the host. gVisor = userspace kernel, Kata = hardware virtualization. gVisor is lighter weight; Kata provides stronger isolation.

Q3
When would you use a sandboxed runtime instead of the default runc?
Show Answer
Answer

Use sandboxed runtimes for: (1) Untrusted workloads (user-uploaded code, multi-tenant environments), (2) Workloads processing sensitive data where container escape would be catastrophic, (3) CI/CD pipelines running arbitrary build code. The tradeoff is performance — gVisor has ~5-10% overhead, Kata has ~15-20% overhead vs native runc.

Q4
What happens if you specify runtimeClassName: gvisor but gVisor is not installed on the target node? How do you prevent scheduling to incompatible nodes?
Show Answer
Answer

The pod gets stuck in ContainerCreating with error: failed to create shim task: runtime "runsc" not found. Prevention: (1) Use nodeSelector with a label like sandbox-runtime: gvisor that only exists on nodes with gVisor installed. (2) Use nodeAffinity with requiredDuringScheduling. (3) Label nodes automatically at provisioning time: kubectl label node <name> sandbox-runtime=gvisor. (4) Verify the RuntimeClass handler name matches the containerd config.

Explanation

This is the #1 operational issue with RuntimeClasses. The scheduler doesn't know which nodes have which runtimes — it only checks the RuntimeClass resource exists. You MUST use nodeSelector/affinity to ensure sandboxed pods land on compatible nodes. On the CKS exam, if a sandboxed pod won't start, check: (a) RuntimeClass handler name, (b) containerd config, (c) nodeSelector.

Q5
How do you configure containerd to support gVisor? Write the containerd config section and explain the handler name mapping.
Show Answer
Answer
# /etc/containerd/config.toml
version = 2
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runsc]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runsc.v1"
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc.options]
    SystemdCgroup = true

The RuntimeClass handler: runsc maps to the containerd runtime name runsc in the config. Kubernetes passes the handler name to containerd, containerd looks it up in its config, and launches the pod with the matching runtime binary (/usr/bin/runsc for gVisor).

Explanation

The handler name in RuntimeClass must match the runtime name in containerd config EXACTLY. Common mistake: naming the RuntimeClass handler "gvisor" but containerd has it as "runsc" — these must match. On the CKS exam, you may need to verify containerd config and RuntimeClass are consistent.

Q6
Can you apply Seccomp profiles to a gVisor-sandboxed pod? What's the interaction between gVisor's sentry kernel and Kubernetes Seccomp?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes Seccomp is NOT applied inside gVisor. gVisor's sentry kernel implements its OWN syscall filtering that is separate from the host kernel's Seccomp. When you specify a Seccomp profile on a gVisor pod: (1) The host Seccomp filters gVisor's own limited syscalls (gVisor only makes ~50 safe syscalls). (2) The application's full set of syscalls is intercepted by gVisor's sentry kernel in userspace — Seccomp never sees them. In most cases, you don't need Seccomp on gVisor pods because gVisor itself provides stronger isolation than Seccomp.

Explanation

gVisor renders Seccomp unnecessary because the application never makes direct syscalls to the host. All syscalls are intercepted and handled by gVisor's user-space kernel, which implements its own security policies. On the CKS exam: if you're already using gVisor, you don't NEED to also apply Seccomp — it's redundant. But it doesn't hurt to have both (defense in depth).

Q7
What container escape techniques does gVisor protect against that runc does NOT? List at least 3 specific vulnerabilities that gVisor would have prevented.
Show Answer
Answer

gVisor protects against kernel exploit-based container escapes because the application's syscalls never reach the host kernel. Specifically: (1) CVE-2019-5736 (runc escape): Overwrites runc binary via /proc/self/exe — gVisor has no /proc/self/exe to the host runc. (2) CVE-2022-0492 (cgroups escape): Release agent escape via cgroups — gVisor's sentry kernel doesn't expose cgroups to the container. (3) Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195): Kernel race condition — gVisor runs in userspace, kernel exploits don't apply.

Explanation

The fundamental difference: runc shares the host kernel with containers. A kernel exploit in a runc container can compromise the entire node. gVisor runs the application in a sandboxed userspace kernel — even if the application exploits "the kernel," it's only exploiting gVisor's sentry, not the host. This is the strongest container isolation available without hardware virtualization (Kata/VMs).

Q8
Write a Kyverno policy that mutates any pod in the "untrusted" namespace to use runtimeClassName: gvisor automatically.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: enforce-gvisor-untrusted
spec:
  rules:
  - name: set-gvisor-runtime
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
          namespaces: [untrusted]
    mutate:
      patchStrategicMerge:
        spec:
          runtimeClassName: gvisor

Any pod submitted to the "untrusted" namespace is automatically mutated to use gVisor. Developers don't need to remember to set it — the policy handles it transparently.

Explanation

Policy automation is the CKS approach to security at scale. Instead of relying on developers to remember runtimeClassName: gvisor, a Kyverno policy enforces it automatically. This is a mutation (changing the pod spec) rather than validation (rejecting the pod). On the CKS exam, prefer mutation policies for security defaults — they reduce friction while maintaining security.

Q9
What's the difference between gVisor's ptrace platform and kvm platform? Which provides better isolation?
Show Answer
Answer

ptrace (default): gVisor's sentry uses Linux ptrace to intercept syscalls. Works everywhere but ~10% overhead. kvm: gVisor uses hardware virtualization (KVM) to create a sandboxed address space. Better isolation (ring-1 vs ring-0 attacker can't escape) but requires KVM support. kvm platform blocks speculative execution attacks (Spectre/Meltdown) that ptrace platform might be vulnerable to. For CKS: kvm platform is recommended for highest-security workloads.

Explanation

This is advanced gVisor configuration. On the CKS exam, you probably won't need to configure the platform, but you should know: (1) ptrace is the default and works everywhere, (2) kvm provides stronger isolation but requires hardware virtualization support on the node, (3) the platform is configured in containerd's config.toml under the gVisor runtime section.

Q10
A multi-tenant cluster runs workloads from different customers. What isolation strategy combines RuntimeClass with NetworkPolicy and PSS? Design the namespace configuration.
Show Answer
Answer
# Namespace setup for a tenant "tenant-a"
kubectl create ns tenant-a
# 1. Pod Security: enforce Restricted
kubectl label ns tenant-a pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
# 2. Network isolation: default-deny NetworkPolicy
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny, namespace: tenant-a}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF
# 3. Runtime isolation: auto-inject gVisor via Kyverno
# (policy from Q8 above — matches namespace tenant-a)
# 4. RBAC: tenant users only have access to their namespace
kubectl create role tenant-a-admin --verb=* --resource=* -n tenant-a
kubectl create rolebinding tenant-a-admin --role=tenant-a-admin --user=tenant-a-user -n tenant-a
Explanation

Multi-tenant isolation requires layered defenses: PSS (can't run privileged pods), NetworkPolicy (can't talk to other tenants), gVisor (can't escape container via kernel exploits), RBAC (can't access other namespaces). No single control is sufficient. On the CKS exam, when asked about multi-tenancy, always propose at least 3 layers of defense.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Check available RuntimeClasses
kubectl get runtimeclass  # Shows all installed sandboxed runtimes

# 2. Apply a RuntimeClass to a pod (EXAM PATTERN)
# Pod spec: runtimeClassName: gvisor
kubectl run sandboxed --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml | sed 's/containers:/runtimeClassName: gvisor\n  containers:/' | kubectl apply -f -

# 3. Verify the runtime used by a running pod
kubectl get pod sandboxed -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'
kubectl exec sandboxed -- dmesg | grep -i gvisor  # gVisor adds its own kernel messages

# 4. Check if containerd supports the runtime
cat /etc/containerd/config.toml | grep -A5 "plugins.*runtime"  # Should list runc, gvisor, kata
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 21 Traps
  • RuntimeClass must be installed FIRST: The RuntimeClass resource AND the runtime binary (gVisor/Kata) must exist on the node BEFORE you create a pod referencing it. If the RuntimeClass exists but the runtime isn't installed on the target node, the pod gets stuck in ContainerCreating with a cryptic "failed to create shim task" error.
  • Not all nodes support all runtimes: gVisor/Kata must be installed on EVERY node that might run sandboxed pods. Use nodeSelector or node affinity to ensure sandboxed pods only land on nodes with the runtime installed.
