Chapter 22: mTLS and Service Mesh Security

By default, pod-to-pod traffic inside a Kubernetes cluster is plaintext HTTP. Any process that can sniff the CNI network — a compromised pod, a malicious node exporter, a network administrator with tcpdump access — can read every request and response between your services. Database queries, API keys in headers, session tokens, user data — all visible. Mutual TLS (mTLS) solves this by encrypting pod-to-pod traffic AND authenticating both ends of every connection. A service mesh like Istio automates mTLS by injecting a sidecar proxy (Envoy) into every pod — handling certificate issuance, rotation, and enforcement without changing a single line of application code. This chapter teaches you how mTLS works, how Istio implements it, and how to secure every anihpj service-to-service connection with automatic, transparent encryption.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 🔗 mTLS 🌐 Service Mesh

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why pod-to-pod traffic is plaintext by default — and what attackers can see
  • ✅ How mTLS works — the full handshake with both client AND server certificates
  • ✅ How Istio automates mTLS with Envoy sidecar proxies and automatic cert rotation
  • ✅ How to configure PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy for anihpj
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% Supply Chain Security 20%

22.1 Why Pod-to-Pod Traffic Is Insecure by Default

Kubernetes does not encrypt pod-to-pod traffic. NetworkPolicy (Ch6) controls WHO can talk to whom, but does not encrypt the traffic itself. TLS at the Ingress (Ch7) encrypts external-to-cluster traffic, but once inside the cluster, traffic between pods is plain HTTP. An attacker with any foothold in the cluster can sniff this traffic:

Pod-to-Pod Traffic — Without mTLS vs With mTLS
  WITHOUT mTLS (plaintext — the Kubernetes default):
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  anihpj pod ──── HTTP GET /jobs?search=engineer ────▶ postgres pod
              ◀──── SELECT * FROM jobs... ──────────
                    (database results in plaintext)

  Attacker pod on same node: tcpdump -i any port 5432
  → Captures: SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE title LIKE '%engineer%'
  → Captures: All job listing data in the response
  → Captures: Database credentials in the connection string
  → Captures: Session cookies, auth tokens in HTTP headers

  WITH mTLS (encrypted + authenticated — Istio default):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  anihpj pod ──TLS──▶ postgres pod
  (cert: anihpj-sa)     (cert: postgres-sa)
  Both sides verify each other's certificate.
  Traffic is AES-GCM encrypted.
             ◀──TLS───

  Attacker pod: tcpdump → sees only encrypted bytes. Cannot decrypt.
  Attacker pod: tries to connect → has no valid cert → REFUSED.

22.2 Mutual TLS (mTLS) — How It Works

Regular TLS (what HTTPS websites use) only authenticates the SERVER. The client (your browser) verifies the server's certificate, but the server doesn't verify the client. mTLS adds a second step: the client also presents a certificate, and the server verifies it. Both sides must prove their identity before any data is exchanged:

mTLS Handshake — anihpj → postgres, Step by Step
  anihpj pod (client)                         postgres pod (server)
       │                                              │
       │ 1. ClientHello (supported ciphers, SNI)      │
       │ ──────────────────────────────────────────▶ │
       │                                              │
       │ 2. ServerHello + Server Certificate          │
       │    (cert contains: CN=postgres.anihpj.svc)   │
       │ ◀────────────────────────────────────────── │
       │                                              │
       │ 3. anihpj VERIFIES postgres cert:            │
       │    ✅ Signed by Istio cluster CA?            │
       │    ✅ CN matches postgres.anihpj.svc?        │
       │    ✅ Not expired?                            │
       │    ✅ Not revoked?                            │
       │    All checks pass → continues               │
       │                                              │
       │ 4. Server: "Send me YOUR certificate"        │
       │ ◀──────── CertificateRequest ────────────── │
       │                                              │
       │ 5. anihpj sends its OWN certificate          │
       │    (cert contains: CN=anihpj-sa.anihpj)     │
       │ ──────────── ClientCertificate ───────────▶ │
       │                                              │
       │ 6. postgres VERIFIES anihpj cert:            │
       │    ✅ Signed by Istio cluster CA?            │
       │    ✅ CN matches allowed identity?           │
       │    ✅ Not expired?                            │
       │    All checks pass → continues               │
       │                                              │
       │ 7. ✅ BOTH sides authenticated!              │
       │    Encrypted TLS 1.3 tunnel established     │
       │ ◀═══════════ AES-GCM encrypted ═══════════▶ │

  WHAT HAPPENS IF AN ATTACKER POD TRIES TO CONNECT:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Attacker pod → tries to connect to postgres:5432
  postgres: "Send me YOUR certificate"
  Attacker: has NO valid certificate (not signed by Istio CA)
  postgres: Connection REFUSED — TLS handshake fails
  Result: Attacker cannot even establish a TCP connection.

TLS vs mTLS — The Key Difference

🔒 Regular TLS (HTTPS)
  • Server proves identity
  • Client is ANONYMOUS
  • Any client can connect
  • Use: Public websites
🔐 mTLS (Pod-to-Pod)
  • Server AND Client prove identity
  • Both authenticated
  • Only authorized clients connect
  • Use: Service-to-service communication

How Istio Automates Certificate Management — The Citadel (istiod) CA

Manual mTLS is a nightmare: generate a cert for every pod, distribute it, rotate it before expiry, revoke compromised certs. Istio's istiod (formerly Citadel) handles all of this automatically. Every Envoy sidecar gets a certificate from the Istio CA, rotated every 24 hours, without the application ever knowing:

Istio Certificate Lifecycle — Automatic Issuance and Rotation
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ISTIO CERTIFICATE AUTOMATION                                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: POD STARTS — SIDECAR REQUESTS A CERTIFICATE                    │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────                         │
  │  • Envoy sidecar starts alongside the application container.             │
  │  • Sidecar reads its ServiceAccount JWT token from the pod's filesystem. │
  │  • Sidecar sends a CSR (Certificate Signing Request) to istiod:         │
  │    POST /istiod/v1/certificate                                           │
  │    {                                                                       │
  │      "csr": "",                                          │
  │      "token": ""                                       │
  │    }                                                                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2: ISTIOD VALIDATES AND ISSUES                                     │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │  • istiod verifies the ServiceAccount JWT via Kubernetes TokenReview.   │
  │  • istiod extracts the pod's identity:                                    │
  │    spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj-prod/sa/anihpj-sa                    │
  │  • istiod signs a certificate with the Istio root CA:                     │
  │    CN = anihpj-sa.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local                           │
  │    SAN = spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj-prod/sa/anihpj-sa              │
  │    TTL = 24 hours                                                         │
  │  • Returns the signed cert + private key to the sidecar.                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 3: AUTOMATIC ROTATION (every 12 hours)                             │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                             │
  │  • The Envoy sidecar watches the certificate's expiry.                   │
  │  • At 50% of TTL (12 hours into a 24-hour cert), the sidecar            │
  │    automatically requests a NEW certificate from istiod.                 │
  │  • The new cert is loaded WITHOUT restarting the application.            │
  │  • The old cert remains valid until expiry (graceful overlap).           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚡ SECURITY PROPERTIES:                                                  │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │
  │  • Short-lived certs (24h): stolen cert useless after 24 hours.          │
  │  • Per-pod identity: cert bound to ServiceAccount (SPIFFE ID).           │
  │  • Automatic rotation: zero human intervention.                           │
  │  • Compromise response: delete the pod → new pod gets new cert.          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

22.3 Istio — Service Mesh for Automatic mTLS

Istio automates mTLS by injecting an Envoy proxy sidecar into every pod. Your application code sends plain HTTP to localhost — the Envoy sidecar intercepts it, encrypts it with mTLS, and sends it to the destination pod's Envoy sidecar, which decrypts it and forwards it to the destination app. Zero application code changes:

YAML — PeerAuthentication: enforce STRICT mTLS for anihpj namespace 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: anihpj-mtls
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT     # ALL pods in this namespace MUST use mTLS

# STRICT: All connections must use mTLS. Plaintext REJECTED.
# PERMISSIVE: Accept both mTLS and plaintext (migration mode).
# DISABLE: No mTLS (insecure — don't use).

How the Envoy Sidecar Intercepts Traffic — The iptables Redirect

How does the Envoy sidecar intercept traffic from the application without the application knowing? Istio configures iptables rules in the pod's network namespace that redirect ALL outbound TCP traffic through Envoy (localhost:15001). The app thinks it's connecting directly to postgres:5432 — iptables silently redirects to Envoy, which then handles mTLS:

Istio Sidecar Traffic Interception — iptables Redirect Architecture
  APPLICATION: connect("postgres.anihpj.svc", 5432)
  │
  ▼
  POD'S iptables (injected by Istio init container):
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -p tcp -j REDIRECT --to-port 15001
  → ALL outbound TCP → redirected to localhost:15001 (Envoy)
  │
  ▼
  ENVOY SIDECAR (localhost:15001):
  ───────────────────────────────
  1. Receives redirected connection.
  2. Reads original destination (SO_ORIGINAL_DST): postgres:5432.
  3. Looks up in Istio service registry → selects a postgres endpoint.
  4. Establishes mTLS to postgres's Envoy sidecar.
  5. Both sides present certs → verify → encrypted tunnel.
  │
  ▼
  DESTINATION ENVOY → decrypts → forwards to localhost:5432 (postgres).

Istio vs Cilium vs Linkerd — Which Service Mesh for mTLS?

FeatureIstioCiliumLinkerd
mTLS✅ Auto (Citadel)✅ Auto (Cilium identities)✅ Auto (identity-based)
Proxy modelSidecar (Envoy)Sidecar-free (eBPF in kernel)Sidecar (linkerd-proxy, Rust)
Performance overhead~5-10ms latency~1-2ms (near-native)~1-3ms
ComplexityHigh (many CRDs)Medium (K8s-native)Low (simplest UX)
NetworkPolicy + mTLS✅ Combined✅ Combined (single CRD)⚠️ Separate configs
CKS exam relevance⭐⭐ Most common⭐ Growing⭐ Simple alternative

Verifying mTLS Is Actually Working

Bash — Test that mTLS encrypts traffic and plaintext is rejected
# 1. Verify STRICT mTLS is enabled in the namespace
kubectl get peerauthentication -n anihpj-prod
# Should show: default  STRICT  (mode: STRICT)

# 2. Deploy a test pod WITHOUT an Istio sidecar
kubectl run test-no-sidecar --image=nginx -n anihpj-prod \
  --overrides='{"metadata":{"annotations":{"sidecar.istio.io/inject":"false"}}}'

# 3. Try to curl the anihpj service from the test pod
kubectl exec test-no-sidecar -n anihpj-prod -- \
  curl -s http://anihpj:8000
# Expected: curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
# ✅ PLAINTEXT REJECTED — mTLS requires encrypted traffic!

# 4. Try from a pod WITH a sidecar — should work
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj -n anihpj-prod -- \
  curl -s http://anihpj:8000/healthz
# Expected: OK (200)
# ✅ SIDECAR-TO-SIDECAR TRAFFIC WORKS (mutual TLS)

# 5. Inspect the certificates in use
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj -n anihpj-prod -c istio-proxy -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:15000/certs | jq .
# Shows: certificate chain, expiry dates, SAN names

# 6. Check Istio's certificate authority
kubectl get secrets -n istio-system | grep cacerts
# These are the CA certs Istio uses to issue workload certificates

22.4 Securing anihpj with Istio mTLS

Here is the complete Istio security configuration for the anihpj application. It enforces STRICT mTLS for all pods in the production namespace and creates AuthorizationPolicies that only allow specific service-to-service communication:

YAML — Complete Istio security for anihpj 
# ── Enforce mTLS for ALL pods in anihpj-prod ──
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

# ── Only allow ingress-gateway → anihpj (port 8000) ──
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-django
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/ingress-gateway"]
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["8000"]

# ── Only allow anihpj → postgres (port 5432) ──
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: postgres-access
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj-prod/sa/anihpj-sa"]
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["5432"]

22.5 Pod-to-Pod Encryption — Istio mTLS + Cilium WireGuard

The official CKS curriculum explicitly calls out Pod-to-Pod encryption (Cilium, Istio). While Istio provides identity-based mTLS at L7 via sidecars, Cilium provides transparent L3 encryption using WireGuard — without sidecars or application changes. Both satisfy the CKS requirement at different layers:

FeatureIstio mTLS (L7)Cilium WireGuard (L3)
EncryptionSPIFFE certs, sidecar proxiesWireGuard kernel module, no sidecars
IdentitySPIFFE (workload identity)Node identity (IP-based)
Overhead~5-15% (sidecar proxy)~1-3% (kernel WireGuard)
Requires sidecarYes (istio-proxy)No — transparent at kernel
💡 CKS Exam: Pod-to-Pod Encryption

If the exam asks for pod-to-pod encryption: (1) Istio PeerAuthentication STRICT mTLS (if Istio installed), or (2) Cilium with WireGuard enabled. Verify: istioctl authn tls-check for Istio, cilium status | grep Encryption for Cilium.

📊 Chapter 22 Visual Summary — mTLS & Service Mesh at a Glance

⚠️
Default (22.1)

Pod-to-pod = plaintext HTTP. Anyone on the network can sniff all inter-service traffic.

🔐
mTLS (22.2)

Both sides present certificates. Encrypted + authenticated. Unauthorized pods REFUSED.

🌐
Istio (22.3-4)

Envoy sidecar automates mTLS. Zero app changes. STRICT mode for anihpj-prod.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam tests mTLS and service mesh concepts at a high level. Know: (1) Pod-to-pod traffic is plaintext by default — NetworkPolicy controls WHO but not encryption, (2) mTLS encrypts AND authenticates both ends, (3) Istio uses Envoy sidecars to automate mTLS without app changes, (4) PeerAuthentication sets mTLS mode (STRICT/PERMISSIVE/DISABLE) per namespace. The exam is unlikely to ask you to install Istio — focus on the conceptual understanding and YAML configuration of PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy.

🔧 Under the Hood — mTLS Handshake: How Envoy Sidecars Establish Mutual TLS Without Application Changes 
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   ISTIO mTLS — Transparent Encryption Between Pods                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │   Pod A (anihpj)                          Pod B (postgres)                │
  │   ┌──────────────┐                       ┌──────────────┐                │
  │   │  App         │                       │  Postgres    │                │
  │   │  (plaintext) │                       │  (plaintext) │                │
  │   └──────┬───────┘                       └──────▲───────┘                │
  │          │ connect(postgres:5432)               │                         │
  │          ▼                                      │                         │
  │   ┌──────────────┐    TLS handshake      ┌──────────────┐                │
  │   │  Envoy       │◄─────────────────────►│  Envoy       │                │
  │   │  (sidecar)   │   Cert presented      │  (sidecar)   │                │
  │   │              │   by BOTH sides        │              │                │
  │   └──────┬───────┘                       └──────▲───────┘                │
  │          │ encrypted TCP                         │                         │
  │          └───────────────────────────────────────┘                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │   🔑 The app sends PLAINTEXT to localhost. Envoy intercepts, encrypts,    │
  │      sends to destination Envoy, which decrypts and forwards to app.      │
  │      The applications have NO IDEA mTLS is happening.                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 22 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between TLS and mTLS? When would you use mTLS in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

TLS: Server presents certificate, client verifies. mTLS: BOTH client AND server present certificates. Use mTLS for pod-to-pod communication when you need to verify the IDENTITY of both ends — not just encrypt traffic. In Kubernetes, pod-to-pod traffic is plaintext by default; mTLS via service mesh provides encryption + mutual authentication without application changes.

Q2
Write an Istio PeerAuthentication that enforces STRICT mTLS in namespace "anihpj-prod".
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: anihpj-mtls
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT  # PERMISSIVE allows plaintext fallback, STRICT requires mTLS
Q3
What is SPIFFE and how does Istio use it for pod identity in mTLS? What does a SPIFFE ID look like for a Kubernetes pod?
Show Answer
Answer

SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone) is an identity standard. Istio issues each pod a SPIFFE ID in the format: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/<namespace>/sa/<serviceaccount>. Example: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj-prod/sa/anihpj-api. This ID is embedded in the X.509 certificate the sidecar proxy presents during mTLS. The receiving sidecar validates: (1) the cert is signed by the mesh CA, (2) the SPIFFE ID matches the expected identity, (3) any AuthorizationPolicy allows traffic from that identity.

Explanation

SPIFFE is the identity layer of zero-trust networking. Every pod gets a unique, cryptographically-verifiable identity based on its ServiceAccount. This enables RBAC-style authorization at the network level: "allow traffic from SA anihpj-api in namespace prod to SA postgres in namespace database." On the CKS exam, understand that SPIFFE IDs replace IP-based trust with identity-based trust.

Q4
Write an Istio AuthorizationPolicy that allows ONLY the anihpj-api ServiceAccount in namespace prod to send traffic to postgres ServiceAccount in namespace database on port 5432.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: postgres-access
  namespace: database
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/anihpj-api
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["5432"]
Explanation

AuthorizationPolicy is Istio's Layer 7 RBAC for network traffic. The principals field uses SPIFFE IDs to identify source workloads. This is much stronger than IP-based NetworkPolicy because it can't be spoofed — the identity is cryptographically verified via mTLS. On the CKS exam, combine NetworkPolicy (L3/4) with AuthorizationPolicy (L7) for defense in depth.

Q5
What's the difference between Istio's PERMISSIVE and STRICT mTLS modes? When would you use PERMISSIVE mode in production?
Show Answer
Answer

PERMISSIVE: Accepts BOTH mTLS and plaintext traffic. Used during migration when not all pods have sidecars yet. STRICT: REJECTS all non-mTLS traffic. Every pod must have a sidecar proxy. PERMISSIVE mode is a migration tool, not a production security posture. In production, use STRICT for all namespaces with sensitive data. The only valid use of PERMISSIVE is during a phased rollout where you're adding sidecars to existing workloads incrementally.

Explanation

PERMISSIVE is NOT a security control — it's a migration aid. If you leave namespaces in PERMISSIVE mode, an attacker who bypasses the sidecar (hostNetwork pod, compromised node) can send plaintext traffic that's accepted. On the CKS exam, if asked to "enable mTLS," the answer includes STRICT mode. PERMISSIVE is only acceptable during the rollout phase.

Q6
How does Istio's sidecar proxy (Envoy) handle TLS certificate rotation? What happens if the cert expires during a connection?
Show Answer
Answer

Istio's Citadel (now istiod) issues short-lived certificates (default 24 hours) and the sidecar proxy automatically renews them BEFORE expiry. The flow: (1) Sidecar requests a new cert from istiod when >50% of TTL remains. (2) istiod issues a new cert signed by the mesh CA. (3) Envoy hot-reloads the cert without dropping existing connections. (4) Existing TLS sessions continue with the old cert until natural termination. New connections use the new cert immediately. No connection drops during rotation.

Explanation

Automatic certificate rotation is one of Istio's key security features. Unlike manual TLS where cert expiry causes outages, Istio handles rotation transparently. On the CKS exam, understand that mTLS in a service mesh eliminates the operational burden of certificate management — it's fully automated.

Q7
What happens to pod-to-pod traffic if istiod (control plane) goes down? Do existing mTLS connections keep working?
Show Answer
Answer

Existing connections: YES, they keep working. Envoy sidecars operate independently of the control plane for the data path. mTLS is performed sidecar-to-sidecar using already-cached certificates. New connections: YES, they still work as long as certificates haven't expired (24-hour default TTL). What fails: New sidecar injection (no istiod to mutate pods), certificate renewal (certs expire after 24h → new mTLS connections fail), configuration updates (new AuthorizationPolicies aren't propagated). The control plane is critical for management but not for the data path.

Explanation

This is the "data plane survives control plane failure" design principle. It's a key architecture concept for CKS. The sidecar proxies form a peer-to-peer mesh that functions independently of the control plane. On the exam, this is important for high-availability planning: a control plane outage is a security degradation (no cert renewal, no policy updates) but not a service outage.

Q8
Compare service mesh mTLS (Istio/Linkerd) with manual mTLS using cert-manager. What are the tradeoffs?
Show Answer
Answer
AspectService MeshManual mTLS (cert-manager)
SetupInstall mesh, inject sidecarsGenerate certs, mount Secrets, configure app
RotationAutomatic, transparentcert-manager auto-rotates Secret, but app must reload
App changesNone (sidecar handles TLS)App must support mTLS (code changes)
GranularityPer-pod identity (SPIFFE)Per-service identity (shared cert)
ComplexityHigher (sidecar overhead)Lower (no sidecar)
Explanation

Service mesh is the CKS-recommended approach for mTLS because it's transparent to applications and provides per-pod identity. Manual mTLS is simpler but requires application changes and provides coarser identity (per-service, not per-pod). On the exam, choose service mesh for greenfield deployments and cert-manager for lightweight mTLS where the mesh overhead isn't acceptable.

Q9
How do you enable automatic sidecar injection in a namespace? Write the command and explain when pods get the sidecar.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl label namespace anihpj-prod istio-injection=enabled
# Or for revision-specific injection:
kubectl label namespace anihpj-prod istio.io/rev=stable

Pods get the sidecar at CREATION time. Existing pods are NOT retroactively injected. To inject existing pods, you must restart them: kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj-prod. The sidecar injection is performed by a mutating admission webhook that runs when the pod is created — it adds the istio-proxy container and istio-init init container to the pod spec.

Explanation

Sidecar injection is a mutating admission webhook — it happens at Gate 4 (Admission). The namespace label tells Istio's webhook to modify pods in that namespace. On the CKS exam, you may need to: (1) enable injection on a namespace, (2) verify injection with kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' (should include istio-proxy), (3) troubleshoot failed injection by checking the webhook configuration.

Q10
A pod with an Istio sidecar can reach postgres.database.svc.cluster.local:5432 but the connection fails with "TLS error: bad certificate." The destination pod also has a sidecar. What's the likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

Most likely: mTLS mode mismatch. The source namespace has PERMISSIVE mode (allows plaintext) but the destination namespace has STRICT mode (requires mTLS). The source sidecar sends plaintext (because PERMISSIVE allows it), the destination sidecar expects mTLS → rejects. Fix: set both namespaces to STRICT, or at minimum set the destination to STRICT and the source will auto-negotiate mTLS if both have sidecars.

Other causes: (1) Istio CA certificates expired or not trusted, (2) clock skew between nodes (cert validity period check fails), (3) different trust domains (source and destination in different meshes with different CAs).

Explanation

mTLS debugging is a common CKS scenario. The key insight: even in PERMISSIVE mode, if BOTH pods have sidecars, Istio will attempt mTLS. But explicit PERMISSIVE + STRICT mismatch across namespaces can cause confusion. On the exam, always check PeerAuthentication settings in BOTH namespaces when debugging mTLS issues. Use istioctl authn tls-check <pod> to see the actual TLS mode per connection.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Check mTLS status in the mesh
istioctl authn tls-check <pod> -n <ns>  # Shows TLS mode for each port
kubectl get peerauthentication -A  # List all mTLS policies

# 2. Enable STRICT mTLS namespace-wide
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: strict-mtls
  namespace: prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
EOF

# 3. Verify mTLS is working between two pods
istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -n prod  # Shows the SPIFFE certs
kubectl exec src-pod -- curl -v http://dst-svc:8080  # Should work with STRICT mTLS

# 4. Check sidecar injection status
kubectl get namespace -L istio-injection  # Shows which namespaces have auto-injection
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 22 Traps
  • PERMISSIVE ≠ disabled: PERMISSIVE mode accepts BOTH mTLS AND plaintext traffic. It's a migration tool, not a security control. For security, use STRICT. The exam will likely ask you to switch from PERMISSIVE to STRICT.
  • mTLS requires sidecars: If a pod doesn't have the Istio sidecar injected (no istio-proxy container), mTLS policies don't apply to it. Check: kubectl get pod -o json | jq '.spec.containers[].name' — should include istio-proxy.
  • NetworkPolicy + mTLS = defense-in-depth: NetworkPolicy operates at L3/L4 (IP:port). mTLS operates at L5 (identity). An attacker who spoofs an IP bypasses NetworkPolicy but can't bypass mTLS because they don't have the SPIFFE certificate.

Chapter 23: Image Security — Scanning and Minimizing Attack Surface

A container image is not just your application code — it's an entire Linux distribution frozen in time: an operating system, system libraries, a language runtime, package managers, shells, and hundreds of packages you never explicitly asked for. Every one of those packages is a potential CVE (Common Vulnerability and Exposure) — a publicly known security vulnerability with a CVSS score. The average container image from Docker Hub contains 100+ known vulnerabilities at the time of pull. Worse, images are immutable snapshots — the vulnerabilities baked in at build time stay there forever unless you rebuild. This chapter teaches you to minimize your image attack surface (distroless, multi-stage builds), scan every image with Trivy in CI/CD, and enforce that only images from approved private registries can run in your cluster. You cannot secure what you cannot see — and you cannot see what's inside an image without scanning it.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔍 Image Scanning 📦 Supply Chain

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ The CVE lifecycle: How vulnerabilities are discovered, scored, published, and how they end up in YOUR images
  • ✅ Image anatomy: How layers accumulate risk, why base images grow stale, and the mathematics of image bloat
  • ✅ Attack scenarios: Step-by-step exploitation of real CVEs in a Django container — and how to stop each step
  • ✅ Distroless architecture: Why "no shell, no package manager" is the strongest security posture you can adopt
  • ✅ Trivy internals: How vulnerability databases work, how Trivy matches CVEs to packages, CI/CD integration patterns
  • ✅ Registry enforcement: Authentication flow, admission controller patterns, preventing public image poisoning
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

23.1 Why Container Images Are a Security Risk — The Full Picture

When you write FROM python:3.12 in your Dockerfile, you are not just getting Python. You are pulling approximately 1,000+ Debian packages into your application's runtime environment — curl, wget, bash, openssl, libc, systemd libraries, perl, and hundreds more. Many of these packages have known, publicly documented vulnerabilities with exploit code available online. The fundamental problem: images are static snapshots that rot over time. The day you build them, they may have zero known CVEs. Six months later, 23 new CVEs are discovered in packages you didn't even know were in the image — and your production pods are still running that old image.

The CVE Lifecycle — How a Vulnerability Ends Up in Your Container

1Discovery

A security researcher or attacker finds a bug in curl 7.74.0 — a buffer overflow triggered by a malicious SOCKS5 proxy response.

2CVE Assignment

MITRE assigns CVE-2023-38545. The vulnerability is now publicly tracked with a unique identifier. NVD (National Vulnerability Database) picks it up.

3CVSS Scoring

NVD analysts assign a CVSS score: 9.8 (CRITICAL). Attack vector: Network, complexity: Low, privileges: None, user interaction: None. This is as bad as it gets.

4Publication

The CVE is published in NVD, MITRE, and security feeds. Trivy's vulnerability database ingests it within hours. Exploit code often appears on GitHub within days.

5Distribution Lag

Debian maintainers backport the fix to curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u7. But your image was built 6 months ago with curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u2 — the vulnerable version. The fix exists, but YOUR image didn't get it because images don't auto-update.

6Exploitation Window

Your production pods running anihpj:v1 are now vulnerable to CVE-2023-38545. Any network request your app makes could be intercepted. Trivy would catch this — but only if you scan.

⚠️ The Core Insight: Images Are Immutable — Vulnerabilities Are Not

Unlike a VM where you run apt upgrade and fix vulnerabilities, container images are immutable by design. The only way to fix a CVE in a running container is to rebuild the image with updated packages and redeploy. This means every image in your registry is a ticking time bomb — secure today, vulnerable tomorrow, without a single line of your code changing. This is why continuous scanning (not one-time scanning) is essential.

Image Layer Anatomy — Why Risk Accumulates in Layers

Every Dockerfile instruction creates a new filesystem layer. Each layer adds packages, libraries, and configuration files — and each layer can introduce vulnerabilities independently:

Docker Image Layer Stack — anihpj:v1 (Debian-based, 6 layers)
  LAYER 6: COPY . /app                                    [your Django code — ~50MB]
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 5: RUN pip install -r requirements.txt             [Python packages — ~200MB]
  │  Introduces: Django 4.2, gunicorn, psycopg2, celery, redis, ... 
  │  Risk: Python package CVEs (e.g., CVE-2024-xxx in Django itself)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 4: RUN apt-get install gcc postgresql-client ...   [build tools — ~300MB]
  │  Introduces: gcc-10, libpq-dev, build-essential, make, git
  │  Risk: Compiler CVEs (CVE-2023-4039: gcc stack protector bypass)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 3: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl   [utilities — ~50MB]
  │  Introduces: curl 7.74.0, libcurl4, ca-certificates
  │  Risk: CVE-2023-38545 — CRITICAL RCE via SOCKS5 (CVSS 9.8)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 2: RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade           [system updates — ~100MB]
  │  Introduces: openssl 1.1.1n, libc6 2.31, libssl1.1
  │  Risk: CVE-2023-44487 — HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DoS (CVSS 7.5)
  │  Risk: CVE-2023-4911 — glibc Looney Tunables LPE (CVSS 7.8)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 1: FROM python:3.12                                [base OS — ~350MB]
  │  Introduces: Debian 12 (bookworm), systemd libs, perl, bash, apt, dpkg
  │  Risk: Hundreds of OS-level packages, many with latent CVEs
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  🔴 TOTAL: ~1,050MB image. ~1,200 packages. 23 known CVEs after 6 months.
  🟢 GOAL:  ~20MB distroless image. ~5 packages. 0-1 CVEs.

CVSS Scoring Explained — What Those Numbers Actually Mean

CVSS RangeSeverityWhat It MeansAction for CKS
9.0–10.0CRITICALNetwork-exploitable, no auth needed, no user interaction. Wormable. Example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0).🚨 BLOCK DEPLOYMENT. Fix immediately. This is the "drop everything" severity.
7.0–8.9HIGHCan lead to RCE, privilege escalation, or data breach. May require some conditions. Example: Looney Tunables (CVE-2023-4911, CVSS 7.8).⚠️ Fix within SLA (e.g., 30 days). Document the risk acceptance if deferred.
4.0–6.9MEDIUMDifficult to exploit or limited impact. Example: Information disclosure via timing attack. Often requires local access.📋 Track and fix in next release cycle. Don't block deployment.
0.1–3.9LOWMinimal impact, theoretical exploit, or requires unrealistic conditions.✅ Acknowledge, fix when convenient. Low priority.

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Exploiting CVE-2023-38545 (curl SOCKS5 RCE) in anihpj:v1

ATTACK SCENARIO How an Attacker Exploits a Known CVE in Your Container
1
Reconnaissance

Attacker scans your cluster's external endpoints. They discover your Django app at jobs.anihpj.com. The HTTP response headers reveal: Server: gunicorn/21.2.0. They fingerprint the stack. They also find your public Docker image anihpj/anihpj-django:v1 on Docker Hub. They pull it and scan it with Trivy themselves — discovering CVE-2023-38545 (curl heap buffer overflow, CVSS 9.8).

2
Weaponization

The attacker crafts a malicious SOCKS5 proxy server. When curl (inside your container) connects to this proxy, the proxy sends a specially crafted response that overflows curl's heap buffer — giving the attacker arbitrary code execution as the user running curl (UID 1000 in your container). The attacker hosts the malicious proxy at evil-proxy.attacker.com:1080.

3
Delivery — How curl Gets Triggered

Your Django app has a feature: "Import jobs from external URL." A user pastes a URL, the backend does requests.get(user_url) → which internally might use curl or libcurl if compiled with it. Or: your Celery task downloads a file from a user-supplied S3 URL using curl as a subprocess. The attacker submits a URL pointing to their malicious proxy: socks5h://evil-proxy.attacker.com:1080. Your container's curl connects to it.

4
Exploitation — Code Execution Inside the Container

The malicious proxy sends the exploit payload. curl's heap buffer overflows. The attacker achieves Remote Code Execution (RCE) inside the anihpj container — as UID 1000, inside the container's namespace. They now have a shell-equivalent inside your container. They can read /app/anihpj/settings.py (with your Django SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL). They can access the PostgreSQL database at postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:5432 because the container has network access to the DB service.

5
Lateral Movement

From inside the container, the attacker reads the mounted ServiceAccount token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. They use this token to list pods: curl -k https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/pods. If the ServiceAccount has excessive RBAC permissions (common mistake!), they can now deploy their own malicious pods, exfiltrate secrets, or access other namespaces.

🛡️
How to Stop This Attack — Defense in Depth

(1) Scan with Trivy BEFORE deploying — would have caught CVE-2023-38545 immediately. (2) Use distroless base image — no curl binary to exploit. (3) NetworkPolicy — block egress from app pods to internet (only allow DB and API egress). (4) Seccomp — block socket() syscalls to prevent outbound connections. (5) RBAC — least-privilege ServiceAccount with no pod listing permissions. (6) readOnlyRootFilesystem — prevents writing exploit tools to disk. Each layer alone is not enough. All six together make exploitation nearly impossible.

Decision Tree: Should I Worry About This CVE?

CVE Risk Assessment for Container Images
  NEW CVE FOUND in your image
  │
  ├─ Is the vulnerable package INSTALLED in the image?
  │  ├─ NO  → ✅ Low risk. But check if it's a transitive dependency.
  │  └─ YES → ▼
  │     ├─ Is the vulnerable package EXECUTED at runtime?
  │     │  ├─ NO (e.g., curl exists but app never calls it)
  │     │  │  └─ ⚠️ MEDIUM risk. Attacker could still execute it if they get RCE via another vector.
  │     │  └─ YES → ▼
  │     │     ├─ Is the vulnerability NETWORK-EXPLOITABLE? (AV:N in CVSS vector)
  │     │     │  ├─ YES → ▼
  │     │     │  │  ├─ CVSS ≥ 9.0 → 🔴 CRITICAL — BLOCK deployment. Fix NOW.
  │     │     │  │  ├─ CVSS 7.0-8.9 → 🟠 HIGH — Fix within SLA. May block deployment.
  │     │     │  │  └─ CVSS < 7.0 → 🟡 MEDIUM — Fix in next release.
  │     │     │  └─ NO (Local access required) → ▼
  │     │     │     ├─ Is the container running as root? → 🟠 HIGH (LPE risk)
  │     │     │     └─ Container runs as non-root → 🟡 MEDIUM (Harder to exploit)
  │     │     └─ Is there a KNOWN PUBLIC EXPLOIT? (ExploitDB, Metasploit)
  │     │        ├─ YES → 🔴 ESCALATE — treat as CRITICAL regardless of CVSS
  │     │        └─ NO  → Follow CVSS-based assessment above
  │     └─ Is the package in a LAYER that could be removed? (build-only layer)
  │        └─ YES → 🟢 Remove it entirely. Multi-stage build can eliminate build tools from final image.
CVE Severity Distribution — Average Docker Hub Python Image (6 months old)
CRITICAL: 2
HIGH: 6
MEDIUM: 10
LOW: 5
NONE: 2

Total: 25 CVEs | CRITICAL: 8% | Actionable (CRITICAL+HIGH): 32% | Fix cost: Rebuild + redeploy (~30 min)

23.2 Minimizing Image Attack Surface — The Distroless Revolution

Every package you remove is an attack vector eliminated forever. There is no patch, no CVE, and no exploit for a package that simply does not exist in your image. The goal is a minimal image that contains ONLY your application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no curl/wget/git/nc/perl. This is the philosophy behind Google's distroless images: "If you don't need it, it shouldn't be in the image."

Distroless Architecture — Why "No Shell" Is the Ultimate Security Win

Distroless Image Anatomy — What's Present vs What's Absent
  DISTROLESS IMAGE (gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12)
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ✅ PRESENT (essentials only):
     • /usr/bin/python3.11          — Python interpreter
     • /usr/lib/python3.11/         — Python standard library
     • /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6  — glibc (Python needs it)
     • /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2  — dynamic linker
     • /etc/passwd, /etc/group      — user/group database (for USER directive)
     • /etc/ssl/certs/              — CA certificates (for TLS)
     • /tmp/                        — writable tmp (scratch space)
     • Your application files       — copied from builder stage

  ❌ ABSENT (attack vectors eliminated):
     • /bin/bash, /bin/sh           — NO SHELL. kubectl exec → fails.
     • /usr/bin/curl, /usr/bin/wget — NO download tools. Cannot pull malware.
     • /usr/bin/apt, /usr/bin/dpkg  — NO PACKAGE MANAGER. Cannot install tools.
     • /usr/bin/gcc, /usr/bin/make  — NO COMPILER. Cannot build exploits.
     • /usr/bin/git, /usr/bin/nc    — NO dev tools. Cannot clone repos.
     • /usr/bin/perl, /usr/bin/python2 — NO legacy runtimes with known CVEs.
     • /usr/bin/ssh, /usr/bin/scp   — NO remote access tools.
     • /usr/bin/cron, /usr/sbin/cron— NO job scheduler. Cannot persist tasks.
     • /bin/chmod, /bin/chown       — NO permission modifiers (in some distroless variants)
     • systemd, init scripts        — NO init system. PID 1 is your app.

  📊 RESULT:
     • Image size: ~20MB vs ~1,050MB full Debian image
     • Package count: ~5 vs ~1,200 packages
     • Attack surface: REDUCED BY ~99.6%
     • CVEs: 0-1 vs 23 in the full image
     • kubectl exec anihpj -- /bin/bash → "exec: /bin/bash: no such file or directory"
     • This is a FEATURE, not a bug. Attackers cannot get a shell either.
💡 The Distroless Mindset Shift

Many developers resist distroless because they can't kubectl exec into the container to debug. This is the wrong instinct. In production, if you need a shell, your observability is broken. Fix your logging, metrics, and tracing instead. Use kubectl logs, Prometheus metrics, and distributed traces. If you absolutely need debugging access, use an ephemeral debug container: kubectl debug -it anihpj-pod --image=busybox --target=anihpj. This attaches a separate debugging container with a shell WITHOUT modifying the production image.
