📊 Chapter 24 Visual Summary — Admission Control at a Glance

🚪
Built-in Plugins (24.1)

~30 plugins, 8 critical for CKS. Plugin chain runs mutating first (sequential), validating second (parallel). Configured via --enable-admission-plugins on API server. Always keep existing plugins when adding new ones.

🪝
Webhooks (24.2)

Mutating: sequential. Validating: parallel. TLS certs require CN matching Service DNS. failurePolicy: Fail = secure but risky. Ignore = available but insecure. objectSelector for fine-grained matching.

📜
OPA Gatekeeper (24.3)

Rego language. Logic programming paradigm. ConstraintTemplate defines logic, Constraint applies it with parameters. Audit mode for safe rollout. Rego reusable across K8s, Terraform, CI/CD.

🏛️
Kyverno (24.4)

Pure YAML. Validate/Mutate/Generate/VerifyImages. Auto-create NetworkPolicies for new namespaces. PolicyReport CRDs for compliance. CLI testing with kyverno test.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam tests admission control in multiple ways: (1) Enable admission plugins — edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, modify --enable-admission-plugins, keep existing plugins, verify with kubectl describe. (2) Configure ValidatingWebhookConfiguration — know clientConfig.service, caBundle (base64 CA cert), failurePolicy (Fail vs Ignore), namespaceSelector, objectSelector. (3) Write OPA ConstraintTemplate in Rego — know the violation[{"msg": msg}] pattern, iterate with containers[_], use input.review.object path, handle initContainers and ephemeralContainers. (4) Write Kyverno ClusterPolicy in YAML — know validate.deny.conditions, JMESPath expressions like {{ request.object.spec.containers[].image }}, mutate with patchStrategicMerge. (5) Order matters: Mutating runs BEFORE validating. Mutations are visible to validators. If a mutating webhook times out with failurePolicy: Fail, the request is denied before validators even run.

🔧 Under the Hood — Admission Webhook Flow: MutatingWebhook → ValidatingWebhook → PSS → OPA → Kyverno — Execution Order and Interaction 
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   ADMISSION CONTROL EXECUTION ORDER                                        │
  │                                                                           │
  │   Pod creation request arrives                                             │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │   1. MUTATING ADMISSION (runs FIRST, can MODIFY object)                   │
  │      • Built-in mutating plugins (DefaultStorageClass, etc.)              │
  │      • MutatingWebhookConfigurations (Kyverno mutate, custom mutators)   │
  │      • If failurePolicy=Fail and webhook fails → REJECT pod              │
  │      • Output: modified pod object (mutations applied)                    │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │   2. OBJECT SCHEMA VALIDATION                                              │
  │      • API server validates the object against OpenAPI schema             │
  │      • Catches: wrong field names, invalid types, missing required fields │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │   3. VALIDATING ADMISSION (runs SECOND, can only ACCEPT/REJECT)           │
  │      • Built-in validating plugins (PodSecurity, NodeRestriction)         │
  │      • ValidatingWebhookConfigurations (Gatekeeper, Kyverno validate)    │
  │      • If failurePolicy=Fail and webhook fails → REJECT pod              │
  │      • If failurePolicy=Ignore and webhook fails → ACCEPT pod (risky!)   │
  │                                                                           │
  │   🔑 A mutating webhook can ADD securityContext fields. A validating     │
  │      webhook then checks if those fields meet policy. This is how         │
  │      Kyverno can both auto-fix AND validate in one ClusterPolicy.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 24 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between a MutatingWebhookConfiguration and a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration?
Show Answer
Answer

MutatingWebhooks run FIRST and can MODIFY the incoming object (e.g., inject sidecars, add default securityContext). ValidatingWebhooks run SECOND and can only ACCEPT or REJECT the request. Both are called via HTTP POST to external webhook servers with JSON payloads containing the admission review.

Q2
What does failurePolicy: Fail vs failurePolicy: Ignore mean for an admission webhook, and which is more secure?
Show Answer
Answer

Fail: If the webhook server is unreachable, the admission request is REJECTED (fail-closed). More secure — prevents bypass by taking down the webhook. Ignore: If the webhook server is unreachable, the admission request proceeds as if the webhook doesn't exist (fail-open). Risky — an attacker could DoS the webhook server to bypass all its policies. Always use Fail for security-critical webhooks.

Q3
Write a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration that intercepts ALL pod CREATE/UPDATE operations and sends them to a webhook service opa.default.svc on /v1/admit.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata: {name: opa-validator}
webhooks:
- name: opa.default.svc
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
    resources: ["pods"]
    scope: Namespaced
  clientConfig:
    service:
      name: opa
      namespace: default
      path: /v1/admit
      port: 443
    caBundle: <base64-encoded-CA-cert>
  admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
  sideEffects: None
  failurePolicy: Fail
Explanation

This is the baseline webhook configuration for CKS. Key fields: rules (what to intercept), clientConfig (where to send), failurePolicy (Fail = secure), sideEffects: None (required for dry-run support). The CA bundle must be the base64-encoded PEM certificate of the webhook server's TLS. On the exam, you may need to create this from scratch or debug a broken one.

Q4
What is the sideEffects field and why must it be set to None for most admission webhooks? What happens if it's set incorrectly?
Show Answer
Answer

sideEffects declares whether the webhook has side effects beyond the admission decision. None means the webhook only returns an admission decision — no external API calls, no database writes. If set to None, the API server can call the webhook during dry-run requests (--dry-run=server). If set incorrectly (e.g., "None" but the webhook actually writes to a database), dry-run requests will incorrectly trigger side effects. If the webhook HAS side effects, you MUST set sideEffects: Some or sideEffects: NoneOnDryRun. The API server won't call webhooks with side effects during dry-runs.

Explanation

sideEffects is a safety mechanism. On the CKS exam, webhooks that only validate (like OPA) should have sideEffects: None. Webhooks that log to external systems should have sideEffects: Some. Incorrect declaration causes unexpected behavior with dry-run or causes the API server to reject the webhook configuration entirely.

Q5
What's the namespaceSelector in a webhook config, and how would you use it to only apply a validating webhook to namespaces labeled env: prod?
Show Answer
Answer
webhooks:
- name: prod-validator.default.svc
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      env: prod
  # OR exclude specific namespaces:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
      operator: NotIn
      values: [kube-system, kube-public]

namespaceSelector limits which namespaces the webhook applies to. Without it, the webhook applies to ALL namespaces. On the exam, use this to scope webhooks to production namespaces and exclude system namespaces.

Explanation

Scoping is critical for production use. A webhook that validates all pods in all namespaces can break system components (kube-system pods may not meet your policies). Always exclude kube-system and kube-public from custom webhooks unless you specifically need to validate them.

Q6
Explain the order of execution: built-in admission plugins, mutating webhooks, and validating webhooks. What happens if a mutating webhook modifies a field that a validating webhook checks?
Show Answer
Answer

Order: (1) Built-in MUTATING admission plugins (e.g., NamespaceLifecycle, ServiceAccount), (2) External MUTATING webhooks (alphabetically by name), (3) Built-in VALIDATING admission plugins (e.g., PodSecurity), (4) External VALIDATING webhooks (alphabetically by name). If a mutating webhook modifies a field, the validating webhook sees the MODIFIED object. This is intentional: validating webhooks validate the final state, including mutations. If you don't want a mutation to affect validation, validate the field in a MUTATING webhook (which runs before validating).

Explanation

This ordering is critical for debugging. If your OPA policy is rejecting a pod that looks fine in the original YAML, check if a mutating webhook (like Istio sidecar injection) modified the pod before OPA saw it. Use kubectl get pod -o yaml to see the final mutated spec. On the CKS exam, understand that mutations happen before validations.

Q7
A webhook with failurePolicy: Fail is causing ALL pod creations to fail because the webhook server is down. How do you recover without deleting the webhook permanently?
Show Answer
Answer
# Option 1: Patch failurePolicy to Ignore temporarily
kubectl patch validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/webhooks/0/failurePolicy","value":"Ignore"}]'
# Fix the webhook server, then change back to Fail

# Option 2: Delete the webhook (save the YAML first)
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> -o yaml > webhook-backup.yaml
kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>
# Fix the server, then reapply: kubectl apply -f webhook-backup.yaml
Explanation

This is a real production incident scenario. When a security webhook fails, it takes down the entire admission chain. Option 1 (patch to Ignore) is faster and preserves the webhook config. Option 2 (delete + reapply) is safer because you can verify the webhook config is intact before reapplying. On the CKS exam, you may face a cluster where "nothing can be created" — check webhook status first.

Q8
What is the ImagePolicyWebhook admission plugin and how does it differ from a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration for image validation?
Show Answer
Answer

ImagePolicyWebhook: A BUILT-IN admission plugin specifically for image validation. Enabled via --enable-admission-plugins=...,ImagePolicyWebhook with --admission-control-config-file pointing to a config file. It sends image attributes (name, tag, digest) to an external webhook that approves/denies. ValidatingWebhookConfiguration: A general-purpose external webhook that can validate ANY resource, including pods and their images. More flexible but requires more setup. ImagePolicyWebhook is simpler if you ONLY need image validation; a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration is better if you need complex pod-level policies.

Explanation

This is a CKS distinction. ImagePolicyWebhook is a single-purpose, built-in plugin for approving images. It's less flexible than a full admission webhook but easier to configure for simple "allow/deny image" use cases. On the exam, you may be asked to configure either — know both exist and when to use each.

Q9
You have 3 validating webhooks and 2 mutating webhooks. A pod creation request arrives. In what order are they called, and what happens if webhook #2 rejects the pod after webhook #1 already mutated it?
Show Answer
Answer

Order: Mutating webhooks #1, #2 (alphabetically) → Validating webhooks #1, #2, #3 (alphabetically). If validating webhook #2 rejects the pod: (1) The pod is NOT created. (2) The mutation from mutating webhooks is discarded — it never reaches etcd. (3) The API server returns the rejection error to the client. (4) Other validating webhooks (#3) are NOT called (short-circuit on first rejection). (5) The client can fix the issue and resubmit — the mutating webhooks will run again on the new request. Mutations only persist if the request is ultimately accepted.

Explanation

This is the complete admission flow. Key insight: mutations are "tentative" until the request is accepted. If a later validating webhook rejects, the mutations are rolled back. Also, validating webhooks short-circuit — the first rejection stops the chain. On the CKS exam, this ordering is tested when debugging why a pod modification isn't taking effect.

Q10
Write a MutatingWebhookConfiguration that injects a seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault into every pod in namespace "secure" that doesn't already have one. What's the advantage of mutation over validation for this use case?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata: {name: seccomp-injector}
webhooks:
- name: seccomp.default.svc
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      security: strict
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    operations: ["CREATE"]
    resources: ["pods"]
  clientConfig:
    service:
      name: seccomp-webhook
      namespace: default
    caBundle: <ca-cert>
  failurePolicy: Ignore  # Don't block pods if webhook is down
  sideEffects: None

Advantage of mutation: Developers don't need to remember to add Seccomp — the webhook adds it automatically. Validation would REJECT pods without Seccomp, creating friction. Mutation is transparent and ensures compliance without developer effort. Use mutation for defaults, validation for hard requirements.

Explanation

Mutation vs validation is a key design choice. Mutate when you want to AUTO-APPLY a security setting. Validate when you want to ENFORCE that the developer explicitly sets it (or a specific value). On the CKS exam, use mutation for security defaults (Seccomp, securityContext) and validation for hard policies (no privileged pods, must use specific registry).

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. List all admission webhooks
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl describe validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>  # Check rules, CA, fail policy

# 2. Check which admission plugins are enabled
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins

# 3. Test a webhook by creating a pod that should be rejected
kubectl apply -f test-pod.yaml --dry-run=server  # If webhook rejects, error shown
kubectl get events -n <ns> --field-selector reason=Failed  # Shows webhook rejection events

# 4. Temporarily disable a webhook for debugging
kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>  # Remove entirely (can reapply later)
# Or patch: kubectl patch validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> --type=json -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/webhooks/0"}]'
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 24 Traps
  • CA bundle must be valid base64: The caBundle field in a webhook configuration must be valid base64-encoded PEM certificate. If the CA doesn't match the webhook server's TLS certificate, ALL admission requests fail with "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority."
  • failurePolicy: Ignore creates a bypass: If the webhook server is down with failurePolicy: Ignore, all requests that the webhook was supposed to validate pass through unchecked. For security webhooks, always use failurePolicy: Fail.
  • timeoutSeconds too low causes flakiness: Webhook timeout is 10s by default. If your webhook does complex validation (e.g., external API call), it may timeout, and with failurePolicy: Fail, legitimate requests get rejected. Test at scale.

Chapter 25: Static Analysis — Scanning Manifests Before Deployment

Admission controllers (Ch24) catch bad configurations at the API server gate. But by the time a manifest reaches the API server, developers have already written it, reviewed it, merged it, and deployed it. The best security is prevention at the source: catching misconfigurations the moment a developer writes them — in their IDE, in their pull request, before they ever reach a cluster. This is Shift Left Security: moving security checks as close to the developer as possible. Static analysis tools — kube-linter, kubesec, and conftest — scan Kubernetes YAML manifests for security issues without ever touching a live cluster. They find privileged containers, missing securityContexts, writable root filesystems, and images with floating tags before they become production incidents. The cheapest vulnerability to fix is the one that never reaches production.

🟢 Beginner-Friendly ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔍 Static Analysis 📦 Supply Chain

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ Shift Left Security: Why catching misconfigurations at YAML level is 100x cheaper than fixing them in production — the security testing pyramid explained
  • ✅ kube-linter internals: How the template-based check engine works, 30+ built-in checks, creating custom checks, pre-commit hook integration
  • ✅ kubesec scoring deep dive: The full scoring algorithm, HTTP server mode for CI/CD, score tracking over time, comparison with kube-score and polaris
  • ✅ conftest Rego patterns: Fixture-based testing, Dockerfile + Terraform policies, data/warn rules beyond deny, IDE integration
  • ✅ Production CI/CD patterns: Pre-commit hooks for local dev, decision tree for tool selection, performance optimization, artifact-based score tracking
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

25.1 Why Static Analysis of YAML Matters — Shift Left Security

Every Kubernetes security incident begins with a YAML file. A developer writes a Deployment, sets privileged: true "just to make it work," commits it, and six months later that privileged container is the entry point for a cluster-wide breach. In February 2018, Tesla's Kubernetes cluster was breached because an unprotected dashboard allowed attackers to deploy crypto-mining pods — a misconfiguration that static analysis would have caught instantly. Static analysis catches these mistakes before they become incidents. Unlike admission controllers (which catch problems at deploy time) and runtime detection (which catches problems after they're exploited), static analysis works at the earliest possible moment — when the YAML is written.

The Security Testing Pyramid — Where Static Analysis Fits

The Security Testing Pyramid — From Code to Runtime
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    SECURITY TESTING PYRAMID                                │
  │                                                                           │
  │                         ▲                                                 │
  │                        /█\        🔴 RUNTIME DETECTION                    │
  │                       /███\       Falco, audit logs, threat detection     │
  │                      /█████\      (Catch attacks IN PROGRESS)              │
  │                     /███████\     SLOWEST feedback, HIGHEST cost          │
  │                    /█████████\                                              │
  │                   /███████████\   🟡 DYNAMIC TESTING                       │
  │                  /█████████████\  Admission controllers, CI/CD deploy     │
  │                 /███████████████\ (Catch issues AT DEPLOY TIME)            │
  │                /█████████████████\ Medium feedback, medium cost             │
  │                                    🟢 STATIC ANALYSIS                      │
  │               ███████████████████  kube-linter, kubesec, conftest          │
  │               ███████████████████  (Catch issues AT CODE TIME)             │
  │               ███████████████████  FASTEST feedback, LOWEST cost           │
  │               ███████████████████                                           │

Static Analysis vs Admission Control — Complementary, Not Competing

DimensionStatic Analysis (Ch25)Admission Control (Ch24)
WhenBefore commit, during CI/CDAt kubectl apply time
WhereDeveloper machine, CI runnerAPI server
What it seesYAML files on diskLive API requests
Can modify?No (analysis only)Yes (mutating webhooks)
Cluster required?No (works offline)Yes (must reach API server)
False negatives?Possible (e.g., Helm template not rendered)Very rare (sees final rendered object)
Best forDeveloper feedback, CI/CD gatesEnforcement, default injection
StrategyShift LEFT: Catch earlyShift RIGHT: Enforce at gate

BOTH are essential. Static analysis catches problems the developer can fix in seconds. Admission control catches problems that slip through CI/CD. Together they form a defense-in-depth strategy: catch early, enforce always.

The Static Analysis Tool Landscape — What Each Tool Checks

🔍
kube-linter

Linter for K8s YAML. 30+ built-in checks. Detects: privileged containers, missing limits, hostNetwork, writable root FS, latest tags. Written by StackRox (Red Hat).

📊
kubesec

Risk scorer (0-10). Scores manifests on security posture. Checks: capabilities, seccomp, readOnlyRoot, runAsNonRoot, AppArmor, serviceAccount.

📜
conftest

OPA Rego policy testing. Test any YAML/JSON against Rego policies. Not K8s-specific — works with Dockerfiles, Terraform, etc.

🛡️
checkov

Multi-cloud scanner. Bridgecrew's IaC scanner. Checks K8s, Terraform, CloudFormation, Helm. 750+ built-in policies. Graph-based analysis.

📝 Real-World Incident: Tesla Kubernetes Breach (2018)

In February 2018, attackers discovered an unprotected Kubernetes dashboard in Tesla's AWS environment. The dashboard had no authentication and was exposed to the internet. Attackers deployed pods running crypto-mining software, consuming Tesla's cloud resources. Static analysis would have caught: (1) the dashboard deployment with no authentication configuration, (2) pods with no resource limits (allowing crypto miners to consume unlimited CPU), (3) missing network policies (allowing pods to reach external mining pools). The breach was discovered by RedLock (now Palo Alto) cloud security monitoring — but static analysis at the YAML level would have prevented it entirely.

25.2 kube-linter — Kubernetes YAML Security Analysis

kube-linter (by StackRox, now Red Hat) is a static analysis tool that checks Kubernetes YAML manifests against 30+ built-in security checks. It's designed to be fast, opinionated, and CI/CD-friendly. Unlike kubesec (which gives a numeric score), kube-linter produces a simple pass/fail result for each check with actionable error messages.

How kube-linter Works Internally — Template Engine + Object Traversal

kube-linter Architecture — From YAML File to Lint Result
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    KUBE-LINTER INTERNALS                               │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 1: YAML PARSE + OBJECT DETECTION                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  kube-linter reads anihpj-deployment.yaml                     │    │
  │  │  → Detects: Kind=Deployment, apiVersion=apps/v1              │    │
  │  │  → Parses the full object tree into memory                    │    │
  │  │  → Identifies: Pod template, containers, volumes, etc.       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  STEP 2: CHECK REGISTRY — Which checks apply to this object?         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  For Object: Deployment → applies to:                          │    │
  │  │  • Deployment-level checks (host-network, host-pid, etc.)     │    │
  │  │  • Pod template checks (container-level)                      │    │
  │  │  • Container-level checks (privileged, run-as-non-root, etc.) │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  Each check is a Go template or Rego rule that traverses       │    │
  │  │  the object tree looking for specific patterns.                │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  STEP 3: CHECK EXECUTION — Run each matching check                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  check: privileged-container                                   │    │
  │  │    target: containers[].securityContext.privileged             │    │
  │  │    logic: if value == true → FAIL                              │    │
  │  │    result: container "anihpj" has privileged=true → ❌         │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  check: run-as-non-root                                         │    │
  │  │    target: containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot            │    │
  │  │    logic: if not set or false → FAIL                            │    │
  │  │    result: runAsNonRoot not set → ❌                             │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  check: latest-tag                                              │    │
  │  │    target: containers[].image                                   │    │
  │  │    logic: if image ends with :latest or has no tag → FAIL       │    │
  │  │    result: image "anihpj-django:latest" → ❌                    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

kube-linter Built-in Checks — The Most Important Ones for CKS

Check NameWhat It DetectsSeverityWhy It Matters
privileged-containerContainer has securityContext.privileged: trueCriticalPrivileged containers have ALL Linux capabilities and access to all host devices. Equivalent to root on the node.
no-read-only-root-filesystemreadOnlyRootFilesystem is not set or is falseHighWritable root FS allows attackers to install tools, write scripts, and modify binaries after exploitation.
run-as-non-rootrunAsNonRoot is not set to trueHighContainers running as root (UID 0) can escape the container via kernel exploits or misconfigured volumes.
host-networkPod has hostNetwork: trueHighHost network access bypasses all NetworkPolicies and exposes pod to host interfaces.
host-pidPod has hostPID: trueHighHost PID namespace access allows listing and signaling all processes on the node.
latest-tagContainer image uses :latest tagMediumFloating tags are mutable — you don't know which image version is actually running.
dangling-serviceService selector matches no podsMediumIndicates a misconfiguration — the Service has no backends.

Running kube-linter — Local, CI/CD, Pre-Commit, and Helm

Bash — kube-linter commands for all scanning scenarios 
# ── Install ──
brew install kube-linter
# Or: curl -LO https://github.com/stackrox/kube-linter/releases/latest/download/kube-linter-linux

# ── Scan a single YAML file ──
kube-linter lint anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── Scan all YAML files in a directory ──
kube-linter lint ./k8s-manifests/

# ── Scan a Helm chart ──
kube-linter lint ./anihpj-helm-chart/

# ── Scan with specific checks ──
kube-linter lint --include privileged-container,run-as-non-root ./manifests/
kube-linter lint --exclude latest-tag ./manifests/

# ── JSON output for CI/CD ──
kube-linter lint --format json ./manifests/ > kube-linter-report.json

Pre-Commit Hook — Catch Issues Before They Leave Your Machine

YAML — .pre-commit-config.yaml — Run kube-linter on every git commit 
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
- repo: local
  hooks:
  - id: kube-linter
    name: kube-linter
    entry: kube-linter lint
    language: system
    files: \.(yaml|yml)$
    pass_filenames: false    # Lint all k8s/ files, not just changed ones
    args: ['k8s/']

# Setup:
# pip install pre-commit
# pre-commit install
# Now EVERY git commit runs kube-linter.
# If it finds issues → commit is BLOCKED.

🔴 Example: What kube-linter Catches in an Insecure anihpj Deployment

INSECURE MANIFEST — anihpj-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      hostNetwork: true          # ❌ host-network
      hostPID: true              # ❌ host-pid
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: anihpj-django:latest  # ❌ latest-tag
        securityContext:
          privileged: true       # ❌ privileged-container
          runAsUser: 0           # ❌ run-as-non-root
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80      # ❌ privileged-ports
kube-linter OUTPUT — 5 Issues Found
$ kube-linter lint anihpj-deployment.yaml

anihpj-deployment.yaml: (object: anihpj/anihpj-django)
  ❌ "host-network" — hostNetwork set to true
  ❌ "host-pid" — hostPID set to true
  ❌ "privileged-container" — container "anihpj"
     is privileged
  ❌ "run-as-non-root" — container "anihpj"
     does not have runAsNonRoot set
  ❌ "latest-tag" — container "anihpj" uses
     image with ":latest" tag

Error: found 5 lint errors
Exit code: 1 → CI/CD pipeline BLOCKED 🛡️

Creating Custom kube-linter Checks — Extend Beyond Built-ins

YAML — .kube-linter.yaml — Custom check: require team annotation on all resources 
# .kube-linter.yaml
checks:
  addAllBuiltIn: true
  exclude:
  - "dangling-service"
  - "no-extensions-v1beta"

  # ── CUSTOM CHECK: Require 'team' annotation ──
  customChecks:
  - name: "required-annotation-team"
    template: "required-annotation"
    params:
      key: "team"
      value: ".*"           # Any value is acceptable

  # ── CUSTOM CHECK: Deny specific namespace ──
  - name: "deny-default-namespace"
    template: "disallowed-object"
    params:
      kind: "Deployment"
      # All Deployments must be in a non-default namespace

  # ── CUSTOM CHECK: Require specific label ──
  - name: "required-label-app"
    template: "required-label"
    params:
      key: "app"
      value: "anihpj-.*"   # Must match pattern

ignorePaths:
- "vendor/"
- "test/fixtures/"

Decision Tree: Which Static Analysis Tool for Which Scenario?

Static Analysis Tool Selection for Kubernetes YAML
  START: I need to check Kubernetes YAML for security issues
  │
  ├─ Do I want BUILT-IN CHECKS with NO configuration?
  │  └─ YES → kube-linter (30+ checks out of the box, zero config needed)
  │
  ├─ Do I want a NUMERIC SECURITY SCORE for each manifest?
  │  └─ YES → kubesec (0-10 score, track improvement over time)
  │
  ├─ Do I need CUSTOM ORGANIZATIONAL POLICIES in Rego?
  │  ├─ YES → conftest (write your own Rego rules)
  │  └─ Also consider: kube-linter customChecks (simpler template-based)
  │
  ├─ Do I need to scan TERRAFORM, DOCKERFILES, or other IaC?
  │  ├─ For K8s + Terraform + Dockerfile → conftest (multi-parser)
  │  ├─ For Terraform specifically → checkov (graph-based, 750+ policies)
  │  └─ For Dockerfile only → hadolint (specialized Dockerfile linter)
  │
  ├─ Am I in CI/CD (PR gate)?
  │  ├─ Lightweight + fast → kube-linter (fastest, simplest)
  │  ├─ Score threshold → kubesec (numeric gate: score ≥ 4)
  │  └─ Custom policies → conftest (organization-specific rules)
  │
  └─ 🟢 RECOMMENDATION: Use ALL THREE in CI/CD
     kube-linter for built-in checks (fast, broad coverage)
     kubesec for scoring threshold (numeric quality gate)
     conftest for custom policies (organization-specific)

25.3 kubesec — Security Risk Analysis for K8s Manifests

While kube-linter gives you pass/fail checks, kubesec (by ControlPlane) gives you a numeric risk score from 0 to 10. Each check contributes or subtracts points, and the final score represents the overall security posture of your manifest. This is invaluable for measuring security improvement over time: "Last month our deployment scored 3/10. After adding securityContexts, it's 7/10."

kubesec Scoring Algorithm — How Points Are Calculated

kubesec Scoring Breakdown — What Adds and Subtracts Points
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    KUBESEC SCORING MODEL (0-10)                            │
  │                                                                           │
  │  SCORE = SUM(points) / MAX_POSSIBLE_POINTS * 10                           │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  CHECK                          │  POINTS  │  CRITICALITY          │  │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────┼──────────┼───────────────────────┤  │
  │  │  containers[].securityContext   │          │                        │  │
  │  │    .runAsNonRoot = true         │  +1      │  CRITICAL (blocks LPE) │  │
  │  │    .readOnlyRootFilesystem=true │  +1      │  HIGH (blocks writes)  │  │
  │  │    .allowPrivilegeEscalation=fls│  +1      │  HIGH (blocks setuid)  │  │
  │  │    .privileged = false          │  +1      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    .capabilities.drop = [ALL]   │  +1      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    .capabilities.add = []       │  +1      │  HIGH                  │  │
  │  │    .seccompProfile = set        │  +1      │  HIGH                  │  │
  │  │    .appArmorProfile = set       │  +1      │  MEDIUM                │  │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────┼──────────┼───────────────────────┤  │
  │  │  DEDUCTIONS (negative points):  │          │                        │  │
  │  │    privileged = true            │  -5      │  IMMEDIATE FAIL        │  │
  │  │    allowPrivilegeEscalation=true│  -3      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    runAsNonRoot = false         │  -3      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    capabilities.add includes    │          │                        │  │
  │  │      SYS_ADMIN or NET_ADMIN     │  -3      │  HIGH                  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                           │
  │  SCORE INTERPRETATION:                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │
  │  0-3:  🔴 CRITICAL — Do not deploy. Missing essential controls.           │
  │  4-5:  🟠 HIGH — Only dev/staging. Needs improvement.                     │
  │  6-7:  🟡 MEDIUM — Acceptable for production with monitoring.             │
  │  8-9:  🟢 LOW — Good security posture.                                    │
  │  10:   ✅ IDEAL — All recommended controls. Rare.                         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Running kubesec — CLI, HTTP Server, and CI/CD Integration

Bash — kubesec commands, HTTP server mode, and CI/CD score gating 
# ── CLI: Scan a manifest file ──
kubesec scan anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── CLI: Pipe from kubectl or helm ──
kubectl get deployment anihpj-django -n anihpj -o yaml | kubesec scan -
helm template ./anihpj-chart | kubesec scan -

# ── HTTP SERVER MODE: Run kubesec as a service (for CI/CD) ──
kubesec server --port 8080 &
curl -sSX POST --data-binary @anihpj-deployment.yaml \
  http://localhost:8080/scan | jq .

# ── CI/CD SCORE GATE ──
SCORE=$(kubesec scan anihpj-deployment.yaml | jq -r '.[0].score')
if [ "$SCORE" -lt 4 ]; then
  echo "❌ Score $SCORE below threshold (≥4 required)"
  exit 1
fi

# ── TRACK SCORE OVER TIME: Save score as CI artifact ──
kubesec scan k8s/*.yaml | jq '[.[] | {object: .object, score: .score}]' \
  > kubesec-scores-$(date +%Y%m%d).json
# Archive this artifact — track score trends across builds

Interpreting kubesec Output — anihpj Before and After Hardening

kubesec Scan Result — anihpj Deployment Before and After Hardening

Featurekubeseckube-scorepolaris

Checks~15 security checks~25 checks (probes, limits, policies)~30 checks across 5 categories

25.4 conftest — Testing YAML with OPA Rego Policies

conftest tests structured configuration data (YAML, JSON, HCL, TOML, Dockerfiles) against policies written in OPA Rego — the same language used by OPA Gatekeeper (Ch24). Unlike kube-linter (fixed built-in checks) and kubesec (fixed scoring algorithm), conftest lets you define your own policies. This is the ultimate flexibility: enforce your organization's specific security standards, naming conventions, labeling requirements, and resource structure rules.

conftest vs OPA Gatekeeper — Same Language, Different Stage

Featureconftest (Ch25)OPA Gatekeeper (Ch24)
WhenPre-deployment (CI/CD, CLI, IDE)Deployment time (API server admission)
InputStatic YAML/JSON files on diskLive AdmissionReview API requests
LanguageRego (identical syntax)Rego (identical syntax)
Can test non-K8s✅ Dockerfiles, Terraform, HCL, TOML, JSON❌ Kubernetes only
BlockingBlocks CI/CD (non-zero exit code)Blocks API request (403 Forbidden)
Policy input pathinput.spec.template.spec.containers[_]input.review.object.spec.containers[_]

Fixture-Based Testing Pattern — Test Policies with Expected Results

conftest Fixture Testing — Policy + Test Fixtures + Expected Results
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    FIXTURE-BASED TESTING                               │
  │                                                                       │
  │  Directory structure:                                                 │
  │  policies/                                                            │
  │  ├── security.rego          ← Policy rules to test                    │
  │  ├── security_test.rego     ← Test assertions                         │
  │  └── fixtures/                                                        │
  │      ├── good-pod.yaml      ← Should PASS all policies               │
  │      └── bad-pod.yaml       ← Should FAIL specific policies           │
  │                                                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  # policies/security_test.rego                                │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  package main                                                 │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  # Test: good-pod.yaml should have 0 deny results             │    │
  │  │  test_good_pod_has_no_violations {                            │    │
  │  │      count(deny) == 0 with input as yaml_unmarshal(           │    │
  │  │          file("fixtures/good-pod.yaml")                       │    │
  │  │      )                                                         │    │
  │  │  }                                                             │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  # Test: bad-pod.yaml should have at least 1 deny result      │    │
  │  │  test_bad_pod_has_violations {                                │    │
  │  │      count(deny) > 0 with input as yaml_unmarshal(            │    │
  │  │          file("fixtures/bad-pod.yaml")                        │    │
  │  │      )                                                         │    │
  │  │  }                                                             │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  # Run tests: conftest verify --policy policies/              │    │
  │  │  # Output: 2 tests passed, 0 tests failed                     │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rego Policies for conftest — Security + Data + Warnings

Rego — policy/security.rego — Deny, warn, and data rules for anihpj 
package main

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DENY RULES: Block the CI/CD pipeline (exit code 1)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

deny[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    not container.securityContext
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing securityContext", [container.name])
}

deny[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    container.securityContext.runAsUser == 0
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' running as root (UID 0)", [container.name])
}

deny[msg] {
    input.spec.template.spec.hostNetwork == true
    msg := "hostNetwork is not allowed"
}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# WARN RULES: Show warnings but DON'T block (exit code 0)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

warn[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    not container.resources.limits.cpu
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing CPU limit (recommended)", [container.name])
}

warn[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    endswith(container.image, ":latest")
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' uses mutable ':latest' tag", [container.name])
}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DATA RULES: Extract information (always runs, informational)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

images[image] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    image := container.image
}

container_count := count(input.spec.template.spec.containers)

Running conftest — CLI, Multi-Parser, and Fixture Testing

Bash — conftest commands for all testing scenarios 
# ── Install ──
brew install conftest

# ── Test K8s manifests against Rego policies ──
conftest test anihpj-deployment.yaml
conftest test k8s/*.yaml

# ── Test with custom policy directory ──
conftest test --policy ./org-policies anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── Test Dockerfile ──
conftest test --parser dockerfile Dockerfile

# ── Test Terraform ──
conftest test --parser hcl1 terraform/*.tf

# ── Test with JSON output (for CI/CD) ──
conftest test --output json anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── Fixture-based testing (verify policies are correct) ──
conftest verify --policy policies/

# ── Combined pipeline ──
conftest test k8s/*.yaml && echo "✅ All passed" || echo "❌ Violations found"

25.5 Integrating Static Analysis into anihpj CI/CD — The Complete Security Gate

Each tool alone is useful. But together, they form a layered security gate that catches different classes of problems at different stages. The goal: no insecure manifest ever reaches the cluster. The pipeline starts at the developer's machine (pre-commit hooks), continues through PR review (CI checks), and culminates in image signing before deployment.

Developer Workflow — Pre-Commit Hooks for All Three Tools

YAML — .pre-commit-config.yaml — Run all three static analysis tools before git commit 
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
# Install: pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install
# Now EVERY git commit runs these checks. Blocked if any fail.
repos:
- repo: local
  hooks:
  # ── kube-linter: Built-in K8s checks ──
  - id: kube-linter
    name: kube-linter (K8s security checks)
    entry: kube-linter lint
    language: system
    files: ^k8s/.*\.(yaml|yml)$
    pass_filenames: false
    args: ['k8s/']

  # ── kubesec: Security score threshold ──
  - id: kubesec
    name: kubesec (security scoring)
    entry: bash -c
    language: system
    files: ^k8s/.*\.(yaml|yml)$
    args:
    - |
      for f in k8s/*.yaml; do
        SCORE=$(kubesec scan "$f" | jq -r '.[0].score')
        if [ "$SCORE" -lt 4 ]; then
          echo "❌ $f scored $SCORE (needs ≥4)" && exit 1
        fi
      done

  # ── conftest: Custom Rego policies ──
  - id: conftest
    name: conftest (custom Rego policies)
    entry: conftest test --policy policies/
    language: system
    files: ^k8s/.*\.(yaml|yml)$
    pass_filenames: false
    args: ['k8s/']

The Complete anihpj Security CI/CD Pipeline — 4 Gates

anihpj Security Pipeline — Developer Push → Production Deploy
  Developer pushes code → opens PR
         │
         ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  GATE 1: YAML SECURITY (kube-linter + kubesec + conftest)       ║
  ║  ✅ No privileged containers | ✅ Score ≥4 | ✅ Rego policies    ║
  ║  ❌ FAIL → PR blocked with inline violation comments             ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
         │ ✅
         ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  GATE 2: DOCKERFILE SECURITY (hadolint)                         ║
  ║  ✅ Non-root USER | ✅ No ADD from URLs | ✅ COPY before RUN    ║
  ║  ❌ FAIL → PR blocked                                           ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
         │ ✅ PR merged
         ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  GATE 3: IMAGE SCAN (trivy)                                     ║
  ║  ✅ CRITICAL CVEs = 0 | ✅ HIGH CVEs ≤ 2 (documented)          ║
  ║  ❌ FAIL → image NOT pushed                                     ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
         │ ✅
         ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  GATE 4: IMAGE SIGNING (cosign)                                 ║
  ║  ✅ Image cryptographically signed | ✅ SBOM attached           ║
  ║  ❌ FAIL → deploy blocked                                       ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
         │ ✅
         ▼
  Deploy → Kyverno verifyImages checks signature ✅

  🔑 IF ANY GATE FAILS: Pipeline STOPS. Manifest NEVER reaches cluster.

Gate Summary — What Each Tool Catches and Where

GateToolRuns OnBlocks IfWhat It Catches

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam may ask you to scan a Kubernetes manifest with static analysis tools and fix the findings. Know: (1) kube-linter lint <file> — produces pass/fail results; add securityContext to fix privileged/run-as-non-root errors. (2) kubesec scan <file> — produces 0-10 score; know what adds points (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRoot, seccomp, drop ALL caps) and what deducts (privileged: -5, SYS_ADMIN: -3). (3) conftest test <file> — tests against custom Rego policies; know the deny[msg] and warn[msg] patterns; understand the input path difference between conftest (input.spec.template.spec...) and OPA Gatekeeper (input.review.object.spec...). (4) The exam may ask you to fix a manifest to pass a specific score threshold — add runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop ALL capabilities, use a non-root user, and set a custom ServiceAccount. (5) Shift left: these tools run BEFORE deployment. They complement admission controllers (Ch24), not replace them. Static analysis catches at code time ($0 cost), admission control enforces at deploy time.

🔧 Under the Hood — OPA Rego Engine: How Policies Are Compiled, Evaluated, and Cached for Performance 
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   REGO POLICY EVALUATION — OPA Internals                              │
  │                                                                      │
  │   1. PARSE: Rego source parsed into AST (Abstract Syntax Tree)       │
  │   2. COMPILE: AST compiled to OPA internal rule representation       │
  │   3. INDEX: Rules indexed by path for fast lookup                    │
  │   4. EVALUATE: For each pod admission request:                       │
  │      input = { review: { object: pod-spec } }                        │
  │      Evaluate rules top-to-bottom                                     │
  │      violation[{msg}] — partial set: each match = one violation      │
  │      If ANY violation rule matches → constraint returns violations   │
  │   5. CACHE: Compiled policies cached until source changes             │
  │                                                                      │
  │   KEY REGO PATTERNS FOR CKS:                                          │
  │   container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]  # Iterate     │
  │   not condition  # Negation — true when condition is false            │
  │   some var       # Existential quantifier                             │
  │   count(set)     # Count elements in a set                            │
  │   sprintf("container %v has no CPU limit", [container.name])         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 25 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Write an OPA ConstraintTemplate in Rego that blocks pods without CPU limits.
Show Answer
Answer
package k8srequirecpulimits
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
  not container.resources.limits.cpu
  msg := sprintf("container %v has no CPU limit", [container.name])
}
Q2
What is the difference between conftest and Gatekeeper? When would you use each?
Show Answer
Answer

Conftest runs Rego policies against YAML files in CI/CD (pre-deployment). Gatekeeper runs Rego policies as an admission controller inside Kubernetes (at deployment time). Use conftest to catch violations BEFORE they reach the cluster (shift-left). Use Gatekeeper to enforce policies at the admission gate (defense-in-depth). Both use the same Rego language. Conftest input path: input.spec.template.spec.... Gatekeeper input path: input.review.object.spec....

Q3
Write a Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate + Constraint that requires all pods to have runAsNonRoot: true. Include both resources.
Show Answer
Answer
# ConstraintTemplate
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata: {name: k8srequirednonroot}
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names: {kind: K8sRequiredNonRoot}
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8srequirednonroot
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot == true
        msg := sprintf("container %v must set runAsNonRoot: true", [container.name])
      }
---
# Constraint
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredNonRoot
metadata: {name: require-run-as-non-root}
spec:
  match:
    kinds: [{apiGroups: [""], kinds: ["Pod"]}]
Explanation

Gatekeeper uses a two-resource model: ConstraintTemplate (defines the Rego policy logic) and Constraint (applies the policy with parameters). This separation allows reuse — one ConstraintTemplate can have multiple Constraints with different parameters. On the CKS exam, you create the template first, then the constraint.

Q4
What's kubesec and what does a score of 7 mean? What specific checks does it perform on a pod spec?
Show Answer
Answer

kubesec scores pod security from 0-10. A score of 7 means the pod has good security but could be improved. It checks: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities.drop, seccompProfile, hostPID, hostNetwork, privileged, resource limits. Each check adds or deducts points. Critical deductions: privileged:true (-30), hostPID:true (-20), no capabilities drop (-10). Additions: runAsNonRoot (+2), readOnlyRootFS (+2), drop ALL capabilities (+2). A score of 10 requires ALL security features enabled.

Explanation

kubesec is a quick security scoring tool for CI/CD. On the CKS exam, you may be asked to scan a pod spec and identify what's causing a low score. The scoring breakdown tells you exactly which fields to add. A score below 3 is critically insecure; above 7 is production-ready.

Q5
Write a Rego policy for conftest that blocks pods using the :latest tag.
Show Answer
Answer
package main
deny[msg] {
  container := input.spec.containers[_]
  endswith(container.image, ":latest")
  msg := sprintf("container %v uses :latest tag", [container.name])
}
deny[msg] {
  container := input.spec.containers[_]
  not contains(container.image, ":")
  msg := sprintf("container %v has no tag (defaults to :latest)", [container.name])
}
Explanation

:latest tags are mutable — they can change without notice, bypassing image scanning and signing. The second rule catches images with NO tag, which also default to :latest. On the CKS exam, always enforce specific tags or digests. Use conftest in CI/CD to catch this before deployment.

Q6
What's kube-linter and how does it differ from Trivy? Which one scans live clusters vs YAML files?
Show Answer
Answer

kube-linter: Scans Kubernetes YAML manifests for security misconfigurations and best practices. Runs in CI/CD or against files. Checks: securityContext, resource limits, liveness probes, etc. Trivy: Scans container IMAGES for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and also scans YAML configs. kube-linter is YAML-only; Trivy is image + YAML. kube-linter focuses on Kubernetes best practices; Trivy focuses on vulnerability databases. Use BOTH: kube-linter for config hygiene, Trivy for CVE detection.

Explanation

These tools are complementary. kube-linter catches "this pod runs as root" (config error). Trivy catches "nginx:1.25 has CVE-2024-XXXX" (vulnerability). On the CKS exam, you may use both — scan the manifest with kube-linter, scan the image with Trivy.

Q7
Write a Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate that blocks pods from using any container image registry EXCEPT anihpj.azurecr.io.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata: {name: k8sallowedrepos}
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names: {kind: K8sAllowedRepos}
      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          properties:
            repos:
              type: array
              items: {type: string}
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sallowedrepos
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        not startswith(container.image, input.parameters.repos[_])
        msg := sprintf("container %v uses disallowed registry: %v", [container.name, container.image])
      }

Constraint: parameters: {repos: ["anihpj.azurecr.io/"]}

Explanation

Registry allowlisting is a supply chain security control. By restricting images to your private registry, you ensure: (1) all images have been scanned before being pushed to the registry, (2) no one can deploy images directly from Docker Hub, (3) every image is signed by your CI pipeline. On the CKS exam, this is a common Gatekeeper policy task.

Q8
You scan a pod YAML with kubesec and get 2/10. The deductions show: privileged:true (-30), hostNetwork:true (-20), no seccompProfile (-5). Write the corrected pod securityContext to achieve 9+/10.
Show Answer
Answer
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
# Remove: privileged: true, hostNetwork: true, hostPID: true
Explanation

This is the CKS pattern: start with the kubesec deductions, fix each one, rescan. privileged:true alone can take a score from 10 to 2. hostNetwork and hostPID are almost as bad. The corrected securityContext above should score 9+/10 (only missing resource limits which kubesec also checks but are optional for security). On the exam, iteratively fix and rescan.

Q9
How does conftest integrate into a CI/CD pipeline? Write the pipeline step that fails the build if ANY Rego policy violation is found.
Show Answer
Answer
# In CI/CD (GitHub Actions / Jenkins)
conftest test deployment.yaml --policy policies/ --fail-on-warn
# --fail-on-warn: Fails if even a warning-level violation is found
# Exit code 1 = policy violation, pipeline stops

# Test multiple files
conftest test k8s-manifests/*.yaml --policy policies/

# Structured output for reporting
conftest test deployment.yaml --policy policies/ --output json | \
  jq '.[] | select(.failures | length > 0)'
Explanation

CI/CD integration is the "shift-left" approach. conftest should run BEFORE any image is built or deployed. If policies fail, the pipeline stops. On the CKS exam, the supply chain security domain (20%) heavily tests CI/CD integration — know how to add security gates to pipelines.

Q10
Compare OPA Gatekeeper vs Kyverno for admission control. What are the key differences in architecture, language, and use case?
Show Answer
Answer
AspectOPA GatekeeperKyverno
LanguageRego (declarative policy language)YAML (Kubernetes-native)
ArchitectureConstraintTemplate + ConstraintClusterPolicy (single resource)
Learning curveHigher (Rego syntax)Lower (YAML, K8s-like)
MutationSeparate product (OPA, not Gatekeeper)Built-in (generate/mutate rules)
CKS ExamGatekeeper is more commonly referencedGrowing in popularity
Explanation

Both are CNCF projects and valid CKS answers. Gatekeeper is more mature with a larger ecosystem. Kyverno is simpler (no Rego required) and supports mutation natively. On the CKS exam: if the question mentions "Rego" or "ConstraintTemplate," the answer is Gatekeeper. If it mentions "ClusterPolicy" or "YAML-based policies," it's Kyverno. Know both architectures.

# 1. Scan a manifest with kube-linter
kube-linter lint pod.yaml  # Checks for security best practices
kube-linter lint --include "run-as-non-root,no-privileged" pod.yaml

# 2. Get a security score with kubesec

⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 25 Traps
  • conftest input path vs Gatekeeper input path: conftest evaluates YAML files directly, so the Rego input is the raw YAML structure: input.spec.containers[_].securityContext. Gatekeeper receives the AdmissionReview object, so: input.review.object.spec.containers[_].securityContext. Same Rego language, different input paths.
  • kubesec score is not absolute: A score of 7/10 might pass your threshold but still have dangerous configurations. Always check WHY points were deducted, not just the final score.

Chapter 26: Image Signing — Cosign and Sigstore

You've built anihpj:v2. Trivy says zero CRITICAL CVEs. kubesec scores it 8/10. kube-linter gives it a clean bill. You push it to your private registry. But here's the terrifying question: how does your Kubernetes cluster KNOW that the image in the registry is actually YOUR image? An attacker who compromises your registry credentials could push a malicious image with the exact same tag — and your cluster would pull it without hesitation. This is where image signing comes in: cryptographic proof, verified at admission time, that the image was built by you and only you. Cosign (part of the CNCF-backed Sigstore project) signs container images with digital signatures stored alongside the image in the registry. Kyverno verifies those signatures before allowing pods to run. Together, they close the supply chain's final gap: proving that what you built is what you deploy.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours ✍️ Image Signing 📦 Supply Chain

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ Cryptographic foundations: How ECDSA digital signatures work, why digest-based signing is essential, and the in-toto attestation framework
  • ✅ Cosign key-based signing: Key generation with password protection, signing and verifying, key rotation strategies, multi-signer workflows
  • ✅ Kyverno verifyImages deep dive: Key rotation policy patterns, troubleshooting common failures, enforcement level decision framework
  • ✅ Keyless signing internals: Fulcio certificate chain of trust, Rekor transparency log querying, OIDC identity binding, and when to choose keyless over key-based
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

26.1 Why Image Signing Matters — Trust But Verify

You build anihpj:v2 in CI/CD, push it to registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2, and deploy. The cluster pulls the image and runs it. But how does the cluster know it's really your image? Registry credentials prove you can push — they don't prove what you pushed is what you built. Image signing solves this: you cryptographically sign the image digest with your private key. The cluster verifies the signature against your public key at admission time. If the signature doesn't match, the image is rejected — even if it came from the right registry with the right tag.

The Cryptography Behind Image Signing — ECDSA and Digest Immutability

How Digital Signatures Work — ECDSA Signing and Verification
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    ECDSA DIGITAL SIGNATURE BASICS                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Cosign uses ECDSA-P256 (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)     │
  │  with the P-256 curve — same cryptography as TLS certificates.           │
  │                                                                           │
  │  SIGNING (in CI/CD):                                                      │
  │  ──────────────────                                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  1. Image manifest is hashed: SHA256(manifest) → abc123def456   │    │
  │  │     (The hash is a fixed 256-bit fingerprint of the image)      │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  2. Hash is signed with PRIVATE key:                             │    │
  │  │     Sign(private_key, abc123def456) → signature (r,s)           │    │
  │  │     (Only the private key holder can create this signature)      │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  3. Signature + metadata is pushed to the registry as an         │    │
  │  │     OCI artifact: sha256-abc123.sig                              │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  VERIFICATION (in Kyverno):                                               │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  1. Image manifest is hashed again: SHA256(manifest) → hash     │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  2. Signature is retrieved from registry: sha256-abc123.sig     │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  3. PUBLIC key verifies the signature against the hash:          │    │
  │  │     Verify(public_key, hash, signature) → TRUE/FALSE            │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  4. If TRUE: The signature was created by the holder of the      │    │
  │  │     private key AND the image hasn't been modified since.        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 WHY DIGEST-BASED SIGNING IS ESSENTIAL:                                │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  • Tags like "anihpj:v2" are MUTABLE — the same tag can point to         │
  │    different digests over time                                            │
  │  • Digests like "sha256:abc123..." are IMMUTABLE — they uniquely          │
  │    identify a specific image manifest                                     │
  │  • Cosign ALWAYS signs digests, never tags                                │
  │  • Even if an attacker overwrites the "v2" tag to point to their         │
  │    malicious image, the signature is bound to the DIGEST, not the tag     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Supply Chain Attack Vector — Without vs With Image Signing

Supply Chain Attack — Without vs With Image Signing
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    WITHOUT IMAGE SIGNING                                   │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CI/CD                    REGISTRY                     KUBERNETES          │
  │  docker build         ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐     │

  │                        │ (legitimate) │              │ anihpj:v2 ✅ │     │
  │                        └──────────────┘              └──────────────┘     │
  │                                                                           │

  │                                                                           │

  │                    WITH IMAGE SIGNING (Cosign + Kyverno)                   │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CI/CD                    REGISTRY                     KUBERNETES          │

  │                                                      └──────────────┘     │
