How Image Signing Works — Cryptography in Plain English

1Generate Key Pair

cosign generate-key-pair creates an ECDSA-P256 private key (kept SECRET, used only in CI/CD) and a public key (shared with Kyverno for verification).

2Sign the Image Digest

cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 resolves the tag to an immutable digest (sha256:abc...), hashes the manifest, signs with the private key, and stores the .sig OCI artifact.

3Verify at Admission

Kyverno fetches the .sig from registry, verifies it against the configured public key. If the signature is cryptographically valid → ALLOW. If missing or invalid → DENY.

4Transparency (Keyless)

With keyless signing, the signing event is also recorded in Rekor's public transparency log — providing an immutable, auditable record of who signed what and when.

The in-toto Attestation Framework — Beyond Signatures

Image signatures answer "who signed this image?" But in-toto attestations answer deeper questions: "How was this built? From what source? Using which builder? With what dependencies?" Cosign supports in-toto attestations, allowing you to attach SLSA provenance, vulnerability scan results, and SBOM references as signed metadata alongside the image signature:

in-toto Attestation Model — Predicates Signed by the Builder
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    IN-TOTO ATTESTATION FRAMEWORK                       │
  │                                                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ATTESTATION = Envelope {                                      │    │
  │  │    subject: [{                                                 │    │
  │  │      name: "registry.anihpj.com/anihpj",                      │    │
  │  │      digest: { sha256: "abc123..." }                          │    │
  │  │    }],                                                          │    │
  │  │    predicateType: "https://slsa.dev/provenance/v0.2",         │    │
  │  │    predicate: {                                                 │    │
  │  │      builder: { id: "https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj/..." },  │    │
  │  │      buildType: "https://github.com/actions/runner@v1",       │    │
  │  │      invocation: {                                              │    │
  │  │        configSource: { uri: "git+https://github.com/...",     │    │
  │  │          digest: { sha1: "def456..." },                        │    │
  │  │          entryPoint: ".github/workflows/build.yml" }           │    │
  │  │      },                                                         │    │
  │  │      materials: [{ uri: "git+https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj",│    │
  │  │        digest: { sha1: "def456..." } }]                         │    │
  │  │    }                                                            │    │
  │  │  }                                                              │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  🔑 ATTESTATIONS PROVE:                                               │
  │  • WHO built it (builder identity)                                    │
  │  • HOW it was built (build type, entry point)                        │
  │  • FROM WHAT source (git repo + commit SHA)                          │
  │  • WITH WHAT materials (dependencies, base images)                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

26.2 Cosign — Signing and Verifying Container Images

Cosign is the flagship signing tool of the Sigstore project (CNCF-backed, open-source). It signs container images by creating digital signatures and storing them directly in the OCI registry alongside the image — no separate signature server needed. Cosign supports both key-based signing (traditional public/private key pairs) and keyless signing (OIDC identity + Rekor transparency log). It works with any OCI-compliant registry: Docker Hub, AWS ECR, GCP Artifact Registry, Azure ACR, Harbor, and more.

Cosign Key-Based Workflow — Generate, Sign, Verify

Bash — Complete cosign key-based workflow with password protection 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 1: Generate a password-protected key pair
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign generate-key-pair
# Prompts for a password — ALWAYS use one in production!
# Creates:
#   cosign.key   ← PRIVATE KEY (encrypted with password)
#   cosign.pub   ← PUBLIC KEY (give to Kyverno)

# To use the password in CI/CD non-interactively:
export COSIGN_PASSWORD="${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY_PASSWORD }}"

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 2: Sign the image
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
# What happens internally:
#   1. Resolves tag → digest (sha256:abc123...)
#   2. SHA256(manifest) → hash
#   3. ECDSA-Sign(private_key, hash) → signature
#   4. Pushes .sig as OCI artifact to registry

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 3: Verify the signature
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
# ✅ VALID: shows signature details + claims
# ❌ INVALID: "Error: no matching signatures found" (exit code 1)

Cosign Key Rotation Strategy — Signing with Old + New Keys During Transition

Bash — Key rotation: sign with both keys during transition period 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# KEY ROTATION STRATEGY (3-phase)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# PHASE 1: Generate new key pair (new key NOT yet trusted by Kyverno)
cosign generate-key-pair
# → cosign-v2.key, cosign-v2.pub

# PHASE 2: TRANSITION — Sign with BOTH old and new keys
cosign sign --key cosign-v1.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.1
cosign sign --key cosign-v2.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.1
# Image now has TWO valid signatures (old key + new key)

# PHASE 3: Update Kyverno to trust BOTH keys, then remove old key
# After all running pods use images signed with new key:
cosign sign --key cosign-v2.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.2
# (No longer sign with old key)
# → Remove old public key from Kyverno ClusterPolicy
# → Securely delete cosign-v1.key

Cosign in CI/CD — GitHub Actions Integration

YAML — GitHub Actions: Build → Scan → Push → Sign anihpj image 
name: Build and Sign anihpj
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-sign:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Build image
      run: docker build -t registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }} .
    - name: Trivy scan
      uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
      with:
        image-ref: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
        exit-code: 1
        severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    - name: Push to registry
      run: docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
    - name: Install Cosign
      uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
    - name: Sign image (key-based)
      run: |
        cosign sign --yes --key env://COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY \
          registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
      env:
        COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        COSIGN_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY_PASSWORD }}

Multi-Signer Workflows — Release Manager + CI/CD Co-Signing

Bash — Multiple signers: CI/CD key + release manager key 
# CI/CD pipeline signs the image with the CI key:
cosign sign --key ci-cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# Release manager manually verifies and co-signs with release key:
cosign verify --key ci-cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
cosign sign --key release-cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# Image now has TWO signatures: CI key + release key
# Kyverno policy requires BOTH signatures (count: 2):
# attestors:
# - count: 2
#   entries:
#   - keys: { publicKeys: ci-cosign.pub }
#   - keys: { publicKeys: release-cosign.pub }

# Verify both signatures exist:
cosign verify --key ci-cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
cosign verify --key release-cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

How Cosign Stores Signatures — OCI Registry Internals

Cosign Signature Storage — OCI Registry Layout
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj
  ├── 📦 Manifest (tag: v2.0.0) → sha256:abc123def456...
  ├── sha256:abc123def456.sig    ← Signature (ECDSA over manifest hash)
  ├── sha256:abc123def456.att    ← Attestation (in-toto SLSA provenance)
  └── sha256:abc123def456.sbom   ← SBOM (SPDX/CycloneDX)

  🔑 Signatures reference digests (immutable), never tags (mutable).
     Multiple signers = multiple .sig objects, all for the same digest.

26.3 Kyverno verifyImages — Enforcing Signed Images in Kubernetes

Signing images is only half the battle. The cluster must verify those signatures before running pods. Kyverno's verifyImages rule type does exactly this: at admission time, Kyverno retrieves the image's signature from the registry, verifies it against the configured public key(s), and either allows or denies the pod.

Kyverno verifyImages ClusterPolicy — Full Configuration with Key Rotation

YAML — Kyverno ClusterPolicy with key rotation support 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-cosign-signature
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
  - name: check-cosign-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources: { kinds: [Pod] }
    exclude:
      any:
      - resources: { namespaces: [kube-system, kyverno] }

    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences:
      - "registry.anihpj.com/*"

      # ── Require at least 1 valid signature ──
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              MFkwEwYHKoZIzj0CAQYIKoZIzj0DAQcDQgAE...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
        # ── Key rotation: also accept OLD key during transition ──
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              (previous key — remove after rotation complete)
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

Verification Flow — What Kyverno Does When a Pod Is Created

Kyverno verifyImages Flow
  kubectl apply → API Server → Kyverno Webhook
  │
  ├─ STEP 1: Resolve tag → digest (sha256:abc123...)
  ├─ STEP 2: GET registry/.../sha256-abc123.sig
  │   ├── 404 → ❌ DENY: "image is not signed"
  │   └── 200 → Continue
  ├─ STEP 3: cosign verify --key anihpj.pub
  │   ├── VALID ✅ → Pod allowed
  │   └── INVALID ❌ → 403: "signature validation failed"
  └─ STEP 4: (Optional) Check attestation predicates match policy

Troubleshooting Kyverno verifyImages Failures

Error MessageLikely CauseFix
image is not signed.sig artifact not found in registryRun cosign sign in CI/CD after docker push. Check registry permissions.
signature validation failedPublic key in Kyverno doesn't match private key used to signVerify cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image> locally. Check key mismatch.
no matching signaturesImage was signed with a different key or the signature expiredCheck which key signed the image: cosign verify --key <each-key>
certificate expiredKeyless certificate TTL (10 min) elapsed before verificationUse Rekor log for verification instead of time-limited certs.
registry auth failedKyverno can't pull .sig from private registryAdd imagePullSecrets or configure registry credentials in Kyverno.

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Registry Credential Theft — Stopped by Kyverno

ATTACK SCENARIO How Signing Prevents Registry Credential Compromise from Becoming a Breach
1
Credential Theft

Attacker phishes DevOps engineer, obtains ECR push credentials for registry.anihpj.com.

2
Malicious Push

Attacker builds backdoored anihpj:v2.0.1, pushes to your private registry. Has valid credentials — push succeeds.

3
Deployment Attempt

New pod references registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.1. Kubelet authenticates to ECR — pull succeeds.

🛡️
Kyverno BLOCKS

verifyImages rule fires: resolves digest → looks for .sig → NOT FOUND (attacker lacks private key). Returns DENY: "image is not signed." Pod NEVER created. Attack stopped at signature verification gate.

26.4 Keyless Signing with Sigstore — The Future of Image Signing

Traditional key-based signing has a fundamental problem: private key management. You must generate, store, rotate, and protect the private key. Keyless signing (Sigstore's Fulcio + Rekor) eliminates long-lived private keys. The signer proves identity using OIDC, Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate, and Rekor records the event in an immutable transparency log.

Keyless Signing Architecture — Fulcio + Rekor + OIDC

Keyless Signing — Ephemeral Keys + OIDC Identity + Transparency Log
  CI/CD (GitHub Actions)
  │
  ├─ 1. OIDC Token: "I am repo anihsj/anihpj on main branch"
  │     ↓
  ├─ 2. Fulcio CA: Verifies OIDC token → Issues 10-min X.509 cert
  │     Cert binds: identity → ephemeral public key
  │     ↓
  ├─ 3. Cosign signs image with ephemeral private key
  │     ↓
  ├─ 4. Certificate + signature → Rekor Transparency Log
  │     Immutable, public, auditable record
  │     ↓
  └─ 5. Signature (with Rekor reference) → OCI Registry

  🔑 KEYLESS = No long-lived secrets. Identity proven per-signature via OIDC.
     Compromise of CI/CD runner doesn't expose any persistent signing key.

Rekor Transparency Log — Querying and Auditing

Bash — Querying Rekor for signature transparency records 
# ── Search Rekor for entries related to an image ──
rekor-cli search --artifact registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# ── Get details of a specific Rekor entry ──
rekor-cli get --uuid <entry-uuid>

# ── Verify the Rekor inclusion proof ──
cosign verify --key cosign.pub \
  --rekor-url https://rekor.sigstore.dev \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# ── Verify with identity + OIDC issuer (keyless) ──
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj/.github/workflows/build.yml@refs/heads/main \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

Key-Based vs Keyless — Decision Framework

FeatureKey-Based (cosign.key)Keyless (OIDC + Fulcio + Rekor)
Key management🔴 Generate, store, rotate, revoke🟢 No long-lived key to manage
Key compromise🔴 Catastrophic — attacker signs anything🟢 Minimal — no persistent key to steal
Identity binding"Whoever has the key"OIDC identity: repo + branch + workflow
Transparency❌ None by default✅ Rekor — immutable, public, auditable
Offline/air-gapped✅ Works offline🔴 Requires internet (Fulcio + Rekor)
CKS Exam✅ Primary — cosign sign --key⚠️ Know concept + --keyless flag
Best forAir-gapped, simple, CKS examProduction CI/CD, zero-trust, compliance

🔐

Registry credentials ≠ trust. ECDSA signatures over immutable digests. in-toto attestations prove build provenance. Without signing, stolen credentials = instant compromise.

✍️

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam expects you to understand image signing. Know: (1) cosign generate-key-pair creates the key pair, cosign sign --key cosign.key <image> signs, cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image> verifies. (2) Kyverno verifyImages enforces at admission — know the YAML structure with attestors.entries.keys.publicKeys. (3) Key rotation: sign with both old + new keys during transition, update Kyverno to accept both. (4) Keyless: cosign sign <image> (no --key), identity verification via --certificate-identity and --certificate-oidc-issuer. (5) Signatures reference immutable digests, never mutable tags. Even if an attacker overwrites a tag, the signature is bound to the original digest and will fail verification.

SBOM in Practice — The Log4Shell Wake-Up Call

REAL-WORLD EVENTDec 2021 — Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0)
1
CVE Published

Remote code execution in Log4j 2.x via JNDI lookups. CVSS 10.0 — maximum severity.

2
Without SBOM

WEEKS of manual auditing. Engineers grep Dockerfiles, Maven POMs, JAR files.

3
With SBOM — 30 Seconds

SBOM generated in CI/CD. When Log4Shell hits: grype sbom:image.sbom.json → results in 30 seconds: "anihpj:v2 — NOT affected."

4
The Lesson

SBOMs transform vulnerability response from weeks to seconds. US Executive Order 14028 now requires SBOMs for federal software.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ✍️ Image Signing 📦 Supply Chain

Complete Supply Chain Attack — SolarWinds-Style Scenario

ATTACK SCENARIOHow an Attacker Infiltrates the Build Pipeline Without Detection
1
Source Compromise

Attacker gains access to the anihpj GitHub repository via a compromised developer SSH key. They modify settings.py to add a secret backdoor that exfiltrates all Django SECRET_KEY values to a C2 server.

2
Build Poisoning

The compromised code passes CI checks (Trivy scan, kube-linter pass). Docker build succeeds. Without signing: the poisoned image is pushed to the registry. With signing: the CI pipeline signs the image with cosign, but the SIGNATURE IS VALID because the build happened legitimately — the source was compromised, not the build.

3
Where Signing Helps (and Doesn't)

Signing proves the image was BUILT by your CI pipeline — it does NOT prove the source code is clean. This is why SLSA Level 3 requires two-person review — someone must review the code before it's built. With SLSA L2+L3: (a) Provenance is signed → proves the build happened, (b) Two-person review required → prevents tampered code from being built, (c) SBOM attached → rapid CVE response when vulnerabilities are found in dependencies.

4
The Multi-Layer Defense

① Code review (SLSA L3) catches malicious PR. ② If missed: cosign signature proves the build pipeline produced this image (not an attacker pushing directly). ③ If deployed: Kyverno verifyImages confirms the pod is running the signed image. ④ If exploited: SBOM enables rapid identification of affected images. ⑤ Falco detects the exfiltration at runtime. Five layers — the attacker must defeat ALL of them.

Cosign Internals — How Signing Works Under the Hood

Cosign Architecture — Key-Based and Keyless Signing
  KEY-BASED SIGNING (traditional):
  ─────────────────────────────
  1. cosign generate-key-pair → cosign.key (private) + cosign.pub (public)
  2. cosign sign --key cosign.key IMAGE@sha256:abc...
     → Computes SHA-256 hash of image manifest
     → Signs hash with private key → creates .sig payload
     → Pushes .sig to registry as a separate OCI artifact
     → Tag: sha256-abc123.sig (stored alongside the image)
  3. cosign verify --key cosign.pub IMAGE@sha256:abc...
     → Downloads .sig from registry
     → Verifies signature against public key
     → Confirms: "This digest was signed by the holder of cosign.key"

  KEYLESS SIGNING (Sigstore):
  ──────────────────────────
  1. OIDC token from CI (proves: "I am repo X on branch Y")
  2. Fulcio CA issues short-lived cert (10 min) binding identity to public key
  3. Ephemeral private key signs the image digest
  4. Certificate + signature uploaded to Rekor transparency log
  5. cosign verify checks: identity matches, cert from Fulcio, entry in Rekor

  🔑 CKS EXAM: Know both methods. Key-based is simpler for the exam
     (generate key → sign → verify). Keyless is production best practice
     but requires OIDC infrastructure (GitHub Actions, GCP SA, etc.).
🔧 Under the Hood — Sigstore Architecture: How Keyless Signing Works — OIDC → Fulcio → Ephemeral Key → Rekor → Certificate Chain 
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   SIGSTORE KEYLESS SIGNING FLOW                                       │
  │                                                                      │
  │   1. GitHub Actions provides OIDC token to cosign                    │
  │      {"sub": "repo:Anihs-Canvas/DEV-DOCs:ref:refs/heads/main"}     │
  │                                                                      │
  │   2. cosign generates EPHEMERAL key pair (exists only for signing)   │
  │                                                                      │
  │   3. cosign sends OIDC token to Fulcio CA                             │
  │      Fulcio validates token → issues short-lived certificate (10min) │
  │      Certificate binds: OIDC identity → ephemeral public key         │
  │                                                                      │
  │   4. cosign signs image digest with ephemeral PRIVATE key            │
  │                                                                      │
  │   5. Certificate + signature uploaded to Rekor transparency log      │
  │      Rekor returns: entry UUID, log index, integrated time           │
  │                                                                      │
  │   6. VERIFICATION: cosign verify checks:                              │
  │      (a) Signature matches image digest using cert public key        │
  │      (b) Certificate chains to Fulcio root                            │
  │      (c) Certificate identity matches expected OIDC subject          │
  │      (d) Entry exists in Rekor transparency log                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 26 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Generate a cosign key pair and sign an image. Write the exact commands.
Show Answer
Answer
cosign generate-key-pair  # Creates cosign.key + cosign.pub
cosign sign --key cosign.key ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
cosign verify --key cosign.pub ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
# Must use DIGEST (@sha256:...), NOT tag (:latest)
Q2
What is the difference between key-based and keyless cosign signing?
Show Answer
Answer

Key-based: You generate a long-lived key pair, store cosign.key securely, and distribute cosign.pub for verification. Simpler, works anywhere. Keyless: Uses OIDC token (from GitHub, GCP, etc.) + Fulcio CA for short-lived certificates. No key management. Requires OIDC provider. Cert appears in Rekor transparency log. Keyless is recommended for CI/CD pipelines.

Q3
What is the Rekor transparency log and why does cosign use it? How does it prevent supply chain attacks?
Show Answer
Answer

Rekor is an immutable, append-only transparency log that records every signing event. When you sign with cosign, the signature is recorded in Rekor. This provides: (1) Non-repudiation: an attacker who compromises your signing key can't remove old signatures from Rekor. (2) Auditability: you can verify when and by whom every image was signed. (3) Tamper detection: if a signature appears that's NOT in Rekor, it's suspicious. Rekor prevents the "stolen key" scenario where an attacker signs malicious images and you can't prove which signatures are legitimate.

Explanation

Rekor is the "trust but verify" layer of sigstore. Even if your signing key is compromised, the attacker's signatures MUST appear in Rekor (if verification checks Rekor). This creates an audit trail you can use to identify the exact point of compromise. On the CKS exam, keyless signing automatically records in Rekor; key-based signing requires --rekor-url flag.

Q4
You sign anihpj:v2.1 with cosign. Later, a new image is pushed with the same tag. Can the attacker's image be verified with your signature?
Show Answer
Answer

No. cosign signs the DIGEST of the image content, not the tag. If you signed anihpj@sha256:abc... and the tag :v2.1 now points to sha256:xyz..., your signature only verifies against sha256:abc.... The new image at sha256:xyz... has NO valid signature. However, if you signed using the TAG (cosign sign anihpj:v2.1), the signature follows the content (cosign resolves the tag to a digest at signing time). The signature is ALWAYS tied to a digest, never a tag. This is why you should always reference images by digest in production.

Explanation

The key insight: cosign signatures are cryptographically bound to image DIGESTS. Tags are just pointers. If you deploy using tags, you might accidentally deploy an unsigned image even though "the tag was signed previously." On the CKS exam, always use digests for deployment: image: ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc....

Q5
How do you verify a cosign signature in a Kubernetes admission controller? What component checks the signature before allowing the pod to deploy?
Show Answer
Answer

Use the Sigstore Policy Controller (or a custom ValidatingWebhook) that calls cosign verify. The controller intercepts pod creation, extracts the image reference, and runs cosign verify against it. If verification fails, the pod is rejected. Alternative: use Kyverno's verifyImages rule or Connaisseur. The key configuration is the public key (or Fulcio CA) that the controller trusts for verification.

Explanation

Signing without enforcement is useless. The CKS supply chain domain expects you to close the loop: (1) sign images at build time (cosign), (2) verify signatures at deploy time (admission controller), (3) reject unsigned images. On the exam, you may be asked to configure the admission controller to enforce signature verification.

Q6
What is Sigstore's Fulcio CA, and how does keyless signing work without you ever creating a private key?
Show Answer
Answer

Fulcio is a certificate authority that issues short-lived (10 minutes) code-signing certificates based on OIDC identity. Flow: (1) CI pipeline authenticates to OIDC provider (GitHub Actions → token). (2) OIDC token sent to Fulcio. (3) Fulcio validates the token and issues an ephemeral X.509 certificate with the OIDC identity embedded. (4) cosign uses this certificate to sign the image. (5) The certificate expires in 10 minutes — no long-lived private key exists. Verification uses Fulcio's root CA + the OIDC identity claim.

Explanation

Keyless signing eliminates the #1 problem of code signing: key management. No private keys to protect, rotate, or lose. The "key" is your OIDC identity, which is tied to your CI platform's authentication. On the CKS exam, understand that keyless = no key management + identity-based verification.

Q7
Write the cosign command to verify a keyless-signed image from GitHub Actions, checking that the identity is https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main.
Show Answer
Answer
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity="https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...

This verifies: (a) the signature is valid (cryptographic check), (b) the certificate was issued to the expected GitHub Actions workflow, (c) the OIDC issuer is GitHub (not a fake IdP). This ensures the image was built by YOUR pipeline, not impersonated.

Explanation

Identity-based verification is the keyless verification pattern. Instead of checking "is this signed with the right key?" (key-based), you check "was this signed by the right CI workflow?" (identity-based). On the CKS exam, you may need to construct this verification command with the correct identity and issuer.

Q8
What is an attestation in cosign/sigstore? How do you sign an SBOM attestation for an image?
Show Answer
Answer

An attestation is a signed statement ABOUT an image (metadata, not the image itself). Common attestations: SBOM (software bill of materials), SLSA provenance (how the image was built), vulnerability scan results. Sign an SBOM attestation:

# Generate and sign an SBOM attestation
cosign attest --predicate sbom.spdx.json --type spdx \
  ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
# Verify the attestation
cosign verify-attestation --type spdx \
  --certificate-identity=... ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
Explanation

Attestations extend signing beyond "is this our image?" to "what's in this image and how was it built?" SBOM attestations prove you know exactly what's in your image. SLSA provenance attestations prove the image was built through your CI pipeline (not a developer's laptop). On the CKS exam, attestations are tested in the supply chain security domain.

Q9
You're deploying to production and the admission controller rejects your image because "cosign verification failed." What are the 3 most likely causes and how do you check each?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Wrong digest: You specified the tag in the pod spec, the admission controller resolved it, but the tag now points to a different (unsigned) digest. Check: cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image>@sha256:<latest-digest>. (2) Wrong key: The admission controller has an outdated public key — the image was signed with a rotated key. Check: cosign verify --key <correct-key>.pub <image>. (3) Image not signed: The CI pipeline built and pushed the image but the signing step failed silently. Check: cosign triangulate <image> --type=signature to see if any signatures exist.

Explanation

This is a real debugging scenario. On the CKS exam: (1) always check the digest first — tag-based deployment is the most common cause, (2) check key rotation — if you rotate keys, update the admission controller, (3) verify the signing step actually succeeded — CI pipelines can fail silently.

Q10
Write a complete CI pipeline step (GitHub Actions) that builds a Docker image, pushes it, generates an SBOM, and signs BOTH the image and the SBOM attestation with keyless signing.
Show Answer
Answer
- name: Build and Sign
  run: |
    IMAGE=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
    # Build and push
    docker build -t $IMAGE .
    docker push $IMAGE
    DIGEST=$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' $IMAGE)
    # Generate SBOM
    syft $IMAGE -o spdx-json > sbom.json
    # Sign image (keyless via GitHub OIDC)
    cosign sign --yes $DIGEST
    # Attest SBOM
    cosign attest --predicate sbom.json --type spdx $DIGEST
  env:
    COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL: "1"  # Enable keyless signing
Explanation

This is the complete supply chain security pipeline for CKS. Key points: (1) ${{ github.sha }} ensures each commit gets a unique tag, (2) --yes skips the interactive prompt, (3) COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 enables keyless signing before it's GA, (4) the DIGEST (not tag) is signed. On the exam, recognize each step and its security purpose.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Generate key pair and sign (EXAM PATTERN)
cosign generate-key-pair
cosign sign --key cosign.key ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
cosign verify --key cosign.pub ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...

# 2. Keyless signing with GitHub Actions OIDC
cosign sign ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...  # Auto-detects OIDC env

# 3. Verify with identity (keyless)
cosign verify --certificate-identity=anihpj@anihpj.com --certificate-oidc-issuer=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...

# 4. Check Rekor transparency log
cosign verify --key cosign.pub --rekor-url=https://rekor.sigstore.dev ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
rekor-cli get --uuid <entry-uuid>  # Inspect the log entry
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 26 Traps
  • DIGEST, not tag: cosign sign ghcr.io/anihpj/api:latest signs the tag, not the digest. If :latest changes, the signature becomes invalid. Always sign the digest: cosign sign ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc....
  • cosign.key is your private key: If you lose it, you can't sign new images. If an attacker steals it, they can sign malicious images in your name. Protect it like a root CA key — use a KMS or Vault for production.
  • OIDC token expiry: Keyless signing uses short-lived OIDC tokens. If your CI job takes too long, the token may expire before signing completes. The signature appears valid but verification fails with "token expired."

Chapter 27: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and SLSA

You scan your images with Trivy (Ch23), analyze your YAML with kube-linter (Ch25), and sign every image with Cosign (Ch26). But when Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0) was discovered in December 2021, organizations worldwide spent weeks manually auditing their software to answer one question: "Are we affected?" An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — a complete, machine-readable inventory of every component in your software — answers that question in seconds. And SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts) provides a framework to verify that your build pipeline hasn't been tampered with. Together, SBOM and SLSA close the final supply chain gaps: knowing what's in your software and proving how it was built.

🟢 Beginner-Friendly ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📋 SBOM & SLSA 📦 Supply Chain

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ SBOM fundamentals: What an SBOM is, why it's critical for vulnerability response, and how the US Executive Order made SBOMs mandatory for federal software
  • ✅ Generating SBOMs: Using Syft, Trivy, and Docker to generate SPDX and CycloneDX SBOMs — and attaching them to images with Cosign
  • ✅ SLSA framework: The 4 levels of supply chain integrity (0-3), from basic provenance to hermetic, isolated builds — and how to implement SLSA Level 2 for anihpj
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

27.1 What Is an SBOM and Why Does It Matter?

An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is a complete, structured list of every component, library, and dependency in a software artifact — think of it as a nutrition label for software. For a container image like anihpj:v2, the SBOM lists every OS package (curl, libssl, glibc), every Python package (Django, gunicorn, psycopg2), and every transitive dependency — each with its exact version. When a critical CVE like Log4Shell drops, you query your SBOM database instead of manually auditing hundreds of images. SBOM → query → "anihpj:v2 does not use Log4j. Next." — in seconds, not weeks.

The Log4Shell Incident — Why SBOMs Became Mandatory

Log4Shell Response — Without SBOM vs With SBOM
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    DECEMBER 10, 2021 — LOG4SHELL DROPS                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  WITHOUT SBOM (what actually happened):                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                                    │
  │  • CVE-2021-44228 published — CVSS 10.0, remote code execution           │
  │  • Security teams: "Are we affected?"                                     │
  │  • Manual audit begins: check every Java app, every container image      │
  │  • Weeks of work across hundreds of teams                                │
  │  • Many organizations didn't know they were affected for MONTHS          │
  │  • US government: "This cannot happen again"                              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  WITH SBOM (what should happen):                                          │
  │  ──────────────────────────────                                           │
  │  • CVE-2021-44228 published                                               │
  │  • Security team: grep SBOMs for "log4j"                                 │
  │  • Query returns: "anihpj:v2 — log4j NOT FOUND"                          │
  │  • Query returns: "legacy-app:v1 — log4j-core 2.14.1 — AFFECTED!"      │
  │  • Response time: SECONDS, not weeks                                     │
  │  • Targeted fix: update ONLY the affected images                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 SBOMs turn vulnerability response from a MANUAL AUDIT into           │
  │     a DATABASE QUERY. This is why the US Executive Order 14028           │
  │     (May 2021) requires SBOMs for all federal software.                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SBOM Formats — SPDX vs CycloneDX

FeatureSPDXCycloneDX
Full nameSoftware Package Data ExchangeCycloneDX (OWASP project)
Standard bodyLinux Foundation (ISO/IEC 5962:2021)OWASP Foundation
FormatsJSON, YAML, RDF, tag-valueJSON, XML
FocusLicense compliance + securitySecurity + vulnerability management
K8s ecosystem✅ Syft default, Kubernetes SIG✅ Trivy, Dependency-Track
VEX support✅ Native VEX integration✅ VEX extension
CKS exam✅ Know it exists, syft -o spdx-json⚠️ Know it as an alternative format

What's Inside an anihpj SBOM — Real Example

JSON — Excerpt from anihpj:v2 SBOM (SPDX format, generated by Syft) 
{
  "spdxVersion": "SPDX-2.3",
  "name": "registry.anihpj.com/anihpj",
  "packages": [
    {
      "name": "Django",
      "versionInfo": "5.0.6",
      "supplier": "Organization: Django Software Foundation",
      "licenseConcluded": "BSD-3-Clause",
      "externalRefs": [
        {"referenceCategory": "SECURITY",
         "referenceType": "cpe23Type",
         "referenceLocator": "cpe:2.3:a:djangoproject:django:5.0.6"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "libssl1.1",
      "versionInfo": "1.1.1n-0+deb11u4",
      "supplier": "Organization: Debian",
      "externalRefs": [
        {"referenceCategory": "SECURITY",
         "referenceType": "cpe23Type",
         "referenceLocator": "cpe:2.3:a:openssl:openssl:1.1.1n"}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "relationships": [
    {"spdxElementId": "anihpj-image",
     "relatedSpdxElement": "Django-5.0.6",
     "relationshipType": "CONTAINS"}
  ]
}

VEX — Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange

An SBOM tells you what packages are in your software. A VEX document tells you whether a CVE in those packages is actually exploitable in YOUR specific context. For example: your anihpj image contains libssl1.1 which has CVE-2023-44487 (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DoS, CVSS 7.5). But your Django app runs behind an ALB that TERMINATES HTTP/2 — the vulnerable code path is never reached. A VEX document says: "CVE-2023-44487 in anihpj:v2 → NOT AFFECTED (HTTP/2 terminated at ALB)." This prevents false-positive driven fire drills.

SBOM + VEX = Complete Vulnerability Intelligence
  SBOM: "anihpj:v2 contains libssl1.1 1.1.1n — has CVE-2023-44487 (CVSS 7.5)"
     │  ← This alone triggers PANIC: "We have a HIGH CVE!"
     │
     ▼
  VEX: "CVE-2023-44487 in anihpj:v2 → NOT AFFECTED"
     │  ← VEX provides CONTEXT:
     │     • HTTP/2 is terminated at the ALB, not at the container
     │     • The vulnerable code path is never executed
     │     • No action needed — this is a FALSE POSITIVE in our context
     │
     ▼
  RESULT: Security team does NOT get paged. No emergency rebuild.
          VEX saved hours of investigation for a non-exploitable CVE.

  🔑 SBOM = "what's in the box" | VEX = "can it hurt us?"
     Together: actionable vulnerability intelligence, not just noise.

27.2 Generating SBOMs for anihpj Images

Three primary tools generate SBOMs for container images: Syft (by Anchore, most popular), Trivy (by Aqua, already used for CVE scanning), and Docker SBOM (built into Docker CLI). All three produce SPDX or CycloneDX output. Once generated, SBOMs should be attached to the image using Cosign and stored in the registry alongside the signature.

SBOM Generation Tools — Syft, Trivy, Docker

Bash — Generate SBOMs with Syft, Trivy, and Docker 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# SYFT (Anchore) — Most feature-rich, recommended
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Install: curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin

# Generate SPDX JSON SBOM
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o spdx-json > anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json

# Generate CycloneDX JSON SBOM
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o cyclonedx-json > anihpj-v2.sbom.cdx.json

# Generate table output (human-readable)
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o table

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# TRIVY — Already in your pipeline for CVE scanning
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Generate CycloneDX SBOM
trivy image --format cyclonedx --output anihpj-v2.cdx.json registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2

# Generate SPDX SBOM
trivy image --format spdx-json --output anihpj-v2.spdx.json registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DOCKER — Built-in, no extra tools needed
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
docker sbom registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
docker sbom --format spdx-json registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 > anihpj-v2.spdx.json

Attaching SBOMs to Images with Cosign

Bash — Generate SBOM and attach to image in CI/CD pipeline 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Complete CI/CD step: Build → SBOM → Sign → Attach
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

IMAGE=registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

# 1. Build and push
docker build -t $IMAGE .
docker push $IMAGE

# 2. Generate SBOM with Syft
syft $IMAGE -o spdx-json > anihpj.sbom.spdx.json

# 3. Sign the image (Ch26)
cosign sign --key cosign.key $IMAGE

# 4. Attach SBOM to the image
cosign attach sbom --sbom anihpj.sbom.spdx.json $IMAGE

# 5. Verify SBOM is attached
cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub --type spdxjson $IMAGE
# Output: verified + shows SBOM metadata

# 6. Download SBOM from registry (for CVE impact analysis)
cosign download sbom $IMAGE > anihpj-downloaded.sbom.spdx.json

SBOM → CVE Impact Analysis — The Real Value

SBOM-Powered Vulnerability Response — From CVE to Fix in Minutes
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    SBOM-DRIVEN VULNERABILITY RESPONSE                      │
  │                                                                           │
  │  1. NEW CVE PUBLISHED: CVE-2024-xxxx in libssl1.1 (CVSS 9.8)            │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  2. QUERY SBOM REPOSITORY:                                                │
  │     $ grype db search CVE-2024-xxxx                                       │
  │     $ jq '.packages[] | select(.name=="libssl1.1")' anihpj-*.sbom.json   │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ├── "anihpj:v2" → libssl1.1 1.1.1n → AFFECTED 🔴                  │
  │       ├── "anihpj:v3" → libssl1.1 1.1.1w → NOT AFFECTED 🟢              │
  │       └── "sidecar:v1" → no libssl → NOT AFFECTED 🟢                     │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  3. TARGETED RESPONSE:                                                    │
  │     • Only anihpj:v2 needs rebuilding                                     │
  │     • anihpj:v3 and sidecar:v1 can stay as-is                             │
  │     • Fix time: rebuild one image (~10 min)                               │
  │     • WITHOUT SBOM: audit all images manually (~days)                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Grype — SBOM-Based Vulnerability Scanning

Once you have SBOMs, scan them for vulnerabilities without re-scanning the image. Grype (by Anchore, same creators as Syft) matches SBOM components against vulnerability databases:

Bash — Scan SBOM for vulnerabilities with Grype 
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json --fail-on critical
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json -o json > grype-results.json
# 🔑 Store SBOM once, scan many times. New CVE? Download SBOM → grype scan.

SBOM Tool Comparison — Syft vs Trivy vs Docker SBOM

FeatureSyft (Anchore)Trivy (Aqua)Docker SBOM
FormatsSPDX, CycloneDX, Syft JSON, tableCycloneDX, SPDX, Trivy JSONSPDX, CycloneDX
Speed🟢 Fastest (Go, optimized)🟡 Moderate (also does CVE scan)🟢 Fast (Docker-native)
Deepest coverage🟢 OS + Python + Node + Java + Go + Rust🟢 OS + Python + Node + Java + Go🟡 OS + Python + Node (limited)
Already installed?❌ Separate install needed✅ If using Trivy for CVE scanning✅ Built into Docker CLI (≥20.10)
Cosign integration✅ syft + cosign attach sbom✅ trivy + cosign attach sbom⚠️ Manual attachment needed

Best forDeepest SBOM, best Cosign integrationAlready in your pipeline for CVE scanningQuick one-off SBOM with no extra tools

SBOM Storage Strategies — Where to Keep Your SBOMs

SBOM Storage Decision — Registry vs Database vs Both
  I have SBOMs for my images — where should I store them?
  │
  ├─ OPTION 1: Attach to image in OCI registry (cosign attach sbom)
  │  ✅ SBOM travels WITH the image — always available
  │  ✅ Immutable — same digest, same SBOM
  │  ❌ Hard to query across images ("find all images with log4j")
  │  Best for: individual image verification, audit trail
  │
  ├─ OPTION 2: Store in SBOM database (Dependency-Track, OWASP)
  │  ✅ Query across ALL images — "show me every image with libssl1.1"
  │  ✅ Trend analysis — "are our SBOMs getting better or worse?"
  │  ❌ Requires additional infrastructure
  │  Best for: CVE impact analysis, compliance reporting
  │
  ├─ OPTION 3: Both (registry + database) — RECOMMENDED
  │  ✅ Attach to image for provenance (audit trail)
  │  ✅ Also upload to database for cross-image queries
  │  Best for: production environments with compliance requirements
  │
  └─ OPTION 4: Git repository (for development)
     ✅ Version-controlled, easy to diff
     ❌ Not suitable for production (SBOMs belong with images)

Grype — SBOM-Based Vulnerability Scanning

Once you have SBOMs, you can scan them for vulnerabilities without re-scanning the image. Grype (by Anchore, same creators as Syft) takes an SBOM file and matches every component against vulnerability databases. This is faster than Trivy image scanning because the SBOM has already done the package inventory work:

Bash — Scan SBOM for vulnerabilities with Grype 
# Install Grype
curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/grype/main/install.sh | sh

# Scan an SBOM file (faster than image scan)
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json

# Scan with severity filter
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json --fail-on critical

# Output as JSON for pipeline processing
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json -o json > grype-results.json

# 🔑 KEY ADVANTAGE: Store SBOM once, scan many times
#    • Generate SBOM in CI/CD → attach to image
#    • When new CVE drops: download SBOM → grype scan
#    • No need to re-pull or re-scan the full image

27.3 SLSA — Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts

SLSA (pronounced "salsa") is a security framework from Google and the OpenSSF that defines four levels of supply chain integrity. Each level builds on the previous one, providing increasing guarantees that your software hasn't been tampered with between source code and deployment. SLSA is to software supply chains what seatbelts → airbags → crumple zones are to car safety: progressive, layered protections.

The Four SLSA Levels — Progressive Supply Chain Integrity

LevelNameRequirementsWhat It Preventsanihpj Status
0 None No guarantees. Build may be entirely undocumented. Nothing. Any compromise goes undetected. Starting point 🔴
1 Provenance Exists Build process produces provenance (who, what, how, when). Provenance is NOT signed, NOT verified. Honest mistakes. Accidental misconfigurations. Syft SBOM generated 🟡
2 Hosted Build Platform Build runs on a hosted platform (GitHub Actions, GCB). Provenance is SIGNED and VERIFIABLE. Source + build are version-controlled. Tampering after the build. Unsigned provenance modifications. GitHub Actions + cosign attest ✅
3 Hardened Builds Isolated, ephemeral build environment. Builds are hermetic (no network, deterministic). Two-person review required. Compromised build platform. Insider threats. Cache poisoning. Future goal 🟡

Generating SLSA Provenance with Cosign Attest

Bash — Generate and attach SLSA provenance in CI/CD 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 1: Generate SLSA provenance predicate (JSON)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cat > slsa-provenance.json << 'EOF'
{
  "builder": {
    "id": "https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj/.github/workflows/build.yml@refs/heads/main"
  },
  "buildType": "https://github.com/actions/runner@v1",
  "invocation": {
    "configSource": {
      "uri": "git+https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj",
      "digest": {"sha1": "${{ github.sha }}"},
      "entryPoint": ".github/workflows/build.yml"
    }
  },
  "materials": [
    {
      "uri": "git+https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj",
      "digest": {"sha1": "${{ github.sha }}"}
    }
  ]
}
EOF

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 2: Sign and attach SLSA provenance as in-toto attestation
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign attest --key cosign.key \
  --predicate slsa-provenance.json \
  --type slsaprovenance \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 3: Verify SLSA attestation (in Kyverno or locally)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub \
  --type slsaprovenance \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

SLSA Threat Model — What Each Level Defends Against

SLSA Threat Model — Attack Vectors Blocked at Each Level
  LEVEL 0 — No defenses: source mods → build → deploy, all undetected
  LEVEL 1 — 🛡️ Catches honest mistakes. ❌ Provenance can be forged (unsigned).
  LEVEL 2 — 🛡️ Provenance cryptographically signed. 🛡️ Platform identity verified.
  LEVEL 3 — 🛡️ Isolated + hermetic + deterministic. Defends against insider threats.

SLSA Level 2 Practical Checklist — anihpj Implementation

RequirementImplementationStatus
Version-controlled sourceGitHub + branch protection + PR reviews✅
Hosted build platformGitHub Actions, ephemeral runners✅
Signed provenancecosign attest with SLSA predicate✅
Build as codeWorkflow YAML versioned with source✅
Ephemeral environmentFresh runner per build, no shared state✅
IsolationNo cross-build cache or volume sharing⚠️

27.5 Supply Chain CI/CD Integration — Artifact Repository Security

The CKS curriculum requires you to understand your supply chain including CI/CD and artifact repositories. An artifact repository (like Harbor, Artifactory, ECR, GAR, ACR) is the bridge between your CI pipeline and your Kubernetes cluster. Securing it is as critical as securing the cluster itself:

Artifact Repository Security — Controls at Each Stage
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CI/CD PIPELINE                     ARTIFACT REPOSITORY              │
  │  ─────────────                      ───────────────────              │
  │                                                                      │
  │  1. git push ──→ 2. Build ──→ 3. Scan ──→ 4. Sign ──→ 5. Push     │
  │                                                    │                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                │
  │  │                                                                    │
  │  ▼                                                                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  🏪 ARTIFACT REPOSITORY (Harbor / ECR / GAR / ACR)           │   │
  │  │                                                               │   │
  │  │  ✅ Image signed (cosign signature verified at push)          │   │
  │  │  ✅ SBOM attached (SPDX/CycloneDX)                            │   │
  │  │  ✅ Vulnerability scan (Trivy integrated)                     │   │
  │  │  ✅ Tag immutability (prevent :latest overwrite)             │   │
  │  │  ✅ Pull-by-digest only (sha256:abc...)                       │   │
  │  │  ✅ Retention policies (auto-delete old/unscanned images)    │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                    │
  │  6. Kubernetes pulls from repository                               │
  │     │                                                               │
  │     ├─ ImagePolicyWebhook checks: approved registry?               │
  │     ├─ OPA/Gatekeeper checks: image signed? scan passed?           │
  │     └─ Pod starts ONLY if all checks pass                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 CKS Exam: Supply Chain

Key supply chain controls: (1) Only push signed images (cosign sign in CI). (2) Repository enforces tag immutability. (3) Admission controller verifies signature before deployment. (4) SBOM generated at build, attached to image. (5) Periodic re-scanning of stored images for newly discovered CVEs.

📋
SBOM (27.1)

Nutrition label for software. Lists every OS package, language dependency, and transitive library with versions. SPDX (license-focused) and CycloneDX (security-focused) formats. Turns CVE response from days to seconds.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam expects you to understand SBOM and SLSA as the final supply chain security concepts. Know: (1) SBOM generation: syft <image> -o spdx-json or trivy image --format cyclonedx <image>. (2) Attach SBOM: cosign attach sbom --sbom <file> <image>. (3) SLSA levels: 0=none, 1=provenance, 2=hosted+signed, 3=hardened+hermetic. (4) SLSA attestation: cosign attest --key cosign.key --predicate slsa-provenance.json --type slsaprovenance <image>. (5) SBOM + SLSA together enable complete supply chain transparency: know what's in your software AND prove how it was built.

Distroless Images — The Ultimate Minimal Attack Surface

ComponentStandard python:3.12python:3.12-slimdistroless python
Image size~1 GB~120 MB~50 MB
Shell?✅ bash, sh✅ sh❌ No shell
Package manager?✅ apt (full)✅ apt (minimal)❌ None
Utilities (curl, wget)?✅ Many⚠️ Few❌ None
CVEs (typical)30-505-100-2
Attacker capability if compromisedFull shell, download tools, scriptBasic shell, limited toolsNo tools — trapped!

The tradeoff: Distroless images are harder to debug. There's no kubectl exec -- sh. You must rely on logs (stdout/stderr) and health checks. For production workloads — where security outweighs developer convenience — this tradeoff is almost always worth it. For development environments, use the slim variant for a balance of security and debugability.

SPDX vs CycloneDX Comparison — Choosing the Right SBOM Format

FeatureSPDX 2.3CycloneDX 1.6
OriginLinux Foundation (2011)OWASP (2017)
Primary focusLicense compliance + supply chainSecurity + vulnerability management

Vulnerability dataVia VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) extensionBuilt-in; can embed CVE IDs and severity directly

Automated SBOM Generation in CI/CD Pipeline

SBOM Generation Pipeline for the anihpj Django App
 1. Checkout code
 2. Build Docker image: anihpj/api:v2.1.0
 3. Generate SBOM BEFORE pushing:
    $ syft anihpj/api:v2.1.0 -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
    $ trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.cdx.json anihpj/api:v2.1.0
 4. Sign SBOM:
    $ cosign sign-blob --key cosign.key sbom.spdx.json
 5. Push image:
    $ docker push anihpj/api:v2.1.0
 6. Attach SBOM as OCI artifact:
    $ cosign attach sbom --sbom sbom.spdx.json anihpj/api:v2.1.0
 7. Sign image:
    $ cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj/api:v2.1.0
 8. Upload SBOM to Dependency-Track for continuous monitoring

 RESULT: Image is signed + SBOM-attached + monitored forever
 QUERY:  cosign download sbom anihpj/api:v2.1.0 | jq .
💡 SBOM Anti-Patterns to Avoid

DO NOT: Generate SBOM AFTER pushing the image to a public registry — that's too late. DO NOT: Store SBOM in the same repo as the source code without signing it — the SBOM itself can be tampered with. DO NOT: Use a single SBOM for all environments — dev dependencies differ from production. DO INSTEAD: Generate SBOM in CI, sign it with cosign, attach it to the image, and upload it to a central SBOM registry (Dependency-Track, Anchore, or graph-db). The SBOM is only valuable if it's (a) accurate, (b) signed, and (c) discoverable.

🔧 Under the Hood — SBOM Generation Internals: How Syft Reads Filesystem Layers and SPDX/CycloneDX Formats Differ 
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   SBOM GENERATION — Syft Internals                                    │
  │                                                                      │
  │   1. Syft pulls image layers from OCI registry                       │
  │   2. For each layer, Syft reads the FILESYSTEM TREE                 │
  │   3. Each file checked against CATALOGERS:                            │
  │      deb cataloger:  /var/lib/dpkg/status → .deb packages           │
  │      rpm cataloger:  /var/lib/rpm/Packages → .rpm packages          │
  │      apk cataloger:  /lib/apk/db/installed → Alpine packages        │
  │      go cataloger:   go.sum, go.mod → Go module dependencies        │
  │      python cataloger: requirements.txt, setup.py → pip packages    │
  │      java cataloger: pom.xml, build.gradle → Maven/Gradle deps     │
  │   4. Detected packages assembled into SBOM in chosen format:         │
  │      SPDX: JSON/YAML/tag-value. Package-version-checksum-triples    │
  │      CycloneDX: JSON/XML. Bom + components + dependencies graph     │
  │   5. SBOM attached to image or exported to file                      │
  │                                                                      │
  │   CKS EXAM NOTE: For the exam, know syft + trivy SBOM commands.      │
  │   syft scan → output SPDX/CycloneDX → attach with cosign.            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 27 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Generate an SBOM for a container image using syft. Write the exact command.
Show Answer
Answer
syft ghcr.io/anihpj/api:latest -o spdx-json
syft ghcr.io/anihpj/api:latest -o cyclonedx-json
syft ghcr.io/anihpj/api:latest --output sbom.spdx.json
# Common options: -o (format), --catalogers (which scanners to use)
Q2
What is SLSA Level 3? What additional guarantee does it provide over Level 2?
Show Answer
Answer

SLSA Level 3 — Auditable: Build is fully auditable — the build platform cryptographically attests to the recipe, source, and output artifact. Key difference from Level 2: Level 2 provides signed provenance but relies on the build platform being trusted. Level 3 adds hermetic builds (no network access during build) and isolated builds (each build in its own environment). This means even if the build platform is compromised, the provenance log will show tampering. Level 3 requires hardened build platforms like Tekton chains with TPM attestation.

Q3
What is an SBOM and why is it critical for supply chain security? What information does it contain?
Show Answer
Answer

An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is a machine-readable inventory of every component in a software artifact. It contains: package names, versions, licenses, dependencies, checksums, and supplier information. Critical because: (1) when a CVE is published, you can immediately query SBOMs to find affected images, (2) you can verify images contain only expected components, (3) license compliance auditing becomes automated. Without SBOMs, you have no idea what's in your containers.

Explanation

SBOMs are the foundation of supply chain security. The CKS exam tests SBOM generation (syft), signing (cosign attest), and consumption (Trivy scanning). The key scenario: CVE announced → query SBOMs → find affected images → remediate in hours instead of weeks.

Q4
What are the four SLSA levels? For each level, what guarantee does the consumer receive?
Show Answer
Answer

L1 Documented: Provenance exists but not verified. L2 Authenticated: Provenance is SIGNED by a trusted build service. L3 Auditable: Hermetic + isolated build — even if platform is compromised, tampering is detectable. L4 Unforgeable: Full auditability, two-person review, reproducible builds. Most organizations target L2-L3.

Explanation

SLSA levels are the maturity model for supply chain security. L1 is documentation only (no security), L2 adds cryptographic signing, L3 adds build environment hardening, L4 is the gold standard. On the CKS exam, know each level's consumer guarantee.

Q5
How do you attach an SBOM to a container image and retrieve it later? Write both commands.
Show Answer
Answer
cosign attach sbom --sbom sbom.spdx.json ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
cosign download sbom ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123... > retrieved-sbom.json
cosign attest --predicate sbom.spdx.json --type spdx ghcr.io/anihpj/api@sha256:abc123...
Explanation

SBOMs can be stored as OCI artifacts (attach) or signed attestations (attest). Attesting is preferred because it cryptographically binds the SBOM to the image and records it in Rekor.

Q6
You discover an image contains log4j-core:2.14.0 vulnerable to Log4Shell. Using SBOM, how do you find ALL images with this vulnerable version?
Show Answer
Answer
for image in $(list-all-images); do
  cosign download sbom $image 2>/dev/null | \
    jq -e '.packages[] | select(.name=="log4j-core" and (.versionInfo | startswith("2.14")))' && \
    echo "VULNERABLE: $image"
done

Without SBOMs, you'd rescan every image (hours/days). With SBOMs, you grep through inventory (seconds).

Explanation

This is the SBOM value proposition — turning vulnerability response from "scan everything" to "query your inventory." On the CKS exam, this scenario demonstrates why SBOMs are critical infrastructure.

Q7
What makes a build "hermetic" and "isolated" for SLSA Level 3? What build platform supports this?
Show Answer
Answer

Hermetic: All inputs declared and versioned. No network access during build. Same inputs = same output. Isolated: Each build in its own ephemeral environment. No shared state. Previous builds cannot contaminate current builds. Platform: Tekton Pipelines with Tekton Chains, GitHub Actions with SLSA Generator, or Google Cloud Build. Tekton Chains provides SLSA L2 out of box and L3 with hermetic configuration.

Explanation

Hermetic + isolated = the build is self-contained and tamper-evident. L3 is the threshold where you transition from "trust the platform" to "verify the platform." On the CKS exam, Tekton Chains is the Kubernetes-native SLSA implementation.

Q8
Compare SPDX and CycloneDX SBOM formats. Which does syft support?
Show Answer
Answer

syft supports BOTH. SPDX (Linux Foundation): ISO standard (ISO/IEC 5962:2021). Richer metadata for license compliance. CycloneDX (OWASP): Focused on security use cases. More widely adopted in commercial tools. For CKS: use whichever is specified. If unspecified, SPDX-JSON is a safe default.

Explanation

Both serve the same purpose. SPDX is stronger for license compliance; CycloneDX for vulnerability management. Know syft -o spdx-json and syft -o cyclonedx-json.

Q9
What is Tekton Chains and how does it implement SLSA for Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Tekton Chains watches Tekton PipelineRuns and automatically: (1) generates in-toto provenance (build recipe, source, builder identity), (2) signs the provenance with cosign, (3) stores the signature as an OCI artifact. Provides SLSA L2 out of box, L3 with hermetic builds. Chains automates supply chain attestation — no manual cosign steps needed after each build.

Explanation

Tekton Chains is the Kubernetes-native bridge between CI/CD and supply chain security. On the CKS exam, if asked about "automated SLSA in Kubernetes," the answer is Tekton Chains.

Q10
A new zero-day is announced. You have SBOMs for 200 images. Walk through your triage process: find affected images, prioritize, remediate, and verify.
Show Answer
Answer
1
Query SBOMs

Grep all SBOMs for the vulnerable package. Seconds, not hours.

2
Prioritize

Production → staging → dev. Internet-facing before internal.

3
Patch and rebuild

Update package, rebuild, scan with Trivy, sign with cosign.

4
Deploy

Rolling update. Admission controller verifies new signature.

5
Verify

Trivy Operator confirms zero affected images in production.

Explanation

This end-to-end workflow demonstrates SBOM value. Without SBOMs, step 1 takes days (rescanning). With SBOMs, step 1 takes seconds. On the CKS exam, this is the supply chain security incident response pattern.

# 1. Generate SBOM with syft (EXAM PATTERN)
syft ghcr.io/anihpj/api:latest -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
syft ghcr.io/anihpj/api:latest -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cdx.json

⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 27 Traps
  • SPDX vs CycloneDX: Both are valid SBOM formats. SPDX is Linux Foundation standard (tag-value, JSON, YAML). CycloneDX is OWASP standard (JSON, XML). Tools have preferences — syft supports both. On the exam, use whichever the question specifies.
  • SBOM is a snapshot, not a live inventory: An SBOM generated at build time reflects dependencies AT BUILD TIME. If a new CVE is discovered the next day, the SBOM won't know about it. SBOMs must be continuously scanned, not just generated once.
