How ArgoCD Syncs ConfigMaps — Falco Rule Deployment in Detail

When you update a Falco rule in Git and ArgoCD syncs the ConfigMap, it does NOT automatically reload Falco. The DaemonSet must detect the ConfigMap change and restart. Here's the full chain:

1Git change pushed

You edit falco/falco-rules-anihpj.yaml in Git. Push to feature branch, open PR, CI passes, merge to main.

2ArgoCD detects (≤3 min)

ArgoCD polls Git, detects new commit, diffs the ConfigMap. The data field has changed. ArgoCD applies the updated ConfigMap to the cluster.

3ConfigMap updated in K8s

The ConfigMap falco-custom-rules in namespace falco now contains the new rules. But Falco pods are still running with the OLD rules!

4Kubelet syncs ConfigMap to node (≤1 min)

The kubelet on each node detects the ConfigMap change and updates the mounted file at /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml. But Falco reads rules ONCE at startup — it won't see the update.

5Falco must reload or restart

Option A: kubectl rollout restart ds/falco -n falco (manual, causes brief gap). Option B: Use a sidecar that watches the ConfigMap and sends SIGHUP to Falco. Option C: Configure ArgoCD to trigger a Job that restarts Falco after ConfigMap sync.

Policy Versioning Strategy — Semantic Versioning for Security Policies

VersionExampleWhat ChangedRollout Strategy
MAJOR (v2.0.0)Switch from Gatekeeper to KyvernoCompletely new policy engine. Breaking changes expected.New ArgoCD Application, deploy in parallel, cut over when verified
MINOR (v1.2.0)Add 3 new Falco rulesNew detection capabilities. Backward compatible — old rules still work.Standard PR → CI → merge → ArgoCD sync. Monitor for false positives.
PATCH (v1.1.1)Fix false positive in existing ruleBug fix: rule was matching too broadly. Reduces noise.Quick PR → merge. Low risk — only reduces alerts, doesn't add new ones.

Policy Rollback — git revert Saves the Day

Bash — Roll back a broken security policy via Git + ArgoCD 
# SCENARIO: A new Falco rule is causing 500 alerts/minute (false positive storm).
# You need to roll back NOW — before the on-call engineer quits.

# Step 1: Find the bad commit (the one that added the noisy rule)
git log --oneline -5
# a1b2c3d Add new Falco rules (including reverse shell detection) ← BAD
# e4f5g6h Update NetworkPolicy for postgres
# i7j8k9l Initial security policies

# Step 2: Revert the bad commit (creates a NEW commit that undoes it)
git revert a1b2c3d --no-edit
git push origin main

# Step 3: ArgoCD detects the revert within 3 minutes
# The revert commit REMOVES the noisy rule from the ConfigMap.
# ArgoCD syncs: ConfigMap updated, Falco rules reloaded.
# Alerts return to normal.

# Step 4: Verify the rollback
kubectl get configmap falco-custom-rules -n falco -o yaml | \
  grep "rule:"  # Should NOT include the noisy rule
argocd app sync anihpj-security-policies  # Force immediate sync (optional)

# Total recovery time: ~4 minutes (git revert + ArgoCD sync)
# Without GitOps: ~15 minutes (find old file, SSH, re-apply manually)

Disaster Recovery with GitOps — Full Cluster Security Reconstruction

If your cluster is completely destroyed, GitOps enables full reconstruction of your security posture in minutes:

Bash — Rebuild entire security posture from Git after catastrophic failure 
# SCENARIO: Production cluster destroyed (ransomware, cloud account compromise, etc.)
# You have: Git repository with all security manifests.
# You have: Container images in ghcr.io (signed + SBOM attached).

# Step 1: Provision new cluster (Terraform, kOps, EKS, etc.)
terraform apply    # ~10 minutes

# Step 2: Install ArgoCD on the new cluster
kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Step 3: Apply the ArgoCD Application that manages security policies
# This is a BOOTSTRAP Application — it deploys everything else.
kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml
# ArgoCD syncs ALL security manifests from Git:
#   → RBAC (ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings)
#   → NetworkPolicies (default-deny + 5 allow rules)
#   → PSS labels (Restricted on prod, Baseline on dev)
#   → Gatekeeper (ConstraintTemplates + Constraints)
#   → Kyverno (verifyImages ClusterPolicy)
#   → Falco (custom rules via ConfigMap)
#   → Audit policy (ConfigMap mounted to API server)
#   → kube-bench CronJob

# Step 4: Verify everything is synced
argocd app list
argocd app get anihpj-security-policies

# Step 5: Deploy applications (separate ArgoCD Application)
kubectl apply -f argocd/application-anihpj.yaml

# ✅ Full security posture restored in ~15 minutes.
# ✅ All images verified via Kyverno (cosign signatures).
# ✅ All policies enforced from first pod creation.
# ✅ Complete audit trail: Git history = who deployed what.
🔧 Under the Hood — How ArgoCD Detects and Corrects Configuration Drift: Kubernetes Watch API → SHA Comparison → Three-Way Diff → Self-Healing Sync
🗺️ ArgoCD Drift Detection — The Self-Healing Engine

ArgoCD's self-healing is what makes GitOps truly powerful. When someone runs kubectl edit networkpolicy directly on the cluster, ArgoCD detects the deviation and automatically reverts it. Here's exactly how:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   ARGOCD DRIFT DETECTION & SELF-HEALING — The Complete Cycle              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  1. GIT POLL (every 3 minutes)                                           │
  │     argocd-repo-server polls git repo: HEAD is commit abc123             │
  │     Last synced commit was also abc123 → NO CHANGE in Git                │
  │                                                                           │
  │  2. CLUSTER POLL (every 3 minutes, same cycle)                           │
  │     argocd-application-controller queries Kubernetes API:                │
  │     GET /apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/               │
  │         networkpolicies/default-deny-all                                  │
  │     → Returns: {"spec": {"ingress": [{"from": [{"podSelector": {}}]}]}}   │
  │     Wait — ingress rule was ADDED! Someone ran kubectl edit!             │
  │                                                                           │
  │  3. THREE-WAY DIFF                                                        │
  │     A: Previous desired state (from last sync): no ingress rules         │
  │     B: Current desired state (from Git): no ingress rules                │
  │     C: Live state (from cluster): HAS an ingress rule                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │     Diff: B ≠ C → DRIFT DETECTED!                                        │
  │     ArgoCD marks Application as "OutOfSync"                              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  4. AUTO-CORRECTION (if selfHeal: true)                                  │
  │     ArgoCD applies the desired state from Git:                           │
  │     PATCH /apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/             │
  │          networkpolicies/default-deny-all                                 │
  │     Body: {"spec": {"ingress": [], "egress": [], "policyTypes": [...]}}   │
  │     → The manually-added ingress rule is REMOVED.                        │
  │     → NetworkPolicy is back to Git's desired state.                      │
  │     → ArgoCD marks Application as "Synced" + "Healthy"                   │
  │                                                                           │
  │  5. NOTIFICATION (optional)                                               │
  │     ArgoCD notifications controller sends:                               │
  │     → Slack: "anihpj-security-policies: drift detected + auto-corrected" │
  │     → Audit log: who made the manual change (from K8s audit log)         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 CRITICAL: selfHeal only works if the resource's Live state differs   │
  │     from Git. If someone also commits the change to Git, ArgoCD sees     │
  │     it as a legitimate desired state change and syncs it. This is why     │
  │     BRANCH PROTECTION on main is essential — no unreviewed commits.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 How ArgoCD Avoids Sync Loops — The Reconciliation Throttle

Without throttling, ArgoCD could get stuck in an infinite loop of detecting drift → syncing → detecting drift. Here's how it avoids that:

  SYNC LOOP PREVENTION:
  1. ArgoCD syncs → writes desired state to cluster
  2. Cluster acknowledges the write (ResourceVersion incremented)
  3. ArgoCD's next poll reads the ResourceVersion
  4. If ResourceVersion == expected → no drift, no sync
  5. If ResourceVersion > expected → someone else changed it → drift!
  6. Sync corrects it → ResourceVersion increments again
  7. Next poll: ResourceVersion matches → stable

  SYNC WAVE ORDERING (critical for dependencies):
  Wave -1: Namespaces (must exist before anything else)
  Wave 0:  CRDs, Admission Webhooks (must register before use)
  Wave 1:  RBAC, ServiceAccounts, ConfigMaps
  Wave 2:  Deployments, Services, NetworkPolicies
  Wave 3:  Kyverno Policies, Gatekeeper Constraints
  Wave 4:  Falco ConfigMaps (last — Falco restarts on change)
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

GitOps and automation appear on the CKS exam as CI/CD pipeline scenarios. Know: (1) GitOps principle: Git is the single source of truth. Every security change goes through PR review → CI validation → ArgoCD deployment. (2) Self-healing: syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true auto-corrects manual kubectl edit changes within 3 minutes. (3) CI/CD security gates: kubesec (score ≥ 5), Trivy (0 CRITICAL), conftest (Rego policies pass), cosign (sign before push). (4) Policy as Code: Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplates, Kyverno ClusterPolicies, Falco rules, and audit policies — ALL in Git. Never edit policies directly on the cluster. (5) Disaster recovery: git clone + ArgoCD = full security posture restored in ~15 minutes.

📝 Chapter 35 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
A developer runs kubectl edit networkpolicy default-deny-all -n anihpj-prod and adds an ingress rule allowing port 22 from anywhere. ArgoCD is configured with selfHeal: true. What happens to this manual edit, and how quickly?
Show Answer
Answer

Within 3 minutes (default ArgoCD sync interval), ArgoCD detects that the live NetworkPolicy differs from Git. It performs a three-way diff, identifies the manual ingress rule as drift, and auto-corrects by applying the desired state from Git — removing the unauthorized ingress rule. The Application status briefly shows "OutOfSync" then returns to "Synced." If notifications are configured, Slack receives a drift-detected + auto-corrected message. The developer's manual change survives less than 3 minutes.

Q2
Your GitHub Actions security pipeline runs on every PR. List the four tools that should run on PR checks, what each validates, and which one should FAIL the pipeline (block merge) for a CRITICAL finding.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) yamllint — validates YAML syntax (should FAIL on syntax errors). (2) kube-linter — checks Kubernetes best practices (should FAIL on privileged containers, hostPath mounts). (3) kubesec — scores security posture (should FAIL if score < 5). (4) Trivy — scans for CVEs (should FAIL on CRITICAL CVEs — use --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL). All four should block merge for their respective failure conditions. Additionally, conftest validates Rego policies and cosign signs the image (on merge, not PR).

Q3
Your production cluster is destroyed. You have a Git repository at github.com/Anihs-Canvas/anihpj-security with all security manifests and an ArgoCD Application definition. List the exact steps to restore the full security posture in under 15 minutes.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Provision new cluster (Terraform/EKS/GKE)
terraform apply   # ~10 min
# 2. Install ArgoCD
kubectl create ns argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
# 3. Deploy the bootstrap Application
kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml
# 4. Verify sync
argocd app sync anihpj-security-policies
argocd app get anihpj-security-policies
# ✅ RBAC, NetworkPolicies, PSS labels, Gatekeeper, Kyverno,
#    Falco rules, audit policy, kube-bench CronJob — all restored.
Q4
You've stored Falco rules, Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplates, and the Kubernetes audit policy in Git. ArgoCD deploys them. A team member suggests "just run kubectl apply from my laptop — it's faster." Give three concrete reasons why this is a security anti-pattern.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) No audit trail: kubectl apply from a laptop leaves no record of WHO changed WHAT. Git commits provide author, timestamp, diff, and PR review chain. (2) No review: Direct kubectl apply bypasses PR review. A malicious or mistaken change is applied instantly with no second pair of eyes. GitOps requires approval before merge. (3) No drift detection: If the same person later edits the policy directly on the cluster again, there's no automatic correction. ArgoCD with selfHeal: true detects and reverts unauthorized changes within 3 minutes.

Q5
What is the difference between ArgoCD selfHeal and automated sync? When would you use each for security policies?
Show Answer
Answer

Automated sync: ArgoCD automatically applies changes from Git when it detects a new commit. It does NOT revert manual cluster edits. Self-heal (selfHeal: true): ArgoCD continuously monitors the cluster and reverts ANY change that doesn't match Git — including manual edits, accidental deletions, and unauthorized modifications. For security policies, ALWAYS use selfHeal: true. Without it, an attacker who gains kubectl access can edit NetworkPolicies/rules and the changes persist until the next Git commit (which may never come).

Explanation

SelfHeal is the security-critical setting. It turns GitOps from "deploy from Git" into "enforce Git as the single source of truth." On the CKS exam, selfHeal: true is the answer to "how to prevent unauthorized changes to security policies."

Q6
Write the ArgoCD Application that deploys all CKS security policies with selfHeal enabled. What critical annotation prevents ArgoCD from being used as an attack vector?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: {name: security-policies, namespace: argocd}
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/Anihs-Canvas/anihpj-security
    targetRevision: main
    path: policies/
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: argocd
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
    - Validate=true
    - CreateNamespace=true

The syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true is critical. Also: restrict which repos ArgoCD can sync — never allow arbitrary public repos. Use private repos with branch protection and required reviews.

Explanation

ArgoCD itself must be secured. If an attacker compromises your Git repo, ArgoCD will happily sync malicious policies. Mitigation: branch protection rules, required PR reviews, signed commits, and restricting ArgoCD to specific repos/projects.

Q7
How does GitOps for security policies help with compliance audits? What evidence can you provide to auditors?
Show Answer
Answer

GitOps provides: (1) Complete change history: git log shows every policy change with author, timestamp, and diff. (2) Approval evidence: PR reviews prove changes were reviewed before deployment. (3) Deployment evidence: ArgoCD sync history shows when each change was applied to the cluster. (4) Drift evidence: ArgoCD logs show if/when manual changes were detected and auto-reverted. (5) Rollback capability: git revert proves you can restore previous state. For auditors: "show me who changed this firewall rule and who approved it" — GitPR has both answers in seconds.

Explanation

Compliance is a key GitOps benefit. Traditional approaches require manual evidence gathering. GitOps makes audit evidence inherent to the process. On the CKS exam, GitOps is the recommended approach for managing security policies at scale.

Q8
A CI/CD pipeline runs 8 security tools. One of them (kubesec) is flaky and sometimes fails for legitimate configs. How do you handle this without removing kubesec or allowing insecure code through?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Advisory mode: Run flaky tools as "advisory" — they report results but don't block the pipeline. Example: kubesec scan --exit-code 0. (2) Threshold-based blocking: Only block if score is critically low (< 3) but warn if 3-7. (3) Dashboard review: Publish advisory results to a dashboard; SecOps reviews weekly. (4) Fix the root cause: Investigate why kubesec is flaky — update rules, fix false positives. Never completely disable a security tool — reduce its blocking power but keep it in the pipeline for visibility.

Explanation

Security tooling must balance rigor with developer productivity. The pattern: block on critical/high-confidence findings, warn on medium, ignore low. On the CKS exam, never suggest removing a security tool from the pipeline — adjust its failure threshold instead.

Q9
How do you prevent secrets from being committed to Git in a GitOps workflow? What tools scan for secrets in CI?
Show Answer
Answer

Pre-commit: (1) detect-secrets or git-secrets — scans staged files for API keys, tokens, passwords BEFORE commit. (2) pre-commit hooks — configured in .pre-commit-config.yaml. CI pipeline: (3) truffleHog or Gitleaks — scans all commits in the PR for secrets. (4) git-secrets — scans commit history. Post-commit: If a secret is detected after commit: (a) rotate the secret IMMEDIATELY, (b) use git filter-branch or BFG Repo-Cleaner to remove from history, (c) force-push to overwrite. Never assume "it was only there for a minute" — consider it compromised.

Explanation

Secrets in Git are the #1 GitOps security failure. The CKS approach: prevent (pre-commit hooks), detect (CI scanning), respond (rotate + purge). On the exam, always recommend pre-commit hooks as the first line of defense.

Q10
Design the complete GitOps security pipeline: from developer branch to production deployment. What security checks happen at each stage, and what tools enforce them?
Show Answer
Answer
1
Pre-commit (Developer Laptop)

detect-secrets, yamllint, kube-linter (optional). Block commit if secrets found.

2
PR Checks (CI Pipeline)

yamllint → kube-linter → kubesec → conftest → Trivy → Gitleaks. Block merge if CRITICAL findings.

3
Merge (CI Pipeline)

cosign sign + attest SBOM. Push signed image. SBOM uploaded to registry.

4
ArgoCD Sync (Cluster)

ArgoCD applies manifests. selfHeal: true immediately reverts unauthorized changes.

5
Admission (Cluster)

Kyverno verifyImages (cosign). Gatekeeper validating policies. PSS Restricted enforcement.

6
Runtime (Cluster)

Falco monitoring. Trivy Operator continuous scanning. kube-bench CronJob weekly audit.

Explanation

This is the complete end-to-end CKS security pipeline. Every stage has specific tools and failure criteria. On the exam, you may be asked to identify which stage is missing or what tool should be added at a specific point. Know this flow.

⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 35 Traps
  • Secrets in Git = disaster: Even encrypted, secrets in Git are risky. Use External Secrets Operator (Ch 20) or SealedSecrets. Never commit plaintext secrets — the CKS exam will flag this as a critical violation.
  • ArgoCD needs RBAC too: The ArgoCD ServiceAccount needs cluster-wide read access (to detect drift) and write access to managed namespaces. Don't give it cluster-admin — scope it to managed namespaces only.

Chapter 36: CKS Exam Strategy — Time Management & Approach

You've mastered the theory and practiced the hands-on skills. Now the final challenge: the exam itself. The CKS is a 2-hour, performance-based exam with 15-20 tasks on a live Kubernetes cluster inside a locked-down browser. No notes, no bookmarks, no IDE — just you, a terminal, and the official Kubernetes documentation. Strategy matters as much as knowledge. This chapter covers the exam format, a battle-tested 3-pass time management strategy, the critical habit of context switching, and every file path you'll need to know from memory. Read this chapter the night before your exam.

🎯 Exam Strategy ⏱️ ~45 minutes 📋 Essential 🔴 Part 9

🎯 What You'll Learn — Exam-Day Mastery

  • ✅ Master the exam environment: Know exactly what to expect — the PSI browser, the terminal, the allowed resources, and the scoring system
  • ✅ Execute the 3-pass strategy: Maximize your score by prioritizing easy tasks first, saving hard ones for last, and never getting stuck
  • ✅ Never lose points to context errors: The #1 cause of CKS failures — solving the right problem on the wrong cluster. Build the habit that prevents this.
  • ✅ Memorize critical file paths: Save 5-10 minutes per task by knowing where config files live without searching the documentation
🎓 CKS Exam Domain Coverage
All Domains 100%

36.1 Exam Format and Environment

The CKS is not a multiple-choice test. It's a live terminal session where you solve real Kubernetes security tasks on actual clusters. Understanding the environment before you enter it prevents panic and wasted time.

The PSI Browser Environment — Exactly What to Expect

1Check-in (15-30 min before exam)

Download PSI Secure Browser. Show government ID to webcam. Proctor verifies your identity. Take photos of your workspace (all four walls, desk surface, under desk). Remove all prohibited items. Proctor approves entry.

2The Terminal

You get a Linux terminal inside the browser. Multiple tabs available. Shell is bash. Editor is vi/vim (nano may also be available). tmux/screen are NOT available. The terminal has kubectl pre-configured with multiple cluster contexts.

3The Allowed Browser Tabs

Only these domains open: kubernetes.io/docs, kubernetes.io/blog, falco.org, github.com/falcosecurity/falco, kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx, github.com/kubernetes. You can have 1-2 tabs open at a time. BOOKMARK these URLs before the exam.

4What You CAN'T Do

❌ No copy-paste between your machine and the exam terminal. ❌ No external websites (StackOverflow, Google). ❌ No personal notes or cheat sheets. ❌ No AI tools. ❌ No phone or second screen. ❌ No leaving your seat during the exam.

Exam Day Preparation Checklist

🖥️
Night Before

Test PSI browser compatibility. Charge laptop. Prepare ID. Clear desk of all papers. Test webcam + microphone. Set up in a quiet room with a closed door. Tell family/roommates you cannot be disturbed for 2.5 hours.

⏰
Morning Of

Wake up 2+ hours before. Eat a proper meal. Drink water (but not too much — no bathroom breaks!). Do a 10-minute warmup: kubectl run test --image=nginx, write a quick NetworkPolicy, scan an image with Trivy. Get your brain into terminal mode.

📋
During Exam

Read every question twice. Always run kubectl config use-context FIRST. Use the notepad feature to track completed tasks. If stuck for >3 minutes, SKIP and return later. Save verification commands as proof.

How CKS Scoring Works — Points, Weighting, and Partial Credit

The CKS scoring system is not disclosed in detail by the Linux Foundation, but years of candidate experience reveal consistent patterns:

AspectWhat We KnowImplication for You
Task weightingTasks are weighted by difficulty. A simple RBAC task may be worth 4%, while a complex encryption-at-rest task may be worth 8-12%.Don't skip hard tasks assuming they're worth the same as easy ones. But don't spend 30 min on an 8% task either.
Partial creditYES — many tasks award partial credit. If you create the EncryptionConfiguration correctly but forget to mount it, you might get 60-70% of the points.Always submit SOMETHING. Even a partial solution is better than a blank task. The kubectl command that creates the resource is often worth points by itself.
Verification is scoredSome tasks explicitly ask you to VERIFY your work (e.g., "Verify encryption is working"). The verification step IS part of the score.Read the entire task. The last sentence often says "Verify that..." — that's scorable. Run kubectl get or kubectl describe as your verification.
IdempotencyThe scoring script runs multiple times. If your solution isn't idempotent (fails on re-run), you may lose points.Use kubectl apply not kubectl create. Write manifests, don't run imperative commands. The scoring system re-applies your YAML.
No negative scoringWrong answers don't subtract from correct ones. A wrong answer = 0 points for that task, not -X.ALWAYS attempt every task. There's no penalty for being wrong. A lucky guess or partial solution earns points.

How to Use the Kubernetes Documentation Effectively

🔍Search, Don't Browse

Type kubernetes.io/docs into the address bar, then use the search box. Don't click through the navigation tree. Search for exact resource names: "NetworkPolicy", "PodSecurityPolicy", "EncryptionConfiguration". The search is fast and accurate.

📋Copy the YAML Example

Every concept page has a YAML example. COPY IT. Paste into vi and modify only the fields you need. This is 3× faster than writing YAML from memory and avoids indentation errors.

🏷️Use Task References

The CKS exam references specific Kubernetes versions (e.g., v1.30). Use the version selector at the top of the docs page to match. API fields change between versions — using the wrong version's example may fail.

⚡Pre-Bookmark Critical Pages

Before the exam, practice searching for: Falco Rules, NetworkPolicy, Pod Security Standards, EncryptionConfiguration, Audit Policy, RBAC, Seccomp, AppArmor. Know exactly which search term finds the right page in <3 seconds.

36.2 Time Management — The 3-Pass Strategy

The #2 reason people fail the CKS (after context switching errors) is poor time management. They spend 20 minutes on one hard task, run out of time, and leave 5 easy tasks untouched. The 3-pass strategy prevents this by categorizing tasks by difficulty and allocating time accordingly.

Time Management Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do

🚫
Reading ALL tasks before starting ANY

Some candidates spend 15+ minutes reading every task in detail. You don't need to understand every task upfront. Scan for 30 seconds each — just enough to classify difficulty. Start solving immediately.

🚫
Perfecting one answer for 20 minutes

A task is worth the same whether you spend 3 minutes or 20 minutes on it. If you're 8 minutes in and not close to done, SKIP. Come back in Pass 3. A partial solution may earn partial credit.

🚫
Not using the documentation

The Kubernetes docs are YOUR notes. You don't need to memorize YAML syntax — copy from the docs. Search for "NetworkPolicy" → copy the example → modify it. This is faster than writing from scratch and less error-prone.

What To Do When You're Stuck — The 60-Second Decision Tree

You've been working on a task for 3 minutes and aren't sure how to proceed. What now?
Do you know the RESOURCE TYPE? (e.g., NetworkPolicy, ClusterRole)

→ YES: Search the docs for the resource. Copy the example YAML. Modify it. If this takes more than 3 more minutes → mark as SKIP and move on.

→ NO: Immediately mark as SKIP. You can't solve what you can't name. Return in Pass 3 with more context or a lucky guess.

Are you fighting YAML syntax, not security concepts?

→ YES: Don't waste time on indentation. Write a minimal version. If kubectl apply fails, check kubectl explain <resource> --recursive for the correct field paths.

→ NO: You genuinely don't know the solution. SKIP immediately. Return in Pass 3. Use the remaining time to maximize points on tasks you CAN solve.

Time Tracking Without a Clock — Use the Terminal

Bash — Quick time checks during the exam 
# Check current time (exam clock is in UTC — confirm at start)
date

# Set a mental checkpoint every 15 minutes
# Pass 1 should end at T+45min
# Pass 2 should end at T+105min
# Pass 3 starts at T+105min, exam ends at T+120min

# If you have watch available (not guaranteed):
watch -n 300 'echo "Check time!"'   # Reminder every 5 min

# Simpler: write the target end time in your notepad:
# "Pass 1 ends: XX:XX"  (calculate: start time + 45 min)
# "Pass 2 ends: XX:XX"  (start time + 105 min)
# "HARD STOP: XX:XX"    (start time + 120 min)

# At each checkpoint, count completed tasks:
# Pass 1 (45 min): 5-8 done → on track. 3-4 → behind, speed up.
# Pass 2 (105 min): 9-12 done → on track. 6-8 → behind, focus on high-value tasks.
# Pass 3 (120 min): Every point counts. Verify, fill gaps, submit.

36.3 Context Switching — The Most Important CKS Exam Habit

This single mistake causes more CKS failures than any other: forgetting to switch cluster contexts between tasks. The exam provides multiple clusters (typically 2-4). Each task specifies which cluster to use. If you solve Task 3 on Cluster A when it asked for Cluster B, you get zero points — even if your solution is perfect.

The Context Switch Ritual — Do This Every Single Time

Bash — The EXACT workflow for every CKS exam task 
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 0: BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING — SWITCH CONTEXT FIRST
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# 1. COPY the context command from the task description
#    Task says: "Context: mk8s-cluster-2"
kubectl config use-context mk8s-cluster-2

# 2. VERIFY you're on the right cluster
kubectl config current-context
# Expected output: mk8s-cluster-2

# 3. VERIFY you can see the expected resources
kubectl get nodes
# If you see 0 nodes or "not found" → WRONG CLUSTER!

# 4. CHECK which namespace the task expects
# Task may say: "Namespace: security" or imply it
kubectl get ns
# If the task says "Create in namespace 'prod'" and you don't see it:
kubectl create ns prod    # Create it! Don't assume it exists.

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# THE RITUAL (repeat for EVERY task):
#   ☐ 1. Read the context name
#   ☐ 2. kubectl config use-context 
#   ☐ 3. kubectl config current-context (verify)
#   ☐ 4. kubectl get nodes (sanity check)
#   ☐ 5. NOW solve the task
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Common Context Switching Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

MistakeConsequencePrevention
Typing context name wrongkubectl config use-context mk8s-cluster2 (missing hyphen) → silently fails, you're still on the previous clusterAlways run kubectl config current-context AFTER switching. If it doesn't match, you typed it wrong.
Assuming the namespace existsYou create all resources in the default namespace. Task asked for namespace "web". Zero points.Read the task carefully. If a namespace is specified, CREATE it first: kubectl create ns <name>
Forgetting between tasksYou solve Task 4 on the context from Task 3. Task 4's solution is on the wrong cluster. Zero points.Make the ritual automatic. Train yourself: every time you read a new task, your fingers type kubectl config use-context automatically.
SSH context confusionTask says "SSH to node01". You run commands on the wrong node. Zero points.After SSH: hostname to verify. Some tasks use ssh node01, others use ssh mk8s-node-1. Pay attention to the exact hostname.

The Notepad Trick — Track Your Progress

The exam terminal includes a built-in notepad (accessible from the exam UI, not the terminal). Use it to track:

Text — Your exam notepad template (fill in as you go) 
=== CKS EXAM TRACKER ===
☐ Task 1: [EASY]   Context: cluster1  √ DONE
☐ Task 2: [SKIP]   Context: cluster3  ← Return in Pass 3
☐ Task 3: [EASY]   Context: cluster1  √ DONE
☐ Task 4: [MED]    Context: cluster2  √ DONE (verified)
☐ Task 5: [SKIP]   Context: cluster4  ← Return in Pass 3
☐ Task 6: [EASY]   Context: cluster1  √ DONE
...
☐ Task 15:[MED]    Context: cluster2  IN PROGRESS

PASS 1: 6 done (Tasks 1,3,4,6,8,10)
PASS 2: 4 done (Tasks 7,11,12,15)
PASS 3: 2 attempted (Tasks 2,5) — partial? Not sure.

- 2:00 — TIME

Real Exam Task Format — What You'll Actually See

CKS tasks follow a consistent format. Recognizing this structure saves time and prevents missed requirements:

Text — Typical CKS exam task format (annotated) 
Task 7 of 18: Secure the web-frontend namespace

Context: mk8s-cluster-2          ← ALWAYS COPY THIS FIRST

A developer has deployed a web application in the 'web-frontend'
namespace. The application currently runs with default settings.

1. Create a NetworkPolicy named 'web-deny-all' in the 'web-frontend'
   namespace that blocks all ingress and egress traffic.       ← THE ASK

2. Modify the NetworkPolicy to allow ingress traffic from pods
   in the 'ingress-nginx' namespace on TCP port 8080.          ← THE ASK

3. Verify that pods in the 'default' namespace cannot reach
   pods in the 'web-frontend' namespace.                       ← VERIFICATION

You may use the Kubernetes documentation at kubernetes.io/docs.

→ Scoring: Part 1 = 4%, Part 2 = 3%, Part 3 = 2% (Total: 9%)

Verification Commands That Prove Your Work

Always end each task with a verification command. If the scoring script checks your work, it looks for the expected state. These commands also help YOU confirm you solved it correctly:

Task TypeVerification CommandWhat It Proves
RBACkubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user> -n <ns>The subject has the exact permissions you configured
NetworkPolicykubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- wget -qO- --timeout=5 <url>Traffic is blocked/allowed as expected
PodSecurityContextkubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep -E 'CapEff|Seccomp'Capabilities dropped, Seccomp active
Encryption at restETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/<ns>/<name> | hexdump -CSecret is encrypted (garbled) in etcd
Falco rulecat /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml or falco --validate <file>Rule file exists and is syntactically valid
Audit policycat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq . | head -50Audit logs are being generated
Image scantrivy image <image> --severity CRITICAL — shows 0 resultsNo CRITICAL CVEs in scanned image

36.4 File Locations You Must Know (No Internet Search Needed)

In the CKS exam, searching the Kubernetes documentation for file paths wastes precious minutes. These paths appear in nearly every exam task. Memorize them. Write them on a piece of paper and review them 5 minutes before your exam starts (during the check-in process, you'll have a few minutes while the proctor verifies your ID).

Critical File Paths — Categorized by Component

File / DirectoryComponentPurposeCommon Task
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kubeletStatic pod manifests directory. Any YAML here is automatically run as a static pod.Edit API server, controller-manager, scheduler, or etcd configuration
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yamlAPI ServerAPI server static pod manifest. Add flags here to configure encryption, audit, admission plugins.Enable encryption at rest, configure audit policy, disable anonymous auth
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yamlController ManagerController manager static pod manifest.Configure ServiceAccount token signing, enable/disable controllers
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yamletcdetcd static pod manifest. Configure TLS, peer URLs, data directory.Enable TLS for etcd, change data directory
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yamlkubeletKubelet configuration file (YAML). Contains authentication, authorization, cgroup driver settings.Disable anonymous auth, enable webhook authorization, set Seccomp default
/etc/kubernetes/pki/PKICluster certificate authority and key files.Inspect certificate expiration, rotate certificates
/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/etcd PKIetcd-specific certificates and keys.Configure etcd TLS, verify peer certificates
/var/lib/etcd/etcdetcd data directory. Contains the actual key-value store data.Backup, restore, check data size
/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yamlAPI ServerAudit policy file. Defines WHAT to log and at what detail level.Create or modify audit policy, enable audit logging
/etc/falco/falco.yamlFalcoFalco main configuration file. Output channels, rules files, engine settings.Change output format, enable/disable rules, configure alerting
/etc/falco/falco_rules.yamlFalcoDefault Falco rules. Shipped with Falco installation.View default rules for reference when writing custom rules
/etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yamlFalcoLOCAL custom rules file. Add your custom rules here (never edit the default file).Write custom Falco rules for specific applications
/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/kubeletDirectory for local Seccomp profiles. Place custom JSON profiles here.Create and apply custom Seccomp profiles
/etc/apparmor.d/AppArmorAppArmor profile directory. Place custom AppArmor profiles here.Load and apply custom AppArmor profiles to pods
/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yamlAPI ServerEncryptionConfiguration file. Defines encryption providers and keys.Enable encryption at rest for Secrets

Memorization Strategy — How to Remember These Paths

🧠
Group by Parent Directory

Most paths live under 3 parents: /etc/kubernetes/ (API server, PKI, audit), /var/lib/kubelet/ (kubelet config, Seccomp), and /etc/falco/ (Falco rules). Memorize the 3 parents first, then the specific files under each.

📝
Write Them Before Starting

During the NDA/check-in screen (you have a few minutes), mentally recite these paths. As soon as the terminal appears, type them into the notepad: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml. Your future self will thank you.

🔗
Associate with Tasks

Don't memorize in isolation. Link each path to a specific task: "If I need to enable encryption → edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml". "If I need to write a custom Falco rule → edit /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml". The association makes it stick.

Additional Critical Paths — The Extended Reference

File / DirectoryComponentWhy You Need It
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yamlSchedulerStatic pod for kube-scheduler. May need to edit for profiling, authentication settings.
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yamlKubeletTHE kubelet config file. Contains authentication, authorization, seccompDefault, rotateCertificates. Edit this for most kubelet hardening tasks.
/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crtPKICluster CA certificate. Used to verify API server TLS, etcd TLS, and service account tokens.
/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crtAPI ServerAPI server certificate. Check expiration: openssl x509 -in <file> -text -noout | grep -A2 Validity
~/.kube/configkubectlKubeconfig file. Contains clusters, users, and contexts. kubectl config view to see all configured contexts.
/etc/containerd/config.tomlcontainerdContainer runtime configuration. May need to check for insecure registries or runtime settings.
/etc/kubernetes/admission-control/API ServerDirectory for admission webhook configurations (ImagePolicyWebhook, etc.).
/usr/local/bin/SystemWhere tools like trivy, kube-bench, etcdctl are installed. Check with which <tool>.

Exam Task → File Path Quick Reference

Every CKS exam task maps to one or more of these files. Here's the cheat sheet:

🔐
Encryption Tasks

Create /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml → Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml → Add --encryption-provider-config flag + volume mount → Verify with etcdctl get

📝
Audit Tasks

Create /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml → Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml → Add --audit-policy-file + --audit-log-path flags + volume mounts → Check /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log

🛡️
Kubelet Hardening

Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml → Set authentication.anonymous.enabled: false, authorization.mode: Webhook, readOnlyPort: 0 → Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet

🔍
Falco Tasks

Edit /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml → Write custom rules → Validate: falco --validate <file> → Restart Falco: systemctl restart falco or kill -1 $(pidof falco)

📦
Seccomp Tasks

Create profile in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ → Reference in Pod securityContext.seccompProfile.localhostProfile → Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp

🛡️
AppArmor Tasks

Create profile in /etc/apparmor.d/ → Load: apparmor_parser -r <file> → Reference in Pod annotation → Verify: cat /proc/<pid>/attr/current

🎓
Exam Format (36.1)

2 hours, 15-20 tasks, PSI browser, 67% to pass. Allowed tabs: kubernetes.io, falco.org. No notes, no AI.

⏱️
3-Pass Strategy (36.2)

Pass 1 (45min): 5-8 quick wins. Pass 2 (60min): 4-7 medium tasks. Pass 3 (15min): hard tasks + verify.

🔄
Context Switching (36.3)

#1 failure cause. Ritual: use-context → current-context → get nodes → verify namespace. Every. Single. Task.

📁
File Paths (36.4)

15 critical paths memorized. 3 parent directories. Group by component. Write them in the notepad as soon as exam starts.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam is a test of efficiency, not just knowledge. Know: (1) Context switch ritual: kubectl config use-context → current-context → get nodes — do this for EVERY task. (2) 3-pass strategy: Easy first (45 min) → Medium (60 min) → Hard + verify (15 min). Never spend >8 minutes stuck on one task. (3) Copy from docs: Search kubernetes.io for the resource name, copy the YAML example, modify it. 3× faster than writing from memory. (4) Verification earns points: Many tasks have explicit "Verify that..." requirements. Run kubectl get, kubectl describe, kubectl auth can-i as proof. (5) Partial credit exists: Submit SOMETHING for every task. A partial EncryptionConfiguration that's missing the volume mount still earns 60-70%. A blank task earns 0%.

📝 Chapter 36 — CKS Exam Strategy Practice Questions

Q1
You're 35 minutes into the exam. You've completed 4 tasks. Task 5 asks you to configure encryption at rest — you know it requires editing the API server manifest, creating an EncryptionConfiguration, and verifying with etcdctl. You estimate it'll take 12 minutes. What should you do?
Show Answer
Answer

SKIP Task 5 and mark it for Pass 3. Encryption at rest is a HARD task (8-15 min). At T+35, you're still in Pass 1 (45 min). You should have 5-8 easy tasks done by now. Spending 12 minutes on one hard task in Pass 1 would put you behind schedule. Mark it in your notepad: "Task 5: SKIP — Encryption at rest — Return Pass 3." Move to Task 6. You'll return to it in the final 15 minutes when you've banked all the easy/medium points.

Q2
Task says: "Context: cluster2-prod". You type kubectl config use-context cluster2prod (missing the hyphen). kubectl config current-context still shows cluster1-dev. You don't notice and solve the task. What's the result?
Show Answer
Answer

Zero points. You solved the task on cluster1-dev when it asked for cluster2-prod. The scoring script checks resources on the CORRECT cluster — it won't find your solution. This is the #1 cause of CKS failures. Prevention: ALWAYS run kubectl config current-context AFTER switching and verify it matches the task's context name EXACTLY. If the output doesn't match what the task says, you typed it wrong.

Q3
You have 8 minutes left. You've attempted 14 of 17 tasks but are unsure about Tasks 9, 12, and 16. You haven't verified any of your earlier answers. What's the best use of your remaining 8 minutes?
Show Answer
Answer

VERIFY your Pass 1 answers (the easy tasks you solved confidently). A wrong context switch on an easy task invalidates it completely. Spend 5 minutes verifying: check kubectl config current-context, confirm resources exist with kubectl get, run verification commands from 36.3. Then spend the last 3 minutes attempting ONE of the uncertain tasks — pick the one you're closest to solving. A partial solution earns partial credit. A verified easy task = guaranteed points. A desperate hard task = possible points.

Q4
You need to create a NetworkPolicy but can't remember the exact YAML structure. What's your fastest path to a working solution — writing from memory, searching the Kubernetes docs, or using kubectl explain?
Show Answer
Answer

Search the Kubernetes docs (fastest). Type kubernetes.io/docs in the browser, search "NetworkPolicy", scroll to the example YAML, copy it, paste into vi, modify. This takes ~60 seconds and guarantees correct syntax. kubectl explain (useful for field paths): kubectl explain networkpolicy.spec shows the structure but NOT a working example. Writing from memory (risky): You might forget policyTypes or misindent ingress.from. Time cost of fixing YAML errors > time saved by not searching docs. The allowed browser tabs ARE your external memory.

Q5
What's the 3-pass strategy for the CKS exam? Describe what you do in each pass and roughly how long each takes.
Show Answer
Answer

Pass 1 (0-45 min): Speed Run. Solve ONLY easy tasks (2-4 min each). Skip anything that looks hard or unclear. Goal: 8-10 tasks done, ~50% of exam. Pass 2 (45-90 min): Medium Tasks. Tackle medium-difficulty tasks (5-8 min each). These need more steps but you've practiced them. Goal: another 5-7 tasks done, ~85% of exam. Pass 3 (90-105 min): Hard Tasks + Verify. (a) Attempt hard tasks (encryption, Falco rules, AppArmor) — 10-15 min. (b) Verify Pass 1 answers — context switches, resource existence. (c) Last 5 min: submit.

Explanation

This is the proven CKS time management strategy. Pass 1 banks easy points and builds confidence. Pass 2 tackles what you expected. Pass 3 is for stretch goals and verification. Never do hard tasks first — you'll burn time and panic.

Q6
What are the 5 most common CKS exam mistakes that cause point loss? List each and the prevention technique.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Wrong cluster context — forgetting kubectl config use-context. Prevent: run kubectl config current-context after EVERY switch. (2) Not saving YAML files — editing in vim and closing without :wq. Prevent: always cat the file after editing to confirm. (3) Not waiting for API server restart — editing manifests then immediately testing. Prevent: wait 30-60s, check kubectl get nodes. (4) Missing volume mounts — adding flags to API server manifest without the corresponding volume/volumeMount. Prevent: always check all three (flag, volumeMount, volume). (5) Not verifying solutions — assuming it works. Prevent: run the verification command after every task.

Explanation

These 5 mistakes account for ~80% of point loss on CKS. Memorize them and practice their preventions. On the exam, check for these before submitting each task.

Q7
You have 20 tasks and 120 minutes. What's the rough time allocation per task? Which tasks should you plan to spend 10+ minutes on?
Show Answer
Answer

Average: 6 minutes per task (120 min ÷ 20 tasks). But allocate unevenly: Easy (2-4 min): RBAC roles, NetworkPolicy, SA creation, PSS labels, kube-bench scan. Medium (5-8 min): Audit policy, Falco rules, Seccomp profiles, TLS Secrets, upgrade. Hard (10-15 min): EncryptionConfiguration setup, AppArmor profile creation + loading + pod annotation, complete pod securityContext hardening, etcd backup/restore. Plan to spend 10+ on: EncryptionConfiguration (requires API server manifest edit + volume mounts + verification), AppArmor (requires profile creation + parser load + pod annotation + test), and any "from scratch" security configuration.

Explanation

Task triage is essential. Going into the exam, you should know which topics are hard and budget time accordingly. On the exam, don't spend 15 minutes on an "easy" task (you're overthinking it) and don't spend 3 minutes on a "hard" task (you're not solving it properly).

Q8
What kubectl commands should you ALWAYS alias before starting the exam? What's the benefit?
Show Answer
Answer
alias k=kubectl
export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
alias kn="kubectl config set-context --current --namespace"
# Usage: k get pods, k run nginx --image=nginx $do, kn default
# Time saved: ~2 seconds per command × 100+ commands = 3+ minutes saved

Also enable kubectl autocomplete: source <(kubectl completion bash). Combined with k alias, this saves 5-10 minutes over the exam.

Explanation

Aliases and autocomplete are the easiest time-savers. Set them up in the first 30 seconds of the exam. On the CKS exam, every second counts — 3 minutes saved is one more verification pass or one more attempted task.

Q9
The CKS exam allows 1 browser tab for kubernetes.io/docs. What's the most efficient way to find what you need? Give specific URL patterns for common tasks.
Show Answer
Answer
# Quick URL patterns for common CKS topics:
kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/encrypt-data/  # Encryption config
kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/pod-security-policy/     # PSS
kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/  # securityContext
kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/   # NetworkPolicy
kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/apparmor/  # AppArmor
kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/audit/                 # Audit policy
kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/       # RBAC

Click the "Example" heading — the doc page has working YAML you can copy. Don't read the full page; scroll to examples.

Explanation

The allowed browser is your external memory. Memorize URL patterns, not YAML syntax. On the exam: type the URL fragment in the search bar → click the page → Ctrl+F "Example" → copy → paste → modify. 60 seconds to a working solution.

Q10
It's T+118. You have 2 minutes left. You haven't completed Task 20 (AppArmor). You DO have 15 completed tasks verified. What's your final action?
Show Answer
Answer

Submit the exam. Do NOT attempt Task 20. With 15 verified tasks, you likely have 75%+ score (CKS passing is 66%). Attempting a hard task in 2 minutes: (a) you probably won't finish — zero points, (b) you might make a mistake that invalidates partial work from other tasks (unlikely but possible with cluster-wide configs), (c) rushing creates stress that doesn't improve your score. A verified 75% is a pass. An attempted 80% with unverified tasks is risky. Submit with confidence.

Explanation

Knowing when to stop is a test-taking skill. The CKS passing score is 66%. If you've verified 15 tasks, you're almost certainly passing. The last 2 minutes are for submission, not last-minute heroics. On the exam: submit at T-2 min if you're confident in your verified answers.

🔧 Under the Hood — How the CKS Scoring Engine Actually Works: The Grading Pipeline from Terminal to Score Report
🗺️ The CKS Grading Pipeline — What Happens After You Click Submit

Understanding HOW your work is scored helps you maximize points. The grading engine doesn't watch your screen — it runs scripts against the cluster AFTER you submit:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   CKS GRADING PIPELINE — From Your Terminal to Your Score                 │
  │                                                                           │
  │   1. YOU CLICK "END EXAM"                                                │
  │      → Your terminal session is SAVED (frozen snapshot)                  │
  │      → No further changes possible                                        │
  │      → The cluster state at this moment is what gets graded              │
  │                                                                           │
  │   2. GRADING SCRIPTS RUN (automated, 5-10 minutes)                       │
  │      For EACH task (1-20), the grading engine:                           │
  │      a) Switches to the task's cluster context                            │
  │      b) Runs kubectl/SSH checks against the cluster                       │
  │      c) Compares expected vs actual state                                 │
  │      d) Assigns: FULL (100%), PARTIAL (40-80%), or ZERO (0%)             │
  │                                                                           │
  │   3. WHAT GETS CHECKED (by task type):                                    │
  │      RBAC:       kubectl auth can-i --as=           │
  │      NetPol:     kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget       │
  │      Encryption: etcdctl get /registry/secrets/... | hexdump -C         │
  │      Falco:      cat /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml                  │
  │      Audit:      ls /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log && tail -5            │
  │      Seccomp:    kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec...seccomp}'        │
  │      kube-bench: kube-bench run --targets master --json                  │
  │                                                                           │
  │   4. SCORE CALCULATION:                                                   │
  │      Raw score = SUM(task_points × completion_percentage)                │
  │      Must reach 67% to pass (approximately 10-13/15 tasks)               │
  │                                                                           │
  │   🔑 The grader checks CLUSTER STATE, not terminal history. It only      │
  │      sees: does the cluster match expected state? This is why             │
  │      VERIFICATION matters — if you didn't verify, neither can the grader. │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎭 What Exam Day Actually Feels Like — A Minute-by-Minute Narrative
  T-30min: Proctor verifies ID, room scan, desk check. Nervous? Normal.
  T-15min: "Waiting for proctor..." Mentally recite file paths.
  T+0min:  Terminal appears. 17 tasks. Deep breath. Context switch. Go.
  T+5min:  First task DONE (easy RBAC). Confidence boost.
  T+30min: 6 tasks done. Encounter hard task → SKIP. Move on. Smart.
  T+90min: Fatigue sets in. Search docs, don't guess. Copy YAML, modify.
  T+115min: Final 5 minutes = VERIFY high-value tasks.
  T+120min: Terminal closes. Survey. Score email in 24 hours. Breathe.

  🔑 120 minutes feels like 45. The 3-pass strategy keeps you moving.
     You must ACT on each task within SECONDS of reading it.
🔁 Muscle Memory Drills — Practice Until Automatic
# 3-PASS STRATEGY DRILL (Practice this rhythm)
# PASS 1 (60 min) — Easy tasks first:
#   Read ALL tasks. Mark each as: ✅ Easy, 🤔 Medium, ❌ Hard
#   Complete all ✅ tasks first. These are your points.
# PASS 2 (40 min) — Medium tasks:
#   If stuck for >5 min on a 🤔 task → SKIP → come back
# PASS 3 (20 min) — Hard tasks + review:
#   Attempt one ❌ task. Re-verify ✅ tasks are complete.
#   Run kubectl commands to verify, not just check YAML.

# SPEED DRILL: Timed mini-tasks (target: 5 min each)
# Task: Create NetworkPolicy denying all ingress
# Task: Create ServiceAccount with no API access
# Task: Apply seccomp RuntimeDefault to a deployment
⚠️ Exam Gotchas — Ch 36 Traps
  • Don't spend 20 min on a 5-min task: Every task is weighted. A 4% task isn't worth 20 minutes. If you're stuck at the 5-minute mark, flag it and move on. Come back in Pass 3 if you have time.
  • Read the ENTIRE task before typing: CKS exam tasks often have a twist in the last sentence. "Create a NetworkPolicy... oh, and also ensure DNS traffic is allowed." Read fully, then plan, then type.
  • Verify, don't assume: After completing a task, run a verification command. Don't just check that kubectl apply succeeded — check that the policy actually BLOCKS traffic.
